Yarim Tepe (Iraq) is an archaeological site in Iraq's Sinjar Valley that emerged ca. 6000 BCE. Its later phases are associated first with the Hassuna culture, and then the Halaf and Ubaid cultures.
An island bordering the Chuka Channel in the southeastern Aegean sea; two shipwreck sites (dating to the fourth and seventh centuries A.D.) are located off its southern coast.

Yazılıkaya (also known as 'Midas City') is an archaeological site in Eskişehir Province, Turkey, known for its Phrygian rock-cut monuments, facades, altars, and niches dedicated to the Mother Goddess Matar.

The remains of a Roman settlement at Yeovil have been identified via partial excavation just to the south of Westland Road. Structural remains were documented, as well as evidence for drainage and town planning. The occupation dates range from the first to the fourth centuries CE.

The Yukarı Anzaf Fortress ("Upper Anzaf Fortress") is situated in the Van region in southeast Turkey. It was built by the Urartean King Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) who reports about his building activity in several building inscriptions. The fortress is situated close to Aşağı Anzaf Fortress ("Lower Anzaf Fortress") which had been built by Minua's father Išpuini.
The Great Zab river originates near Lake Van and flows some 400 km until it joins the Tigris River.
Zabas Mikros/Kapros?/Zerbis? fl. (Little Zab River) flows from the Zagros Mountains to the Tigris River.
A place from the TAVO Index

The historical town of Zabid in Yemen is noted for its architecture. It served as the capital of Yemen from the 13th to the 15th century and played an important role in the Arab and Muslim world for many centuries because of its Islamic university.
An island in the Ionian Sea.
Site of an Early Iron Age settlement on the western coast of the island of Andros (ninth-eighth centuries B.C.).
An ancient settlement on the Aegean island of the same name.
Zama Regia/Zama *Maior in Africa Proconsularis was the site of the Battle of Zama on October 19, 202 B.C., at the close of the Second Punic War fought between Rome and Carthage.
A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources that is identified with modern Tell ar-Rimāḥ.
A place from the TAVO Index

A cave sanctuary, dedicated to the Nymphs, located on the east side of Mount Ossa's western "Psila Dendra" ridge north of the modern village of Spilia. Epigraphic and other evidence indicates the sanctuary was active from the Classical through Roman periods.
Evidence for second millennium B.C. copper working were discovered at the site.

Zela (modern Zile, Turkey) was an important ancient city of north-central Asia Minor; Strabo claimed Semiramis had founded the site. Iulius Caesar prevailed in the Battle of Zela against Pharnaces II of The Kingdom of Pontus, coining the phrase "veni, vidi, vici".

An ancient place in Van province, Turkey. It had a street grid, fortifications of mud brick on a polygonal masonry foundation, and at least 14 building inscriptions in Aramaic from the Parthian period. Professor Rafet Çavuşoğlu began a program of excavations in 2021, which appears to be unpublished as of October 2025.
Zetis was an ancient city of Carmania, although its location can no longer be determined.
Zeugitana is the name given to the northern portion of Africa Proconsularis.
The temple of Zeus Olympios on Mt. Olympus
An ancient settlement, modern Khirbet as-Sadaqa in Jordan.
An ancient settlement of Arcadia, probably to be located at modern Zoni or Palamari.
A Minoan settlement dating from ca. 1800 BC onwards, Zominthos is well known for a large Minoan building discovered in 1982.
An important prehistoric settlement located in the Valley of Kleonai in the Corinthia of the northeast Peloponnese. Carl Blegen was the original excavator of the site.

The Zygritai were a Libyan people mentioned by Ptolemy and thought to have been localized in the vicinity of the ancient town of Zygris, for which Ptolemy separately provides coordinates. Desanges (whence RE) puts them in the vicinity of modern Sidi Barrani in Egypt's Matruh governorate. BAtlas writes the label just east of Sidi Barrani, between it and Marsa Matruh.
An Arabian city of lower Mesopotamia, located some 420 km south-east of Baghdad.
The early settlement history of [Feraria] (modern Ferrara) remains uncertain. The name Ferrara appears in AD 753 in a document of the Lombard king Desiderius.
Nuzi was an ancient city of Mesopotamia located southwest of Arrapha.
[Terqa]/Asicha? was an ancient city located at the site of Tell Ashara on the banks of the Euphrates river.
A Roman vicus on the Nahe river.

The toponym "ad Capita bubula" is attested in Suetonius and refers to a place located at the northeast corner of the Palatine Hill in Rome near the Curiae Veteres. Here, there was a domus of one Caius Octavius, a Roman politician who was the biological father of Octavian. It is possible that Octavian was born in this domus, and the sources suggest that the location was later commemorated with the
The territory of Motyca in the Roman province of Sicilia that, according to Cicero, supported 187 farmers.
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index
An important later Etruscan and Celtic settlement in the Po Plain with signs of occupation in the Late Bronze Age and then again between the fifth and second centuries BC.
A place from the TAVO Index
Remains of a Roman-era site in the modern Algerian municipal territory of el Karimia (Chlef province).
El-Kurru is the site of a necropolis used by Nubian royalty. Many of the royal tombs date to the Kushite period.

el-Bara (also Bara or al-Bara (Arabic: بارة)) is numbered among one of the so-called "Dead Cities" of northwestern Syria. The settlement originates in the fourth century CE and flourishes during the fifth and sixth centuries. It benefited from a favorable position along the route between Antioch and Apamea.
funeral monuments of the Via Iulia Augusta

A Roman necropolis located along the course of the Via Iulia Augusta in modern Albenga, Italy. The archaeological area includes the remains of at least nine tombs dating to the first and second centuries CE. These family tombs faced the ancient roadway. Nino Lamboglia carried out the first archaeological fieldwork here in the 1930s.

According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, nu-x-ù/nu-HAR-UD (name fragmentary and not reconstructable) was one of the four city districts of the western half of the inner city of Babylon.

Ägelmoos is an archaeological site located in Beinwil am See in the Swiss canton of Aargau. It is a now-submerged site that was once a lakeside settlement and was occupied between ca. 4500 BCE and 850 BCE.

Modern name for an otherwise unnamed ancient settlement. It may have been a possession of the Ptolemies, Rhodes, and the Attalid kingdom, and was at least peripherally involved with Rome's war against Aristonikos as a Roman ally.
A place from the TAVO Index

Çelebibağı is a modern city in the Van province in south-east Turkey. Here a stele with an inscription (CTU A 11-1) of the Urartian king Argišti II, son of Rusa (8th / 7th century BCE) was found which reports the creation of an artificial lake in this mountainous region.
An Early to Middle Bronze Age site located on the southern shore of the Dardanelles.
Megalithic temple on the island of Gozo; named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980

The Šamaš Gate, which was given the Akkadian ceremonial name Šamaš-mušakšid-ernittīya ("The God Šamaš Is the One Who Makes Me Triumph"), is the first of the eight city gates of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon") listed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) in inscriptions recording the construction of his new capital. This gate is the first of the east-facing entrances to the city.

When Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud) became the principal administrative center of the Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC, king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) built (or rebuilt) numerous temples. One of those was dedicated to the goddess Šarrat-niphi (an aspect of Ištar).

According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, Šuanna was one of the six city districts of the eastern half of the inner city of Babylon and it contained two temples. Šuanna is also a name of Babylon itself (starting in the twelfth century BC).
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index

A village in today's Amasya, Turkey. According to Mehmed Neşrî (Vol. 1, pp. 374-9 (1949)), Kara Devletşah, a commander in the Timurid Sultanate, stayed in this village and was defeated here or nearby by Bayezid I.
A place from the TAVO Index
Settlement east of Acre with remains from the Neolithic through the 12th century. The site was destroyed to make a highway in 1991.
Small Iron Age fortress in the Northern Negev with a surrounding wall and three buildings making up the fortress.

A late Iron Age IIa (ca. ninth century BCE) site located in the north-eastern part of the Jezreel Valley, Ḥorvat Tevet has produced archaeological evidence of a large, pillared building that has been interpreted as an administrative site belonging to early monarchic Israel.
A Sumerian city located on the Diyala River known for its Early Dynastic temples.
Ṣanʿāʾ is the largest city in Yemen. Its "Old City" was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index
‘A(n)dros’ Ins., referred to as Edrou Heremos by Ptolemy was perhaps originally a coastal island, but is now connected to the mainland by a narrow strip of land, thus forming a peninsula.
‘Abone’ or Abonae was a Roman port located on the Avon (Abona) river, now Sea Mill, Bristol, Great Britain.

'Cedreaticum' is a suggested editorial emendation offered by Bean for 'Tetraticum' in Mela, based on the conjecture that it is naming only the "innermost portion" (i.e., narrower eastern end) of the Gulf of Kos/Gökova (ancient Kerameios/Doridis) and therefore takes its name from the settlement of Kedreai (on modern Şehir Adası).
Roman fort and civil settlement or castrum established by the Roman legions invading Wales and now located at Abergavenny.
Possibly originally named Praesidium, this small Roman fort located in modern Jordan is known today as Khirbet al-Khalde.
According to the Antonine Itinerary, ‘Vernemeto’ was located 13 Roman miles north of Ratae Coritanorum (Leicester) along the Fosse Way.
A church (but not a basilica) in Ravenna, Italy, established by Bishop Ecclesius in 526 AD and consecrated ca. 547 AD.
A first-century AD colonnaded structure south of the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis, perhaps a gymnasium or a sanctuary dedicated to the Imperial cult.

A small 1st-century AD temple south of the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis, which was identified by the original excavator as a Mithraeum. This is unlikely to be correct. Other suggestions include that it was devoted to the cult of Augustus.

The "Ponte Sanguinario" at Spoleto is a late republican to early imperial Roman bridge. The remains of the bridge are now below street level in the Piazza della Vittoria, not far from the Porta San Gregorio.
The ruins of the Sabaean temple dedicated to Almaqah and its associated burial ground are located near the town of Mārib, Yemen.
An Iron Age site near the modern town of Rosh Ha'ayin.
(A)Esica, also known as Great Chesters, was a fort on the line of Hadrian's Wall.
BAtlas 62 G2 (Col. Iulia Aug. Felix) Germa
A body of water separating the Apennine Peninsula of Italy from the Balkan Peninsula.
A Gallic tribe inhabiting the modern Burgundy region during the La Tène and Roman periods.
An ancient Sasanian royal residence, located close to Persepolis.
A Gallic people of the Languedoc. Their chief town was Tolosa.
Mentioned by Pliny and other ancient authors, Abalus may correspond to the modern German island of Helgoland.
A river of Liguria. The modern Vara in Italy.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: around Brumano.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Vitolište MAC.

A sanctuary in the territory of the Paeligni dedicated to Hercules Curinus situated on an artificial terrace on the slopes of Mount Morrone. The terrace sanctuary looks over Sulmo in the valley below.
Egitania (Civitas Igaeditanorum) was a Roman city whose name was bestowed by the Swabians and Visigoths. This settlement achieved municipal status under the Flavian emperors.
*Incerulae, an ancient sanctuary site in the territory of the Vestini.
*Letocetum was an important military post near the junction of Watling Street and Icknield Street.
*Sedunum was the principal settlement of the Seduni.
*Silina Inss. (Isles of Scilly) form an archipelago off the southwestern tip of the Cornish peninsula of Great Britain.
*Tiddis (or Castellum Tidditanorum) was a Roman city located in the Constantine Province in Algeria.
A Roman settlement located at modern Freixo in Portugal.
The Ambra flows from the foot of Monte Luco to the Arno river.
Roman fort, cited: BAtlas 9 D6 Aballava
An ancient river mentioned by Arrian, possibly to be identified with the modern Lapsta in Georgia.

The Abbey of Sant'Antimo was a Benedictine monastery located in the comune of Montalcino, Italy, about 9 km from the line of the Via Francigena. The abbey grew around the site of an oratory to Saint Anthimus, whose relics may have been relocated here in the eighth century. The site was formerly occupied by a Roman villa.
Abbazia di Santa Maria di Falleri

The Medieval Cistercian abbey church of Santa Maria di Falleri occupies a portion of what was initially the walled area of the ancient town of Falerii, established in 241 BCE. The abbey's name, along with that of the associated hamlet, preserves the ancient toponymy.
A multi-period hilltop settlement with evidence for ancient terrace construction that now supports an abbey of the Benedictine order.
Abbey of San Clemente a Casauria

The Abbey of San Clemente a Casauria (Italian: Abbazia di San Clemente a Casauria) is located along the ancient Via Claudia Valeria in the territory of Castiglione a Casauria, province of Pescara, Abruzzo. Louis II (a great-grandson of Charlemagne) founded the abbey in 871. It was dedicated to Saint Clement in the following year (872).
Abbotsbury Castle is an Iron Age hill fort located on Wears Hill in Dorset, England.
Abd al Kuri is an island located about 65 miles southwest of Socotra in the Indian Ocean and is part of the Socotra Archipelago.
Abdera was a coastal city located on Cape Bulustra, near the estuary of the river Nestos.
Abellinum was a settlement of the Hirpini in Campania.
Attested by the Antonine Itineraries and the Geographer of Ravenna, Abelterium is probably to be identified with modern Alter do Chão in Portugal's Portalegre district.
The Abii were an ancient Scythian people.
A low mountain overlooking the port of Ceuta in North Africa.
A settlement of Aethiopia located between the Second Cataract and Syene on the left bank of the Nile River.
Abrettene was a region in northern Mysia.
Burial area in the northwestern portion of the Giza Necropolis containing burials dated to the Fourth-Fifth Dynasties.
Pharaonic archaeological site located 8 km north of Giza, including the pyramid of King Djedefre and several necropolises.
A Roman-era fort and associated well at Deir Umm Deheis in modern Egypt's Eastern Desert.

The site of two temples constructed by Ramesses II, one dedicated to the triad of Amun, Ra-Horakhty, and Ptah, as well as the deified Ramesses, and another dedicated to Hathor and the pharaoh's wife Nefertari. The temple was relocated between 1964 and 1968 to prevent its submersion under Lake Nasser after the construction of the Aswan High Dam.
An Old Kingdom necropolis serving the ancient Egyptian city of Memphis.
Abusina was the site of a Roman auxiliary fort along the Danube, some 30 km SW of Regensburg (at the modern village of Eining).
Minor site from which inscribed bricks have been found.
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index
An archaeological site, location of Plato's philosophical school
Acalander fl.. a river of Lucania emptying into the Gulf of Tarentum.
The Inhulets River is a right tributary of the Dnieper River that flows through the Ukraine.

Established in 280 BCE, the second Achaean League was centered in the northern and central Peloponnese. Allied to Rome in the Second Macedonian War (200-196 BCE), the league extended its control over all of the Peloponnese. In the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BCE), the League's relationship with Rome deteriorated; in ca. 146 BCE, this led to open warfare, which resulted in the defeat and dissolut
A fortified island in (or fort alongside) the Euphrates mentioned by Ammianus. Possibly to be identified with the modern island of Bidjan or the city of Haditha in Iraq.
A gate in the Themistoklean Wall of Athens, through which the road to Acharnai passed.
This ancient lake is to be identified with the modern Kastri dry lake in Preveza, Epirus (Greece).
A strip of land northwest of Crimea and south of the mouth of the Dnieper river in Ukraine, running nearly due west and east.
Achna is a modern village on Cyprus where evidence exists for an ancient sanctuary dedicated to a goddess perhaps associated with Artemis.
Ancient settlement and center of Buddhism near modern Banpur with remains from the 7th-12th centuries. Demolished in modern times.
Now unlocated, Acidios was a station on the Via Herculia according to the Antonine Itinerary, possibly located in the vicinity of Grumentum in the area of Marsico Nuovo.

A Roman villa at Anguillara Sabazia that may have been built in order to take advantage of mineral springs. The villa dates to the Late Republican period but has only been partially excavated. A large hemicycle with ambulatio is extant; this feature may have been coordinated with the villa's garden.
The modern Acquapendente was settled in pre-Roman times but is known historically from the Middle Ages onward.
The modern Untersee (Lower Bodensee) of Lake Constance, for which Pomponius Mela provides the Latin name Acronus.
The acropolis of the ancient city of Athens in Greece.
The Acropolis of Cumae was used across multiple periods, beginning with the foundation of the Greek colony in the eighth century B.C.
A people of the southern Arabian peninsula, localized around modern al-Qatn in Yemen.
Site of an ancient temple of Apollo near which Octavian erected a monument to commemorate his naval victory over M. Antonius in 31 BCE.

A promontory on the southern side of the entrance to the Ambracian Gulf from the Ionian Sea. It was in the sea off this promontory in 31BC that M. Antonius suffered a famous naval defeat at the hands of Octavian.

Acumincum (modern Stari Slankamen in Serbia) was a settlement of the Scordisci that was later conquered by the Romans. During the Flavian period, the Cohors I Britannica equitata and II Adjutrix were based there.
Site of a Roman settlement that is included on the Antonine Itinerary.
Ad Aquas Salvias was a place on the Via Laurentina.
A statio in Latium located at the intersection of the Via Latina and the Via Labicana, near the modern Valmontone.

A road station located ten Roman miles from Carthage on the road that circumnavigated Lake Tunis on the west and south, Ad Decimum is probably to be located somewhere in the vicinity of modern Sidi-Fathallah. A significant battle between the Vandals and a Byzantine force was fought in the vicinity of Ad Decimum in 533 CE.
A Roman road station attested in the Peutinger map. It is perhaps to be identified with modern Zvornik in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
A Roman road station whose precise location cannot be determined today. It is thought to have been located somewhere in the vicinity of modern Goult in France's Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur department.
Ad Fines was a Roman road station located near present-day Drubiaglio, Avigliana, Italy.
An ancient place located along the road that led from Carthage to Utica, placing it in the vicinity of the modern Sebbalam, Tunisia.
Ad Medias was a mutatio on the ancient Via Appia. It was located at the halfway point of the so-called Decennovium.
Ad Nonas is the name of a now unlocated road station near Cosa; the name is attested in the Peutinger Table.

An unlocated Roman road station in Italy. As represented on the Peutinger Map, it was at least a minor hub in the road network, connected to Ad Grecos (unlocated), Arretium, Clusium, and Manliana. The Barrington Atlas Directory describes its likely general localization as "between Saena and Clusium".

BAtlas tentatively (hollow symbol and question mark) places this road station, mentioned in the Peutinger map on a route between Augusta Vindelicum and Abodiacum, in the vicinity of modern Landsberg am Lech in Bavaria (see also Rathmann).
Ad Pictas is a road station east of Rome, known mostly for its role in Sulla's march on Rome in 88 B.C. The precise location of the statio continues to be debated.

An ancient road station mentioned in the Antonine Itineraries and labeled on the Peutinger Map. It was likely located in the vicinity of modern Albertville at the confluence of the Isère and Arly rivers in France, but its precise location remains uncertain.
Ad Quintanas is the name of a road station on the Via Labicana.
An ancient road station labeled on the Peutinger Map and usually equated with the archaeological remains of a mansio at modern Puech-Crémat-Bas in France (BAtlas 14 I4 Ad Silanum)

A Roman road station on the main highway between Emerita Augusta and Norba. The mansio has not been located archaeologically, but is thought to have been coincident with the modern Spanish village of Casas de Don Antonio.
Ad Statuas was a road station on the Via Labicana located east of Rome.
A Roman road station, mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary. It was probably located somewhere near modern Valiano in the Italian province of Sienna.
BAtlDir, following Bosio 1991, offers two possible modern associations for this attested Roman road station at or near the Meduacus Maior estuary north of the Po delta: Dolo or Sambruson.

Ada / Adalar is a village in Southeast Anatolia. It is located a few kilometres southwest of Malazgirt in the Turkish province Muş. Nearby is a rock inscription of the Urartian King Minua (ca. 810-785/80 BCE), in which he reports the construction of a Canal named "Canal of Minua", which is still in use today. In Late Antiquity, the canal was attributed to the legendary Queen Semiramis by the Armen
The Adda river is a river in northern Italy and a tributary of the Padus fl. (Po river).
A river attested in ancient sources between Cissi and Rusuccuru, it is perhaps to be identified with the modern Oued Sebaou.
Site of a Roman fort that developed in a small Romano-British settlement
A mountain, possibly the source of Sangarius fl.
An ancient market settlement and port on the west coast of the Red Sea near modern Zula in Eritrea.
An ancient tribe of north Africa. Herodotus indicates that they are the first Libyan people encountered west of Egypt.
The temple sacred to the god Apollo on the Palatine Hill in Rome.
The Temple of Ceres, located on the slope of the Aventine Hill in Rome, was originally dedicated by Sp. Cassius in 494/3 B.C.
A temple of Hercules located near the Circus Maximus.
An island lying off the coast of Libya.
The Egadi Islands, a small group of mountainous islands northwest of Sicily.
Aegida was an ancient town of Histria that is mentioned only by Pliny the Elder.
The Roman province of Egypt (Aegyptus) was established in 30 BC after the defeat of Marcus Antonius and Cleopatra VII at the Battle of Actium.
A volcanic archipelago in the Tyrrhenian Sea composed of eight islands.
The Aequi were an ancient Italic tribe of northeast Latium in the first millennium BC.
Aesis fl. (modern Esino river) is a river of the Marche region of Italy and flows into the Adriatic Sea.
The Aesontius, known now as either the Soča or Isonzo river, flows from the Trenta Valley in the Julian Alps to the Adriatic Sea.
The Aestii were an ancient people living on the shores of the Baltic Sea, as described by Tacitus.
An archaeological site near the Mycenaean causeway has been interpreted as a multi-period heroön dedicated to Agamemnon.
A promontory of the northern shore of the Azov Sea, included in Ptolemy's gazetteer. It is perhaps to be associated with the promontory that now extends into the sea near modern Berdyansk.
The Agathyrsoi were an ancient tribe whose territory was located on the upper Mureş river, north-east of that of the Neuri.
A mythic rock formation at Eleusis where Demeter searched for Persephone.
The rural hinterland of the ancient city of Rome.

A multi-period archaeological site on Kastelli Hill, Khania, Crete, that has occupation stretching more than five millennia. Archaeological fieldwork was undertaken by the Greek–Swedish Excavations and the Danish Institute at Athens beginning in 2005.
A fortified architectural complex on the island of Amorgos that dates to the fourth century BCE.
An ancient river of north Africa whose modern location cannot be determined today. It may be identifiable with the Oued Chélif or one of its tributaries, the Oued R(h)iou.
A Mycenaean citadel on Sifnos with continued use in the Iron Age.
The Doric temple at Agios Elias, above Asea in Arcadia, dates to ca. 500 B.C.
The so-called "agora" is a large open courtyard to the northwest of the Middle Minoan palace at Malia.
The marketplace of the ancient city of Athens in Greece.
The Agora of the ancient city of Priene.
Now a municipality in the Urgell comarca of Catalonia, Agramunt originated prior to the 11th century CE.
The modern Ergene river in Turkey's East Thrace region.
Agunia fl. (Agogna river) is a river of northern Italy and a tributary of the Padus fl. (Po river).

An ancient, now-vanished, branch of the Nile River. Geophysical research has demonstrated that the Ahramat Branch, no longer visible to the naked eye, was located west of the main Nile River channel and flowed from south of Lisht to the area of the Giza Plateau area. This channel would have bordered on the complexes of more than 30 ancient pyramids ranging in date from the Old Kingdom to Second In
An ancient Greek sanctuary located at ancient Keryneia in Achaia.

The modern town of Aidepsos (formerly Lispo) in Greece, is usually identified as the original city and/or polis center of ancient Aidepsos. This location lies some three kilometers north of the extensive archaeologically attested spa center at modern Loutra Aidepsou.
A mountain range of Attika that lies between the plains of Athens and Eleusis.
This mountain, mentioned in ancient sources, is to be identified with the modern Gerenion, northeast of the city of Loutraki.
Ain Hersha is the site of a Roman temple located in the environs of Mount Hermon.
Ain Ouassel or Ain Wassel is a rural archaeological site dated to the early Byzantine period. The site contained a mix-use farm.
The Esaro River, the ancient Aisaros, flows into the Ionian Sea just north of Crotone, Italy
The Aisepos river was located in Mysia in northwest Turkey. It is the modern Gönen Çayı.
Aithiopika M. (The Ethiopian Highlands), a rugged range of mountains in Ethiopia in the area of the Great Rift Valley.
Among various features at Aix-en-Diois are the remains of baths that could either pertain to a sanctuary or a villa.
A major Scythian kurgan of the 5th c. BC partially excavated in 1885.
An ancient settlement near Lykosoura, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today
Akathartos Kolpos, an embayment of the Red Sea just north of the Tropic of Cancer.
The second largest of the four islands in Lake Van, in eastern Turkey.
A tributary of the Indus River.
The narrow mountain ridge in Boiotia that, at its eastern tip, supports the acropolis of Orchomenos. Today, the ridge is mostly encapsulated by a modern wildlife refuge.
The Île de Rachgoun is a coastal island of Algeria.
An ancient town of Boeotia located on the eastern edge of the former Lake Copais.
An ancient settlement whose precise location can not be determined today
Akrite Ins. (modern Arkoi) is an island of the Dodecanese archipelago.
An ancient settlement on the Athos/Akte peninsula.
Necropolis on the West Bank of the Nile near Thebes containing tombs from the 18th, 25th, and 26th dynasties.
The Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem was established on the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif in the seventh century. It is the third holiest site of Islam.
Find-spot of a hoard of metal objects dated to the early Iron Age, located on the campus of Sultan Qaboos University in Oman.

An elaborate, rock-cut monument at Petra built ca. 100 BC to AD 200 known as "Al-Khazneh" or "The Treasury". The Nabatean structure, originally used as a tomb, dates to the reign of Aretas IV Philopatris.
Al-Sabaa wa Arbain (Saba‘ wa Arba’īn) is a small modern town in northeastern Syria (al-Hasakah Governorate). The settlement sits atop a small mound of ruins (ancient name not known).
Alabum was a Roman fort in Britain that was occupied until the fourth century A.D.
An ancient Germanic people, whose name in modern works is sometimes also spelled Alemanni or Allemanni.
Alanoi, a group of Sarmatian tribes and nomadic pastoralists of the first millennium AD.
A large-scale Minoan dyemaking and dying establishment overlooking the modern Gulf of Mirabello at Pachia Ammos in Lasithi, Crete.

Α small Μinoan rock shelter of uncertain function discovered alongside a highway on the modern Alatzomouri hill just west of Pacheia Ammos in Lisotho, east Crete. A significant assemblage of broken pottery and tools, all dating to EMIII, were found in the shelter.
Remains of a Roman fort and several marching camps which included a signal tower near Ardoch, Scotland
A Roman fort at present-day Maryport. Part of Cumbrian coastal defenses.
The Alba Fucens Aqueduct is a Roman aqueduct dating from the later first century BCE.
A rural sanctuary in the territory of Poseidonia (Paestum) has been excavated at S. Nicola di Albanella.
Albaniana was the site of a castellum that was part of the Roman frontier system (limes) of Germania Inferior.

A volcanic lake in ancient Latium at the foot of Albanus Mons, Albanus Lacus (Alban Lake) is connected with the site of the city of Alba Longa and, later, with imperial properties of the Flavian house.

A Roman bridge with origins in the first century B.C. that crosses the Albarregas River, a tributary of the Guadiana River. The bridge was been declared a Site of Cultural Interest in 1912 and named a part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Mérida Archaeological Ensemble" in 1993.
A settlement in the interior of southern Corsica
The Albegna is a river of southern Tuscany and flows from Monte Amiata to the Tyrrhenian Sea.
A toponym connected to the semi-legendary topography of Latium as described in the Aeneid.
A port at the mouth of the river Silarus that derived its name from Alburnus mons.

Albus Portus is attested on the Antonine Itinerary and refers to a mansio located between Carteia and Mellaria. Modern scholarship places it at the site of the now-demolished 16th-century Torre de San García at modern Algeciras in Spain.
An oppidum located on Michelsberg hill in Bavaria, occupied from ca. 500 BC until the first century BC.
A six-span stone bridge over the Tagus river, also known as the Puente Trajan.
An ancient settlement in Arcadia that flourished from the Classical to Roman periods.
The Aleksandrovo tumulus or kurgan is a Thracian burial mound located near Aleksandrovo in south-eastern Bulgaria, that dates to the fourth century BC.
Bronze Age settlement and associated burial site located on the left bank of the Tobol river in northern Kazakhstan.
A cave in Diros Bay in Greece used as a settlement in the middle and late Neolithic Period. The site was sealed by an earthquake and abandoned around 3200 BCE.
A Gallic oppidum, the site of Caesar's defeat of Vercingetorix, and afterward a Gallo-Roman town.
An ancient settlement, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today
The Alfar Romano de Cartuja (Roman potters' workshop of Cartuja) was a pottery production center for southern Spain that was active from the 1st century till the later 2nd century CE.
A Samnite settlement occupying a strategic location in the valley of the Sangro river.

Aliler Castle is the modern Turkish name of an Urartian fortress situated near the village of Karaağaç, approx. 11 km southeast of Lake Van. Here, the remains of a column base with a fragmentary preserved Urartian inscription of the Urartian king Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) have been found.
Pausanias observed sanctuaries of both Asclepius and Athena at Aliphera, as well as an altar of Zeus Lecheates.
A settlement located some 40km outside of modern Karachi, Pakistan, dating to the Mature Harappan period. The site was abandoned by the close of the third millennium BCE.
An ancient spa, known in modern times as Paşa Ilıca in Turkey.
The Spanish village of Almoguera is located in the southeast of the province of Córdoba, near Baena. It belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X in the thirteenth century.

Almus (now Lom, Bulgaria) was a place in Moesia Inferior located on the southern bank of the Danube River and near the mouth of a river of the same name (Almus). Both places are noted on the Tabula Peutingeriana.
The modern Spanish island of Isla Plana (also known as Isla Nueva Tabarca) is associated by modern scholars with the ancient Alonis.
A major river of the Northern Caucasus that flows from Georgia to the Caspian Sea.
Alpes Cottiae (Cottian Alps) are a mountain range located the southwestern part of the Alps. They take their name from Marcus Julius Cottius.

A small Alpine province of the Roman Empire organized around the Little St Bernard Pass, roughly corresponding to the eastern portion of the modern-day French department of Savoie. Augustus annexed the territory in 15 BCE; under Diocletian, the periodically joint administration of the province together with Alpes Poeninae was made permanent, forming the province of Alpes Poeninae et Graiae.
A seventh- and eighth-century BC Punic sanctuary on the Awali river dedicated to Eshmun, the Phoenician god of healing.
Althiburos was a city of Africa Proconsularis that became a municipium under Hadrian and a colonia during the third century A.D.
The largest site of the Dzhetyasar culture, Altyn-Asar is a fortified settlement in the Syr Darya region inhabited from the 5th century BCE-8th century CE.

A Roman bridge in the modern Barranco de Aluenda (Aluenda Gorge), which runs down from the northwest to the modern village of Aluenda in Spain's Zaragoza province (Aragon). This bridge was east of ancient Bilbilis on the Roman road to Caesaraugusta.
Occupation of the Roman villa at Alviano Scalo begins in the first century BCE and continues until the fourth century CE.
A river of north Africa, a portion of which formed the boundary between Mauretania and Numidia. Scholars associate the Ampsaga with the modern Oued El Kebir in Algeria.
A stream or torrente that flows 48 km from its source at Monte Soglio to the Po river, of which it is a left side tributary.
A mountain pass that is located on the border between Osmaniye and Gaziantep provinces in south-central Turkey. The pass played an important role in the Battle of Issus, 333 B.C.
A pass through through the Taurus Mountains, the modern Karanlik Kapi.
The Sefīd-Rūd river flows into the Caspian Sea at Rasht.
A 10th-century fortress located on Mount Aragats in modern Aragatsotn province, Armenia.
The Ambiani were an ancient Belgic people.
The Amisia River (modern Ems) is located in northwestern Germany. It flows along a course of more than 360 km and discharges into Dollart Bay that is a part of the Wadden Sea.

An extensive ancient settlement and road station at modern Haidra in Tunisia with evidence for occupation from the Roman, Vandal, and Byzantine eras. The site seems to have been abandoned by the 10th century CE.
An alluvial plain at the mouth of the Gravona river.
This promontory, known today as Ras Kaboudia, is the easternmost point of the coast of Tunisia.
A Graeco-Roman town of Crete located 14 km E of Rethymno.
The modern Karteros river in Crete.

The Amnya River (Russian: Амня) is a left tributary of the Kasym in the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug/Ugra of Western Siberia. It flows predominantly northward through the West Siberian Plain and joins the Kasym about 15 km east of Beloyarsky. The river flows for some 374 km from its source to the point of confluence and drains an area of 7210 km².

The high altar of the present, Gothic-era Pfarrkirche (parish church) of modern Ampass (near Insbruck in Austria) was built over a series of earlier Christian churches, the earliest of which appears to date to the fifth century CE, based on excavated remains of a reliquary vault dating back to that period.
The Amphiareion of Oropos was an ancient sanctuary dedicated in the fifth century BCE to the hero Amphiaraos and located in the hills southeast of the port of Oropos.
A first century A.D. amphitheater at Alba Fucens built during the reign of Tiberius.

Intramural amphitheater located within the military sector on the north side of Dura-Europos. Built on the site of the former Bath F3, which was destroyed by fire. The amphitheater's dedication in 216 CE is attested by an inscription found fallen from above entrance C on the south side of the amphitheater.
Third century A.D. Roman amphitheater; declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
The Flavian amphitheater at Rome (the so-called "Colosseum").
An ancient tribe of Colchis mentioned by Pliny the Elder who places their territory between the Heniochi and the Lazi.
The Ampsivarii were a Germanic tribe whose homeland was close to the Amisia fl.

Amyclanus Sinus, the modern Gulf of Gaeta, is an open body of water along the central-western coast of the Italian peninsula. To the north, Cape Circeo bounds the gulf, while to the south it is bounded by the island of Ischia and the Gulf of Naples. It extends westward to the Pontine Islands.
A river and homonymous spring mentioned by Pausanias in the vicinity of Lerna. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
The Anamares were a people of Gallia Cispadana living along the south bank of the Padus.
Bronze Age burial site of the Alazani-Bedeni culture near the Alazani River in eastern Georgia. The site is dated to the first half of the 24th century BCE.
Modern Kouvelaki, a hill in Arcadia separating the plain of Orchomenos and the plain of Mantineia.
The Ancient Theater of Argos was a Hellenistic theater initially constructed in 320 BCE and later renovated by the Romans.
Archaeological remains of Aegina's military harbor.
The ancient theater of Maroneia was constructed in the Hellenistic period and later remodeled in the Roman period.
Andabalis was a settlement of southern Cappadocia located northeast of Tyana.
Andes is said to be the birthplace of the Latin poet Vergil.
An ancient settlement of the Treveri. Modern Niederanven in Luxembourg.
The island of Jersey is the largest of the Channel Islands in the English Channel.
The Andizetes were an Illyrian tribe that lived in the territory of present-day Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The "Anfiteatro Fausto" or "Amphitheater of Faustus" refers to a Roman amphitheater that was built during the reign of Tiberius (likely 30 or 32 CE) at Terni.
A Roman amphitheater located to the northwest of Nola and dating to the first century BCE.
The so-called "Anfiteatro minore" is a small amphitheater at Puteoli dating to the early Imperial period.
Late Bronze Age site in the Emathia region.
The principal temple of Angkor, the capital city of the Khmer empire, Angkor Wat was constructed in the 12th century CE. Angkor was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.
The Ani citadel is a flat-topped hill that was once known as Midjnaberd (the Inner Fortress). Its defensive walls date to the seventh century A.D.
The Anio river (modern Aniene) is a river of northern Latium.
Anneianum was located in the Etruscan Apennines, along the road from Faventia to Florentia.
Antandros was a city on the coast of the Troad, near the head of the Gulf of Adramyttium.
Anthylla was an ancient settlement located on the Canobic branch of the Nile.
An ancient Roman town mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary and by the Ravenna Cosmographer. Modern Antequera in Spain.
A river, now called the Kuban, flowing from Mount Elbrus to the Sea of Azov.
The Anti-Lebanon mountains, also known as the Eastern Lebanon Mountain Range.

A sacred precinct at the western end of Villa Hadriani, comprising two temples at opposite (north and south) ends of a plaza or garden, and (on the western edge of this complex) a small colonnaded hemicycle. Here, Hadrian may have planned to build a large, semi-circular temple-tomb for Antinous, in place of which his successors built the colonnaded hemicycle.
The archaeological site of Marina el-Alamein.
A mountain range of southeastern Turkey, extending to the north of the Taurus mountains.

A series of fortifications approximately 63 km in length, spanning the breadth of modern day Scotland between the Firth of Forth and the Firth of Clyde. The Antonine Wall was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

Aornos was a mountain fortress and the site of Alexander the Great's last siege during the winter of 327-6 BC. The ancient site likely corresponds to Ūṇa, a peak on the Pīr-Sar west of the Indus river.
Aorsoi refers to a group of tribes of the Sarmatae living to the east of Maiotis.
The Apennine Mountains extend ca. 1,200 km (750 miles) along the length of peninsular Italy.
A city located on the Tigris, where it split into two streams, in the region of Mesene, founded by Antiochos I.
Apatouros Kolpos (Taman Bay) is a shallow bay or gulf on the east coast of the Strait of Kerch.
Aperlae was a coastal settlement of Lycia. Its ancient economy is linked to the production of Tyrian purple.
Minoan tomb in the Mesara Plain in south-central Crete dated to the Early Minoan II period (ca. 2200-2050 BCE) and in use until the Middle Minoan III period (ca. 1750-1675 BCE).

Minoan tomb in the Mesara Plain in south-central Crete constructed during the Early Minoan I period (ca. 3100-2650 BCE) and expanded later in the Prepalatial and Protopalatial periods (through 1700 BCE).
A large Attic deme, located on the Gulf of Kotroni.
A small, ancient island off the southwest coast of the Iberian peninsula where the core of the ancient city of Gades (modern Cádiz) was located. It is now joined to the modern Cádiz peninsula.

Located outside the city walls of Pergamon, this temple, according to an inscription (OGIS 273-9), was supposedly the site of a victory of Attalos I over the Tolistogi, Galatians, and Antiochus Hierax. It was likely later destroyed by Philip V.
Temple dedicated to Aphrodite constructed in the 6th century BCE at the Greek colony of Akrai.
An ancient sanctuary of the goddess Aphrodite, described by Pausanias and located at modern Dafni (Daphne) along the ancient sacred way from Athens to Eleusis.
The worship of Aphrodite is significant in the colonial city of Lokroi Epizephyrioi.
Aphroditopolis was an ancient town of Egypt, modern Kom Isgaw.
Apliki in central Cyprus was the site of Bronze Age copper smelting.
Sanctuary of Apollo Cynneius near or in Temnos, destroyed by Prusias II in 155 BCE. Its precise location is unknown today but certainly lies within Barrington Atlas Map 56 grid E4.
A sanctuary dedicated to Apollo Nasiotas located on the islet of Apsiphia.
Two early Christian basilicae were superimposed over the ancient sanctuary of Apollo Dalios.
The oracular shrine of Apollo Koropaios.
An ancient river on the Mediterranean littoral of what is now France, the Apron is possibly to be associated with the modern Siagne.
Aprustum was an interior town of Bruttium.
A river that flows into the Black Sea.
The Apsyrtides Islands, a group of Liburnian islands located east of Istria.
The Apuani were a Ligurian tribe of northwest Italy.
The Apuli were an ancient tribe of southeastern Italy.
Apulum (modern Alba Iulia) was an important Roman castrum in Dacia and the base of Legio XIII Gemina.
Aqaba - now Aaqbe - is a place located in the Beqaa Governorate in Lebanon. It is the site of a Roman temple that has been classified as belonging to the "Mount Hermon" temple group.
A pre-Constantinian Christian church located at ancient Aila in Jordan.

The earliest of Rome's aqueducts, the Aqua Appia was constructed in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus. The aqueduct runs a course of 16.4 km, entering Rome at the Porta Maggiore. Frontinus estimated the daily volume at 75,537 cubic meters.
Aquae Calidae was an ancient spa depicted on the Peutinger Map. Modern scholarship associates it with archaeological remains found in modern Vichy (France).
An ancient Roman thermal spa in modern Caldes de Malavella
Remains of an Etrusco-Roman thermal complex, dating from the third century B.C. to late antiquity, were documented between 2000 and 2003.
Aquae Statiellae (modern Acqui Terme) was an ancient settlement in Liguria.
An ancient Roman thermal spa and site of the Temple of Sulis Minerva.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Vranjska Banja YUG.

In the 19th century, A. de Caumont hypothesized an aqueduct to supply Augustodurum from the south (i.e., from the modern communes of Juaye-Mondaye and Monceaux-en-Bessin). This idea was repeated in TIR Condate whence BAtlas, but more recently it has been called into question.
A cape on the Mediterranean coast of modern Morocco, mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary. Modern scholars associate it with Pointe Restinga.
A confederation of a number (?20) of Iberian tribes initially subjugated by P. Licinius Crassus in 56 BC.

A Roman province formed in 27 B.C. by Augustus. According to Strabo, it incorporated the territories of the Aquitani and 14 other peoples whose territories were located between the Garumna and Liger rivers.
An early cult center connected with Herakles located in Rome's Forum Boarium.
A fourth to third century B.C. sanctuary at Tarquinia.
Arabicus Sinus/Erythr(ae)um/Rubrum Mare (The Red Sea) is an inlet of the Indian Ocean located between Africa and Asia.
A river that flows through the Hub District, Balochistan, Pakistan. It originates in the Pab Range of southeastern Balochistan and flows into the Arabian Sea.
A prehistoric site of the Torrean civilization in Corsica.
A river of Gaul, the modern Saône.
Araxes fl. is one of the largest rivers of the Caucasus.
Cape Araxos separates the Gulf of Patras from the Ionian Sea.
Rab island in the Adriatic Sea.
A Roman fort at present-day South Shields.
The Kirthar Mountains are located in Balochistan and Sindh provinces of Pakistan.
BAtlas 68 B4 Arca/Herakleia en Phoinike/Caesarea ad Libanum
The Arcadian Gate is a monumental city gate constructed in the fourth century BCE in Messene.
Arch at F Street and 10th Street
Monumentalized passage arch marking the intersection of F Street and the south side of 10th Street in Dura-Europos.

The brick core of an arch monument stands immediately to the west of the Temple of Jupiter in the Forum of Pompeii. It has had various appellations including "Arch of Drusus", referring to Drusus Iulius Caesar the son of emperor Tiberius.
The Arch of Augustus at Ariminum was dedicated in 27 B.C. and marked the end of the Via Flaminia.
Arch of Caius and Lucius Caesar (Pompeii)
An arched entranceway located in the northwest corner of the Forum of Pompeii.

The so-called Arch of Caracalla at Theveste is a tetrapylon arch dating to the third century. Originally dedicated to the deified Septimius Severus with Julia Domna and Caracalla, the arch was repurposed and modified to function as a gate in the Byzantine city wall.
The Arch of Caracalla at Volubilis was constructed in 217 CE by the governor Marcus Aurelius Sebastenus in honor of the emperor Caracalla and his mother Domna Julia.
A Roman triumphal arch monument dedicated to Caracalla, Julia Domna, and the deified Septimius Severus located at ancient Cuicul / Curculum (modern Djémila).
The Arch of Hadrian is a monument in the form of a Roman triumphal arch, constructed by the citizens of Athens in AD 131 or 132 to honor the Roman emperor Hadrian.
A fourth-century A.D. tetrapylon arch stands at the intersection of the Via Flaminia and a road linking the Via Tiberina and Veii.

The so-called "Arch of Marcus Antonius" takes its name from a local tradition that the citizens of Aquinum built the monument in a single day to honor Antonius. In all likelihood, it is a monument connected either to a deductio of veterans sent to Aquinum in 41 BCE or to the work of Caius Calvisius Sabinus who reorganized the via Latina in 27 BCE.

The Arch of Septimius Severus is situated at the northwest corner of the Forum Romanum. It was dedicated in A.D. 203 and serves to commemorate the Parthian victories of Emperor Septimius Severus and his two sons against the Parthians (194/195 and 197–199).
A triumphal arch erected in summa Sacra Via and dedicated to the deified emperor Titus by his brother Domitian, ca. 81 CE.

A triple-bay triumphal arch was erected at the eastern end of the Circus Maximus in honor of Emperor Titus' role in the victory in the Jewish War. The arch is known from architectural and sculptural fragments and from an inscription recorded in the Einsiedeln sylloge.
An arch erected to honor Trajan between A.D. 100 and 116.
A triumphal arch built in honor of Trajan at Beneventum; it marks the Trajanic extension of the Via Appia.

The Arch of Trajan at Dura-Europos is a triple bay arch located outside walls of Dura-Europos ca. 1.7 km NW of the Palmyrene Gate. An inscription records the dedication to Trajan by the Legio III Cyrenaica and was duplicated on each side of the arch.
An ancient necropolis at Carife (Campania) with more than 100 Samnite tombs.
Archaic City Wall and Gate of Phocaea
The archaic period city walls and gate of Phocaea excavated under the Maltepe tumulus.
The agora of the ancient city. The site was located near the center of the city's shoreline and was surrounded by stoas and public buildings.
Center point of Archaic period tholos tomb of Pharsalos, used until the Hellenistic period.
A private, early Christian oratory in Ravenna, Italy, erected by Peter II as archbishop in A.D. 495.
A river of Mesopotamia in the Roman period, and possibly somewhat earlier. It is perhaps to be associated with the modern Shatt al-Gharaf in Iraq.

The so-called "Arco Etrusco" is one of the gates of ancient Perusia. The gate dates originally from the third century B.C. when it was one of seven gates in the Etruscan wall. In 40 B.C. it was refashioned under Augustus.
The so-called "Arco Felice Vecchio" is a city gate of the first century A.D. built under the administration of Domitian.
The so-called "Arco Romano de Dona Isabel" is a second or third century A.D. city gate of Évora, the ancient site of Ebora Liberalitas Iulia.
The Arco di Sant'Ercolano of Perugia is the ancient Porta Cornea of the Hellenistic walls of the city.
An opus quadratum monument with an arched gateway perhaps marking a boundary between the territory of the Equi and the Hernicans.

A mid-first century CE building located east of the Roman Agora in Athens, of unknown purpose. Early 20th-century scholars incorrectly identified it as the Agoranomeion (office of the market inspectors).

A now-lost arch on the ancient Via Lata. It was dedicated to Diocletian either in 293 CE (marking the occasion of his decennalia) or in 303-304 (joint triumph with Maximian). The present church of Santa Maria in Via Lata occupies the site of the arch.

A single-bay triumphal arch dedicated to Tiberius in 16 CE. This arch commemorated the recovery of Varus' standards lost in 9 CE. It stood on the Sacra Via at the northwest corner of the Basilica Iulia.
The Ardiaei were an ancient tribe of Illyria.
A Roman fort of the first and second centuries A.D. at present day Melandra Castle.
An ancient forest region occupying parts of modern Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, and France; its modern remains are known as the Ardennes.

During archaeological excavations carried out between 1926 and 1934 in Casarinaccio (Ardea), a monumental complex was identified. This consisted of a late republican basilica (first century BCE) and the remains of an archaic temple dedicated to Venus.

The remains of an extensive Roman villa have been documented (amongst other phases) in the village of Le Ferriere, on the grounds of the Casale del Giglio winery. This multi-period, multi-phase settlement demonstrates continuity of human activity, albeit with varying loci of focused activity.
Area di Monte Giulio e Capitaneria

The low hill known as Monte Giulio is anthropic, formed by the accumulation of sediment atop an ancient quay. Archaeological investigation beginning in 1968 revealed numerous architectural remains, including a cistern and a bath complex along the via Guidoni. The ruins of the so-called Capitaneria, or Harbor office, are located near the modern stele to the Fallen of Kindu. This complex seems to ha
An island mentioned in ancient sources, possibly to be identified with the modern Italian Isola Palmaria in the Gulf of Genova.

An ancient place mentioned in the correspondence of Pope Gregory the Great (ca.  540 – 12 March 604) wherein Gregory permits the Bishop of Velletri to transfer his seat from Velletri to Arenata. This may refer to the modern comune of Rocca Massima in the Latina province.

Named after a mythical trial of the god Ares, the Areopagus is a rocky outcropping in Athens located to the northwest of the Acropolis. The hill was used as a meeting place for the Council of the Areopagus, which functioned as a council of elders for the city of Athens. The Areopagus is also traditionally identified as the setting for Paul's sermon to Athens.
Arethusae Fons is a spring in Ortygia, Sicily, traditionally connected with the nymph Arethusa.
The Arevaci were a pre-Roman Celtic tribe of northern Hispania who dominated most of Celtiberia from the fourth to late second centuries BC.
Mount Hasan, Hasan Dağı in Turkish, is an inactive stratovolcano and the second highest peak in Anatolia.
Erciyes Dağı in Turkish. A massive volcanic mountain, the highest peak of the Antitaurus range. Commonly depicted on coins from Cappadocia.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Babuna valley MAC.

The Argiletum was a street of ancient Rome that passed from the Forum Romanum and crossed the Suburra. Its route more or less followed that of the modern streets Via Leonina and Via della Madonna dei Monti.
A gulf on the east of the Peloponnese that opens into the Aegean Sea.
Argoura was a city of Thessalian Pelasgiotis that may have been the Homeric Argissa. The city was located on the Peneios river, some 40 stades from Atrax.
Baptistry built by Theodoric the Great in the late fifth or early sixth century AD
Ariassos is located in Pisidia and is mentioned by several ancient sources, including Ptolemy.
Ariolica was a Roman road station located at or near modern La Thuile, Italy.
Ancient Ariolica was an important settlement of the Aulerci Brannovices tribe in Gaul. It has been identified with the modern La Pacaudière.

Described by Pausanias as flowing past the ancient Messenian site of Thouria "in the plain", this river seems to correspond today to a heavily managed stream originating in the vicinity of Pedema and flowing south to the Messenian Gulf, bypassing ancient Thouria on the west.
An ancient road station, possibly to located at modern Tamazim, an abandoned village in Portugal's Bemposta parish (Abrantes municipality).
An island, known today as Kara Ada, that lies between ancient Halicarnassus (Bodrum, Turkey) and the Greek island of Kos.
The Arles Roman amphitheater or Arènes d'Arles was built ca. A.D. 90 and could seat over 20,000 spectators.
Archaeological site on the Nile River.
Aroania M. is the third highest mountain of the Peloponnese (2,355 m asl).

Three rivers of Arcadia bearing this name are mentioned in ancient sources. According to Pausanias, this Aroanios rises in the ancient Erymanthos mountains and flows southward to join other tributaries of the Erymanthos river at ancient Psophis. BAtlas labels the modern Nousaitiko, which matches Pausanias' description.
Arsanias fl. is a river of eastern Turkey and a major source of the Euphrates fl.
A settlement in the Roman province of Mauretania Caesariensis in North Africa.
An ancient fortress located somewhere between Mosul and modern Zakho; its precise location is unknown today.
Arsia fl. is a river of Istria that became the boundary between Italy and Illyricum.
The rock-cut "Arslan Kaya monument" located just west of Lake Emre in Turkey is in the Phrygian Highlands. The monument carries an inscription in Old Phrygian to the goddess Materan.
The Artamis was a river of Bactria. It is possibly to be identified with the modern Ab-e-Khulm in Afghanistan.

This sanctuary is believed to have been active since at least the Geometric period, possibly on the site of a Mycenaean settlement. Ceramic evidence indicates continuous activity at least through the Roman period.
A small island of the Tuscan Archipelago.
The possible site of the temple of Artemis Proseoa beneath the Ag. Georgios chapel, Artemision (Kourbatsi) Euboea.
A mountain located between Argolis and Arcadia, with a temple of Artemis at its summit.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Arsennaria.
A circular Roman temple that stood on the river Carron until it was destroyed in 1743.
A city in Tabal mentioned in royal inscriptions of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (r. 858-824 BC).
Arupium (modern Prozor, Croatia) was a town of the Iapydes in Illyricum.
An early Scythian burial mound located in what is now the Tuva Republic of Russia.
The Roman amphitheater of Lutetia (modern Paris).
The Al Hajar Mountains of northeastern Oman and the eastern United Arab Emirates are the highest mountain range in the eastern Arabian peninsula.

A sanctuary sacred to Zeus (Jupiter) Asbamaeus that was located in Cappadocia. According to Ammianus Marcellinus, a sacred spring could be seen at the sanctuary. Apollonius of Tyana was said to have been born here.
The ancient Aegean island of Ascania is associated by modern scholars with an island now known as Christiani. The name Ascania has migrated to a smaller, neighboring island in modern times.
An ancient lake in Thessaly. Livy locates it near the Perrhaebian Mountains. The lake was drained in the early 20th century, prior to which it was known by the modern name Nézéro.
A Doric temple dated to the sixth century BCE.

The Ashen Hill Barrow Cemetery is located in Somerset, England. These barrows are the most northerly of the sites in this area. The cemetery consists of six bowl barrows and two bell barrows that are aligned on an east-to-west axis.
Asine was an ancient Greek city of Argolis.
An ancient town of Boeotia known as the birthplace of Hesiod.
Ancient Egyptian island fortress on the Nile in the Middle Kingdom, now submerged.
A river of Boeotia and northern Attica that marked the border between the cities of Thebes and Plataea.
Strabo includes the now-unlocated Asopos river of Paros among other similarly named rivers discussed in his geography. This river of Paros is the fourth of four rivers enumerated at 8.6.24.
An island in the Saronic Gulf.
An island attested in ancient sources, it is probably to be identified with the modern Katrancık Adasi off Turkey's southern coast.
An ancient town in Boeotia that was mentioned by Homer in the Iliad.
A volcanic island that formed on the southwestern edge of the Santorini archipelago following a major volcanic eruption that occurred ca. 1625 BC.

An ancient river of north Africa, placed by Ptolemy between Igilgili (modern Jijel) and the mouth of the Amsaga river (modern Oued El Kebir). The Assarath is probably to be identified with the modern Oued Nil in Algeria.
Assembly Hall from Synagogue at Dura-Europos
Assembly Hall with Torah Shrine located on the west side of the Synagogue Phase 2 in Dura-Europos.

In a private house in Assur, cut into by the excavation trench eD10I, researchers found eight clay tablets and a stamp seal. One of the texts can be dated to 717 BC. The group of texts mostly includes school tablets, as well as a purchase document and an incantation in the form of a letter, written in Babylonian script.
Ancient Roman colony in Tunisia, today's Zanfour, Tunisia.
The Gulf of İzmit (Turkish: İzmit Körfezi) is also known as Izmit Bay. This body of water is a bay located at the easternmost edge of the Sea of Marmara.
A river of Colchis that flows into the Black Sea 120 stadia south of Dioscurias/Sebastopolis and 30 stadia north of the river Hippus, according to Arrian.
A wet-weather watercourse in the Argolid, mentioned by Pausanias. Camp in BAtlas marks it on map 58 on a path followed by an intermittent watercourse mapped in OSM and labeled there as "Taksiarchis".
The Asterousia Mountains are a range of southern Crete that separate the Mesara Plain from the Libyan Sea.
Astura was once a coastal island of Latium and is now a small peninsula at the southeastern edge of the Bay of Antium.
The Astura is a river of Latium that flows from the Alban Mount to the Tyrrhenian Sea.
An Aegean island that still carries its ancient name.
Quarry region around the town of Aswan in Upper Egypt.
The Adige River is the second longest river in Italy. It flows from the Alps to the Adriatic Sea.
An ancient Greek city in Aeolis that lies on the mainland opposite the island of Lesbos, northeast of the town of Dikili in modern-day Turkey.

The site of a Roman villa in the locality of Magnone (Potenza) in South Italy. The archaeological site was first identified in 1979. Limited excavations identified a storage complex housing dolia. The presence of African Red Slip pottery suggests a date in the fourth century.
A city of Campania located between Capua and Neapolis.
Atene was a paralia (coastal) deme of Attica and belonged to the phyle Antiochis.
An ancient Greek tribe that inhabited south-eastern Epirus and west Thessaly.
The temple of Athena Kranaia, mentioned by Pausanias, was located near ancient Elateia in Phokis.

The Athenaeum of Hadrian was located in regio VII near the Capitoline Hill in Rome. Founded by the Emperor Hadrian, it was designated for the promotion of literary and scientific studies and named after the city of Athens. Excavations connected to the Metro C line revealed a complex in the vicinity of the modern Piazza Venezia that has been identified as the site of the Athenaeum.

A fortification in Arcadia that was built and destroyed during the Hellenistic period and is mentioned in ancient sources. The site, located on a hill locally called Chemos and near the modern Greek town of Skortsinos, was used in the late medieval period for a castle.
The Athenian Treasury at Delphi, built between 510 and 480 BC, is a building intended to house offerings made to Apollo by the citizens of Athens.
The Atrebates were a Belgic tribe of Gaul and Britain prior to the Roman conquest. In Gallia Belgica, they inhabited the Artois region.
Lagoons of the Po (Padus) river delta near (H)Atria
An ancient settlement of Umbria mentioned only by Pliny the Elder. Numerous inscriptions discovered at the site indicate that Attidium achieved the status of a municipium.
Site of a multi-phase Roman military encampment located in the modern town of Vitoria (Basque Country, Spain). Its ancient name is not known.

An early Imperial building on the Esquiline Hill in Rome, the Auditorium Maecenatis has been connected with Maecenas as it stands in the area of his gardens (horti). While its precise function is unknown, the building may have served as a conservatory.
A dual court grave near the south shore of Strangford Lough in County Down, Northern Ireland.
A probable Samnite center, the Romans captured Aufidena in 298 BC. It only became a municipium after 49 B.C.

Smith (1854) notes that this station was located at the river mouth where a bridge carried the coast road that led from Sipontum to Barium. Its name is corrupted in various forms, appearing as Aufidena in the Antonine Itinerary and as Aufinum on the Peutinger Table.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A sacred mountain of Italy mentioned by Livy; possibly corresponding to Monte Cimone of the northern Apenines.

The Augusteum, or Sebasteion, at Antioch in Pisidia was a monumental architectural complex dedicated to the Roman Imperial cult. Its archaeological remains were first excavated in 1913. Approximately 60 fragments of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti were discovered at the site.
The Aula Palatina is a Roman Imperial Basilica of the emperor Constantine (German: Konstantinbasilika) located at Trier, Germany. It was built ca. A.D. 310 as part of a Roman palace complex.

An ancient, spring-fed lake (modern Çapalı Göl/Çapalı Bataklık/Karakuyu Gölü in Turkey's Afyonkarahisar province) next to which the ancient settlement of Aporidos Come and the Roman castellum known as "Alutrena" were located.
The visible archaeological remains of the settlement of Aunobari cover ca. 5 hectares.
A gold mining region in Dacia.
The modern Djebel Aurès: an eastern extension of the Atlas Mountain System in northeastern Algeria and northwestern Tunisia.
Auridai was a deme of ancient Attica. It originally belonged to the phyle of Hippothontis, but later to Antigonis.
The Aurunci were an Italic tribe of south Italy. Their territory was incorporated into the Roman territory in the fourth century B.C.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
The Auscii were an ancient tribe of Aquitania and submitted to Caesar's legate in 56 BC.
A Confederation of Libyan peoples, cited: BAtlas 37 C3 Austuriani
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group whose territory was located around Ossucio.
The Autariatae were an ancient tribe of Illyria.
The Autrigones were a pre-Roman tribe of Iberia, settled in what in what today is the western Basque country of Spain.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: between R. Saja and R. Nansa valleys.

Avatha (al-Bakhra') is the site of a Late Roman and early Islamic fort that is located south of Palmyra. The fort was originally a Tetrarchic establishment that housed an auxiliary cavalry unit. The fort was modified and expanded during the Umayyad period.
Avebury is a Neolithic henge monument comprised of three stone circles dating to the third millennium BCE.
A river of the Sabine territory.
One of the seven hills of Rome. Until the reign of the emperor Claudius, the hill lay outside the pomerium of the city.
A volcanic crater lake located in the Phlegraean Fields, Lake Avernus served a major ritual role for ancient Romans and Greeks as they viewed it as an entrance to Hades.
Avitta Bibba was a settlement located in the Roman province of Africa Proconsularis.
The Axiakes, a river of Ukraine.
Caches of sculpture discovered in the 19th century by Luigi di Cesnola provide evidence for a cult of a male deity in the area of the modern Ayios Photios church near Athienou on Cyprus.
This place is attested in an inscription found in Algeria's Hamma oasis (north of ancient Cirta) in the late nineteenth century.
A modern town located near the mouth of the Don river in the Russian oblast of Rostov.
Aşağımollahasan höyük is a prehistoric höyük located in Özalp, Turkey.

The Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) surrounded his new capital Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon") with a rectangular-shaped, 16,280-cubit-long inner and outer city wall. The name of the city wall (dūru) was Aššur-mušalbir-palê-šarri-ēpišīšu-nāṣir-ummānīšu ("The God Aššur Is the One Who Prolongs the Reign of Its Royal Builder (and) Protects His Troops") according to some Akkadian royal inscriptio
B(a)elo is located on the northern shore of the Strait of Gibraltar. The town was founded in the late second century BC and achieved municipal status under Claudius.
Roman fort at present-day Beckfoot. Part of the Cumbrian coastal defenses.
Bābā Jān Tepe is an archeological site located in Luristan, some 10 km from Nūrābād, Iran.
Baccanae was a road station along the Via Cassia.

Nineveh’s main (or great) inner wall was called Badnigalbilukurašušu ("Wall Whose Brilliance Overwhelms Enemies"). It was constructed by the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib after he moved the Assyrian capital to Nineveh. Badnigalbilukurašušu’s superstructure was reportedly raised to a height of 200 courses of brick. The visible remains of the twelve-kilometer-long wall and some of its gates are stil

Nineveh’s outer stone wall was called Badnigerimhuluha ("Wall, Terrorizer of Enemies"). It was constructed by the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib after he moved the Assyrian capital to Nineveh. The visible remains of the twelve-kilometer-long wall and some of its gates are still visible today.
The city wall of Sippar. Its Sumerian ceremonial name means "Wall Built in Ancient Times." In the 7th century B.C., the wall was also called Badullisâ ("What Named in Ancient Times").
A settlement of Hispania Baetica in the territory of Castulo that was the site of Scipio's victories over Hasdrubal (209 B.C.), and over Mago and Masinissa (206 B.C.)

Mount Behistun is located in the Kermanshah Province of Iran. It is the site of the so-called Behistun Inscription, a multilingual inscription and rock relief established by Darius the Great (r. 522–486 B.C.).
A megalithic dolmen located in Saumur, France. This is one of the largest dolmens in France.
The so-called "Baths of Nero" are located near the Porta a Lucca in Pisa.
A third century Roman villa with mosaics and a bath complex was discovered at Bagnoli di S. Gregorio in 1986.
Bagras Castle is located in Turkey's İskenderun district in the Amanus Mountains. The tenth-century castle was rebuilt in the twelfth century.
Bahçecik is a village located in Sur, Diyarbakır Province, Turkey. Sarduri built a tower temple and the fortress “Sarduriḫinili” here in the eighth century BCE.
Urartian site containing a ruined building and some rock inscriptions.
Modern Piram island in India's Gulf of Khambhat.
A sanctuary to the west of the Acropolis of Athens, which was the clubhouse for a private religious association called the Iobakchoi, in the 2nd century AD.
Balanea/Leukas was an important Phoenician port.
A fierce mountain tribe of interior Sardinia, said to have descended from Iberian and Libyan mercenaries who had deserted from the Carthaginian army.
A pre-Roman people settled in south-eastern Corsica, mentioned by Ptolemy.
The Balearic Sea or Iberian Sea: coastal waters to the south and east of the Iberian Peninsula.
Balmuildy was the site of a Roman fort on the Antonine Wall in Scotland. This is one of only two Antonine Wall forts found to have stone ramparts.
A fortified Medieval site located in Puglia.
Colonia Iulia Valentia Banasa was one of the three colonies founded by emperor Augustus between 33 and 25 B.C. in Mauretania Tingitana.
A place from the TAVO Index
The Etruscan necropolis of Caere, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

A Roman maritime villa located at the southwest corner of the Istrian peninsula, about six kilometers south of Pola. According to Matijašić 1982, the remains of the villa are visible beneath the waters of Paltana Bay.
The Roman fort at Banna, now known as Birdoswald Roman fort.
Site of Roman settlement attested in the Ravenna Cosmography, referring to either of the small towns situated at Caistor or Horncastle in Lincolnshire.

Buddhist temple at Angkor, located approximately 20 km northeast of the main temple complex. Dedicated to Shiva, the temple was constructed during the 10th century CE during the reigns of Rajendravarman II and Jayavarman V.

An octagonal brick structure erected by Bishop Ursus (late fourth or early fifth century AD) as part of a Basilica (destroyed in 1734). Bishop Neon completed the baptistry at the end of the fifth century AD.
The Bar Hill Fort Bathhouse was built around 140 CE, at the same time as the Antonine wall, and is a long and narrow stone structure with latrines and two heated rooms.
Barbarano Romano is a Medieval town in the province of Viterbo that has produced substantial archaeological evidence of Villanovan and Orientalizing habitation.
Barbarikon was a port city near modern-day Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan, that was important in the Hellenistic period in Indian Ocean trade.

A no-longer-visible villa maritima was identified north of Tergeste in 1887. According to AdriAtlas, a reanalysis by Fontana (1993) places the beginnings of the villa's occupational sequence in the third quarter of the first century BCE.
A Roman signal station on Barcombe Hill, overlooking the Stanegate and Vindolanda.
A Byzantine and Ottoman fortification northeast of (and overlooking) the Azyleia/Mytika plain in Acarnania, Greece. Some commentators have supposed an earlier antecedent on the site.
Military barracks reworked from private house K5-A in Block K5 at Dura-Europos
Archaeological site on the Ob River in Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, Russia containing remains dated to the 6th-4th centuries BCE.
The Gulf of Khambhat is an inlet of the Arabian Sea along the west coast of India.

A hilltop archaeological site in southeastern Albania, presently named after the adjacent modern village, that lies less than 2km northeast of modern Korça. Its precise nature is not yet known, but earlier suggestions that it was a burial mound have been refuted by the discovery of significant stone walls and small finds datable to the Iron Age and possibly the Hellenistic period.
A basilica located at the juncture of the Sacra Via and the Argiletum flanking the Forum Romanum that was initially built in 179 B.C.E.
The Basilica Julia was built on the south side of the Forum Romanum in 46 B.C. on the site of the former Basilica Sempronia.
A building in the Campus Martius that originally dates to ca. 25 BCE.

The Basilica Porcia is considered the first named civil basilica in Rome. The elder Cato is responsible for its construction in 184 BCE. It seems to have been a small structure that took the place of several earlier private atria located between the Clivus Argentarius and the Curia Hostilia. The Basilica Porcia was destroyed by fire in 52 BCE.

The Basilica Ulpia is located in the Forum of Trajan at Rome and derives its name from the emperor Trajan's gentilician nomenclature. The basilica was considered a marvel of ancient Roman architecture by observers, including the historian Ammianus Marcellinus.
A Christian basilica in Milan built in the late fourth and early fifth centuries.

The ruins of a Christian basilica located near the Via Ardeatina on the grounds of the Calixtian complex have been connected with the Basilica of Saint Mark. The site was discovered accidentally in 1991 and is associated with the Catacomb of Balbina.
Basilica di Sant'Agnese fuori le mura
Pope Honorius I commissions the Basilica of Saint Agnes in the seventh century, replacing the earlier Constantinian structure.

The presence of a basilica created with funds donated by Constantine I in region 5 of ancient Ostia was known from textual sources and then confirmed via geophysical prospection and, ultimately, excavation.

The Basilica of Junius Bassus (basilica Iunii Bassi) was a civil basilica on the Esquiline Hill in Rome. Its remains were demolished in 1930 to make way for the Seminario Pontificio di Studi Orientali, in via Napoleone III, 3. Junius Bassus held the consulship in 331 CE. The basilica is particularly known for its opus sectile decorations. In the fifth century, the basilica was remodeled into the c
Basilica of Saint Augustine in Campo Marzio

The Basilica of Saint Augustine of Hippo in Camp Martius is a titular minor basilica of the Roman Catholic church located in the Campus Martius of Rome. The basilica was conceived in 1286 and the current basilica was completed in 1483.
A basilica begun in the sixth century AD by Bishop Ursicinus with financial support from the Greek banker Iulianus Argentarius.
Basilica of Santa Maria in Trastevere
The Basilica di Santa Maria in Trastevere is a titular minor basilica located in the Trastevere district of Rome, Italy.
The Basilica of Septimius Severus belongs to the Severan Forum at Lepcis Magna.
The Basilica of St. John the Evangelist is located in Ephesus on the Ayasuluk Hill. It was built between 548 and 565 CE.
The Casa Herrera Basilica is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida". The paleochristian basilica was built in either the late fifth or early sixth century CE.
Bath building constructed by Roman soldiers in Block C3.
Bath building located in the intramuros military sector of Dura-Europos, replaced by Bath E3 Phase 2.
Bath building constructed by Roman soldiers in Block M7.

The circuit walls of Aquae Sulis, enclosing an area of some 23 ha, began in the Roman period and were later reinforced in the Anglo-Saxon and Medieval periods. Various remains are visible at points along the original circuit.
The Baths of Antoninus at Carthage date to the middle of the second century and are the largest of the Roman public bath complexes in North Africa.
A bath complex of ancient Rome built on the Aventine Hill in 252 CE.

The so-called "Baths of the Philosopher" or "Terme del Filosofo" in region V of the ancient city of Ostia take their modern sobriquet from a bust of Plotinus dating to the middle of the third century CE.
The Batinus flumen is mentioned by Pliny and may correspond to the modern Tordino river.
Bavares, an ancient people of Mauretania.
Site of mid- to late-fourth century Roman fort.
A temple in the Khmer capital of Angkor Thom, constructed in the late 12th or early 13th century CE.
A Bronze Age funereal mound located in Turkey's south-eastern Siirt Province.
Ruins of an ancient city, located in modern Syria. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 as part of the "Ancient Villages of Northern Syria."
Beacon Hill Hill fort is an Iron Age hill fort in Hampshire, England.
An ancient settlement of the Treveri. Modern Bitburg in Germany.
The Ronco River is a tributary of the Montone River, located in Romagna, northern Italy.
Lake Vegoritida, once known as Lake Ostrovo, is a large natural lake located in western Macedonia, northern Greece.
Beit She'arim National Park is the site of a large number of ancient rock-cut Jewish tombs, dating to the second century AD. The necropolis was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015.

A monumental Hellenistic tomb located at the modern Turkish village of Belevi (11km northeast of ancient Ephesus). The tomb may have been prepared for either Antigonus Monophthalmus or Lysimachus. The Seleucid king Antiochus II Theos may have been buried there subsequently.
Founded from Chersonesus in the late fourth century B.C., Beljaus was a fortified agricultural settlement located near the mouth of Lake Donuzlav.
A mountain, probably Silla del Papa, near B(a)elo.
The Bellovaci were a tribe of Gallia Belgica.
An ancient people mentioned by Ptolemy. They are possibly to have been located to the east of modern lake Garda.
At Beltany in County Donegal, Ireland, is a Neolithic stone circle monument comprised of 64 menhirs. The monument dates ca. 1400-800 BC.
A speaker's platform erected in the Theater of Dionysus at Athens in the second century CE.
An ancient settlement of Corinthia, placed near ancient Nemea by Strabo. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
