Ben Shemen Forest is the largest forest in Central Israel and it contains several archaeological sites, including Bir a Shemi, Tel Gimzo, Tel Hadid, and several Hasmonean-period tombs.
Benacus L. (Lake Garda) is the largest lake in Italy.
A late antique harbour site that is linked to the abandonment of the site of Lucentum.

A set of poros benches built on the east slope of the Kolonos Agoraios at the edge of the Athenian Agora in the fifth century BC, which seated 400-500 people and perhaps served as a meeting place for a council or court. They were truncated and rendered inaccessible by further construction in the fourth century BC.
A Middle Kingdom cemetery known for its rock-cut tombs of local officials.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: middle R. Evros valley.
A pyramid built by Pharaoh Sneferu (ca. 2600 BC).
A modern town and a former municipality in Evros, Greece. Site of a 12th century monastic foundation, subsequently fortified.
A nymphaeum on the shores of the Alban Lake that is located in a natural grotto that is assigned to the Flavian period and associated with the complex of the Villa of Domitian.

Berlanga de Duero is a Spanish municipality located in the province of Soria, in the autonomous region of Castile and León. An object dubbed the "Berlanga cup" was discovered here. This object is a hemispherical bowl that belongs to a small group of artifacts referred to as "Hadrian's Wall pans", as these vessels depict places and names from sites along the line of Hadrian's Wall.
A circular Roman mausoleum with a distinctive cupola located at the ninth mile of the Via Appia.
A Roman triumphal arch dedicated ca. 13 BC by Lucius Licinius Sura and perhaps dedicated to Augustus.

Archaeological investigation at the site of Beta Samati, located between Aksum and the Red Sea, has revealed remains of a significant Aksumite administrative center. The archaeological site is located in the vicinity of Yeha, Ethiopia.
Govrin/Eleutheropolis was a Roman city founded on the site of Betaris.

A domus included in Regio III, the house of Betitius Perpetuus Arzygius was located on the Quirinal Hill close to the ara incendii Neroniani. Some of its remains have been documented beneath the present Palazzo delle Esposizioni.
A Roman castrum of the limes Arabicus. In the fourth century, Legio IV Martia was stationed here.

Bewcastle Castle is a Medieval castle that occupies the site of a former Roman fort. The first castle dates to ca. 1092 and was destroyed in 1173. The castle was rebuilt in the fourteenth century and was again renewed in the 1540s.
An archaeological site located in Pakistan's Punjab province that includes some of the earliest remains of the city of Taxila, dating ca. 800–525 BCE.
A "princely burial" at modern Białęcino (formerly Balenthin) in Poland dated to the early Roman imperial period by virtue of coins found deposited with the burial.
An island off the coast of Gedrosia, mentioned by Pliny and Arrian. Due to coastline change and other factors, its precise location cannot be determined today.
Bibbiena likely originated as an Etruscan hilltop settlement. A Medieval castle is eventually built atop the hill, which stands 425 metres (1,394 ft) above sea level.
Bibracte (modern Mont-Beuvray) was an oppidum of the Celtic Aedui, later named Lugdunensis.
Bidis? was a fortress located near Syracuse.
A monumental sanctuary (26 x 20 m) dedicated to Iuppiter.
Thirteenth- and fourteenth-century fortress located in Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi in the Odessa region of southwestern Ukraine.
Bilitio (modern Bellinzona, Switzerland) is an ancient settlement in proximity to both the Po and Ticino rivers. A Roman settlement was established there during the Augustan period.
The Billaios was a river of ancient Bithynia.
A Roman balneum attached either to a Roman townhouse or mansio.

The modern Bingöl Dağları is an extinct shield volcano located to the northeast of modern Bingöl in Turkey, lying between the modern settlements of Karlıova, Tekman, Hınıs, and Varto. The mountain was known in Roman times by the name "Abos".
The Bishop Genesius Church at Jerash (Jordan) may be the earliest Christian church on the site. The church was built in the early seventh century, reusing a preexisting Roman temple.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A province of the Roman Empire on the Black Sea coast that was formed when the former kingdoms of Bithynia (annexed by Rome in 74 B.C.) and Pontus (annexed in 63 B.C.) were joined together.
Bitia was an ancient settlement located in extreme southern Sardinia. It likely had a nuragic phase that was followed by Punic and Roman phases of occupation.
The Bituriges Vivisci were a tribe of Gaul whose capital was at Burdigala.
The pyramid of the Middle Kingdom Pharaoh Amenemhat III.
A Roman fort at present-day Birrens, cited: BAtlas 9 D5 Blatobulgium
The Blemmyes were a nomadic people of Lower Nubia. Strabo places them on the right bank of the Nile River.
A vicus of the civitas Nerviorum.
City block of Dura-Europos labeled according to modern excavators' scheme.
City block of Dura-Europos labeled according to modern excavators' scheme.
City block of Dura-Europos labeled according to modern excavators' scheme.
City block of Dura-Europos labeled according to modern excavators' scheme.
City block of Dura-Europos labeled according to modern excavators' scheme.
City block of Dura-Europos labeled according to modern excavators' scheme. The city's grid plan was established c. 150BCE and the site went out of use in 256 CE.
A lake in Bithynia located between the Ascania Lacus and the river Sangarius.
A small city of northern Italy with Roman origins.
A villa maritima of the first century B.C.

Bodobrica (Kastell Boppard) was the site of a fourth-century CE Roman fortification on the Rhine River. The fort measured approximately 308 × 154 meters and was surrounded by a wall defended by up to 28 interval towers.
The modern River Forth in Scotland.
Boibe was a settlement of ancient Crete.

According to Strabo, Boinoa/Oinoe was an ancient settlement between Pylos and Lasion in Elis that was either also called Ephyra or located near another place with that name. The precise location of this settlement cannot be determined today.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: S Lake Ohrid ALB.
Lake Volvi is located on the Chalkidiki peninsula.
A river located in northern Achaea that drains into the Gulf of Corinth.

Burial complex along a stretch of over 3 km of the northern bank of the Siniukha River, a stream in the Laba River valley (Krasnodar region). The necropolis contains over 200 individual burials dated to the Middle Bronze-Early Iron Ages (3rd millennium BCE-3rd century CE).

The Great Salbyk Mound is the largest burial mound in the Khakassia region of Russia. The mastaba-like tomb, associated with the Bronze Age Tagar culture, was constructed in the 7th century BCE, and may have had an astronomical function.
An ancient sanctuary of the Aventine Hill in Rome.
Boncuklu Tarla is an archaeological site located in the Mardin province of Turkey. The human settlement was occupied from the Late Epipalaeolithic to Pre-Pottery Neolithic B periods.
Bonna (modern Bonn, Germany) began as a Roman military outpost in Germania Inferior ca. 11 BC.
Karadağ Mountain is an extinct volcano located in the Karaman Province of Turkey.
Bordj-Hellal shows evidence for both pre-Roman and Roman phases, as attested by both epigraphic evidence and ceramics.
Tell in Eastern Romania with evidence of habitation in the Gumelnitean and La Tene periods.
A mountain in Arcadia above Asea, perhaps Mt. Gravari.
The northernmost point of the island of Sri Lanka.
A settled area of Campania, especially well known for the Roman country villas of the first century BCE, which were destroyed by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.
A strait that forms part of the boundary between Europe and Asia.

The archaeological site of Bostel is located in Castelletto, municipality of Rotzo, province of Vicenza. The site is located some 850 meters above sea level. This ancient alpine village was inhabited from the fifth to first centuries BCE.
The remains of a Roman legionary fort located in North Lanarkshire near Glasgow, Scotland, that was built in connection with the Antonine Wall (ca. A.D. 142-165).
Bottike was a western area of ancient Chalcidice.

These mines, evidently actively worked in the 19th century and early 20th century but not in more recent times, are mentioned in AAA in passing (without any clear assertion of ancient evidence of exploitation) alongside discussion of some meager Roman remains at Merachiche, 3.5km to the northwest. They are conflated with the former in a single mine/quarry symbol in BAtlas.
The ancient river called Boudoros is associated with the Voudoros Potamos, in Euboia, Central Greece.
The modern Capo Scalambri on Sicily's southern coast.

Constructed during the Hellenistic period, this meeting hall served the Epirote league. It was destroyed and rebuilt multiple times before going out of use for this purpose during the early Roman empire.
BAtlas 58 H4 Bounali tou Barba Spiro
The River Boyne follows a course of some 112 km from Trinity Well, Newberry Hall, near Carbury, County Kildare to the Irish Sea.
An Archaic coastal sanctuary located at Alepochori, Megara, Greece.
Boutadai was a deme of Attica.
Bovium? was the site of a brickworks that supplied the Roman fort of Deva Victrix.

The Boxmoor Roman Villa located at Boxmoor, Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, was occupied from the first to the fourth centuries. During that time at least five occupational phases have been identified.
A settlement mound and archaeological site located in the Troad containing evidence of habitation from the Chalcolithic through the Late Bronze Ages.

At Brading on the Isle of Wight, the remains of a Roman winged corridor type villa, consisting of three blocks, were excavated between 1881 and 1900. The villa was occupied between the second and fourth centuries A.D. The villa is known for its mosaic pavements.
Small settlement in southeastern Crete dated to the Middle-Late Minoan period.

A previously quarried limestone bed on the banks of the Rhone was identified and requarried in the 19th century near the modern French commune of Brangues in Isère. A number of discarded and incomplete stones were identified. The original quarrying has been assumed to have been of Roman date.

A Roman fort was established near the present-day village of Leintwardine ca. 70 CE. The fort was situated close to the confluence of the river Clun with the river Teme, along the Roman road now known as "Watling Street West".
The site of a probable Roman villa, associated with findspot of RIB 3179.
A Scythian burial mound dated to the fourth century B.C. located near the village of Bratolyubivka in Kherson Oblast, Ukraine.
A Roman fort at present-day Kirkby Thore.
Brazda lui Novac de Nord is part of a Roman frontier system in present-day Romania. This frontier system is known also as Constantine's Wall.
A colony of Athens founded c. 445 BC.
A Roman fort at present-day High Rochester.
Brenthe was a city in Arcadia that was reportedly in ruins in Pausanias' time. It was located close to the right bank of the river Alpheius.
An ancient Alpine people whose territory included the Eisacktal valley.
An unnamed bridge over Eurymedon fl.
Bridge over Fosso di Acqua Rossa
The remains of a Roman bridge that once carried a road over the Fosso di Acqua Rossa. Ward-Perkins posits a date of the second or first century BCE based on comparanda in the vicinity.
Brigantium (modern Bregenz) was a Celtic settlement from at least the fifth century B.C. and came under Roman control in the first century B.C.
Brigetio was a legionary camp, cannabae, and municipium along the Pannonian limes.

Britannia I or Britannia Prima was a province of the Roman empire that was established under the Diocletianic reforms of the third century. The capital of the province remains undetermined but the province was mostly likely centered in the present regions of Wales and Cornwall.
A Roman fort at modern Brougham in the United Kingdom (sometimes called Brougham Castle Roman Fort).
The Broch of Mousa is a drystone broch in Scotland, dating ca. 400-200 BC.
A Roman auxiliary fort likely to have been built to support pre-Flavian campaigns in modern Wales.
A large fortified settlement in modern County Wicklow, Ireland, with evidence of occupation in the Late Bronze and Early Iron Ages.
An ancient Italic people of extreme southern Italy, the Bruttii inhabited an area that roughly corresponds to the modern Calabria.
Brylleion/Myrleia/Apamea/Col. Iulia Concordia was a city in Bithynia founded originally by the Colophonians.
A Neolithic mound site on the island of Anglesey.
The ancient Bubasius Sinus is now known as the Gulf of Hisarönü (Hisarönü Körfezi in Turkish). The gulf lies Bozan Burnu to the north and Atabol Burnu to the south.
The Bucinobantes were an Alemannic tribe living in the region of the modern city of Mainz (Germany) on the river Main.
Buciumi was the site of a Roman castrum along the road between Porolissum and Bologa.

Monumental statues of Gautam Buddha were carved into the cliff-face at Bamyan, located in the Bamyan valley in the Hazarajat region of central Afghanistan, The statues were, respectively, 35 and 53 m tall. They were intentionally destroyed by the Taliban in 2001.
Buduntini, the only freshwater lake in Sardinia.

An apsidal structure on the Acropolis of Athens, built in the late 6th-century BC, destroyed in the Persian Sack of 480 BC, and perhaps repaired in the first half of the 5th century. It was probably located on the site of the northwest wing of the later Propylaia, which would have superseded it in 437 BC.
Building III on the Athenian Acropolis

A building on the north side of the Acropolis of Athens with an attached courtyard, built in the second half of the 5th century BC. It is perhaps to be identified with the house of the Arrhephoroi, but other identifications have been proposed.

Bukhara began as part of the Persian empire in the sixth century B.C. The site is especially important as an example of an Islamic city of central Asia. The city center was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
A series of Celtiberian sculptures located near El Tiemblo, Ávila, Spain. These statues were perhaps originally created during the second century BC.
Burano is an island in the Venetian Lagoon. It may have been settled in Roman times by refugees from Altinum.
Burcana Ins. (Borkum) is an island in the North Sea. It is mentioned by Strabo and Pliny the Elder as the Burchana fabaria (island of beans).
A Spanish city located in the north of Spain that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.
The Burgundiones were an ancient Germanic tribe of eastern Germany that perhaps emigrated from the island of Bornholm.

Burkhan Khaldun is a mountain that forms part of one of the Khentii Mountains located in the Khentii Province of northeastern Mongolia. The mountain and/or its vicinity is believed to be the birthplace and site of the tomb of Genghis Khan. The mountain and its landscapes were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 4 July 2015 under the heading "Great Burkhan Khaldun Mountain and its surround
Minor settlement in Upper Syrian Euphrates.
The modern Rienz (German) or Rienza (Italian) river flows from the Dolomite mountains in South Tyrol, Italy, to join the Eisack river at the city of Brixen.
An early imperial villa along the coast of Liguria. Its ancient name is unknown.

Buxio is one of several villas mentioned in a list of "donatio ecclesiae" in the "territorio Carducino" in the Life of Saint Didier, who was bishop of Cahors in the 7th century CE. BAtlas places it with a hollow symbol and a question mark on map 25, offering "Le Buz, Vabre?" in the directory for modern location. Modern Vabre is a French commune in Occitania on the Gijou river. CAG reports that the
A Byzantine fortress located at the site of Thignica.
A sixth century A.D. Byzantine fortress built at Timgad by the governor Solomon.
The Byzantine fortress at Ammaedara is a border fortress located in the far west of the Byzacena. It was built between 534 and 565 and covers 2.55 ha.
An ancient river of peninsular India, known to Pliny as Cabirus and to Ptolemy as Chabēros. Scholars identify it with the modern Kāverī.
Site, in modern France, of a Gallo-Roman settlement whose ancient name is not known.
A terraced pre-Roman settlement located in Premià de Dalt. The site flourished between the fifth and third centuries B.C. and was abandoned by the first century B.C
A Roman fort located in a bend of the Afon Llugwy near Capel Curig in Conwy, Wales.
Amphitheatre of the legionary fortress at Caerleon
Site of a late first century CE Roman auxiliary fort between Cardiff and Gelligaer.
The Mithraeum at Caesarea is only one of two excavated from the eastern half of the Roman empire.

Hellenistic temple constructed by Cleopatra VII and dedicated to Julius Caesar, and later rededicated by Augustus to himself. In 13 BCE Augustus relocated two obelisks from Heliopolis to the site. The temple was converted to a Christian church in the mid-4th century.
The complex, identified as the Caesareum of Palmyra, was converted into a mosque during the Umayyad period.
An 8-hectare Romano-British settlement that developed in the 60s AD and continued in use until the fourth century.

Caimeni is a name ascribed to the geological predecessors of Palea and Nea Kameni, islands in the caldera of Santorini. These two later islands were formed by volcanic activity between AD 1620 and 1850.
An ancient river of the Indian peninsula, mentioned by Pliny and Arrian, that perhaps should be identified with the modern Ken.
Roman town in present-day Lincolnshire. Candidate location for Bannovallum (the other being Horncastle).

The Cala Morell Necropolis is an ancient rock-cut necropolis located at cala Morell on the island of Menorca. The necropolis has two phases of use, the first corresponding to the final Bronze and the other to the Roman period.
An ancient Sicilian city located on the northern coast of the island, founded by Ducetius in 446 B.C.
Calagurris (Nassica) Iulia (modern Calahorra, Spain) was conquered by Rome in 187 BC and later supported Quintus Sertorius in his war against Cn. Pompeius Magnus.
A first century A.D. Roman aqueduct that carried water from the locality known as "Caldaccoli" to baths in Pisa.
A Roman settlement with public baths that was occupied from the later republican period until the fifth or sixth century CE.
The Callaeci Bracari formed part of a large Celtic tribal federation that inhabited Gallaecia, a region roughly corresponding to what is now Galicia (Spain).
The Callaeci Lucenses formed part of a large Celtic tribal federation that inhabited Gallaecia, a region roughly corresponding to what is now Galicia (Spain).
A river of Samnium and a major tributary of the Volturno river.
An Etruscan settlement covering some 17 ha located near the modern village of Gonfienti (Prato).
The largest Yemeni island in the Red Sea.
Camerinum was a town in Umbria on the frontiers of Picenum that was allied to Rome from 309 B.C.
Site of a small Romano-British town.

The place known as "Camp de César" or "Caesar's Camp" is an ancient town covering some 18 ha that was occupied from the fifth century BCE until Late Antiquity. Built fortifications augment the site's natural defensibility.
A large oppidum active in the Late Bronze and early Iron Ages.
Roman baths dating from the first to fourth centuries.
An Italic sanctuary sacred to Hercules located in località Civitella in the comune of Campochiaro. The site is to be connected with the Pentrian Samnites.
The Campus Martius or "field of Mars" is the name given to the level ground between the slopes of the Capitoline, the Quirinal, and Pincian hills, and the Tiber river.
An ancient tribe located in Val Camonica during the Iron Age.
Canauna was a region located on the western coast of Arabia.
The remains of a Roman "Villa rustica" located adjacent to the Sanctuary of the Madonna di Canneto.
The site of a Roman and Iron Age settlement located at Kelvedon.
The Cantabri were an important tribe of the Atlantic coastal region of northern Iberia.

A limestone quarry at Nîmes that is often referred to by the name of the hill into which it was cut. It is located just west of the Temple of Diana and north of the terminus of the Rue de la Càrriere Romaine. Modern structures have been built in and around the quarry and access is gated, but some of the excavated cliff faces are still visible from the terminus of the Rue du Rempart Romain.
The Cantiaci were a Celtic population inhabiting Britain prior to the Roman conquest. They lend their name to a Roman civitas centered on Kent.
Capalbio is a municipality in the Province of Grosseto. It is first attested in A.D. 805 when Charlemagne donated the locality to the Abbey of the Tre Fontane.
The smallest of Rome's hills and one of its most important, the Capitoline Hill served as the citadel (arx) of the city and as the site of its poliadic temple.
The so-called Capitolium of Aquinum is found in the northwest part of the site. It may predate Roman colonization, and it is perhaps sacred to Iuno Regina.
The Capitolium at Thugga dates to the middle of the second century and carries epigraphic dedications to Lucius Verus and Marcus Aurelius dating to the late 160s.
The Capitolium of Brixia was built in A.D. 73.
The so-called Capitolium temple of the Latin colony of Cosa.
Tetrastyle Corinthian temple located in the Roman forum at Sala (modern Chellah) dating from the early Hadrianic period (c.120 CE).
A Tuscanic podium temple that is often referred to as being of the Capitolium type was built at Terracina in the middle of the first century BCE.

The prehistoric village of Capo Graziano dates to the Middle Bronze Age and is located on the island of Filicudi. The site was excavated between 1952 and 1969. It is situated on a terrace some 100 m above sea level. At least 27 agglomerative huts were identified at the site.
A promontory on the northern coast of Sardinia. It is probably to be identified with the "Errebantion Akron" mentioned by Ptolemy.
Capo la Timpa is an archaeological site in Maratea, Italy, with evidence for human settlement beginning in the Neolithic period.
A mountain that Pliny claims Licinius Mucianus identified as the source of the Euphrates. Per T.B. Mitford in BAtlas, it is probably to be identified with modern Kurtlu Tepe.
The site of a villa located between Frascati and Monte Porzio Catone. It is associated with Matidia Augusta on account of an inscribed fistula discovered there in 1888.
Site of a Roman fort occupied during the Flavian and Antonine periods. It lies 4 miles east of Jedburgh in the Scottish Borders, along the line of Dere Street.
A tribe of North Africa, the Caprarianses ("inhabitants of a region full of goats") dwelt in the Montes Caprarienses and were the neighbors of the Abannae.
The north-westernmost of the seven islands of the Tuscan Archipelago.
A Roman road station attested in ancient sources. It is probably to be localized somewhere in the vicinity of the modern Spanish town of Ossa de Montiel (Castilla-La Mancha).

An unlocated Roman road station that, according to the Antonine Itinerary, was located between Agiria (modern Calamocha or Salvacañete?) and Sermonae (Cariñena?) on the Roman road from Laminium (Alhambra?) to Caesaraugusta (Zaragosa). It may be the same place as one "Caraca" mentioned by the Geographer of Ravenna as lying between Complutum (Alcalá de Henares) and "Puteis".
The modern Capo Sant'Elia on the southeast coast of Sardinia.
The so-called "le Carceri Vecchie" is a first-century CE Roman mausoleum. Its original position on the Via Appia placed it outside the walls of ancient Capua.
The Corace river empties into the Gulf of Squillace.
Cardiff Castle incorporates remains of the antecedent Roman fort.
Carecini Infernates, one of the four ancient tribes that made up the Samnite population.
The Carecini Supernates were a tribe of Samnites.
An ancient town on the Via Clodia.
The ancient Cares has been identified with the modern Cher in France. It is a tributary of the Liger (modern Loire).
A coastal mountain range in northern Israel.
Carn Euny is an Iron Age site near near Sancreed in Cornwall.
The Carni were a people of ancient Histria.
A Roman army camp on the Danube River in Noricum; after the first century CE Carnuntum served as the capital of Upper Pannonia.
The Carnutes were a powerful Celtic tribe occupying a territory between the Sequana (Seine) and the Liger (Loire) rivers.
A Neolithic cemetery dated to 3400 to 3100 BC. Fourteen passage tombs have been identified.
A grouping of fourth-millennium BC Neolithic monuments located on the Cúil Irra peninsula near Sligo, Ireland.
The cothon at Carthage was divided into a rectangular merchant harbor and an inner protected harbor reserved for military use.
An oppidum of the Statielli/Statellati, where the Romans defeated Ligurian tribes in 173 BC. Its location is not known.

Located in Transalpine Gaul, Cas(s)inomagus is included on the Peutinger Table. It lies along the road from Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes) to Ausritum, Augustoritum (Lirnmoes), some 25.5 Roman miles from Limoges.
A Roman domus at Cartagena, Spain, dating to the first century BCE.

A structure in Rome built between 1040 and 1065 by one Niccolò, son of Crescenzio and Teodora, in order to control the Ponte Emilio, on whose transit the family charged a toll. The building incorporates ancient spolia.

The House of the Relief of Telephus or Casa del Rilievo di Telefo is one of the largest houses attested in the excavated area of Herculaneum (ca. 1,800 sq. m.). The house was excavated between 1934 and 1936.
A domus at Pompeii partially excavated in the nineteenth century.
The House of Bacchus at Pompeii takes its name from a wall painting featuring the god Bacchus. Excavations were carried out in 1824 and 1826. The site was bombed during World War II in 1943.
The so-called "Casa di Properzio" at Assisi is a Roman domus located near the southern curtain of the ancient city walls. The decorations date the house to the first century B.C.
The so-called Casa di Trittolemo at Pompeii was excavated in 1859 and again in 1871.

Casal Bertone is named for the modern Roman neighborhood where it was discovered, about 2 km east of the Porta Maggiore. The site of Casal Bertone covers more than 3,000 square meters. The eastern portion of the site comprised a residential area that was occupied from about the first century B.C. to the fifth to sixth centuries A.D.
A Roman tomb that supports a Medieval farmhouse (casale) at the sixth mile of the Via Appia. The tomb originally dates ca. 30 BC; it was a large, circular tomb with a diameter of approximately 35 m.
At modern Casalbore, Italy, archaeological evidence includes a significant temple structure and associated material from the Samnite and Roman periods.

A villa located at the eighth mile of the ancient Via Latina. The villa was first built in the first century B.C. and continued in use until the fourth century. During its life span there were several phases of architectural modification and expansion.
A villa at the seventh mile of the Via Latina.
T. Ashby notes the presence of a villa platform to the west of the "upper Casale Vitriano". This platform seems to be a terrace at least 34 m in length.
An ancient people of the southwest coast of Arabia, probably localized in the area immediately south of modern Jazan, Saudi Arabia.

Ashby describes a rich archaeological landscape that once included the remains of Roman-period tombs and villas, the latter appointed with mosaics. The modern toponym "Case Rosse" is said to derive from a well-preserved Roman tomb executed in brick that was purposefully destroyed in 1824.

The remains of a Roman villa in the modern Italian municipality of Casignana in Calabria. The site dates to the first through fifth centuries AD and is located near the Mediterranean coast, along the Strada Statale 106 between Bianco and Bovalino.
Mount Kasion or Kasion Oros as described by Herodotus.
The Caspian Sea is a remnant of a larger, inland sea and is now the world's largest enclosed body of water. It has been classified as both a lake and a sea.

A villa in Tibur that has been incorrectly linked to Gaius Cassius Longinus. In the eighteenth century, the site produced a cache of Egyptianizing sculpture that likely dates to the reign of Hadrian and is now held in the Vatican Museums.

Castel Lagopesole was situated along the line of the ancient Roman Via Herculea between Melfi and Potenza in southern Italy. During the eighth through tenth centuries, the site played a strategic role in the region. The castle's construction between 1242 and 1250 is linked to Frederick II. The castle was the meeting place of Pope Innocent II and Abbot Rinaldo of Montecassino during their war again
An important pre-Roman and Gallo-Roman oppidum overlooking the Gardon gorges north of Nimes.
Castell Henllys is an Iron Age hill fort located in north Pembrokeshire, Wales.
A villa and a number of burials located along the Via Laurentina, dating from the fourth century BC to the second century AD.
A Hellenistic fortified site (?oppidum) near Capranica (Viterbo).
A fortified medieval settlement that succeeds the acropolis of ancient Velia.
BAtlas 47 D4 Castellazzo di Palma di Montechiaro
An Iberian town dating between the fifth century B.C. and the third century A.D. It has a quasi-orthogonal plan and cover approximately 1,000 square meters.
A fortified pre-Roman settlement near lacus Plestinus.
A castle of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries located in Celano, the Province of L'Aquila (Abruzzo), Italy.

The "Castello di Decima" is a fortified complex located in the frazione of Castel di Decima. The fortification is located at the tenth mile of the ancient Via Laurentina. The fortification dates to the early Middle Ages. The earliest mention dates to 1081 when there is mention of a "castrum pontis Decimi".

Local tradition holds that the Castello di Lombardia, located at Enna, was established on the site of a fortified acropolis of the Sicani. The castle is located on a mountain top some 970 meters above sea level.) The castle remains that are visible in the present day belong to a construction phase initiated by Ruggero II of Sicily in 1130.

The castle of Montevetrano is a Medieval fortification atop the Montevetrano hill (258 meters above sea level) in the present-day comune of San Cipriano Picentino, Italy. While the origins of the Medieval fortifications lie in the eleventh century, the hill was fortified as early as the third century BCE. In early modern and modern times, the castle was reused on multiple occasions as a defensive

A 14th-century fortification, built on a hill called Monte Raffe, which is located east of the modern Sicilian town of Mussomeli. The hill was previously the site of a long-lived fortified settlement, dating back at least to the early iron age.
The present late fourteenth-century castle on the site is first mentioned in a papal bull of 1206.
A now-ruined castle with Medieval origins occupying the same range of hilltops as ancient Poira.

The ruined castle of Vicalvi is an eleventh-century fortification that remained in use until the sixteenth century. The Medieval fortifications re-use elements of ancient, pre-Roman polygonal masonry architecture that is presumed to date to the fifth or fourth centuries BCE.
Castellu di Cucuruzzu is a Torrean archaeological site in Corsica.
Castellum Aurelianense Antoninianense/Caput Saltus Horreorum Pardalarii
BAtlas 31 C4 Castellum Aurelianense Antoninianense/Caput Saltus Horreorum Pardalarii
Possibly to be identified with modern Bir el Khreba, according to BAtlDir, which also cites EncBerb wherein Bled Bachir ben Yara (douar Malah-Djiadja) is suggested.
Castellum Pucinum was a settlement in the territory of the Carni in Histria.
A building in Pompeii serving as the distribution point of water originating from the Acquedotto Serino, Claudio or Augusteo. The structure is also referred to as Castellum Divisorium.
A Gallo-Roman site located in the Barguelonne valley that covers some 4,000 square meters. Excavation (1962-1964) suggested the site was likely a rural sanctuary that included a theater and baths.
The Castillo de Cote was built toward the end of the 13th century on the orders of Alfonso X.
Castle Dore is a fort located near Fowey in Cornwall that originated in the Iron Age and was re-occupied in the sixth century AD and again during the Middle Ages.

A large villa complex located at Castle Hill, Whitton. This site is considered to be one of the most important villa complexes known in Suffolk. Excavations were conducted in 1929-32, 1946-50 and 1988-9.
Castle an Dinas is an Iron Age hillfort near St. Columb Major in Cornwall, United Kingdom, built during the third and second centuries BC.
The Castle of Serravalle is a twelfth century castle located in Bosa, province of Oristano, Sardinia. It is connected with the Tuscan Malaspina family.
Roman fort and fortlet on the Antonine Wall, Scotland.
Roman fort and vicus in Netherby.

Leveau (1977) discusses the possible location of this Roman fort on the basis of itinerary sources and prior modern scholarship, concluding only that it must have been near the Oued Damous and its mouth. Potter (BAtlDir) echoes this assertion, but ventures to place a hollow symbol on the map at a location in the vicinity of modern Sidi el Kassadi. No archaeological site corresponding to this topon
A site that originated as a Roman castrum and developed into a town from the fifth century onward. Archaeological remains date from the Roman, Byzantine, and Early Muslim periods.
Located on the Caelian Hill, the Castra Peregrina housed Roman soldiers.
Castra Praetorii Mobeni was a Roman fort associated with the Limes Arabicus. Modern Qasr Bshir in Jordan.
Castra Vetera was established as a Roman fort ca. 15 B.C.
A Roman castrum dating to the reign of Trajan located on the Danube, at Turnu-Severin, Romania.
A Latin settlement that became a Roman municipium.
A fortified Iberian settlement in modern Portugal's Santa Maria da Feira municipality.
A multi-period fortified site with occupation stretching from the Bronze Age to the Middle Ages.
An oppidum of the Castro Culture.
A Pre-Roman oppidum located in the modern Spanish province of Asturias.
Castro de La Garmas is a fortified Cantabrian site located in Omoño (Ribamontán al Monte), Spain.
An Iron Age oppidum of the northwestern Iberian peninsula.
A settlement of the Castro Culture covering > 4 hectares near Santai in Spain.
A pre-Roman castrum of Lusitania located in the Vizela river valley.
A settlement dating to the second through fourth centuries.
The remains of a multi-period fortified settlement located in modern Portugal's Porto district, that dates initially from the ninth century BCE.
A Medieval fortification that incorporates and repurposes the Roman mausoleum of Caecilia Metella.
Castrum Novum was a colonia maritima established on the coast of Etruria.
A river of Lucania that flows from the Apennines near Potentia and into the Gulf of Taranto.
An irregular standing stone bearing a fragmentary Latin inscription, the Cat Stane is likely a Neolithic monument re-used for a burial of the fifth or sixth century AD.
A Paleochristian catacomb at the second mile of the via Portuensis. The catacomb is noted for containing the original tombs of Pope Anastasius I and his son Pope Innocent I.
A Christian catacomb located at the tenth mile of the ancient Via Labicana.

The Catacomb of the Nunziatella or the Catacomb of the Annunziatella is an ancient catacomb located in Rome's Ardeatina neighborhood in the via di Grotta Perfetta. The catacomb was excavated on the site of a large Republican-period necropolis and does not seem to have been connected with any Christian martyrs.
Ancient catacombs in the city of Siracusa, built between AD 315 and 360. The main gallery re-purposes parts of an earlier aqueduct.

The catacombs of San Sebastiano located on the Via Appia are located near the church of the same name. These hypogeal tombs emerged in the third century CE and were linked initially to the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul.
A Christian catacomb located on the via Ardeatina.
A Paleochristian catacomb located at the sixth mile of the via Portuense.
A vast Roman catacomb along the Via Appia that began to be used at the close of the second century A.D.
A Christian catacomb located at the fifteenth mile of the Via Appia in use from the late third century A.D. until the Middle Ages.
The Second Cataract (or Great Cataract) was located in Nubia. It is now submerged under Lake Nasser.
Cathedral of the Holy Cross at Aghtamar
Armenian church built on the island of Aghtamar by King Gagik I Artsruni between 915-921 CE.
Cattedrale di Santa Maria di Amiternum
The ruins of the cathedral of the fifth century are located in an area of the archaeological site of Amiternum that was occupied in the second and third centuries CE.
The Caturiges were an ancient Gallic tribe dwelling in and around the valley of the Durance River.

A Roman-era bridge or causeway, possibly known as "Pons Zitha". Various subsequent versions are attested, and there may have been antecedents. All are thought to have been roughly coincident with the modern causeway, although archaeological evidence is meager to non-existent.
Cavallino was an ancient center of the Messapii.

A cave located below Palaiokastro (Navarino, Pylos) that has been identified with the “cave of Nestor”. This site shows human activity from an early date and has been the subject of various instances of archaeological investigation.
An ancient mountain range, attested in Caesar and Strabo, roughly coincident with the modern Cévennes in France, which inherited the name.
Celadussae Inss., a Dalmatian archipelago in the Adriatic Sea.
Celaletae Maiores, an ancient people living at the foot of the Haemus mountain ranges.
Celaletae Minores, an ancient Thracian tribe that settled in the Rhodope mountains.

This place was created for Barrington Atlas map 43 (A2 no. 1) as a collective place representing ancient Etruscan necropoleis associated with the ancient city of Caere. While the Banditaccia necropolis is the largest and perhaps most well-known, this collective place should also include the Sorbo necropolis, the Monte Abatone necropolis, and the Greppe S. Angelo necropolis.
A cemetery cluster associated with three modern villages, treated by the Barrington Atlas as a single symbol on the map.
A burial ground for the the Christian martyrs Gordianus, Epimachus, and Apronianus at the seventh mile of the Via Latina.
The Cenomani were a Celtic people whose territory centered on the valley of the Maine river; Vindinum or Suindinum was their principal center.

The ancient name of this fortified grain-house is known only from a Latin inscription describing its restoration by a governor of Mauretaniae Caesariensis in the mid 290s CE under Diocletain and his tetrarchic colleagues. The inscription's findspot, near a spring in Algeria's Kefrida Pass depression, is close to remains of Roman fortifications noticed by French scholars in the 19th century on eith
A Late Roman fortlet in Tunisia, known today as Ksar Tarcine.

The so-called Cento Camerelle at Bacoli is an archaeological site that dates initially to the late republican period. A multi-story structure with provisions for a water system and cisterns, the building is linked initially to the Roman consul Quintus Hortensius Hortalus and later to Antonia Minor, the mother of the emperor Claudius.
A bath complex (IX, 4, 5-18) located at the intersection of the Via Stabiana and Via di Nola that was built following the earthquake of AD 62.
A public bath complex at Herculaneum, dating to the first century A.D. It was subdivided into "male" and "female" sectors.
The Villa dei Centroni, located on the modern via Anagnina, lay at the ninth mile of the ancient via Latina. It dates from the first century B.C. onward.
An ancient Roman camp, located near the modern Romanian town of Surducu Mare.
The Cerbani were an Arabian tribe mentioned by Pliny the Elder.
A now-unlocated place near Florentia in Etruria (Regio VII) known from epigraphic sources. Caius Caesar, the father of Iulius Caesar, helmed a veterans' colony there.
A group of islands lying off the east coast of Tunisia in the Gulf of Gabès, the islands were a place of exile in Roman antiquity.
The Roman temple dedicated to Ceres and Faustina received patronage from Herodes Atticus. Its remains were eventually repurposed in the construction of the church of Sant'Urbano.
A settlement of the Marsi and a Roman road station on the Via Valeria.
A Samnite temple dedicated to Flora.
The Cerro de las Cabezas is an archaeological site located approx. 8 km south of  Valdepeñas, in the province of Ciudad Real, Spain.
A ruined Roman mausoleum on the grounds of the Caffarella regional park. The so-called Cessati Spiriti mausoleum was once clad in travertine.
Vicus on the Meuse river along the road from Noviomagus to Atua(tu)ca.
Chabala was the ancient capital of the Caucasian Albania from as early as the fourth century BC.
A fortified settlement site with evidence of occupation in the Kushan (first–fourth century CE) and the Pre-Mongol Islamic (tenth-thirteenth century) periods.
A city at the mouth of the Axius river.
Augustus uses the generic term Chalcidicum to describe a porch he built as an approach to the Curia Iulia.
The Chalybes or Chaldoi were an ancient people inhabiting Pontus and Cappadocia in Asia Minor.
A sanctuary located at the boundary of the civitas of the Suessiones and that of the Silvanectes.
Mentioned by Pausanias, this mountain is securely identified with the modern Megavouni (Greece).
Chapel for the Sacred Barque of Amun-Ra in Karnak, established by the Egyptian pharaoh Hakor of the Twenty-ninth dynasty who reigned from 392/1 to 379/8 BCE.
Ptolemy places the "headland of Charidemos" on the southern coast of the Iberian peninsula between Abdera and Barea. Scholars have identified it as the modern Cabo de Gata.
Charybdis was a sea monster that was rationalized in the form of a whirlpool located in the Strait of Messina.
An ancient deme of Athens, possibly to be localized at modern Fyli (formerly Chasia).
The Chauci were a German tribe occupying the territory between the Ems and Elbe rivers.
A Roman road linking Lutetia and Rotomagus, the construction of which was begun by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa. The modern French Route nationale 14 follows the course of the ancient road.
An archaeological site located in the Zeydun plain south of the provincial city of Behbahan, Iran.

A group of islands located off Cape Gelidonya on the south coast of Anatolia, modern Beşadalar (Five Islands), Turkey. Ancient commentators vary on the number of islands in the group, some counting only the largest two.

The Kastro Chelmou was a medieval castle, built probably in the 13th century of the modern era inside the ancient Athenaion fortress in Arcadia. It is located on the hill of Agios Konstantinos, southeast of the modern town of Skortsino.
A settlement of ancient Egypt, modern Kasr el-Saijad.
An archaeological site near Aubigné-Racan in western France.
The promontory now known as Capo Teulada.

A major city of the Khitan People of Mongolia. The city was built in 1004, but has layers from before this period and up to the 16th-17th centuries. It was built on the site of an earlier settlement, Kedun.
A small archipelago composed of two islands - San Pietro and San Paolo - in the Gulf of Taranto.
An ancient settlement, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today
The Choragic Monument of Lysicrates is a round structure erected in 335/4 BC in Athens to honor the victory of a choregos in a dramatic competition.

A desert monastery, founded in the fifth century CE, which was located where the 19th-century Greek Orthodox monastery of Deir Mar Jirys now stands on the north cliffs above the Wadi Qelt/Kelt in the West Bank, nearly 5km west from the center of modern Jericho.
Church adapted from a private house building in Dura-Europos.
A river of central Sicily: the modern Fiume Dittaino.

According to Cicero, the shrine of Chrysas (the god shares a name with the nearby river) was located along the road from Assorus to Henna. A cult image in marble, described as being "beautiful", was to be found there and was ultimately spared from the depredations of Caius Verres.
An ancient river that flowed into the Black Sea. It is probably to be identified with the modern Kelasuri in Georgia.
Chrysoun Oros is the highest mountain on the island of Corsica.

The ancient Chulcul river has been tentatively identified by scholars with the modern Oued Bou Zenna/Oued Zouara in Tunisia. This river and its environs were largely inundated by the construction of the Sidi El Barrak dam in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Ruins of a church likely built around the fifth century AD, on the summit of the low hill of Sidi Khiribech in Berenike. The character of the building and its position has suggested to some archaeologists a defensive as well as a religious purpose.
Church of Saint Alexander Nevsky, Jerusalem
The nineteenth century Russian Orthodox church preserves within it remains of Constantine's original fourth century church of the Holy Sepulchre.
A seventh century AD church dedicated to the patron saint of Thessalonica; the present basilica stands on the site of a precursor with phases beginning in the fourth century AD.
Church of Saint Martin at Moissac
A Christian church built, at least in part, atop the ruins of a Gallo-Roman building that include a hypocaust.

A church in Athens, excavated and demolished between 1859 and 1861, which was built on top of a section of the post-Herulian wall incorporating several hundred inscriptions and sculptures, mostly from the Diogeneion gymnasium.
A twelfth-century AD Christian church was built atop the remains of the Roman temple of Apollo.

The church of the Annunziatella is a Catholic church located in Rome's Ardeatino district. It is situated between the via Ardeatina and via di Grotta Perfetta. The church was established in the thirteenth century, as an inscription of Pope Honorius III attests.
Church of the Archangels at Sige

Church in the village of Sige (modern Kumyaka) on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara. Constructed under Constantine VI in 780, the structure was restored twice, in 1448 and 1819. It remained in continuous use until it was ultimately abandoned in 1922.
Church of the Holy Apostles at Constantinople

Construction of a church dedicated to the Twelve Apostles at Constantinople began in 330 CE under Constantine the Great, and was completed during the reign of his son Constantius II (331-367). A larger church was established on the same site in 550 by Justinian I. The church was demolished by Mehmed II in 1462, and the Fatih Mosque was constructed on its site.

A church that many claim marks the birthplace of Jesus Christ is located in Bethlehem, now in the State of Palestine in the West Bank. The original church built on the site was commissioned by Constantine I and dedicated in May 339 CE. The church was destroyed by fire, likely in 529, and replaced by Justinian I.
Chysauster Ancient Village is an Iron Age settlement comprised of stone-walled homesteads known as 'courtyard houses'.
Cidamus (modern Ghadamès, Libya) became allied to Rome after Lucius Cornelius Balbus prevailed against the Garamantes in 19 BC.
A plain that abuts the plain of the Cayster river. Strabo remarks that it is fertile.
Cilpe/*Lacilbula? was an Ibero-Roman settlement in Baetica.
A Germanic tribe that made war against the Roman Republic between 113 and 101 BC.
A major Roman necropolis and catacomb along the Via Nomentana.
A strait between the modern Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
A settlement of the Vestini, now unlocated, that, according to Livy, Iunius Brutus captured in 325 B.C.
Pliny the Elder classifies the Cinithii as an indigenous community (civitas) that could be considered among the nationes.
A Roman limes fortress located in Mesopotamia, along the Khabur river, near the point where it flows into the Euphrates.
Fortification wall surrounding the sanctuary of Apollo at Thermon
The Roman circus of Tarragona dates from the reign of Domitian. The circus measures ca. 325 meters in length and ca. 100 to 115 meters in width.
The Circus of Maxentius is part of a complex of buildings built by emperor Maxentius on the Via Appia between A.D. 306 and 312.
The capital city of the ancient Berber Kingdom of Numidia.

Cissbury Ring is an Iron Age hillfort located north of Worthing in West Sussex, England, and is the second largest hillfort in England. The hillfort, surrounded by earthworks, covers about 24 ha. It was likely abandoned by 50 CE.

A section of the ancient city wall of Salamis, dating to the fourth century BCE, has been excavated protruding from the north shore of Ampelaki Bay, where it was partly built into an early modern jettty.
The Cividade de Bagunte is a fortified Iron Age site that became Romanized. It is located in the municipality of Vila do Conde in the Porto district of Portugal.
A settlement of the Castro culture founded ca. 900 BC.

The Civil Basilica at Aphrodisias was a three-aisled public hall measuring approximately 145 by 30 meters. It opened off the southwest corner of the South Agora. It dates to the late first century CE.

The Civita Giuliana is located in the northern suburbium of Pompeii, about 700 meters from the city walls. Thus far the site has produced archaeological evidence of suburban villas in Pompeii's hinterland. Early twentieth-century excavations were carried out here, only to be published in 1994. Clandestine looting at the site brought about a cooperative effort to resume excavations in the interests
Clanis fl. (Chiana river) is a river of central Italy that flows into the Tiber river.
A river of Campania that likely flowed into the Tyrrhenian Sea near Liternum.

A road station listed in the Antonine Itineraries on the Agedincum → Augustobona road. It is perhaps to be localized in the modern French commune of Paisy-Cosdon (Aube department), where ceramic fragments of Gallo-Roman date and associated stone architectural elements were identified in a construction excavation in the 20th century.

Listed on the Peutinger map, Clarenna has been identified by modern scholars with a Flavian-era military post near modern Donnstetten in Germany. It continued as a civilian settlement into at least the third century CE.

Distyle in antis temple of the fourth century BCE, built from the salvage of the large archaic temple, likely destroyed in the earthquake of 373 BCE. This temple remained in use until the first or second centuries CE.
A mansio listed in the ItBurd. BAtlas follows Hammond 1974 in placing it in the vicinity of modern Urakë in Albania. Bitrakova-Grozdanova 1994 would place it at modern Radožda in Macedonia.

A Roman rural tribe that was one of the most ancient of Rome's gentes. The gens Claudia traced its history to the earliest days of the Roman Republic. Appius Claudius Sabinus Regillensis, in 495 B.C., was the first of its members to hold the consulship.

The so-called Clausura Bir Oum Ali is part of a defensive barrier that formed part of the Limes Numidiae of the ancient Roman empire. This system of military outposts and fortifications closed off the Roman province of Africa Proconsularis to the south.
A Late Roman villa and necropolis located at modern Imola in Italy.

The Oropos Amphiareion clepsydra is a hydraulic inflow clock serving the Sanctuary of Amphiaraus. Situated on the southeast bank of the sacred spring of Amphiaraus, this inflow hydraulic clock dates to the 4th century BCE.
A major river and tributary of the Po River of northern Italy.
The principal road leading to the Capitolium and the Arx in the city of Rome.
A street that ascended from the depression between the Palatine and the Caelian hills.
Cicero describes the villa of Publius Clodius Pulcher as being located at the thirteenth mile of the Via Appia near Bovillae.
Clostra (Romana) was a place in Latium along the Via Severiana. It was located 15 miles from Circei and 9 miles from Astura.
The River Clyde, the eighth-longest river in the United Kingdom, flows into the Firth of Clyde.
Co(n)silinum/Cosilianum was a statio on the Via Popilia (Annia) in ancient Calabria.
Coastal Tower 16b, part of the Hadrian's Wall Coastal defences
A pre-Roman tribe that settled in what today is southwestern France, to the north of the river Adour. They were bounded by the Tarbelli to the south and the Boiates to the north.
A Pre-Roman Iberian oppidum located in the region of Bages.
An ancient Iberian settlement in southeastern Spain, located near Jumilla.

Survey and excavation at Montelabate overlooking the upper Tiber valley in the territory of Perugia have revealed evidence for an Etruscan settlement on the hill of Col di Marzo (Perugia). This place is located some 10 km from Arna and rises to 645 meters above sea level.
Probably to be associated with a complex of Roman forts at modern day Camelon, just to the north of the Antonine Wall.
A courtyard building of a non-military nature dating to the later Roman period (second to third century CE) was located on the seafront at modern Barry (Wales, United Kingdom).

The remains of a Romano-British villa with at least 12 rooms were first uncovered via ploughing in 1838 on a tract of land called "The Allotment" near Colerne, Wiltshire, England. Excavations took place in 1854. Fragments of an inscribed mosaic reading either "Servivs" or "Severvs" were documented at the site.

Excavations in the late 1970s revealed evidence for a multi-phase sanctuary. The Iron Age site was of circular plan, while the Romano-British site, of two phases, consisted of a walled enclosure with two shrines.
Colle Madore is an archaeological site connected with the Sicanians.
A hilltop villa near Tifernum Tiberinum commonly associated with one of the villas of Pliny the Younger.
Colle Rotondo was the site of a prehistoric settlement inhabited from the Bronze Age until the early Iron Age.
A Pre-Roman fortified center in the territory of Frosinone.
Colle Vitriano is the site of a Roman villa supported on two artificial terraces that utilize megalithic walling in the polygonal masonry technique as well as caementicium.
The so-called College of the Augustales at Herculaneum was built at the end of the first century BC. The brothers A. Lucius Proculus and A. Lucius Iulianus served as patrons of the project.
A building that has been identified as the seat of a Collegium because of its internal structure and size, was previously known as the"House of the Exedra".
Sixteen columns in the Corinthian order that once belonged to a Roman temple were relocated to the square adjacent to the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Milan.
The remains of a Roman temple of the first century CE.
A port city founded by Aeolian settlers at the mouth of the River Avci.
The so-called Columbarium of Constantine is a second-century tomb that was later repurposed as a mill.
A columbarium was discovered by chance in the Via di Pietralata in Rome in 2012.

The Columnae Herculis (Pillars of Hercules) are the twin promontories that flank the Straits of Gibraltar, namely the rock of Gibraltar on the northern side and a debated southern promontory, likely either Monte Hacho (the ancient Abila Mons) or the Jebel Musa.
BAtlas 65 D3 Comama/Col. Iulia Augusta Prima Fida
The site of a Romano-British villa of the winged corridor type, probably late 3rd century CE in date.
Combretovium is a 60-hectare open settlement that was occupied from the late Iron Age and Claudian periods through to the middle of the fourth century CE.
The Commercial Market or Tetragonos Agora was one of the main squares of ancient Ephesus.
This stoa was built against a fourth century BCE seawall sometime in the Hellenistic era. The seawall shows evidence of later Roman repairs.
A Roman road station, attested in ancient sources. It is probably to be localized in the modern commune of Cognac (Charente)
A fort and associated vicus on Hadrian's Wall.
An ancient settlement, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today
The Condrusi were a Germanic tribe of ancient Belgium.
A Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall, cited: BAtlas 9 D6 ‘Congavata’
A Spanish village located in the north of the province of Sevilla that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.
The Convenae were a tribe of Aquitania whose territory lay on the north side of the Pyrenees.
Coombe Hill in East Sussex is the site of a Neolithic causeway enclosure built ca. 3200 B.C.
Now drained, Lake Copais was a lake located in the center of Boeotia to the west of Thebes.
A Celtic tribe of Galicia whose territory was located south of Noega; described by the elder Pliny and Ptolemy.
A Latin center in the Monti Lepini that was already a Roman municipium by 211 B.C.

Now unlocated, Corbio was the chief settlement of the Suessetani. Livy discusses Corbio in the course of describing the campaigns of Aulus Ternentius Varro and Publius Sempronius Longo in 184 BCE. Varro captured Corbio, lying north of the River Ebro, in Hispania Citerior. Livy uses the Latin term "oppidum" to describe Corbio.
A Roman fort probably to be equated with the site at present-day Castledykes.
Corent was the site of a Celtic and Gallo-Roman oppidum.

The Corinth Canal cuts across the Isthmus of Corinth, connecting the Gulf of Corinth to the Saronic Gulf and the Aegean Sea. Several abortive attempts in antiquity were made at creating the canal, although its final (and functional) realization occurred in modernity.

The origins of the theater at Corinth lie in the fifth century B.C. The complex was further expanded during the Hellenistic period. An elaborate renovation during the reign of Hadrian further improved the complex and added a new orchestra and scaenae frons.
The Cornacates were a Celtic tribe that migrated to Pannonia in Illyria.

The Roman dam at Cornalvo is a gravity dam with associated reservoir and aqueduct. It dates to the first or second century AD. The earthen dam and its stone cladding remain in use. The site is a part of the Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
An ancient settlement of Boeotia, located about 4 km north of the modern Greek city that now bears its name.
A Gallo-Roman site located near the junction of the Saône and Coney rivers.
The Corsi were an ancient tribe occupying a region of ancient Sardinia that is now known as Gallura.
Settlement on the northern shore of Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland containing the inundated remains of a Bronze Age village, inhabited ca. 1010-955 BC.
A Spanish village located in the north of the province of Huelva that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.
Corycus was an ancient city in Cilicia Trachaea.
The ancient station of Cosa lay along the road from Toulouse to Cahors near the Aveyron river. It was a significant site from the time of Augustus onward.
A site with votive activity from the Archaic period and a later Roman house in addition to the basalt-paved Roman road.
An ancient castle, located in modern Syria. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006 as part of the "Crac des Chevaliers and Qal’at Salah El-Din" listing.
Crathis/Crater fl., now the Crati, is a river in Bruttium in southern Italy.
Site of a small Roman fort between Castledykes and Tassiesholm. The fort was discovered in 1938 and excavated in 1961-66.
The hill in the province of Trapani known as Cresta di Gallo has evidence for Bronze Age occupation in the form of a necropolis that is linked with the nearby site of Mokarta.
The Sea of Crete is the sea located south of the Aegean Sea, north of the island Crete, and south of the Cyclades islands.
Modern day site of a Romano-British settlement in Wiltshire dating from first to fourth centuries A.D.
Fourth-century B.C.E. fortifications located in the Croccia Cognato forest near Oliveto Lucano in Lucania, south Italy.
A major necropolis of Volsinii that reaches its maximum extent between 550 and 450 BC. The necropolis is especially noteworthy on account of its orthogonal layout.
The river known today as the Creuse.

A square sacred enclosure in the northwest corner of the Agora, in front of the Stoa Basileios at the meeting point of the west road and the Panathenaic Way. It was built ca. 430 BC around a sacred rock. It was gradually obscured by the rising ground levels and built over in the 3rd century AD.
Roman ruins were discovered on the shores of Lake Balaton.
A Phoenician port of southeastern Sardinia.
A nuragic site near Cagliari, Sardinia.
Road and postal station on the Roman road Virunum-Iuvavum, which is recorded in the Tabula Peutingeriana.
Cabo de Santa Maria is the southernmost point of mainland Portugal.
The modern archipelago of Maddalena off northern Sardinia is comprised of seven main islands and numerous other small islets.
Construction of the Curia Julia was begun by Julius Caesar and completed by Augustus in 29 BCE. It replaced the former senate house, the Curia Hostilia.
A large island in the Adriatic Sea.
A station located along the course of the Danube River in Lower Pannonia between Acumincum (Stari Slankamen) and Malata-Bononia.
A lake located near ancient Reate.
An island group in the Aegean Sea composed of over 200 islands.
The Cyclopean Bridge of Agios Ioannis is located one kilometer south of the citadel of Mycenae.
Daesitiates were a tribe of ancient Illyria.
A Bronze Age settlement mound located in the Akhisar District of Turkey.

Dal'verzin tepe is an archaeological site located in Uzbekistan. The site is located near the Surkhan­darya River, approximately 60 km northeast of Termez. The settlement has its origins as a Greco-Bactrian town that developed into a larger, fortified settlement.
The third tell near Dalma, Iran, that remains unexcavated.
An unexcavated Bronze Age site located in the modern Chahar Burjak District of Afghanistan's Nimruz province.

Sited at an ancient crossing-point over the river Jordan, between Neapolis and Philadelpheia, a Roman-era bridge is thought to have been one of many. The modern bridge and its antecedents are often referred to as the "Damia Bridge".

An Iranian people of ancient Central Asia, the Daoi/Dahae were composed of a confederation of three tribes – the Parni, Xanthii, and Pissuri. These peoples occupied an area that corresponds with much of modern Turkmenistan.

The current Daphni Monastery in Attica dates to the eleventh century, yet its earlier Christian phases belong to the sixth century AD when a Christian site grew atop the abandoned and destroyed sanctuary of Apollo Daphnaios.
A coastal villa known especially for its polychrome gladiatorial mosaics was excavated at Dar Buk-Ammarah, located on the coast some 4.5 km to the north of Zliten, Libya.

Darenth Court Roman villa numbered among the largest Roman villas in Britain. This courtyard villa included numerous components, among them a bath complex. The villa measured ca. 370 by 414 feet upon excavations in 1894 and 1895. An assemblage of Roman coins (53 in number) range in date from Domitian to Gratian.
An ancient settlement, listed by Ptolemy in Paropamisadai. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
A fortress in Armenia Minor on the river Euphrates, some 75 Roman miles from Zimara.
An island of the Cyclades that is now uninhabited. The Cambridge Keros Project identified a large Bronze Age settlement on the island.
Also called "Aphnitis Limne" in antiquity, according to Strabo. Modern Lake Kuş/Lake Manyas in Turkey.

Strabo describes the Debai of southwestern Arabia as a semi-Nomadic people. He notes that they live in a land that is rich in resources (like gold) for which these people have no use. This description is part of his narrative of "primitive" peoples at the margins of the Roman world.
Decastadium?, a Roman road station that possibly corresponds to Melito di Porto Salvo in Calabria, Italy.
A Pre-Roman Celtic tribe of Wales whose territory was located in what is now north-east Wales and parts of Cheshire, England.
Deciana is an important pass through the Pyrenees. The ancient Roman Via Augusta passes through Deciana.

The remains of a stone, arched Roman bridge at Decimomannu, to the west of Assemini, Sardinia. Three of the original six arches survive today. The bridge may originally have been as much as 160 meters in length. R.J. Rowland considered it to be of Iulio-Claudian date.

Late Antique rural settlement located in Gaziantep Province, Turkey, less than 2km southeast of the tell at Tilbaşar Kalesi. Salvage excavations were carried out on the site in 2016-2018 prior to the construction of the Doğanpınar Dam.

A Roman fort in the Ghozza district of the Egyptian Eastern Desert, located in the Deir el-Atrash wadi along an ancient route between Kaine (modern Qena) and the quarries at Mons Porphyrites (modern Gebel Dokhan).
Deir el-Bahari is a complex of mortuary temples and tombs that constitute a part of the Theban necropolis located on the west bank of the Nile river, opposite Luxor.
The workers' village of the artisans who worked on the New Kingdom tombs in the Valley of the Kings.
A monastery located in the modern Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, likely founded in the 6th century CE. The ancient church and some of its early decorative program survive.
Deiradiotai?, an Attic deme of the tribe Leontis.
A lake located to the north of Byzantium, now called Derkoz Gölü (Turkey).
Delminium was an ancient city of Illyria and a capital of the Dalmatae.

Recent geophysical investigation and analysis have led to a new reconstruction of the main harbor of Delos ca. 100 BCE that identifies a shallow-draft (1-2m) harbor with broad beach area significantly different from the modern situation. Infill of wetland areas for construction in antiquity, combined with contemporary and subsequent sea level rise, dredging, and modern interventions have all contr
An ancient settlement located on the west bank of the Bosporus, just opposite Chrysopolis.
An ancient settlement and fortress on the island on Chios, mentioned in Thucydides.
An ancient settlement of Attica on the Euboean Gulf. At modern Kamaraki in Greece.
The Hellenistic- and Roman-period sanctuary of Apollo Delphinios is located northeast of the North Market at Miletos.
A round defensive tower located to the east of the Dema Wall in Attica.
The so-called Dema wall was a built fortification of ancient Attica that was intended to a close a gap between between Aigaleos and Parnes. The wall's course originally ran more than 4 km.
An Iron Age Celtic people who inhabited modern Pembrokeshire and Carmarthenshire in south-west Wales.

A temple complex at Aegae-Yuntdağı, associated with the cult of Demeter and Kore based on epigraphic evidence, may also have been sacred to other divinities. The site is located to the west of the Scaenae frons of the theater complex.
A gate in the Themistoklean city wall of Athens, located on the northwest slope of the Hill of the Nymphs.
An ancient Settlement located in Eskişehir Province, Turkey.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: upper Struma BUL.
The River Dee flows from the Cairngorms to the North Sea at Aberdeen.
A Roman fort at present-day Papcastle, cited: BAtlas 9 D6 Derventio
A river of modern Yorkshire, known today as the Derwent (one of several rivers so-named in the UK).
An ancient settlement, modern Debelt in Bulgaria.
Deva or Deva Victrix (modern Chester) was a legionary base in Britannia. It was originally founded by the Legio II Adiutrix in the AD 70s and completed by the Legio XX Valeria Victrix.

This river, known by various names in antiquity, was an upstream tributary (via the Karun river) of the final stage of ancient Tigris/Pastigiris, ultimately debouching into the Persian Gulf. Today its waters still join the Karun. The modern course of the Dez lies within the modern country of Iran.

Değirmenköy is a modern Turkish settlement with an Urartian fortress situated nearby. Here, a cylindrical stone with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua, son of Išpuini (9th / 8th century BCE) has been found mentioning a "barzudibiduni building of Minua" (CTU A 5-64).
A Bronze Age necropolis located near the village of 'Ayn Samiyah in the West Bank.
Modern name of a seventh-century Pallava cave temple in Mahābalipuram.
Modern name of a seventh-century Pallava rock-cut temple in Mahābalipuram.
An island near Sardinia recorded by Ptolemy and Stephanus. It is possibly to be identified with the modern Isola Piana.
A small island group off the west coast of Syme.
Diana Veteranorum was a vicus in Numidia founded for veterans of Legio III Augusta. It became a municipium in A.D. 162.
The Greater Liakhvi River, a tributary of the Kura River in the South Ossetia region of the Republic of Georgia.
The ancient sanctuary of Apollo near Miletos (modern Didim, Turkey).
An ancient group of islands, identified by scholars with the modern Diliktaş Adaları in the Gulf of Fethiye on Turkey's southern coast.
A river in eastern Crete, probably to be associated with the modern Sitianos/Stomios, which is known today primarily as the Pentelis Rema and which empties into the Mediterranean Sea at Sitia.
A stream in the ager Sabinus.

Dikili Tash is a prehistoric tell in eastern Macedonia, approximately 1.5 km east of ancient Philippi. The site has been excavated by the École française d’Athènes in stages since 1920. Neolithic and Bronze Age deposits have been investigated.
A sanctuary located at Menies bay in Chania, Crete, with remains ranging in date from Hellenistic period to Late Antiquity.
20th century BCE Dilmun temple on the highest part of the ancient settlement mound at Saar in modern Bahrain.
Din Lligwy is the site of a prehistoric village near the east coast of Anglesey in Wales.
The highest point on Kapu Dagh.
The modern Arayit (Günüzü) Dağı in Turkey, below the western slopes of which lay ancient Pessinous (modern Ballıhisar).
The whirlpool Dine, located in the Argolic Gulf, is discussed by Pausanias in a discussion of the flow of water in the Argolid.
A small frontier settlement dated to the Neo-Asssyrian period, located in the Peshdar Plain near the banks of the Lesser Zab River.

The site of Dinkha Tepe is located in the Ushnu valley of Iranian Azerbaijan. Sir Aurel Stein initially identified second-millennium BCE funereal deposits there. The University of Pennsylvania Museum, under Robert H. Dyson, jr. and Oscar White Muscarella, carried out further excavations in the late 1960s.
An Adriatic archipelago north of Mons Garganus. Modern Isole Tremiti.
Diomeia was a deme of Attica, and it was located both within and outside the walls of Themistocles at Athens. The deme was named after the hero Diomos, a son of Kollytos.
An island grouping off the north coast of Crete, opposite Siteia. Known today also as the Yanisades Islands.
The Divi or Diveni were the ancient inhabitants of the Lakshadweep or Laccadive Islands, an archipelago located off the western coast of the Indian subcontinent.

A porticus constructed by Domitian in A.D. 80 on the eastern Campus Martius on the site of the Villa Publica, whose northern entry—a triumphal arch—was flanked by two small temples in honor of Titus and Vespasian.
An elite tomb structure constructed in the late 4th to early 3rd century BCE near the Hellenistic settlement of Callatis.
Dolichiste Ins. (Kekova) is a small island of Ionia.

A megalithic stone circle dating to the third millennium BCE located in Peraleda de la Mata in eastern Extremadura, Spain. The monument is usually submerged beneath the waters of the Embalse de Valdecañas, a reservoir of the Tagus river.
"The Dolmen of the four Maols" is a cist and dolmen tomb in County Mayo, Ireland.
A sprawling palace complex begun by Nero after A.D. 64 that aimed to connect the Esquiline, Caelian, and Palatine hills.

The house of Lucius Fabius Cilo, praefectus urbi in 203, consul in 193 and 204, and a close friend of the emperor Septimius Severus. The house was a gift of the Severans and appears on the Severan marble plan. Its site is now occupied by the basilica of Santa Balbina on the "little Aventine".
Domus and Mitreo delle Pareti Dipinte

The complex known as "Domus and Mitreo delle Pareti Dipinte" began its life in the later second century BCE and was remodeled during the time of Augustus. A mithraeum is built in the northwest part of the building in the later second century CE.
The so-called Domus dei Coiedii is a domus located at Suasa. It dates to the first century B.C.
The so-called House of A. Octavius Primus was excavated in 1859 and again in 1872.
A well-appointed domus of the first century CE located on the Molinete hill in Cartagena, Spain.
A Roman domus traditionally associated with Vespasia Polla, mother of the emperor Vespasian.
The so-called "Domus of the figurative emblem" is a well-appointed domus at Privernum.
A ruined Roman townhouse located on the boundary between Mdina and Rabat, Malta that was discovered in 1881. It dates to the first century B.C.
Dorchester-on-Thames was the site of a Roman vicus, although its name is no longer known.
A fortified hilltop settlement overlooking the Soulima Valley in northern Messenia. Dorion appears in the Catalogue of Ships in Homer's Iliad.
An ancient Thracian settlement, located west of the Hebrus river.
A Neolithic cursus monument spanning some 10 km of Cranborne Chase in east Dorset, United Kingdom.

Dragoncello is a modern district of Rome's metropolitan area where archaeological evidence for a series of late republican villas was uncovered. At least four in number, these villa rustica sites have evidence for domestic production.
Drapsaka (modern Kunduz) was an ancient settlement in central Asia.
The Draus or Dravus River, now the present-day Drava River, flows through Italy, Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, and Hungary.
An ancient cemetery at modern Drepano in Greece, uncovered in rescue excavations since the 1970s.
A peninsula and associated islet that extends south-southeastward on the same axis as the Gebel Zeit in modern Egypt's Red Sea Governorate, separating Zeit Bay from the Gulf of Suez.
Called the Durance (French), a tributary of the Rhone.
The Drôme river, a tributary of the Rhône.
Drusiana Fossa was a canal constructed by Nero Claudius Drusus ca. 12 BC in order to connect the Rhine delta with Lake Flevo.
The ancient Dubis is the modern Doubs river.
A Mithraeum near Duino, in the province of Trieste, north-eastern Italy, that is located within a natural cave.
A road station, possibly located at or en route to modern al-Ǧauf in Saudi Arabia, that epigraphic evidence from another location indicates was garrisoned by Roman soldiers during the Severan period.

In several rooms of the Red House, located in the central part of the lower town of Dur-Katlimmu, an archive of ca. 150 clay tablets inscribed in Assyrian cuneiform and ca. 50 tablets inscribed in Aramaic alphabetic script, along with many more small fragments, was discovered. The texts found at in the Red House date between 828 and 600 BC, after the fall of the Assyrian Empire. Many of the texts
A place on the Tigris River mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus.
The Duranius or Duranus, the modern Dordogne, is a river of Aquitania that flows into the Atlantic Ocean.
Duria (Bautica) fl. (Dora Baltea) is a river of northern Italy that is a tributary of the Padus fl. (Po river).
One of two tributaries of the Po river named Duria, the modern Dora Riparia.
Durnomagus (modern Dormagen) was a Roman settlement along the frontier (limes) in Germania Inferior. It was first occupied by Legio I Germanica.
Durocobrivis (Dunstable) was a Romano-British station along Watling Street.
Durocornovium (Wanborough, Wiltshire) was a vicus on the Ermine Street.
The site of a Romano-British Settlement is located at Little London, Chigwell. The site is located above the flood plain of the River Roding.
Dushanbe is the capital and largest city of Tajikistan. In antiquity, the settlement was part of the Graeco-Bactrian kingdom.
A Chalcolithic necropolis located in Antequera, province of Málaga, Andalusia, Spain. The Antequera Dolmens Site was enrolled as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
An ancient ceremonial site located in County Kildare, Ireland. The circular enclosure once covered ca. 13 ha.
A prehistoric fort in the Aran Islands of County Galway, Ireland, dating ca. 1100 BC.
A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources that is identified with modern Anaz Höyük.
Partially excavated military barracks reworked from private houses in Block E5 at Dura-Europos.
Unexcavated military barracks reworked from private houses in Block E6 at Dura-Europos.

When Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud) became the principal administrative center of the Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC, king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) built (or rebuilt) numerous temples. One of those was dedicated to the god Ea and the goddess Damkina. Although its location is not known, the Ea-Damkina temple at Kalhu is thought to have been situated within the Ninurta temple

A building in the southeastern corner of the Athenian Agora, built in the mid-second century BC as the eastern side of the South Square complex and its main entrance from the Panathenaic Way. It was destroyed in the Sullan Sack of 86 BC, but repaired in the Imperial Period.
The temple of the god Šamaš at Sippar. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ebabbar means "Shining House."
The Eburones were an ancient people of Gallia Belgica.
The Gallic tribe known as the Eburovices was a branch of the Aulerci.
Eburum (modern Eboli) was an ancient Lucanian settlement.
The Ecdinii were an Alpine tribe. They are mentioned both on the inscription of the Tropaeum Augusti and on the Arch of Augustus at Susa.
A Galatian settlement founded on the road from Ancyra to Tavium; a statio on the Tabula Peutingeriana.
Edin's Hall Broch, also known as Odin's Hall Broch, is a second-century AD broch near Duns in Scotland. The function of the broch, a drystone roundhouse structure, is a matter of some debate.
A Thracian people dwelling in the lower basin of the Strymon river.
The ziggurat of the god Šamaš at Larsa. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eduranna means "House, Bond of Heaven."

The dais of the Igīgū gods, Edurkuga (“House, Pure Abode”), was located in the TE.E (read as either Tê or Kisīri) district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of two daises in that part of Babylon.

From the classical period onward, a complex of moles and fortifications at the mouth of the Piraeus harbor. Hellenistic fortifications are the most obvious component of the visible archaeological assemblage today.
A Hittite sacred spring located 80 km west of Konya, Turkey.
The temple of the goddess Gula (as Ninisinna) at Isin. The Sumerian ceremonial name Egalmah means "Exalted Palace."
The Giparu-House at Ur was the temple of the high-priestess of the moon-god.
An ancient settlement on the east coast of the Red Sea at modern al‑Wajh (Saudi Arabia).
The temple of the god Sîn at Harran. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ehulhul means "House which Gives Joy."
The temple of the god Lugal-Marda at Marad. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eigikalamma means "House, Eye of the Land."
