A peak sanctuary on the Kounados hill of Paros, where sacred activity, including votives, indicates venerations of Zeus Hypatos along with Eileithyaia and Aphrodite.
The Cave of Eileithyia outside Heraklion on Crete is an ancient sanctuary sacred to the goddess of childbirth. The shrine was active during Neolithic, Minoan, and Mycenaean phases.
A city of southeast Boeotia mentioned by Homer.
An Eretrian colony located at the mouth of the Strymon river.

The dais of the Anunnakū gods, Ekagula (“House, Big Gate”), was located in the TE.E (read as either Tê or Kisīri) district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of two daises in that part of Babylon.
The temple of the god Ea within the Esagil(a) complex at Babylon. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ekarzagina means "Pure Quay"or "Quay of Lapis Lazuli."
The temple of the goddess Aya at Sippar. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ekinu means "House, Bed-Chamber."
The monumental central staircase in the agora of Morgantina has been identified as the Ekklesiasterion. They date after the middle of the third century B.C.
A building complex located in the city's agora, the Ekklesiasterion/Theater is dated ca. 625-300 B.C.
The temple of the god Bunene at Sippar. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ekurra means "House of the Mountains."
A barrel-vaulted cistern complex located to the immediate north of Tubusuctu that could hold nearly 12,000 cubic meters of water. It was fed by the so-called "Western Aqueduct" of Tubusuctu.
A celtiberian settlement located just south of modern Berrueco in Spain's Zaragoza province.

An aqueduct tunnel, near Saldae, sometimes referred to as the Nonius Datus tunnel. It was a component of a Roman aqueduct that delivered water from the area of modern Toudja to Saldae (modern Bejaia in Algeria's Kabylia province). The tunnel's modern name derives from the nearby village of El Habel, which is located just north of Meccuc in the municipal district of Bejaia.
A fortified, pre-Roman oppidum located to the north of modern Camporrobles in Spain's Valencia region.
Evidence of Roman-era settlement has been uncovered at modern El Poyo in the Calamocha municipality of Teurel province, Aragon, Spain.
Bronze Age fortified site located on the Euphrates in Syria.

Ptolemy places this cape on the east coast of the island of Cyprus, enumerating it between the ancient city of Salamis and the Kleides promontory at the terminus of the island's distinctive northeast peninsula.
Elaious was the southernmost town of the Thracian Chersonese.
Structure in the the necropolis of Carmona (near Seville) named for a small sculpture of an elephant found inside it. Rather than a tomb, it may have been a sanctuary or temple.

Site of the most completely excavated timber-built auxiliary fort (with annexe) in the Roman Empire, situated in present-day Midlothian, Scotland. Roman occupation was short-lived, having been established in the early 70s CE and abandoned in or shortly after 86. Now completely built over by the Royal Bank of Scotland Data Centre.
In the village of Elst, located between Arnhem and Nijmegen, the remains of two quadrangular Romano-Celtic-type temples were discovered beneath the parish church following World War II.
The temple of the goddess Ištar of Agade at Babylon. The Sumerian ceremonial name Emašdari means "House of Animal Offerings." The Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus rebuilt/renovated it.
An ancient settlement and sanctuary site on the Cnidus (modern Reşadiye/Datça) peninsula.
The temple of the god Nergal at Cutha. The Sumerian ceremonial name Emeslam means "House, Warrior of the Netherworld."
A Roman mine at St Barbara in Germany where copper and the mineral ingredients for an azurite pigment now known as "Wallerfanger Blau" were extracted.
An artificial canal originally dating to the fourth century BCE that was built by the inhabitants of Ariccia in order to regulate the waters of Lake Nemi.
Emshi tepe is located in Jauzjan Province to the northeast of Shibarghan. Material on the site dates to the Hellenistic, Kushan, and Sassanian/Kushano-Sassanian periods.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: N Lake Ohrid MAC.
An ancient Thracian hilltop settlement whose site is located on a hill 2 kilometers north of the later site of Amphipolis.
The Isola di San Pietro is one of the principal islands of the Sulcis archipelago.
The ḫilṣu-building of the goddess Ningal inside the Egišnugal temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Enunmah means "House of the Exalted Prince."
An unnamed Roman bridge on the Via Aemilia over the ancient Incia river. Located near modern S. Ilario d’Enza in Italy.
A Hellenistic settlement with Illyrian antecedents located at modern Stobreč in Croatia. The city flourished into late antiquity.
An ancient settlement in Elis on the Selleis river, between Pylos and Lasion. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
A Roman fort at present-day Whitley Castle.

A koinon (league) of Epirote tribes, which grew out of the earlier Molossian League, was established between 370 and 320 BCE. The league dissolved during the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BCE) as its constituent cities chose different sides in the conflict.
Episcopal complex of Eio-el Tolmo de Minateda (Héllín, Albacete, Spain)

The episcopal complex of Eio at El Tolmo de Minateda dates to the terminal sixth century CE and was in use during the following two centuries. Its construction may have been directed by Visigothic officials in Toletum.
The highest mountain on the island of Ischia.
An ancient site at modern Echternach in Luxembourg.
A river which flowed into the Ganges river at Patna, mentioned by both Arrian and Pliny.
The Eravisci were a Celtic tribe that occupied the area of Aquincum prior to the Roman conquest.
Erchia was an inland deme of the tribe Aigeis in Attica.
Erebidai? or Erebidae, an ancient tribe of north Africa that were counted among the Lotophages, according to Philistos.
Erek Dağ is a mountain in the Van Province in eastern Anatolia. It is the second-highest peak of the province of Van, rising to 3200 meters above sea level.

The cavern of San Michele was a hermit's dwelling place that is located near a cavern known as the "cave of San Colombano". This hermitage lies in a relatively solitary area of the valley of the Curiasca di San Michele stream, a tributary of the Trebbia river (Italian municipality of Coli, province of Piacenza).
A stream that flowed from the Lykabettos, through the Agora to the Kerameikos.
The Erigon is the largest tributary of the Axius river in Macedonia.
Erk Kala, founded in the sixth century B.C., was at the center of Merv.
The Helmand River flows some 1,150 km (710 mi) from the Hindu Kush mountains to the Sistan basin.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.

The temple of the god Lugalbanda, Esag (“Foremost House”), was located in the Kullab district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of four temples in that part of Babylon.
The modern Dakhla (Dakhleh) Oasis in Egypt's western desert.
Essalois was originally an oppidum of the Segusiavi.

A limestone quarry from which was sourced the stone used in the construction of the Pont du Gard. The quarry was excavated in the late 1990s and early 2000s on a site 600-700 meters northeast of the aqueduct bridge.
The Domu de Orgia at Esterzili is the largest nuragic "megaron" structure thus far discovered in Sardinia.
The Estiones were a sub-tribe of the Vindelici.
Roman-era marble extraction in the vicinity of modern Estremoz in Portugal can be documented by use of the local stone throughout the western part of the Iberian peninsula.

A fourth century A.D. church located in Ejmiatsin, Armenia. This is the central cathedral of the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin of the Armenian Apostolic Church and was enrolled as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
The Euenos (modern Evinos) is a river of western Greece that flows into the Gulf of Patras.
The ziggurat of the god the god Nabû at Borsippa. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eurmeiminanki means "House which Gathers the Seven (Me's) of Heaven and Underworld."
Eurotas fl. (Evrotas) is the principal river of Laconia.

The temple of the god Nabû, Eurunanam (“House, the Very City”), was located in the New City district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was the only dais in that part of Babylon.

A sanctuary dedicated to Eurysakes, son of Ajax on the Kolonos Agoraios in Athens, which served as the central sanctuary of the tribe Aiantis. It has not been located archaeologically, but the findspots of related inscriptions suggest it was somewhere southwest of the Hephaisteion.
A small islet located northeast of Paros, Greece, with the remains of a Byzantine fort (ca. seventh century CE).
A mountain on the island of Tinos with archaeological evidence for habitation beginning in the Late Bronze Age and concluding with the remains of a Venetian fortress.
The temple of the god Nergal at Me-Turnat. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ešahula means "House of the Happy Heart."

The temple of the god Ea, Eʾešmah (“Exalted House”), was located in the Kumar district of Babylon, in the western half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of seven temples in that part of Babylon.
Military barracks located north of the camp wall in the northern part of Block F5 at Dura-Europos.
Military barracks located north of the camp wall in the northern part of Block K5 at Dura-Europos.
A Tyrrhenian coastal port opposite Elba. Modern Piombino.
The Wadi al Qattafi in Jordan's Black Desert is the site of numerous sites of occupation dating to the Neolithic period.

The cathedral in Faras, founded in 620 and rebuilt in the 8th and 10th centuries, respectively, was the seat of the Diocese of Faras. The site had well-preserved wall paintings from the 8th to 9th centuries. The cathedral was flooded by the creation of Lake Nasser in the 1960s.
A first to third century AD castrum site on the Galician coast.
Fern Pass (elevation 1212 m) is a mountain pass of the Tyrolean Alps.
A fortified ancient hilltop, Ferrazzano is usually identified as a Samnite site.
An Etruscan necropolis located on a tufaceous plateau overlooking the valley of the Fosso della Lenta. The tombs in the necropolis date between the seventh and fifth centuries BCE.
The Fidenates number among the lost peoples of Latium enumerated by Pliny the Elder.
An ancient place, known only from the Tabula Peutingeriana, perhaps located near Khoi and Marand, northwest of Lake Urmia.
An archaeological site with nine burial mounds, including an intact royal mound (kurgan), located in the Southern Ural Region of Russia dating from the 6th-4th centuries BCE.
The approximate location of the fourth century BCE archaeological deposit that is referred to as either the Kabul or Chaman-i Ḥaz̤ūrī Coin Hoard.
A Gallo-Roman site lying along the Roman road from Lyon to Saintes.
A high mountain forming part of the central and most elevated chain of the Apennines. Pliny indicates that it was the source of the river Nar.

Flag Fen is a Bronze Age ritual site near Peterborough, England, comprised of 60,000 timbers arranged in five rows that connect Whittlesey Island with Peterborough. Dendrochronological evidence has dates the site to ca. 1365–967 BC.

The so-called "Flaminio Obelisk" at Rome was created in Egypt during the Nineteenth Dynasty under Pharaoh Seti I. The obelisk was erected at Heliopolis under Ramesses II. In 1 BCE, the obelisk was transported to Rome on the orders of Augustus. It was transported with the Obelisk of Montecitorio. The Flaminio Obelisk was re-erected on the spina of the Circus Maximus. It was discovered in a fragment
The Flavian Amphitheater at Puteoli is an amphitheater constructed in the port town of Puteoli under the Flavian dynasty around 80 CE.
A small Gallo-Roman settlement south of Béziers, located on the coast at La Fount de Rome.
An ancient lake which existed in Roman and Medieval times in what is now the Netherlands.
A Roman fort located at modern Ajdovščina in Slovenia.
An elaborate Romano-British villa of the mid-second century A.D. Epigraphic evidence connects the site with the prefect of the Classis Britannica (praefectus classis Britannicae).
Salt springs continuously exploited from the Neolithic period through the early modern era. Also the site of a Roman bath complex.
Modern village on the Taman Peninsula. It was the find-spot of a hoard of first-century didrachms.

The Fontana dell'Acqua Paola or Il Fontanone stands on the Ianiculum near the church of San Pietro in Montorio. It was built in 1612 to mark the end of the Acqua Paola aqueduct after it had been restored by Pope Paul V.
A previously unknown settlement with Roman-period remains was identified near the village of Artieda, Spain.

At Forte Tiburtina the remains of a Roman villa located on the northern edge of the Parco della Serenissima in the eastern suburbium of the city of Rome.
A ruined ninth-century Arabic fort on the shores of Sicily's Lago Arancio.
A sanctuary dedicated to Fortuna Muliebris along the Via Latina. Tradition holds that it was dedicated in 487 B.C.
The "Blessed Islands", equivalent in most ancient literature to the modern Canary Islands (Islas Canarias).
The modern, Portugeuse archipelago of Madeira seems to have been identified by some ancient authors with the "Fortunatae Insulae" or "Blessed Islands".
An ancient road station on the Via Appia located 69 km southeast of Rome.
The Forum of Augustus at Rome was dedicated in 2 BCE, to the northeast of Julius Caesar's Forum. It contained the Temple of Mars Ultor.

The so-called "Forum Boarium" in Pompeii was erroneously named by its 1755 excavators who discovered the bones of large bovids and assigned the name that still is used to describe this insula in Pompeii's Regio II (II, 5).
Rome's so-called "cattle market", the Forum Boarium is a key area of commercial and ritual activity on the east bank of the river Tiber. It is flanked by the Capitoline, Palatine, and Aventine hills.
Forum Domitii was a market created prior to the foundation of Narbonne along the Via Domitia.
The Forum Iulium (or Forum of Caesar, Forum Caesaris) is a forum built by Iulius Caesar and dedicated ca. 46 B.C. The main cult of the forum is that of Venus Genetrix.
An important town of the Ager Falernus, not to be confused with Forum Popili, the modern Polla.
Imperial forum constructed at Rome under Trajan between 105-112 CE.
A town of Liguria located near the source of the Po River (ancient Padus).
The Gallo-Roman forum of ancient Bagacum (Bavay) covers more than 2.5 ha.
Roman granaries of the forum in Pompeii. (VII,7,29).
The forum of Cosa functioned as the administrative center of the town and was the site of key administrative and ritual structures.

The forum of Roman Paestum stands north of the Hera sanctuary and measures ca. 57 x 150 meters. It occupies the site of the Greek agora and was surrounded with a peristyle of re-used Doric columns. Tabernae stood at its south side and baths funded by M. Tullius Venneianus stood to the southwest. A triple-podium structure - lararium? - stands on the western side.
Main forum of the Roman city of Pompeii (VII, 8).

The Fossa Traiana (Channel of Trajan) describes a canal of ca. 45 m width connected with the artificial harbors at Portus. Despite the name, its origins may lie in the Claudian harbor works. The cutting of the channel created an artificial island between Ostia and Portus, the so-called Isola Sacra.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Seguia Bent el Krass.
Fosse Way was a Roman road connecting Isca Dumnoniorum and Lindum Colonia.

A small stream that flows into the Tyrrhenian Sea. It now lies in the territory of the municipalities of Allumiere, Civitavecchia, and Santa Marinella and forms the geographical boundary between the latter two. The watercourse originates at Poggio Ombricolo.

At Fox-Amphoux the remains of a Roman villa were discovered, adjacent to those of a sanctuary ad fines that may have been dedicated to the Capitoline triad. The site was in use from the time of Augustus until the third century AD.

Samuel Lysons excavated a Roman villa at Frampton (Dorset) in 1796. Its unusual mosaics were a subject of keen interest, even attracting the attention of George III. The villa was thought to have been demolished, but Bournemouth University demonstrated that remains of the villa can still be identified in situ in 2019.
The Franci or Franks were a confederation of German tribes inhabiting the valleys of the Lower and Middle Rhine.
An important painted Etruscan tomb dating to the final quarter of the fourth century B.C.

An ancient side road (diverticulum) connecting the Via Appia to ancient Bovillae was rediscovered in 2014 construction work in modern Frattocchie. A section of the road was conserved and can be visited beneath the McDonald's restaurant now occupying the site. Other remains of the road have been identified to the west.
An ancient town of Etruria, Fregenae was located between Alsium and the mouth of the river Tiber.
A small river draining into the Tyrrhenian Sea just south of Luna (the modern Fiume Frigido in Tuscany).
The Friniates were an ancient tribe of Liguria.
The Frisiavones were a Germanic people living near the northern border of Gallia Belgica during the early first millennium CE.
BAtlas 2 G3 Frombork, Młoteczno, Trąbki Małe

A large and minimally excavated site that lies under the modern Aquisgrana industrial park in the eastern part of the city of La Carolina in Spain's Jaén province. Evidence indicates a temporal span for the site from at least the first century BCE to the late first century CE. The site may have served as a central foundry for metallic ore extracted from mines in and around La Carolina and Cerro de
A Roman municipal center and port.
Furfane was a road station located 18 miles to the west of Herdonia, as indicated on the Peutinger map.
This Roman fish-salting workshop located in Setúbal dates to the first century CE. It was discovered in 1979.
Gabellus/*Secia fl. (Secchia river) is a tributary of the Po river.
A Roman fort at present-day Moresby that was a part of the Cumbrian coastal defenses.
A Ptolemaic foundation in northern Jordan that eventually became part of the Decapolis.
A Scythian burial site containing burials from the fourth to second centuries B.C.; located near the Dnieper River, southeast of the modern village of Balky.

A Roman fort located along the Roman road from Brougham to Ravenglass. The previous association with Ambleside is now in doubt since the discovery of a diploma at Ravenglass in 1995, which plausibly links Itunocelum with Ravenglass, and consequently making Ambleside more likely to be identified with *Glannoventa.
A place recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana that is to be located between Equizeto? and Auzia. Talbert notes that Galaxia is attested as a name on the manuscript, but has no symbol.
Galessos was an ancient city on the island of Syros in the Cyclades.
An ancient people whose territory is unlocated
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Galliano di Cantù.
The Gulf of Lion, or Sinus Gallicus.
An evergreen thicket of the area around Cumae.
A settlement of the Treveri (ancient name unknown) at modern Mamer in Luxembourg.
A Gallo-Roman settlement occupied from the late second century B.C. to the middle of the first century A.D.
The remains of a Gallo-Roman settlement.

A pair of archaeological sites in Gallia Narbonensis. The site of Les Orpaillots shows traces of a sanctuary and a group of tombs while Notre-Dame-de-la-Mure showed traces of a late third century Gallo-Roman villa.
Archaeological remains of the Gallo-Roman temple at ancient Nasium, located at Mazeroie, commune Naix-aux-Forges, France.
Remains of the Roman-era settlement at Dalheim.
A Praedium or estate located in Etruria near Siena; the modern Galognano.
A village in Media notable for its agricultural wealth.
An ancient city mentioned by Ptolemy that some have tentatively identified with modern Baku.
This ancient name is probably to be associated with the modern Mahaweli, which is the longest river of Sri Lanka.
The Ganges flows some 2,525 km (1,569 mi) from its sources in the western Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal.
A multi-period hilltop settlement occupied from the Chalcolithic period to Late Antiquity.
Gaochang is the site of an ancient oasis city located on the northern rim of the inhospitable Taklamakan Desert in present-day Xinjiang, China.
The Garamantes, a Saharan People, living in Fezzan region of Libya cited: BAtlas 36 C4

A large residential complex, built in ca. 128 CE as part of the Hadrianic remodeling of Ostia. Its central area was occupied by two blocks, each comprising four houses, surrounded by a garden furnished with six fountains.
An ancient settlement known in modern times as Gardies in France (BAtlas 15 B2 Gardies)
A massif and promontory of Apulia.
Gargettos was an inland deme of the tribe Aigeis in Attica, probably located south of Mt Pentalikon in the area of modern Gerakas.
One of two mountains in the immediate vicinity of the West Bank city of Nablus.
The Garni Temple dates to the first century A.D. and was sacred to the Armenian sun god Mihr.
Gasr Banat (also Qasr Banat or Qasr Isawi) was the site of a Roman-period fortified farmstead referred to as a "centenarium".
Gate at Hag. Dimitrios Loumbardiaris/Gate XIV
A gate in the Diateichisma wall of Athens, built in the 280s or 270s B.C.
Gate north of the Olympieion/Gate IX
A gate in the Themistoklean city wall of Athens, built partially with material spoliated from the archaic temple of Olympian Zeus.
Gatheai was a town of Arcadia in the district of Cromitis, along the river Gatheatas.
An eruptive volcanic vent in the Phlegraean Fields. Modern Monte Gauro (also known as Monte Barbaro).

Gazandži is a village at the Turkish-Armenian border location south of Armavir, on the right bank of the river Arasse, approximately 9 km northeast of Iğdir. Here a cylindrical stone with a building inscription of the Urartian king Argišti I., son of Minua (8th century BCE) was found.
An ancient Macedonian settlement, located near the modern town that bears its name. A likely acropolis has been identified at the church of Hagios Athanasios, northeast of the modern town.

Village in Krasnodar Krai, Russia, located 9 km. southeast of Anapa. Between 1972 and 1986, several separate coin hoards dated to the late Bosporan Kingdom (4th century CE) were found on a farm at the edge of the village.
An ancient river, possibly to be identified with the modern Gail in Austria.
The earliest Roman fort in present-day Gelligaer, Wales.
An ancient settlement located south of modern Kivari in the Peloponnese.
An eastern Germanic tribe that shared a close relation to the Goths.
A fourth century A.D. Roman villa with mosaic pavements. The villa may have extended to some 10,000 square meters in area.
An ancient settlement of Caria located near Ovacik, 12 km S-SE of Çine.
Geridu, located near the comune of Sorso in Sardinia, was the site of a Medieval village active from the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.
The Greek name given to Thracian tribes dwelling south of the Danube river.

Settlement associated with Punic and Roman quarries known today as Ghar El Kebir (previously and perhaps in error: Rhar-el-Kebir). The complex is perhaps to be associated with the ancient name Latomiai.
Ghirza is the site of a Roman town in Libya.
The site of a villa associated with Lucius Vitruvius Mamurra.
A modern settlement on the southwest coast of Sri Lanka. The discovery of Roman bronze coins of the fourth and fifth centuries CE were reported in the early 20th century in the vicinity of Gintota.
A fourth-century A.D. catacomb along the via Salaria at Rome.

Gird-I Matrab is a multi-period settlement site located in Iraqi Kurdistan. The site was first settled during the fifth millennium BCE and, through various phases, shows evidence for human activity across more than six millennia.
A high mound located on the edge of Lake Dukan and now threatened by innundation.
Tall multiperiod settlement mound in Kurdistan Iraq. Preliminary excavations have yielded evidence for occupation and construction ranging from the Chalcolithic to the Iron Age.
The archaeological site of the Girsu Bridge, located in modern Iraq's Dhi Qar governorate, was identified in 1920 and has been dated to the third millennium BCE.
A fourth to third century B.C. circular tower in masonry built atop a Middle Bronze Age mound.
A large Bronze Age fortification of the Mycenaean civilization, Gla dates ca. 1300 B.C.
A training ground for gladiators in Pompeii noted for the more than 100 inscriptions connected to gladiating. (V, 5, 3)
Glanum was a Celtic oppidum that became a Roman city; it was eventually abandoned in the third century AD.
A Roman dam that created the Lac du Peirou and supplied Glanum with water. While the ancient dam was destroyed in the late nineteenth century, the reservoir remains.
A settlement and harbor located in Ionia on Mt. Mykale in what is now western Turkey.
A Roman fort, just over the river Dee from modern Glenlochar in Scotland. The fort, excavated in the 1950s, is largely invisible today. It may correspond to the ancient name Loukopibia.
The Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site located in central Azerbaijan. The 537 ha site comprises more than 6,000 rock engravings covering a period of 40,000 years.
Located along the course of the Via Appia between Fondi and Itri are the remains of a likely sanctuary of Apollo that dates to the fourth and third century BCE.
An archaeological site near the village of Sinemorets. The site of a Thracian aristocratic woman's home, dated to the third to second centuries BCE.
A Roman bridge at modern Golmayo in Spain's Soria province (Castile and León), crossing the modern river of the same name. The modern N-122 highway still makes use of this originally Roman bridge.
A cape located at the northwest corner of the island of Sardinia. Modern Capo Falcone, a promontory in Stintino, Sardinia, Italy.

A multi-period site with evidence of construction and occupation ranging from the Neolithic to the Medieval periods. An iron age farmstead was replaced by a series of Roman-era constructs, including a late first-century CE masonry establishment, often characterized as a Roman villa (the site is located near the site of Verulanium, modern St. Albans). Renovated in the late second century, the farm
Gors Fawr Stone Circle is located in Mynachlog-Ddu, Pembrokeshire, Wales, United Kingdom.
Gough's Cave is located in Cheddar Gorge. A hominin fossil commonly referred to as "Cheddar Man" was discovered in the cave in 1903.
A river on the island of Corsica. The modern Golo.

Early Minoan cemetery located in Gournes, Crete, containing 37 tombs. The site was largely destroyed by the installation of irrigation pipes and the building of the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research and its associated parking lot.

A monumental burial structure in the so-called "Petosiris-Nekropole" at Tuna el-Gebel, excavated in 2021. Immediately north of the tomb, in the street area, stone basins supporting undisturbed lead coffins, as well as other associated burials, were found in situ.
An early town in the neighborhood of Eretria on Euboea. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
The so-called Grand Fortress of Selçuk is situated on the Ayasuluk Hill at Ephesus. Its origins lie in the Byzantine period, following the decline of the Graeco-Roman metropolis of Ephesus.

At Grand Lagneux, a small village in the French commune of Yenne, a rescue excavation in 2020 revealed part of a Roman-era bathing establishment. The excavated site is now buried under a modern home. This find constitutes another possible locality in the commune for attested ancient name "Etanna".
Grange stone circle or Lios na Grainsi is the largest stone circle in Ireland, consisting of 113 stones and was built ca. 2100 BC.
Grave Circle A encloses a royal cemetery within the walls of the citadel of Mycenae; inside it are six shaft graves constructed around 1600 BC.

The Grave of Charmylos is a third-century BCE vaulted tomb located on Kos. The site is understood as a heroön dedicated to the legendary king Charmylos. The ancient site was dismantled and partially reused in the church of Tímios Stávros.

A Chalcolithic to Bronze Age settlement mounded identified in 1989, located on the east bank of the Euphrates River, 75 km southwest of Şanlıurfa. The mound measures ca. 15 meters high and 70 x 60 meters in area.
The primary colonnaded avenue of the ancient city of Palmyra was constructed during the second and third centuries CE. It stretched for more than one kilometer (approximately 0.75 miles).
The Great Mosque of Aleppo, also known as the Umayyad Mosque of Aleppo, is the largest and one of the oldest mosques in the city of Aleppo, Syria.

The Great Temple of Petra is one of the major archaeological and architectural components of central Petra. It is located to the south of the Colonnaded Street and southeast of the Temenos Gate and covers 7560 square meters.
The altar of Athena Polias on the Acropolis of Athens, built in or before the 7th century BC.
A great pit dug to the north-east of the village of Deir el-Medina, where hundreds of objects, particularly ostraca, were found.
The outer entranceway to the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis, completed by the emperor Marcus Aurelius and modelled on the Propylaia of the Acropolis in Athens.
Rock-cut theater of Greek form at Syracuse, Sicily, probably in use from the 5th c. BC to the Late Roman period.
The Greek theater of Taormina was built originally in the third century B.C.
A Roman fort and associated vicus at modern Greta Bridge (UK).

A Roman fortification on the modern Mt. Grociana piccola, east of Trieste. The structure seems to date to the late second and early first centuries BCE, and may have been part of a military fortification network in the area that developed over time.
Cave site in the Aniene Valley in central Italy with signs of human activity from the Early Neolithic period to the early Bronze Age.

The quarries at Grotta Oscura were an important source of high-quality tuff located in the territory of Veii. This was the "tuffo giallo della via Tiberina" that was used at Rome from the Archaic period onward.

The Paglicci cave or Grotta Paglicci is located near Rignano Garganico, Apulia, in southern Italy. Discovered in the 1950s, the cave is an important archaeological site documenting life in the Paleolithic period. In addition to artifact finds and zooarchaeological information, the cave provides evidence of the harvesting of wild oats ca. 36,000 BCE. The cave also includes Paleolithic mural art.

The site of a Roman villa situated on two terraces. The modern toponym "Grotta Papale" derives from a partially subterranean apsidal nymphaeum. The villa was extensive, covering some 23,000 square meters and has both a late republican and an imperial phase.
Grotta Porciosa, near Borghetto, was the site of a small but prosperous settlement in the Ager Faliscus.

The Grotta Trinità is a cave sanctuary located in the comune of Ruffano, province of Lecce, in southern Italy. The cave was in use from the Neolithic period onwards. In the Iron Age, terracotta vessels with incised graffiti date activity to the sixth century BCE and subsequent.
The so-called Grotta dei Massacci located in Osteria Nuova, municipality of Frasso Sabino, Italy, is a monumental, vaulted subterranean tomb structure that likely dates to the second century CE.
A 1-km long ancient tunnel connecting Lake Avernus with Cumae. It dates ca. 38-36 B.C.

Located on the Sirmione peninsula on the southern shore of Lake Garda, "Grotte di Catullo" is the name given to the ruins of a Roman villa dating to the late first century B.C. and the beginning of the first century A.D.
The so-called Grotte di S. Nicola, the remains of the platform and cryptoporticus of a late republican Roman villa.
This group of sanctuaries was carved out of rock along the Coromandel coast in the seventh and eighth centuries. The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
A tributary of the Guadalquivir river that rises in Pozo Amargo in the province of Cadiz.

The so-called "Guglia di Marcello" or "Aguglia d'Agosta" is a Roman funerary monument located along the ancient via Pompei that once connected Syracuse and Messina. It dates to the period from the first century B.C. to the first century A.D.
Guild Temple and Mithraeum of Fructosus

An architectural complex excavated in 1938 at the intersection of Via del Pomerio and Via del Tempio Rotondo in Ostia. The guild temple dates to the reign of Alexander Severus (222 - 235 CE). Based on epigraphic evidence, this shrine may belong to the guild of the stuppatores. A mithraic shrine with a patron named Fructosus is to be found in the substructure of the podium.
A Spanish village located north of Sevilla that belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X.
An ancient coastal settlement, located at modern Sidi Brahim in Algeria, about 4 kilometers west of modern Gouraya.
The so-called "Shapur cave" in the Zagros Mountains contains a colossal statue of Shapur I, the second ruler of the Sasanid Empire.
According to Hind, a sanctuary dating ca. third century BC to second century AD was identified at the Gurzuf Pass. Silver and bronze statuettes of Graeco-Roman divinities were recovered.
A burial, located in the modern village of Gustow in Germany's Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state. Grave goods included Roman materials.
The Gymnasium of Olympia was a practice and training field constructed in 250 BC for male Hellenic athletes competing in the Olympic Games.
An ancient Greek polis located on the Mani peninsula of the Peloponnese. Modern Gytheio.

Gövelek is a village situated 27 km to the east of Van in the southeast of Turkey. Here the upper part of a stela with an inscription of Rusa, son of Erimena (presumably last quarter of 8th century BCE) was found. It reports his military success and describes deportations from the city Ṭušpa, the building of the city Rusaḫinili, and the creation of an artificial lake called "Lake of Rusa". The lak
HaMa'apil is a kibbutz in central Israel, near Ahituv, that sits atop a small mound of ruins, the ancient name of which remains unknown).
A Roman fort at present-day Risingham.
Site of a Romano-British settlement dating from the first-fourth centuries CE, located near modern Wickham Market in Suffolk.
The Arda is a right tributary of the Po River in northern Italy.

Hadrian's Wall or Vallum Aelium was the first of two Roman fortifications built across northern Britannia. The project was begun in A.D. 122 and the works eventually stretched from the River Tyne near the North Sea to the Solway Firth on the Irish Sea. The wall represented the northern limit of the Roman Empire.
A mountain range of northern Thrace: the modern "Balkan Mountains".
One of the three largest settlement mounds located in the Urmia basin, Azerbaijan, that covers some fifty acres.
A major paleochristian, then Byzantine, church in Istanbul; subsequently an Islamic mosque, and today a museum.

Hagia Sophia, Iznik, Turkey, was founded as a Christian basilica in the fourth century CE. Justinian I rebuilt the site in the mid-6th century CE. An earthquake in the eleventh century destroyed that church, and it was then substantially rebuilt following 1065. It is to that rebuilding that much of the present structure pertains. Following the Ottoman conquest, the church became a mosque in 1331.
A natural cave in the side of the Halberg hill at Saarbrücken was enlarged for the use of the Mithras cult.
Halisarna was a small center located in the border regions of Mysia and the Troad.
An ancient river of Asia Minor that scholars identify with the modern Acı Çay upriver from its confluence with the Tatlı Çay south of Çankırı (ancient Gangra).
An ancient city of Thessaly. Modern Alos, Greece.
A sequence of occupational phases at Haltern, Germany, results from the presence of the Roman military following from the earliest period of Roman occupation in the principate of Augustus.
Haltwhistle Burn Roman Fortlet and Camp
Site of Roman fortlet and temporary camp. The fortlet guarded the crossing of the Burn by the Stanegate. It pre-dates the construction of Hadrian's Wall, which passes 0.5 km to the north.
The archaeological remains of Haltwhistle Burn Temporary Camp 4 are visible as a standing earthwork.
The Halykos (modern Platani) is the fifth-longest river in Sicily.
Hamae is an ancient site of Campania located between Capua and Cumae, although its precise location is difficult to fix. The people of Capua gathered there for a solemn religious festival.
An Early Bronze Age settlement located in Central Anatolia to the southwest of Hamam Karahisar Village.
Hambledon Hill is a prehistoric hill fort in Dorset, England, with occupation beginning in the Neolithic period.

The so-called Hammam Beni Guecha is a ruined Roman spa located just north and east of the modern Algerian village of Chouara Torche (Beni Guecha municipality). The site may be associated with a road station recorded on the Peutinger Map: Fons Carmerata.
One of many fortified stations (hydreuma) of Roman date on a route through the eastern desert of Egypt. The station at el-Hammamt is also marked by a modern well, dug by English engineers in 1830.
A large bath complex adjacent to the ancient harbor of Ephesus that measures ca. 160 by 170 meters and was originally built in the late first century CE.
An ancient river of Elis in the Peloponnese, reported by Pausanias to be in his day near the ruins of the city of Harpina. The river's precise location has not been determined.
Located in West Sussex, Hassocks is thought to be the site of a Roman settlement, on the basis of funerary evidence discovered in the area.
A shrine sacred to Hathor connected with the Egyptian mining settlement that was extracting copper in the Timna Valley.
An Ancient Egyptian alabaster quarry used intermittently from the Fourth Dynasty through the Roman period.
Haughey's Fort is a Late Bronze Age hillfort located in County Armagh, Northern Ireland. It dates ca. 1200 BCE and was an important prehistoric center.
The site of a Roman fort and an associated vicus along Dere Street, now buried and bisected by the modern A1.
A mountain, probably Monte Pellegrino (contra Manni 1981, 86-87).
An Aegean island that parallels the southeast coast of Attica (modern Makronisos).

In Greek mythology, Helicon was the site of two springs sacred to the Muses, the Aganippe and the Hippocrene. The mountain is located near the Gulf of Corinth and rises to an elevation of 1,749 meters (5,738 ft).
An ancient estuary, discharging the Mosa and some distributaries of the Rhenus. The modern (though much altered) Waal-Maas-Delta in the Netherlands.
An ancient river of the Peloponnese, mentioned by Pausanias. It empties into the Corinthian Gulf and is identified with the modern Elissonas in the Greek municipality of Sikyona.
Hellas was an administrative region of the Late Roman Empire, included in the prefecture of Illyrikon according to Hierocles.
An ancient river of southeast Crete, possibly to be identified with a modern stream that empties into the Libyan Sea just east of the modern village of Gra Lygia in the Ierapetra municipal region.
A circular public bath building dating to the Hellenistic period in the agora of Amathous.
A Hellenistic bath complex at Syracuse, located near the Greek theater.
Helorus fl. (Tellaro), a river of southeast Sicily.
Helsby Hillfort is an Iron Age hillfort located in Cheshire, northwest England. Helsby Hill has an elevation of 141 meters above sea level.
The Hemnatae were are ancient tribe of interior Arabia described by Pliny the Elder.
The narrowest point in the Hellespont, between Sestos and Abydos.
Herakleia was an ancient settlement of Pisatis in Elis, some 40 or 50 stades from Olympia.
The Strait of Gibraltar, a narrow strait that connects the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea and separates Europe from Africa.
A sanctuary of Herakles located on the island of Lemnos, active from the Archaic period through to the time of the Roman empire.
Heras? Ins. is a small, rocky island located in the southern shore of the Strait of Gibraltar, some 200 meters from the Moroccan coast
An ancient settlement, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today.
A city gate of Pompeii that dates to the time of Sulla.

An ancient forest located east of the Rhine river in southern Germany. The precise location and extent of the forest remains uncertain, although the Black Forest formed the western part of the Hercynian Forest.
Cap Bon is a peninsula of northeastern Tunisia.
Herminius M. (the Serra da Estrela mountains of modern Portugal)
Hermion(e) was a settlement of the eastern Argolid.
An Ionian colony on the Gulf of Taman.
Site of Romano-British settlement or small town
A triangular enclosure with approximately 19 burials (both cremation and inhumation) dating to the Geometric period (ca. 750 BC - ca. 630 BC).
The Heruli? were an East Germanic tribe who migrated from Scandinavia to the Black Sea during the third century AD.
An important hill fort with lower settlement near the source of the Danube, it flourished from the 7th to the 5th century BCE despite one major destruction.
A promontory at the foot of the Kragos mountains, the modern Yedi Burun on Turkey's southwest coast.
Hierapolis in Phrygia, now Koçhisar, Sandıklı, was was part of the Phrygian Pentapolis.
An ancient river mentioned by Ptolemy, now identified with the Alkaliya river in Ukraine.
Hieromyces fl. (Yarmouk river) is the largest tributary of the Jordan river.
A sanctuary that was sacred to Poseidon and Zeus Ourios located at the Black Sea mouth.
The protected, western cove at modern Mytikas in Akarnania, Greece.
A fortified, pre-Roman oppidum with concentric fortification circuits, the site of Hijovejo existed during a transitional phase in Iberia (second century B.C. to first century A.D.)

The Himella River was located in the Sabina, and its modern equivalent is the Fiume Salto. Virgil mentions the river along with the sites of Casperia and Foruli. The Himella debouched into Lacus Velinus.

The Hindu Kush mountain range, which extends through Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Tajikistan, was known to the Greeks and Romans as the Paropamisos or Caucasus mountains. They are not to be confused with the other Caucasus Mountains (greater and lesser) between the Black and Caspian Seas.
A Roman fort built in the mid-first century CE in Wales.
The modern Cap de Garde (Algeria) is probably the proper identification for "Hippo Akra", attested in ancient sources.

The Hippodrome was the great racetrack of the city of Constantinople and was connected to the no longer extant imperial palace. At about 450 m in length, the Hippodrome once accommodated about 100,000 spectators.
Hippoi Inss., an island group off the coast of Ionia near the port of Erythrai.
Hippola was a town of ancient Laconia located to the northwest of Taenarum. Pausanias describes its ruins which included a temple of Athena Hippolaitis.
Hipponensis L. (modern Lac de Bizerte (بحيرة بنزرت))
Hippos was an ancient city that flourished between the third century B.C. and the seventh century A.D. It was abandoned following an earthquake in 749.
The Hirpini were an ancient Samnite people of central Italy.
The remains of an ancient village, perhaps linked to ancient Berenice Troglodytica.
Tumulus covering a rich Celtic burial of ca. 530 BC.
Hod Hill is the site of a large, rectangular Iron Age hill fort. After the Roman conquest, the Romans occupied the site.
A tribe of southern Arabia Felix, occupying territory that is now part of Yemen.
An ancient people, localized to the southwest of Lake Trogitis in modern Turkey.
A Bronze Age burial site located near the modern town of Hordiivka on the southern Bug River.
A Roman 'villa rustica' discovered in 1797 in Horkstow, North Lincolnshire. A large floor mosaic was identified to the east of the nearby modern elite building known as Horkstow Hall.

Site of lesser Roman walled town in present-day Lincolnshire, with occupation possibly as early as 1st century CE. The city walls, however likely do not predate the 4th century CE. Candidate location for Bannovallum (the other being Caistor).

A portion of a warehouse complex dating to the Flavian period, the Horrea Piperataria, was likely destroyed in the fire of 192 CE. Its remains were later incorporated into the substructions of the Basilica Nova (a.k.a. Basilica of Maxentius).

Gardens on the Esquiline Hill that passed into the control of the Iulio-Claudian family from the consul Lucius Aelius Lamia. As imperial property, the gardens were adorned with opulent display architecture and sculpture.

An urban garden of imperial Rome located on the summit of the Esquiline Hill. Based on an inscription dating to the reign of Claudius, it is believed that these gardens were administered by the same magistrate in charge of the Horti Lamiani, an official with the title "procurator hortorum Maianorum et Lamianorum".
Private house located in Block H2 of Dura-Europos.
Remains of a large house with peristyle located within the intramuros military sector of Dura-Europos.
A multiple-household military residence located in Block L7 of Dura-Europos.
Private house preceding the Christian church.
Private house later converted for military use as X7 Barracks.
The House of Argus at Herculaneum is located on the west side of Cardo III adjacent to the House of Artistides.

A domus at Herculaneum that earned its modern sobriquet thanks to the misidentification of a statue found in its ruins. The statue in question was thought to be Aristides, one of the ten Attic orators, when, in fact, it is a statue of Aeschines.

Archaeological excavations in the area of the Aqua Marcia and the Basilica of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem (Rome) in 1887 and 1888 uncovered the remains of lead water pipes identifying this domus as that of one Aufidia Cornelia Valentinilla.
House of the scribe Butehamon in the enclosure of the funerary temple of Ramses III at Medinet Habu, near the western fortified gate.
The House of Lucius Caecilius Jucundus in Pompeii takes its name from one of its latter-day owners, the banker Lucius Caecilius Iucundus who may have perished in the earthquake of A.D. 62.
The House of Pinarius Cerialis and Cassia or Casa dell’orefice or Casa di Ifigenia (III, 4, b).
The House of Julius Polybius (IX 13,1.3) sits on the north side of the Via dell'Abbondanza and dates from the second century BC.
The House of Lucius Cornelius Diadumenus (VII, 12, 26) is a small domus noted for its wall paintings.
A large and well-appointed house located in the so-called "Villa Section" of ancient Olynthus, proposed as an Olynthian type-house.
The House of Marcus Lucretius was excavated in 1846 and 1851.
A Pompeian domus excavated in 1916, 1918, and 1921. (II.2.4).
A Pompeian domus that, upon excavation, was found to have a large supply of colored marble.
The House of Octavius Quartio or the House of Loreius Tiburtinus (II,2,2).
The House of Plotilla, also known as Casa di Apollo e Coronide, was excavated in 1815 and again in 1839. It lies in Regio VIII of Pompeii.
The House of Publius Casca Longus (I, 6, 11) is located on the Via dell'Abbondanza and is also known as the Casa dei Quadretti Teatrali.
The House of Sallust (VI 2,4) is a domus in Pompeii that assumes its final form around the second century B.C.

A house at the southwestern corner of the Athenian Agora, built ca. 500 BC, destroyed during the Persian Sack in 480 BC, rebuilt in the 470s and demolished in the late fourth century BC. Finds suggest that in the third quarter of the fifth century BC it belonged to a shoemaker named Simon, perhaps to be identified with the interlocutor of Sokrates known from literary sources.
House of Venus in the shell
Located on the Via dell'Abbondanza, the so-called "House of Venus in the shell" is also known as the House of D. Lucretius Satrius Valens.
A well-appointed atrium house with Fourth Style wall paintings (VII,4,48).
The House of the Ara Maxima, located on the Via del Vesuvio, is also known as the House of Pinarius and the House of Narcissus (VI, 16, 15-17).
House in Pompeii (VI,3,3) that most likely dates from the second century BC and experienced extensive remodeling after the earthquake of AD 62.
A domus at Herculaneum that occupies a large area in the northern section of the insula.
The site of a domus (VIII.5.38) in Regio VIII where modern botanical gardens of the ancient Vesuvian flora present in Pompeii are maintained.
The so-called House of the Bronze Herm is a domus in Herculaneum (III, 16) that takes its name from a bronze statue found at the site.
A Roman house in Pompeii (I, 6, 15), also known as the House of L. Ceius Secundus. It is also referred to as the House of Fabia and Tyrannus.
A Pompeian domus re-discovered in 1879, the so-called House of the Centenary is among the largest domus in Pompeii.
A large and well-appointed house that takes its name from frescoes of Castor and Pollux (VI, 9, 6).
A domus in Ostia Antica, whose two building phases have been dated, respectively, to the middle and last quarter of the third century CE.
The House of the Four Styles or Casa dei Quattro Stili (I.8.17) is noted for having examples of all four style of Pompeian wall paintings.
The so-called House of the Hotel (Casa dell'Albergo) is an opulent Augustan-period domus that occupies the bulk of the southern end of Insula III at Herculaneum.

The so-called House of the Moralist, also known as the House of M. Epidius Hymenaeus, is located on the Via dell'Abbondanza. The house was formed from two connecting properties that belonged to two related wine-merchants, T. Arrius Polites and M. Epidius Hymenaeus ( III, 4, 2-3).
Large house in Saint-Romain-En-Gaul, France, probably belonging to a wealthy merchant, built around 50 CE and abandoned in the middle of the 3rd century CE.
House of the Prince of Naples
An atrium house with an austere facade located on the west side of the Vicolo dei Vettii (VI 15, 7-8).
A domus excavated in 1832 and 1882. It is noted for its late-stage wall decoations that may call upon public monuments for inspiration.

The so-called "The House of the Skeleton" at Herculaneum is a Roman domus that owes its name to the discovery of a human skeleton during excavations. Carlo Bonucci initially explored it between 1830 and 1831. Amedeo Maiuri completed the excavation in 1927.
The so-called "House of the Skeleton" was constructed in the early first century BCE in the Roman colony of Cosa. It stands an example of the domestic architecture of the Late Roman Republic.
The so-called House of the Surgeon in Rimini may have been the home of a Roman doctor by the name of Eutyches.

A Vespasianic domus in Ostia Antica, built ca. 70-75 CE, situated outside the Porta Marina, and north of the continuation of the Decumanus Maximus. It had a slightly concave façade, comprising six shops and an entrance corridor leading to an interior peristyle garden.

The so-called "House of the Tiles" at Lerna belongs to the Korakou culture in the Early Helladic II period (ca. 2500–2300 BCE). It was a monumental two-story building (12 x 25 meters) and has been interpreted as either a "proto-palace" or administrative center.

The so-called "House of the cithara player" (I,4,5 and 25) opens both on to the Via Stabiana and the Via dell'Abbondanza. One of the largest aristocratic homes in Pompeii, it was formed from two adjoining properties.
The House of the Geometric Mosaics (VIII,2,14-16) is a large domus of more than 60 rooms that was achieved by combining two third to second century BC houses.
A Roman domus in Pompeii facing on to the Via Nocera.
The so-called "House of the Surgeon" is considered to be one of the oldest domus in Pompeii. (VI, 1, 10, 23)

Medieval Armenian monastery in the village of Ohanavan, Aragatsotn Province, Armenia. The site originated as a single-nave church in the 4th century CE, was expanded in the 4th-5th centuries, and was substantially renovated in the 17th-18th centuries.

Hurkum (Dilkaya) is a modern village situated on the southern shore of Lake Van in the Southeast of Turkey near Ishanikom. In its church, a re-used column base with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua, son of Išpuini (9th / 8th century BCE) was found which reports the building of a banquet hall (CTU A 5-65C). Two other column bases with the same inscription have been found in a private house
Hyampolis was a city of eastern Phocis, located some 2.5 km from Abai.
A former island of the Icarian Sea at the location of modern Özbaşı 13.5 km south of Söke.
An ancient thermal site with both nuragic and Roman remains. Now the community of Benettuti on the island of Sardinia.
A river of the Punjab that flows southwest from the western Himalaya and joins the river Acesines.
An ancient settlement of Boeotia. The site is located about 2 km east of modern Loutsi in Greece.

Hymettos is a long mountain in Attica, which separates the plain (pedion) around the city of Athens from the interior of Attica (Mesogaia). It is divided into a northern section (Megas Hymettos) and a southern section (Anydros Hymettos) by the Pinari gorge. It was the site of marble quarries, forests, bee cultivation, and various cults.
The modern Southern Bug river in Ukraine was known in Greek and Roman sources as the Hypanis, one of three distinct rivers with this ancient name.
Hypata was an ancient city located on the north slope of Oeta above the Spercheios river valley.
A mountain mentioned in ancient sources, probably Kardüz Dağı in Turkey.
A corridor tomb located on Menorca that dates ca. 1700-1400 BCE.
A tomb of the fourth century A.D. located on the Via Latina.
A third-century AD hypogeum tomb on the Esquiline Hill in Rome with both pagan and Paleochristian iconography.
A Christian catacomb on the ancient Via Latina used during the fourth century.

The modern Manisa Ovası (Manisa plain) in Turkey stretches to the north, west, and east of the modern city of Manisa (ancient Magnesia ad Sipylum). The plain surrounds the confluences of the Hyllos (modern Demirci Çay) and Pidasos (a tributary of Kum Çay) rivers with the Hermus (modern Gediz).
An ancient, unlocated city located near Celenderis (modern Aydıncık, Turkey) in the region of Cilicia, Anatolia.
A settlement located on the road between Damascus and Emesa.
An ancient people whose territory is unlocated.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: around Occimiano.
Iamneia was a Philistine town on the northwestern border of Iudaea.
An ancient people who lived along the east coast of the Iberian peninsula.
The westernmost portion of the Mediterranean Sea, lying between the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa.
The modern Rio Tinto, which flows from the Sierra Morena mountains to the Gulf of Cádiz at Huelva.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: S Rusubbicari and Cissi.
The Iceni were a Brythonic tribe in Britain, occupying a territory that today lies in East Anglia. They are perhaps best known for their queen, Boudica, who led an anti-Roman revolt in AD 60.
Ichthyophagoi ("fish-eaters"), a people of what is now Pakistan mentioned by Nearchus.

The Roman fort at Theilenhofen, called Iciniacum in antiquity, was a Roman military camp along the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes. The site lies to the northwest of the village of Theilenhofen in the Weißenburg-Gunzenhausen district of Bavaria. The fort was probably built in the middle of the third century CE.
Site of a possible Roman Small Town.
An ancient settlement of the Treveri. Modern Jünkerath in Germany.
A mountain of northwestern Turkey standing to 5,820 ft (1,774 m) above sea level (modern Kaz Dağ).
Idebessos was an ancient city of Lycia.
The village of Igel is known for its funerary monument of the Secundinii dating ca. A.D. 250.
The Ikarian Sea is the southeastern part of the Aegean Sea, extending from Samos to Mykonos.

An ancient settlement located in Sudan's Northern state. The ancient site was situated at the 2nd cataract in Wadi Halfa and contained one of the largest fortresses in Nubia. The site was inundated by the Aswan High dam hydroelectric project.
A sixth century BC settlement on the Nile in Lower Nubia.
The so-called "Il Torraccio (1)" is the cement core of a Roman tomb located at the twelfth milestone of the Via Appia Nuova, on the left side.
A circular mausoleum dating to the Late Republican period along the Via Praenestina.
An Iron Age settlement in Latium.

An ancient settlement reported only by the 4th century CE Roman poet Avienus, who places it on the east coast of the Iberian peninsula. If it is not a fiction, it might be identified as either modern Javea or modern Lérida, north of the river Ebro.
The Ilienses were an important people of the interior of Sardinia who were never subjugated to Roman authority.
Ilipula Minor, modern Repla, south of Osuna.
Tumulus near İznik Lake in Anatolia with Neolithic, Late Chalcolithic, Early Bronze Age, and Early Byzantine remains.
Imbrasos fl. on the island of Samos was said to have been the birthplace of the goddess Hera.
A river of western Greece, known in modern times by several names including Βλαχόρρεμα (Vlachorrema), Bizakos, and Sindekiniotikos.
The modern Enza river in northern Italy.
A river of Asia Minor, now identified with the modern Dalaman Çay, that divided Caria and Lycia.
A Gallic tribe of Northern Italy, giving their name to the region of Insubria.
The island marked "Insula Erkronis" on the Peutinger map may be the island in the Adriatic Sea now known as Silba (Croatia).
A richly appointed insula in Ephesus includes a latrine, which has previously been referred to in scholarship as a brothel.

A Hadrianic insula in Ostia Antica between the north wall of the castrum and the Tiber, comprising the houses of Jove and Ganymede, of the Infant Bacchus, and of the Paintings, arranged according to an L-shaped plan. Its façade faced onto two streets, forming a corner, while its inner sides looked out onto a large garden, without porticoes.
Intercisa/Petra Pertusa was a road station on the Via Flaminia. The toponym derives from the rock-cut tunnel or galleria that dates to the reign of Vespasian.
A Sabine town that was later known as a mansio on the course of the Via Salaria.
The Ionian Sea, located south of the Adriatic Sea, is an elongated embayment of the Mediterranean Sea.
An ancient settlement, located at modern Aytap on the southern coast of Turkey.
The Irish Sea separates the islands of Ireland and Great Britain.
A mountain mentioned in an inscribed Roman boundary demarcation from the area of modern Genova, dating to 117 BCE. Modern scholars place this peak in the vicinity of the modern Passo dei Giovi.
A Bronze Age kurgan site in the Stavropol region.
A hypogeum tomb of the Hellenistic period in Neapolis (now Naples, Italy).
The so-called Hypogeum of the Garlands is an ancient tomb located at the tenth mile of the ancient Via Latina. The tomb dates to either the first or second century CE.
The Scrivia river is a tributary of the Po river.
Iria fl. (Staffora river) is a river of northern Italy that flows from the Ligurian Apennines to the Padus fl. (Po river).
Irni was the site of a Roman municipium located in the Conventus Hispalensis (Baetica) - the Municipium Flavium Irnitanum. Findspot of the Lex Irnitana, a copy of a Flavian municipal law.

The Irno river is a river of Campania that flows into the Tyrrhenian Sea. While its ancient name is unknown, the river valley is the site of first millennium B.C. settlement and also the site of numerous clay beds exploited for pottery production.
A pass through the Hissar mountains in modern Uzbekistan, located just west of the village of Darband/Derbent.
A nuragic shrine with a sacred well.
The Isère River flows into the Rhône River at Pont-de-l'Isère.

A river of Northern Italy and the second longest river in South Tyrol. The river flows from Its source near the Brenner Pass and joins the Adige near Bolzano. The river drains an area of ca. 4,200 km².
An ancient settlement, modern Zengibar Kalesi in Turkey.
An ancient settlement, modern Bozkır in Turkey.
An ancient river of southwest Sicily, the modern Fiume Verdura
Mound, sometimes associated with the ancient city Tummal, which is located in the modern Afak subdistrict of Iraq's Al-Qādisiyyah governorate.
An ancient island or island group, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today

Now lost, the so-called "Isis Tomb" was excavated at Vulci in the 19th century. Based on finds evidence, the tomb is traditionally dated ca. 625 to 550 B.C. Its traditionally assigned name is likely a misnomer, based on a contemporary identification of a bronze bust as representing the Egyptian goddess Isis. The subsequent back-filling of the tomb and uncareful recording at the time have caused th
The River Exe flows into the English Channel at Lyme Bay.
An ancient river, now dried up, that ran through the East side of Thebes.
Isola de San Lazzaro degli Armeni

Small island in the Venetian Lagoon. A church and monastery were constructed on the site during the 9th century CE, and it was used as a leper colony in the medieval and early modern periods. Since 1717 CE, it has been home to an Armenian Catholic (Mkhitarist) monastery, from which the island derives its modern name.
An island in the Ligurian Sea.
Issicus Sinus (the Gulf of İskenderun) is a gulf of the Levantine Sea.

Saka burial ground in modern Issyk, Kazakhstan, containing over 40 kurgans dated from the 4th-3rd centuries BCE. The primary kurgan contained the burial of a richly-dressed individual now known as the "Golden Man."
Isthmia was a major sanctuary located on the Isthmus of Corinth, which was sacred to Poseidon and Melikertes Palaimon, and site of the panhellenic Isthmian games.
A Byzantine fortress erected in the fifth century CE that includes three gates and 21 towers.
A mountain mentioned in ancient sources, probably Ag. Deka (central Kerkyra).
A mountain, probably Pantokrator (in the northern part of Kerkyra).
One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Apulia and Calabria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.
Italic temple of Castel di Ieri
The remains of an Italic temple, in the locality known as "Pié di Francia". The sanctuary dates from the fourth to first centuries B.C.
Modern Mt. Vurkano, Ithome was the principal high point of ancient Messenia and location of the ancient settlement of Messene and principal Messenian sanctuaries.
A Roman road station, mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary. It was located at modern L’Aigüeta in Figures, Spain.
An important Latial sanctuary of Iuppiter located on Mons Albanus (modern Monte Cavo).

A Roman site used for the extraction and preparation of lime. At least six lime kilns have been identified at the site. These were operated by Roman legionaries of the Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix and Legio I Minervia from ca. A.D. 150 to 300.
Bronze age burial site near the banks of the Seversky Donets.
Unexcavated military barracks reworked from private houses in Block J2 at Dura-Europos.
Unexcavated military barracks reworked from private houses in Block J3 at Dura-Europos.
Unexcavated military barracks reworked from private houses in Block J4 at Dura-Europos.
Unexcavated military barracks reworked from private houses in Block J8 at Dura-Europos.

Hill southwest of Mount 'Abd al-'Aziz in Syria. The peak at the southwestern end of the hill is known as Rās et-Tell. Excavations were carried out there by Max von Oppenheim in the early 20th century, uncovering sculptures and graves from the Bronze Age.

An archaeological site in the area of the ancient port of Marseille, the so-called "Jardin des Vestiges" preserves material remains of the many phases of the city's human occupations, including Greek and Roman fortifications, tombs, and port infrastructure.
The ancient Hedyphon River is probably to be associated with the modern Jarahi River.

Jebel Barkal is a mountain that, ca. 1450 BC, was considered the limit of the New Kingdom empire of the Egyptian Pharaoh Thutmose III. Numerous archaeological sites connected with Nubia and the Kingdom of Kush surround Jebel Barka, all of which are listed on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
The Roman-period name of Jebel Moraba is not known.
Settlement south of the village of Khirbet el-Qom in the West Bank with Early Bronze Age remains.
This mountain, which lies on the modern border between Syria and Turkey, has a long history as a sacred site.
A site located in Balkh Province, east of Dilbarjin. The material observed at the site dates to the Hellenistic, Kushan, and Early Sasanian periods.

A Romano-Celtic temple dating probably to the fourth century CE. Its ancient name is unknown. The name of the hill on which it sits is spelled "Jordon" in some twentieth-century works, including the Barrington Atlas.
An ancient settlement of southeastern Spain, whose ancient name is not known today. Occupation of the area seems to stretch from the bronze age up to modern times.

The well of Junia Rufina at Butrint is located near the Lion Gate. The building is a monumentalized spring house with a Greek inscription that names Junia Rufina as patron: "Junia Rufina, friend of the Nymphs." Its construction dates to the reign of Hadrian.

One of the Inner Hebrides islands of Scotland with evidence of human habitation stretching back to the Mesolithic period. It is one possible identification for an ancient "Riginia" island mentioned in ancient sources.
Military barracks located north of the camp wall in the northern part of Block K3 at Dura-Europos.
Military barracks located north of the camp wall in the northern part of Block K5 at Dura-Europos; contains two identifiable units including Barracks K5-A and Barracks K5-B.
Military barracks located north of the camp wall in the northern part of Block K7 at Dura-Europos.
A stone monument located in the Naqsh-e Rustam compound.

Kadembas (Katepants) is a modern settlement in the Van Province in the Southeast of Turkey. Here several rock inscriptions of the Urartian king Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) were found which report the construction of the “Canal of Minua” which is still in use today. Furthermore a rock inscription of Tariria, wife of Minua, (9th / 8th century BCE) is located here which attributes a vineyard to her
Kadmat Island, also known as Cardamom Island, belongs to the Amindivi Subgroup of islands of the Lakshadweep archipelago.

Modern Punta del Pezzo on the Calabrian coast of Italy, opposite Sicily and north of Rhegion. According to Strabo, the promontory was located near the Scyllaean rock, opposite the Pelorus promontory in Sicily.
An ancient settlement of west Macedonia, mentioned by Procopius as one of many whose fortifications were reconstructed under Justinian.
Late Helladic III coastal settlement on the Saronic Gulf in the southeastern Corinthia
Kale Peuke ("beautiful pines") was an ancient settlement of the Troad, located north of Gürgen Dağ. Strabo mentions the site in his text.

Kalecik (formerly known as Aralesk or Lesk) is a modern village situated ca. 5 km north of Van Kalesi in southeast Turkey. In the village church, a re-used cylindrical stone (presumably a column base) with a building inscription of the Urartian king Išpuini, son of Sarduri I (ninth century BCE), was found. Furthermore, a re-used stone slab with an inscription of the Urartian king Argišti, son of M

Kaleköy is a modern village situated ca. 15 km northeast of Mazgirt and ca. 90 km to the north-northeast of Elaziğ in the southeast of Turkey. In the cliff face above the village, lies an Urartian rock-cut tomb. At the left of its entrance is a rock-cut inscription of the Urartian king Rusa, son of Argišti II (seventh century BCE) (CTU I A 12-6). Nowadays the inscription is heavily damaged.
An ancient settlement in Macedonia, located near modern Kalamoto.
A city of the Rhodian Peraea located close to the Gulf of Kos.
A modern settlement on the east coast of Sri Lanka (Ampara district, Eastern province). It was the reported findspot of a single Roman bronze coin.
Find place for a collection of gold and silver objects from the 1st Millenium BCE.

An embayment of the Mediterranean Sea on the southern coastline of Crete, some 7 km east of Cape Lithinon, 2 km west of Lasaia, and 10 km west of Lebena. The location is noted for the visit of the Christian apostle St. Paul in ca. 47 CE.
The Kalon Oros is mentioned in the Periplus Maris Erythraei and has been identified by modern scholars with the modern Jebel Akhdar in Oman.
The Kaloukones? were an ancient tribe located in what is now Germany. Their territory lay close to that of the Suebi.

A modern settlement located in the Puttalam district of Sri Lanka's North Western province. In the early 20th century, Roman bronze coins of the 4th and 5th centuries CE were reported to have been found in the vicinity.
The Mycenaean acropolis of Kanakia is located on the island of Salamis.
Neduntheevu is an island in the Palk Strait, northern Sri Lanka.
An ancient city of India, founded in the 4th century BCE and frequently mentioned in literature thereafter, is still a center of religious life and architecture, as well as the textile industry.

The western-most ancient mouth of the Nile river, located just east of the city of Canopus. It was fed by the Canopic (Kanobikos) branch of the Nile and emptied into the Canopic Gulf (Kanopikos Kolpos).

Kanopikos Kolpos, the modern Abu Qir Bay, is an embayment of the Mediterranean Sea located near Alexandria in Egypt between the Rosetta mouth of the Nile River and Abu Qir. The ancient cities of Canopus, Herakleion, and Menouthis are submerged beneath its waters.
A place from the TAVO Index
Kantharos Limen was the largest harbor area of the Piraeus.
Kantion Akron (South Foreland) is a chalk headland on the coast of southeast England.

An ancient place, located in modern Syria, with remains of an ancient church and residential buildings. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 as part of the "Ancient Villages of Northern Syria."
A Buddhist monastery constructed near the city of Tarmita/Termez in the early second century CE.
Necropolis in western Azerbaijan containing 46 burials dated to the Late Bronze Age/early Iron Age, the Late Antique period, and the 14th century CE.
At Karaftu is a series of rock-cut chambers with a Greek inscription, dating to the fourth or third century BCE. The site is located in Kordestān Province, Iran.

Karagündüz (Armenian name: Charakonis) is a modern village on the eastern coast of Lake Erceç in southeastern Turkey. Here a stela with an inscription of the Urartian kings Išpuini (9th century BCE) and Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) was found which praises the victory over the cites Mešta, Qua, Šaritu, and Nigibi and the land Paršua and gives detailed information about the numbers of soldiers, spo
Karalis (modern Lake Beyşehir or Beyşehir Gölü) is a large freshwater lake in Asia Minor.
Karambis or Carambis was an ancient city of Paphlagonia. The ancient site is tentatively located near Fakas in Asiatic Turkey.

Karataş is a modern settlement situated at the northern bank of Lake Van and 2 km in the east of Erciş in the southeast of Turkey. Here two rock inscriptions of the Urartian king Sarduri II., son of Argišti (8th century BCE) have been found. One of them is of annalistic contents (CTU A 9-10), the other reports the plantation of a vineyard in this region (CTU A 9-11).
A late Hittite fortress (Azatiwataya) located in Cilicia that became a significant Neo-Hittite center after the collapse of the Hittite Empire.
Burial site in the Northern Altai region containing remains associated with the Bulan-Koby culture (2nd-5th centuries CE).
An ancient settlement, located on the Kalanchak estuary, Ukraine.
An ancient river, probably to be identified with the modern Zamantı in Turkey's Adana province.
A place from the TAVO Index

The modern Karun river flows from the Zard-Kuh mountains to the Persian Gulf. In earlier Arabic and Persian sources, it was known as the Dudjayl and may be identifiable with the attested classical Greek Pasitigris.
A city with an extensive circuit wall, temple, theater, and agora.
A tumulus of Macedonian or Roman date located in the hinterland of Amphipolis. The tomb was discovered in 2012 and first entered in 2014.
The site of a pre-Roman Celtic oppidum.
A Roman fort on the Raetian limes, located in what is now Aalen in the modern German state of Baden-Württemberg. It was garrisoned by the Ala II Flavia Miliaria Pia Fidelis.
A Roman border fort and associated vicus located near the modern German town of Schramberg.
Extensive Roman bathhouse associated with the Roman fort at modern Schirenhof in the German municipality of Schwäbisch Gmünd, Baden-Württemberg.
Hill in Khania, Crete, that was the center of the Minoan city of Cydonia and was later a Roman acropolis.

A small fortress on modern Sokha peak between Mytikas and Archondochori in the municipality of Xiromero, Aetolia-Acarnania, Greece. The fortress wall makes use of local stone, mixing polygonal and trapezoidal styles. A rock-cut cistern is located inside the fort, and Hellenistic reliefs have been noted. The site has broad intervisibility with the Mytikas valley and the channel around both sides of
An archaeological site containing Bronze Age burials located near the confluence of the Wadi Zarqa and the Jordan River.
Chance finds and rescue excavations in the vicinity of modern Katerini (Pieria, Greece) indicate the presence of burials and manufacturing facilities in the area during antiquity.

The Kathaioi/Xathroi were a people of ancient India subjugated by Alexander the Great. Their territory lay in the Punjab either to the east of the Hydraotes or between the Hydaspes and Acesines rivers.
J. Ober indicates that Katsimidi was a fortified site that occupied a steep hill on the west side of the Klidi pass, some 7 km north of the town of Barimpompi.
One of two localizations in the Peloponnese given by ancient sources for descendants of a tribe mentioned in Homer. The other was in Triphylia.
One of two localizations in the Peloponnese given by ancient sources for descendants of a tribe mentioned in Homer. The other was in Achaia.
Kefar Nahum/Kapharnaoum was a Hasmonean village located on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee.
The mountain known in antiquity as Kelossa is the modern Megalovouni to the southwest of Nemea.
A "Kenchreai in the Troad," mentioned first by Stephanus, is probably to be identified with a settlement of Roman date, located atop the Kayalı Dağ in modern Turkey.
The site of an Assyrian relief of Shalmaneser III, which is located 10 km away from the Karasu relief.
The modern Botan River in Turkey. It is a tributary of the Tigris River.
A Neolithic site and cemetery on Keos.
A sixth century BC colony of Miletus founded on the Gulf of Taman.
A mountain placed near Colophon by ancient testimony. The modern Karacadağ in Turkey's Izmir province.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A Punic city of northeastern Tunisia, near Cape Bon, abandoned ca. 250 BC (cited: BAtlas 32 H3 Kerkouane)
A complex of 555 megaliths arranged in 13 rows.
An extensive necropolis of the Kerma culture located on Sai Island.
Cave tomb complex located southwest of Jerusalem containing burials dated to the 6th century BCE.
A mountain range that bordered Noricum in the east and Pannonia in the west.
Burial site in western Mongolia containing a stone cairn and several deer stone monuments, dated to the 8th-7th centuries BCE.
Early Islamic town in northern Syria, inhabited during the 8th-9th centuries CE.
Kharaneh IV is an archaeological site located in Jordan. This site has produced evidence of human occupation during the Late Pleistocene, ca. 18,900 to 16,600 BCE.
A fortified site on the banks of the Wadi al-Wala in Jordan inhabited in the Early Bronze IV period.
A small Moabite sanctuary within a walled-in enclosure was discovered on the Wadi ath-Thamad in Jordan.
Necropolis in the West Bank near the modern village of Beit Ummar dated to the Middle Bronze Age.
Settlement near the modern city of Zarqa in Jordan, inhabited during the Early Bronze Age (ca. 3000-2000 BCE).
Fort located near ancient Emmaus in the West Bank, constructed in the Hellenistic period and expanded with additional fortifications during the Roman period.
Settlement in northern Jordan dated to the Early Bronze Age.

Khush Tepe, also known as Tepe Fullol, is a burial site associated with the Oxus Civilization. Discovered in 1966, the site contained gold and silver vessels dated to the Bronze Age (ca. 2600-1700 BCE).
A Classical-period sanctuary at Khondro Teikhos, "said to be somewhere NE of Glossa in Skopelos, Sporades, Magnesia, Thessaly" (according to ToposText).
This decorated gate is located on the western wall of the citadel of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon"), the capital of the Assyrian Empire constructed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC).
This decorated gate was the principal entrance to the citadel of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon"), the capital of the Assyrian Empire constructed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC).
This undecorated gate is the southernmost city gate of the northeast wall of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon"), the capital of the Assyrian Empire constructed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC).
This decorated gate is the northernmost city gate of the southeast wall of Dūr-Šarrukīn ("Fort Sargon"), the capital of the Assyrian Empire constructed by Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC).
An ancient river of Asia Minor, associated by scholars with the modern Küçük Melen Su/Çayi in Turkey.
A deme of ancient Attica that belonged to the phyle of Acamantis.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: upper valley of R. Ostriconi.
The Cilician Gates, a pass through the Taurus Mountains connecting Cilicia to the Anatolian Plateau, by way of the gorge of the Gökoluk River.
A place from the TAVO Index

The Kinaidokolpitai were an ancient people inhabiting the western coastal strip of the Arabian Peninsula. The Barrington Atlas Directory notes that their territory was located from Yanbu' to the west of Baysh in Saudi Arabia.

The King's Stables is an archaeological site located in County Armagh, Northern Ireland. In antiquity, this was an anthropic pool (25 meters in diameter) surrounded by an earthen berm. It dates ca. 1000 BCE and was a site of votive offerings, including weaponry and animal bones; a human cranium was also discovered.
Early Iron Age settlement on the Sea of Galilee covering about 25 acres of a hilltop.

Archaeological site in Burkina Faso occupied from the early first millennium CE through c. 1700. The site consists of a mound spread over approximately 37 hectares. Evidence for ironworking is present along with household structures.
Kirkaion Akron/Veneris Pr. (Monte Circeo) is a mountainous promontory on the Tyrrhenian coast of Italy.
Mountain in central Greece, south of Delphi.
Kish is an island in the Persian Gulf.
Cn. Scipio defeated Hanno somewhere near Kissa in 218 BCE, before capturing the town by assault.
