A fort on Hadrian's Wall known today as Halton Chesters.

This ancient cape of the Peloponnese is now known as the island of Elaphonisas, separated from the mainland reportedly by a fourth-century earthquake. The island's southwestern terminus -- the modern Akra Ag. Maria -- would correspond to the tip of the ancient promontory.

Oostvoorne may correspond to a putative Roman period place that once protected the Meuse river estuary (Helinium) and therefore may have carried its name. Coastal change has long since consumed any remains of the Roman site; a Medieval castle is still attested.
An island located in the southern Sea of Marmara.
Opone, mentioned in the first-century A.D. Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, was a trading center located in the Horn of Africa, likely in the area of present day Hafun, Somalia.
An ancient settlement mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary and usually associated with modern Ksar el Kebir in Morocco.
A Gallic oppidum occupied from the sixth century B.C.
Oram's Arbour, now a park, was the site of Iron Age occupation prior to the establishment of Venta. Location based on OpenStreetMap.
The site of a palatial Roman villa dating to the first and second centuries A.D. Discovered in 1841, the site is noted for its extensive in situ mosaic pavements.
The Orcia originates on Monte Cetona and is a major tributary of the Ombrone.
A Pre-Roman Celtic tribe inhabiting part of what is now Wales, the Ordovices' territory was bonded by the Silures to the south and the Deceangli to the north-east.

Ordu-Baliq, also known as Mubalik and Karabalghasun, was once the capital of the Uyghur Khaganate. The ruins of this settlement are now included as part of the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape World Heritage Site in Mongolia.
Oreine Ins. (Dissei) is an island in the Red Sea.
The Oreioi were a league of states centered in the mountains of western Crete.
An ancient people dwelling on the coast of Gedrosia, and encountered by Alexander the Great during his march from the Indus River to Persia.
Orgus fl. (Orco river) is a river of northern Italy and a tributary of the Padus fl. (Po river).

Ancient Greek and Roman sources refer to the Bay of Bengal, which forms the northeastern portion of the Indian Ocean, by these names. It was also sometimes construed as an ocean entirely surrounding Asia.
A coastal island of Sicily that became the center of ancient Syracuse.
The Osireion at Abydos is located to the rear of the temple of Seti I. It is an integral part of Seti I's funeral complex and was built to resemble an 18th Dynasty Valley of the Kings tomb.
Oskela? (modern Domodossola) was a chief settlement of the Lepontii and was conquered by the Romans in 12 BC.

The ancient synagogue located in Ostia Antica is one of the oldest known synagogues in the world. The structure's earliest phase dates to the reign of Claudius and it continued in use until the fifth century.
A peak of mount Mainalion in Arcadia; perhaps to be identified with the peak accorded this name in modern times.
A large celtic hillfort located in the modern German municipality of Nonnweiler in the northern Saarland.

The "Old Rhine" is now a branch of the Rhine River delta in the Dutch provinces of Utrecht and South Holland. In antiquity, this was a part of the main River Rhine, which forked at the Betuwe into a northern branch, the Rhine, and a southern branch, the Waal.
This ancient river is identified by modern scholars with the Kuma, which empties into the Caspian Sea from the west.
An ancient village site, said by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas) to be located on the left bank of the Oued Chélif (ancient Chulimath), just east of its confluence with the Oued Sly.
Ouedra/Adron fl. flows eastward from the Pennines to the North Sea.
The Celtic Sea is a region of the Atlantic Ocean off the south coast of Ireland.
The modern Aliso river in northern Corsica.

An ancient estuary cataloged by Ptolemy. BAtlas was only confident enough to locate it somewhere in modern Somerset, listing it as an "unlocated" feature in the Map-by-Map Directory. Other scholarly suggestions include the Axe and the Parrett rivers.
The Oval Forum at Jerash dates to the reign of Hadrian.

Ptolemy provides this name for a promontory of Sri Lanka, which BAtlDir identifies with the southern cape of Koddiyar Bay (i.e., the promontory at the tip of which the so-called Foul Point lighthouse now stands).
An ancient people whose territory is unlocated
The Oxubii or Oxybii were a Ligurian tribe inhabiting the coast of France near Massalia.
Minoan cemetery located on a sandy beach in use from very early times until the Late Minoan period.
The Kishon River flows from the Gilboa mountains to the Mediterranean Sea.
A Roman villa located on the Bruna river that was in use from the third century B.C. until the fifth century A.D.
Pagus Meflanus was likely located in the Apennines to the northeast of Beneventum.
The Pagus Vescinus is only attested epigraphically.

At Paikuli, located in what is now the southern part of Iraqi Kurdistan near the modern-day village of Barkal, Sulaymaniyah Governorate, Iraq, are the remains of a stone masonry tower that was erected as a monument to a victory enjoyed by the Sasanian emperor Narseh over his grandnephew. The inscription is now housed in the Sulaymaniyah Museum.

Palace at Ebla dated to the early Bronze Age (24th century BCE), built atop the remains of an older palace (designated G2). Palace G, destroyed around 2300 BCE, contained an extensive archive of clay tablets.
A large-scale building, tentatively identified as a palace, constructed during the 9th century BCE and in use until about 500 CE.
The ruins of a colonnaded structure in marble, perhaps a temple; a well / cistern is also observed by Sealy.
A Classical and Hellenistic settlement featuring a unique, square fortification wall that was located just south of the Kephissos river
A fortified site located on the island of Skyros with Early Bronze Age activity.

Enclosed area at the Iron Age city of Pteria (modern Kerkenes Dağ) containing an audience hall and other elite structures. The complex is in an area of the city that was destroyed by fire, most likely in the mid-5th century BCE.
The central hill of Rome, Italy. Legend held that Romulus founded the city of Rome on the Palatine Hill following an augural contest with Remus, his brother.

Rome's Palazzo Valentini was first built in 1585 on the site of a pre-existing palazzo located adjacent to what was then the piazza dei Santi Apostoli. The palazzo's foundations are entangled with various ancient remains, including perhaps architectural elements of the Forum of Trajan.
The site of one of the twelve villas of Tiberius, and perhaps the largest, on the island of Capreae.
The classical and Hellenistic period acropolis of the island of Nisyros dates from the sixth to the fourth century BCE.
A pair of boiling lakes in Sicily, whose effervescence was attributed to the divine agency of the Palikoi.
Site of a late Bronze Age settlement near the modern village of Alassa, southern Cyprus.
The Pallia is a tributary of the Tiber River.
Main entrance gate in the western city walls of Dura-Europos. Built ca. 150 BCE, the city's fortifications were breached sometime around 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.
Pamphylium Mare, the modern Gulf of Antalya, is an embayment of the Mediterranean Sea.

The Phyle Cave located on Mount Parnes near Fyli (Phyle), Greece, is a small cave that served in antiquity as a shrine sacred to the god Pan. It is one of five such cave sanctuaries dedicated to Pan known in ancient Attica.

The church of Panagia tis Angeloktistis or Panagia Angeloktisti is a Byzantine church located in the village of Kiti, Cyprus. Its origins lies in the fifth and sixth centuries. It was listed as a tentative UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015.

A twelfth-century CE Greek Orthodox church located north of modern Livadia on Cyprus' Karpasia peninsula. Its apse had been adapted from part of an older building and contained a 7th-century mosaic of the Theotokos (i.e., Mary, mother of Jesus).

A stadium in Athens, built in 329 BC under Lykourgos and rebuilt in marble by Herodes Atticus in 139-143 AD. Since its excavation in the late 19th century, the rebuilt stadium has featured in events related to the modern Olympics.
Pandosia was an ancient city of Bruttium.
Pandosia? was a colony founded by Elis on the river Acheron.
A sanctuary with votive deposits dating to the Hellenistic period at Panetelle di Mondragone.
A fortified Phoenico-Punic settlement on Sardinia with two necropoleis.
Located near Mt. Mycale, the Panionion was an Ionian sanctuary dedicated to Poseidon Helikonios that served as the meeting place of the Ionian League.
Site of a late Bronze Age settlement near the modern village of Alassa, southern Cyprus.
An ancient settlement on the Aegean island of Astypalaia.
A narrow, long bay opening on the north side of the modern Küdür peninsula in the Bodrum district of Turkey's Muğla province. BAtlDir offers the modern name "Alaman Gölü".
An ancient harbor (limen) on the north coast of the Peloponnese, mentioned by Pausanias as lying 15 stadia to the east of the Rhion Pr. (modern Rio in Greece).

An ancient harbor or bay, now largely in-filled, that extended eastward inland from modern Turkey's Gulf of Kuşadası. The area of the ancient feature, as reconstructed in BAtlas map 61, is partially coincident today with the western half of the Izmir Selçuk Gebekirse Lake Wildlife Development Area.
Panskoye 1 was an agricultural settlement in the Crimea founded by by Chersonesus in the late fourth century BC.

The estate (tenuta) of Pantano Borghese is one of the oldest land holdings in the Agro Romano and was acquired by the Colonna family in 1613. Much of this low-lying area was once marshland at the margins of the crater lakes of this part of Latium. Thomas Ashby's work on the Roman Campagna documented numerous archaeological and epigraphical remains in this zone, including extensive remains of Roman
The main city and port of the Kimmerian Bosporus, founded by Miletus in the late seventh or early sixth centuries B.C. Modern Kerch.
An ancient river, emptying into the Black Sea. The modern Golyama Kamchiya in Bulgaria.
A mountainous area in the vicinity of the Caspian, possibly to be associated with the Alburz and Talish mountains.
Neolithic tomb located 1km east of the modern village of Paradiimi in Northeastern Greece.

The underwater archaeological park of Baia is a protected marine and cultural heritage area. Submerged beneath the waters of the Gulf of Naples are various Roman-period archaeological remains, including those of harbors, villas, shrines, and nymphaea.
Parco delle Tombe di via Latina
A cluster of Roman Imperial tombs along the Via Latina excavated in the nineteenth century.
BAtlas 24 H3 Paredes de los Mercados
BAtlas 65 E1 Parlais/Col. Iulia Augusta Hadriana

Parndorf was the site of a Roman estate covering some 12 ha. The villa was situated near the Roman road leading from Savaria-Scarbantia to Carnuntum. The site was fortified by means of an enclosure wall ca. 1.5 km long.
A densely forested mountain range located to the north of Athens.
An ancient settlement of Arcadia, possibly to be identified with modern Palaiomoiri.
A river that originates in the Anti-Taurus Mountains and is a major tributary of the Tigris.
On a hill southwest of the modern Greek town of Partheni, a fortified Classical-Hellenistic settlement has been identified with the attested ancient Eritrean deme of Parthenion.
A settlement attested in ancient sources, that was probably located along the modern Ilias Çay in Turkey, downstream from the modern Yortanlı dam.
An ancient river of Asia Minor, emptying into the Black Sea (modern Bartın Irmaği/Bartin Su in Turkey).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: middle Shkumbini valley ALB.
Roman mine on Parys Mountain, Wales.
A small island that is part of the Oinoussai island group, located between Chios and the Ionian peninsula. Its ancient name is unknown.
A group of temples featuring nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary dating to the seventh and eighth centuries CE and connected with the Chalukya dynasty.
An archaeological site located near Malvito in southern Italy, where excavation has revealed a portion of a Roman nucleus of habitation that includes domestic spaces and a bath complex.
A Punic farm site occupied from the fourth to the second century B.C.
Pausilipum was an ancient Graeco-Roman settlement on the Bay of Naples.
An ancient Roman city of Lustiania.
Pech Maho was an indigenous oppidum and Greek way station. The excavated site lies northeast of the modern French town of Sigean in the Occitania administrative region.
A headland in the southeastern part of the island of Cyprus.
Located in Caria, Pedasa is one of the eight Lelegian towns mentioned by Strabo.
Pednelissos was an ancient settlement in Pisidia near to the Eurymedon river.
A gate in the Themistoklean Walls of Athens, through which the road to Peiraeus ran.
An ancient island, probably to be associated with the modern Hekim Adası.
A major city of western Thessaly.
Mycenaean chamber tombs located to the north of Pellana in Laconia.
A lake near Buthrotum that served as a port.
A Roman auxiliary fort in Powys, situated midway along the Roman road linking the forts at Brecon Gaer (Cicutio) and Abergavenny (Gobannio).
The Peneios is the chief river of Thessaly.
Romano-British settlement and military complex located at present day Water Eaton, UK
Pentelikon/Brilessos is a mountain to the northeast of Athens that was famous for its fine-grained marble.
The Pentri were a major tribe of Oscan-speaking Samnites; their chief center was Bovianum Undecumanorum.
An island of the western Aegean Sea (modern Skopelos).
Archaeological excavations at Pépiron in the commune of Saint-Just, near Marennes in Charente-Maritime, France, revealed the remains of a Roman villa rustica.
Cave located near the modern village of al-Buqei'a, used as a burial site in the late Chalcolithic period.
The so-called Great Gymnasium of Pergamon was built in the second quarter of the second century BCE. The complex was then restored in the first century BCE.
An ancient Greek city of Asia Minor and capital of Pamphylia.
Perperakion was an ancient Thracian city located on a high hill in the eastern Rhodope mountains.
Persian and Hellenistic Administrative Building (PHAB), Tel Kedesh
The Persian and Hellenistic Administrative Building was constructed at Tel Kedesh by the Persians in the mid-4th century BCE and was in use through the middle Hellenistic Period (around 143 BCE).
The Persian Gulf is located in Western Asia between Persia and the Arabian Peninsula.
Ancient Peshawar was a capital of the Gandharan kingdom from the second century AD, when it was known as Purushapura.

A Roman legionary encampment (castrum) associated with the Legio X Gemina that later developed into a Roman town. The site is located in the Vidriales valley in the province of Zamora (Castilla y Leon).
Petras Megas (known as Bardia or Bórdi Slemán) is a port settlement located in eastern Libya.

One of several named villas in the territory of Albiga that Desiderius of Cahors gave, from his inheritance, to the church. Its precise location cannot be determined today; BAtlas tentatively places it in the area of modern Peyregoux.
The Peucetii were an ancient tribe of Apulia in southern Italy.
Peukelaotis/Kaspatyros? was an ancient city in Gandhāra located along the trade route connecting Bactria to India.
The island of Fleves in the Saronic Gulf.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Tsambikas, on Rhodos.
Phalakrai, Summit of Ida Mons, cited: BAtlas 56 D2
A fortress named after Phalaris, a tyrant of Acragas and located near the Himera River.
An ancient harbor town located on the northwest coast of Crete.

A promontory, listed by Ptolemy among other coastal features of Euboea, Phalassia is probably to be associated with a promontory on the Malian Gulf in the modern locality of Βασιλίνας (Vasilinas) where a late 19th century lighthouse now stands.
A cemetery at Phaleron with burials ranging in date from the Archaic to the Classical period.

The northwest portion of the Taman' peninsula, which is the modern landmass on the Straits of Kerch' opposite modern Kerch' and the eastern Crimea. Modern geophysical study and ancient testimony indicate that this peninsula was an island in antiquity.
A large ancient sanctuary of Apollo, located on the southwest coast of the island of Chios.
Phara(i) was an ancient settlement of western Achaea, located west of the Peirus river.
Pheradi Maius was a civitas of Africa Proconsularis. The archaeological site is today located near the village of Sidi Khelifa, Tunisia.
Phiale Limne (Lake Ram (Hebrew: בריכת רם‎)) is a crater lake located in the Golan Heights.
A Hellenistic fortified site located southwest of modern Philippaioi in the municipal territory of Grevena in Greece's decentralized administration of Epirus and Western Macedonia
The Philippeion is a tholos at Olympia constructed to celebrate Philip II's victory at Chaeonea in 338 BCE and completed by Alexander the Great.
An ancient city located in the valley of the river Asopos.
An ancient settlement, attested by literary or documentary sources, whose precise location cannot be determined today
Phoinix M. ( Karayüksekdağ) ca. 516 m ASL
Pholegandros is an island in the Aegean Sea located in the southern part of the Cyclades.
Ancient sources separately provide the names Phrourion and Boosoura for capes on the southern coast of Cyprus. Modern scholars tentatively identify both names with modern Cape Aspros/Aspron.

Phrygia was an ancient kingdom of west-central Anatolia, developing around Gordion beginning in the ninth century BCE. According to Strabo, the Cimmerians defeated and overran the Phrygian kingdom in the seventh century BCE.
The Phyrites river is a tributary of the Cayster.
The Pian del Vescovo is the western necropolis of Blera and perhaps the most extensive. A variety of tomb types dating to the seventh and sixth centuries BCE are attested.
A monumental rock-cut necropolis at Tuscania.
A large Christian basilica discovered in 1976 several hundred meters southeast of the Porta Laurentina of Ostia. The original phase dates to the end of the fourth century A.D.
Pianello di Genga, located in Italy's Ancona province, was the site of a Final Bronze Age settlement, as attested by an extensive necropolis.
A Roman cistern dating to the second-third centuries CE.

One of the largest and most luxurious complexes of Villa Hadriani. It is situated at the northern end of the Villa, and consists of a vast building, with a vaulted, octagonal vestibule to the north, a cenatio to the south, and a central quadriporticus, down the middle of which runs a canal.
The Pictones were a Celtic tribe that inhabited an area along the south bank of the Loire river near the Bay of Biscay.
Pieve di Sant'Antonino a Socana, a Medieval parish church, is built atop the remains of an Etruscan sanctuary.
Pieve di San Giovanni Battista a Sillano

A ruined church that was once part of the diocese of Volterra, San Giovanni Battista a Sillano is unique in Tuscany for having a Romanesque-Norman façade. The ruined edifice likely dates to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries although the parish exists as early as the mid-tenth century.
A Late Bronze Age settlement and sanctuary.
Pinara was a city of Lycia located at the foot of Mount Cragus (now Mount Babadağ).
An ancient river located in what is now the country of Turkey. It is probably to be identified with either Deli Çay or Payas Çayı.

The Pincian Hill in Rome likely takes its name from the Pincii, an ancient family. It is not considered a member of the canonical grouping of Rome's hills, but it did lie within the line of the walls built by Aurelian. In the early Imperial period, it is known as a zone of elaborate gardens, hence the moniker "collis hortulorum".

The so-called Pincian obelisk is a monument of red granite that Hadrian brought to Rome from Egypt. It bears hieroglyphics that were likely cut at Rome and seem to indicate that the monument in some way commemorated the place where Antinous was buried. Fragments of the monument were re-erected near the Porta Maggiore in 1570. The Barberini relocated it in 1663, and it was transferred to the Vatica
An ancient mountain in Mysia: the modern Madra Daği in Turkey.
A large mountain range in north and central Greece.
Pirustae were a Pannonian Illyrian tribe that lived in modern Montenegro.
A region of the western Peloponnesus.
A freshwater cistern at Bacoli on the Gulf of Naples, the Piscina Mirabilis likely provided sailors of the Roman fleet with drinking water. Its capacity is estimated at 12,600 cubic meters.
A small shop located in Regio I of Pompeii (I, 8, 7).
Modern Agkistrion in the Saronic Gulf, located to the west of Aegina.
A large island at the entrance to the Argolic Gulf, lying to the southwest off the tip of the peninsula of the Argolid. Modern Spetses.
Pityussae Inss., an ancient island group comprising the islands of Ebusus and Ophiussa.
A Roman necropolis located at Nocera Superiore which was buried by the volcanic ejecta of the Vesuvian eruption of A.D. 79.
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Unnamed minor settlement or villa in the territory of the Machounoi
Described by Ober as a "signal tower and small fortification", Plakoto fort is situated at the northern edge of the Thriasian plain.
An island in the Aegean Sea that is mentioned by Pliny the Elder. It is probably to be identified with the modern Kamilonísi.
Tell site in western Thessaly containing the remains of a settlement and necropolis dated to the early 6th millennium BCE.
Settlement on Crete from the Late Minoan period near Achladia.
A late Minoan tholos tomb in the area of modern Platyskinos/Platyschino on Crete.
A river of northern Italy that flows from the Alps to the Adriatic Sea.
In antiquity, the lacus Plestinus was located in Umbria and was the site of a military engagement during the Second Punic War.

The so-called villa of Pliny the Younger, also known as the Villa della Palombara. The villa's first phases date to the Iulio-Claudian period. It continues in use, and continues to undergo modifications, through the second century A.D.
The Ploutonion at Hierapolis is a walled sanctuary dedicated to Pluto and Kore.
The gathering place of the Athenian Assembly in the Classical Period.

The Iron Age settlement at Poblado de Irulegui is noted as the findspot of the so-called "Hand of Irulegi", a bronze, hand-shaped artifact dated ca. 80 to 72 BCE. This object carries an important inscription written in the Northeastern Iberian script.

Podere Marzuolo was the site of Roman pottery production from the first century B.C. until the early fourth century A.D. The site has yielded evidence for the production of terra sigillata pottery as well as evidence of blacksmithing.
A farm site with a least two occupation phases - one dating between the second century BC and early first century AD and the second between the fourth and fifth centuries AD.
A rural site located in the territory of Volterra.
An Etruscan farm site located in the Albegna valley.
Poetovio (Ptuj, Slovenia) was an ancient city in Pannonia that was the base-camp of Legio XIII Gemina.
Poggibonsi is an ancient and medieval center in the province of Siena on the Elsa river. The city sits along the Via Francigena.
An Etruscan settlement located in the Mugello valley.
An Etruscan tumulus of the fifth century BCE, the tumulus of Poggio Gaiella has been considered by some scholars to be the tomb of Porsenna.
Burial mound near the Sentelek River in Altay, Russia, containing remains associated with the Afanasievo Culture (31st-29th centuries BCE) and the Pazyryk Culture (4th-3rd centuries BCE).
The Roman amphitheater at ancient Pollentia (modern Pollenzo).
Polytimetos fl. (Zeravshan River) is a river of central Asia.
A fortified center of Lucania founded in the fifth century B.C. or earlier, Pomarico Vecchio was influenced by its close contacts with the Greek cities of Magna Graecia.

A building between the Dipylon Gate and the Sacred Gate used for preparing the Panathenaic procession during the Classical and Hellenistic periods, destroyed during the Sullan Sack in 86 B.C., restored ca. A.D. 144, and destroyed again in the Herulian Sack of A.D. 267.
A villa attributed to Cnaeus Pompeius at Albano Laziale.

Pompey (Meurthe-et-Moselle, France) produced archaeological evidence of a Roman productive site located near the junction of the Meurthe and Moselle rivers. This site was discovered in 1962 and has been described as a "villa rustica". There is evidence of baths and painted wall plaster. There is evidence for pottery production at the site, along with agricultural activity. There is a cremation nec
A Roman triumphal column in Alexandria, Egypt.
The Pons Aelius or Aelian Bridge (now Ponte Sant'Angelo) was completed by Hadrian in AD 134 to span the Tiber opposite the new mausoleum of the emperor.
A debated bridge upriver from the modern Ponte Sisto.

A Roman bridge (and possibly coincident road station) on the Via Appia over the Aufidus (modern Ofanto) river in Italy, listed on the Peutinger map and in the Antonine Itinerary. Traditionally it has been identified with a bridge known today as Ponte S. Venere, but recently archaeological work has cast doubt on this view and some scholars now favor an identification with the Ponte romano Pietra de
A Roman bridge across the Cendere Çayı that lies west of Arsameia pros Nymphaio (modern Eskikale in Turkey's Adıyaman Province).

The Pons Sublicius is traditionally held to be the earliest Roman bridge across the river Tiber. The textual tradition assigns its construction to the king Ancus Marcius in 642 B.C. It crossed the Tiber River near the Forum Boarium just downstream from Tiber Island.
A late Republican Roman segmented arch bridge in Padua, Italy.
The bridge known as Ponte Amato carries the Via Praenestina near Gallicano nel Lazio.
A Roman aqueduct bridge located in the comune of Gallicano nel Lazio (Rome, Italy). It was once part of the Aqua Claudia.
The bridge known as Ponte Buriano is located at the hamlet of Ponte a Buriano, Italy. The bridge spans the Arno River and dates initially from 1277.

The Ponte Ceccara, also referred to as the ponte di Terra, is a Republican period bridge located on the fosso di Passerano along the Via Praenestina. It is located within the modern comune of Zagarolo, some 30.5 km southeast of the center of Rome.
Ponte Ezzu or Pont'Ezzu is a Roman bridge of the first century A.D. that crosses the Rio Mannu near Ozieri, Sardinia.
The so-called "Ponte Fabio Massimo" or "Ponte del Diavolo" originally dates to the third century BC with subsequent reworking and reuse continuing to the Middle Ages.
The remains of a late Republican bridge near Benevento (in Località Serretelle).
The so-called Ponte Ladrone was a Roman bridge of the Via Ostiensis located at Acilia. According to L. Quilici, its remaining material vestiges were buried in 1982 by infrastructure works.
Remains of a portion of the Aqua Marcia aqueduct located near Gallicano nel Lazio.
A Roman segmental arch bridge across the Bacchiglione river in Padua, Italy.
A Roman bridge over the Aniene river.
Ponte Romano di Parco dei Medici
The ruins of a second-century A.D. Roman bridge at Magliana Vecchia.
An ancient bridge located to the east of ancient Teanum Sidicinum (modern Teano in Italy).
An ancient bridge, now known as "Ponte Romito" crosses the Arno River to the west of Ponte a Buriano.
An ancient bridge over the Cervaro river between Aecae and Herdoniae on the Via Traiana.
The Ponte Salario is a Medieval bridge with Roman origins. It is located at the point where the Via Salaria crosses the Anio, about 3 km north of the Colline Gate.
The Ponte Sant'Antonio is a Roman aqueduct bridge that was part of the Aqua Anio Novus.
A Roman arched bridge on the Via Flaminia near modern Terni.
An ancient bridge over the Fiora river (the ancient Armenta) near Vulci. Ancient name unknown.
A Medieval bridge across the Serchio River. The bridge was built ca. 1080-1100 and was renovated ca. 1300. It is located along the Via Francigena.

The so-called Ponte della Rocca located on the Via Clodia at Blera is situated adjacent to the Necropolis of San Giovenale and Terrone. Some sources suggest an original date in the third or second centuries BCE.

The so-called Ponte delle Serretelle is an ancient arched bridge located southwest of Benevento, Italy. It lies between the Gran Potenza hill and the Serretelle stream. It may have once been located either at or near the point where the Serretelle and the Calor converged.
A Roman bridge with Augustan origins, known either as Ponte Muto or Ponte delle Vozze, associated with the Via Iulia Augusta and located in the Val Ponci in Liguria.
A Roman arched bridge located near Narni built originally in the Augustan period that remained in use until A.D. 1055.
Ponte di Diocleziano, San Lazzaro di Fossombrone

The so-called "Ponte di Diocleziano" in the local comune of San Lazzaro di Fossombrone was a Roman bridge along the Via Flaminia in the valley of the Metaurus river. The Roman bridge was completely destroyed during the Second World War.
A Roman bridge along the Via Appia.
Remains of a Roman Republican bridge crossing the Fosso di Pratolungo along the line of the via Tiburtina.
The Ponte di Quintodecimo is located near Acquasanta Terme.
Ponte di San Giovanni de Butris
The remains of a Roman bridge along the Via Flaminia that have been incorporated into the thirteenth-century church of San Giovanni de Butris.
Ponte di Traiano at Tor Tre Ponti
A Roman bridge located on the Via Appia at modern Tor Tre Ponti.
The Ponte di Vallerano is a second-century Roman bridge that carried the via Ostiensis across the fosso di Vallerano.

Excavated remains of a Roman bridge located on the modern Via Ponte Romano about 2km southest of Ceggia (Veneto), Italy. Aerial/satellite photographs often show crop marking corresponding to the associated Roman road and now-diverted watercourse spanned by the bridge.
A Roman bridge on the Via Amerina between ancient Nepet and Falerii.

An island placed by Ptolemy off the coast of the Greater Syrtis, along with Maia and Misynos. The name Pontia is used in the plural by Ps. Skylax to identify all three islands as a group. These islands are identified with modern scholars as prominent parts of the modern Legarah reef (Tre Scogli) off the Libyan coast.
An archipelago in the Tyrrhenian Sea off the west coast of Italy.

A number of monumental, rupestral tombs at ancient Amaseia (modern Amasya in Turkey) among which 5 large ones are mentioned by Strabo and attributed to the kings. Mount Harşena and the Rock-tombs of the Pontic Kings were submitted to the Tentative World Heritage Lists in 2005 by the Permanent Delegation of Turkey to UNESCO.
A river, flowing from Monte Leco in the Ligurian Apennines and emptying in the Ligusticum Mare near Genua.
Porolissum was a Roman city in Dacia established in A.D. 106. It became the capital of Dacia Porolissensis in A.D. 124.

At Le Canet, Cm. Port-Ste-Foy-et-Ponchapt, on the west bank of the Dordogne river, a Gallo-Roman villa was discovered in 1922. On the basis of its mosaic decorations, the villa is dated to the later imperial period.
A gate in the Aurelian Wall at the summit of the Ianiculum through which the Via Aurelia passes.
A first century A.D. gate at Verona, the point at which the Via Postumia entered the city.
The Porta Capena was a gate in Rome's Republican city walls ("Servian Wall") located on the south-west slope of the Caelian Hill.
The so-called Porta Eburnea or the Arco della Mandorla is an ancient gate of the Etruscan walls of Perusia.
One of the four gates of the fortified castrum of Allifae. The fortifications are thought to date to the Late Republican period on the basis of building techniques.

The "Porta Flumentana" or "river gate" was a gate in the Republican-period fortifications along the Tiber River. It is now unlocated. While it may have been in the vicinity of the Pons Aemilius, much debate surrounds its topography.
A city gate in the Aurelian Wall that was substantially modified under Honorius in the fifth century A.D.
A Republican gate of Verona dedicated by P. Valerius, Q. Caecilius, Q. Servilius and P. Cornelius.
A city gate at the western terminus of the Strada della Marina.
The so-called Porta Marzia at Perugia began as a third century B.C. gate of the Etruscan city and was engulfed in the fortifications of the Rocca Paolina in 1540.
The Porta Montanara is an ancient Roman gate of Ariminum.
One of the four gates of the fortified castrum of Allifae. The fortifications are thought to date to the Late Republican period on the basis of building techniques.

The so-called "Porta Nigra" is a surviving Roman city gate that dates to ca. A.D. 186-200. It was enlisted as part of the "Roman Monuments, Cathedral of St. Peter and Church of Our Lady in Trier" UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
The Porta Nomentana was a single-arch gateway in the Aurelianic Walls of Rome built between 270 and 273 AD by the emperor Aurelian.
One of the four gates of the fortified castrum of Allifae. The fortifications are thought to date to the Late Republican period on the basis of building techniques.

The Porta Portuensis was one of the gates of the Aurelian Wall of Rome, located in the Transtiberim. The original gate carried an inscription of Honorius and was destroyed during the reign of Pope Urban VIII. The present Porta Portese, built by architect Vincenzo Maculani in 1644, occupies its site.
The Porta Querquetulana was a gateway of Rome's so-called Servian Walls. It derived its name from from a sacred grove of oaks that seems to have vanished by the first century BCE.
The Porta Rauduscula was a gate of Rome's so-called Servian Wall. It is known only from textual sources. Varro's listing places it between the Porta Naevia and the Porta Lavernalis.
One of the four gates of the fortified castrum of Allifae. The fortifications are thought to date to the Late Republican period on the basis of building techniques.
The so-called Porta Romana of Saturnia was once part of the Roman wall of the second century B.C.
An arched gateway built using the Lesbian polygonal masonry technique at Velia.
The Porta Tiburtina is a gate in the Aurelianic Walls through which the Via Tiburtina passes. It is also known today as the Porta San Lorenzo.
The Porta Trasimena or Arco di San Luca is a third-century B.C. gate in the Etruscan wall of Perusia.
Now lost, the Porta Trigemina was one of the main gates of the Servian Wall.
The Porta all'Arco is a city gate of Volterra. Later incorporated into Medieval walls, the gate originates in the fourth and third centuries B.C.
An eleventh-century castle was built on the site of the Roman fort known as Portus Adurni. Portchester Castle is located at Portchester, to the east of Fareham in Hampshire, England.
The Porticus Absidata was an exedra porticata that served as the northern apsidal entryway to the Forum of Nerva, also known as the Forum Transitorium.
A utilitarian porticus and storage building located outside the Porta Trigemina, the Porticus Aemilia was erected in 193 BCE by Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and and Lucius Aemilius Paullus.

A portico that surrounded the Temple of Hercules Musarum in the Campus Martius of ancient Rome. The construction of the portico was the result of the patronage of L. Marcius Philippus, the stepfather of Augustus.
The so-called Portone necropolis is a major Hellenistic necropolis outside the walls of Volaterrae.
The harbor of the Latin colonial city of Cosa in south Etruria.
Portus Dubris (modern Dover) was a key commercial site for trade across the English Channel and was a key site connected with the A.D. 43 Roman invasion of Britain.

The so-called "Portus Iulius" is an ancient Roman port complex on the Bay of Naples. Its remains are now submerged due to the bradyseism of the Phlegraean Fields. The archaeological remains were first rediscovered in 1956.
A port in Carmania, near the lands of the Harmozaei and the Altars of Alexander, known only from literary sources.
A Roman maritime community that may derive its name from a local sanctuary of Venus, Portus Veneris served as the base of the Byzantine fleet until it was destroyed in A.D. 643.
A promontory or cape mentioned by Strabo in his description of coastal northwest Greece. Scholars identify it with modern Akra Skala, Albania.

The so-called "Posto villa" at Francolise was located in the ancient Ager Falernus of Campania. Its remains lie 500 meters from the so-called "San Rocco" villa. This was a small villa rustica whose incipit comes ca. 100 BC.
A settlement and deme of Attica, probably located in the river valley north of Thorikos.
Potentia was the site of a Roman colonial foundation ca. 184 BCE.

Shop no. 29 located in the commercial area along the via dei Sepolcri outside the Porta Ercolano at the northwest corner of Pompeii. Archaeological excavation in 2012 and 2013 undertaken by the École française de Rome in coordination with Ministero per i Beni e le attività cultural demonstrated that, at the time of its destruction, the shop was occupied by a potter.
A necropolis in use from the Neolithic period through to the Iron Age with numerous hypogeum-type tombs.
The Poulnabrone dolmen is a portal tomb in County Clare, Ireland, dating between 4200 and 2900 BCE.

The Pozos de Nieve of Mérida is a Roman archaeological site associated with the ancient city of Emerita Augusta. The site is located at 7 Reyes Huertas Street and is designated as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site. The ruins were discovered in 1920, and various interpretations have been offered for its usage, although it may have been part of a public bath complex.
The 'Pozzo Pantaleo' is a Roman mausoleum that re-used a cistern of the early Imperial period. In a third phase, the site was repurposed as a shrine dedicated to the Christian Saint Pantaleon.
Praetorian Guard Barracks at Amba Aradam Metro Station

Excavations for Rome's Metro C public transit line at the Amba Aradam Station revealed the remains of a second century A.D. barracks connected with the Praetorian Guard, along with a domus identified as that of a praetorian commandant. Although ruinous, the architectural complex demonstrates good preservation of some features, notably floor mosaics and wall paintings. The second century A.D. strat
Praetorium Publilianum was the center of an imperial latifundium in the territory of Teanum Apulum.
An ancient river of the Troad, possibly to be identified with the modern Umurbey Çayı.
An ancient settlement of Laconia, mentioned in a number of ancient sources. The site is located near modern Paralio Leonidi.
An ancient lake in the lower Strymon valley, now erased by modern flood control and land reclamation projects. Its precise borders and extent in antiquity are uncertain.
A headland located south of Meroë in a region referred to as Barbarica, possibly to be identified with the area opposite the island Mafia (Arabic: Manfiya) or Cape Delgado.
Temple at Angkor dedicated in 1191 CE under Jayavarman VII. The temple entered a period of decline beginning in the 15th century.

A small shrine with an altar built before 480 BC on the Acropolis of Athens. The northern colonnade of the Parthenon was built around this shrine, preserving it in situ. It is unknown what cult it housed.
The modern-day site of a Romano-British settlement dating from first and second centuries A.D.
Priddy Circles describes a linear arrangement of circular earthwork enclosures near the village of Priddy, Mendip Hills, Somerset, England.
The Bruna river flows some 70 km from the Colline Metallifere to the Tyrrhenian Sea, passing to the south of Massa Marittima. Its mouth is located at Castiglione della Pescaia.
A coastal lake of Etruria between Vetulonia and Rusellae; its remains can still be seen in the Padule di Raspollino.
An ancient city in Tetras or Achaia Phthiotis in Greece.
One of the Seven gates that surrounds the city of Thebes, on the road to Chalkis. It is possibly to be identified with or proximal to some extant remains of Mycenean fortification walls.
The modern Ionian island of Antipaxos.
Another proposed location of ancient Artulu is at or in the vicinity of modern Kayseri.
A Roman-era reservoir and dam northwest of modern Mérida in Spain, which was tapped to supply Emerita Augusta (modern Mérida) via aqueduct.

The Prytanikon was the seat of the Prytaneis and was located on the west side of the Agora in proximity to the Old Bouleuterion, with which it formed an architectural unit. This structure was supplanted by the later Tholos and its remains are referred to as "Building F". It dates to the later period of the Peisistratids, ca. 550-525 B.C.
A place from the TAVO Index
An island located in the Saronic Gulf.
The Public Bath at Pella is a bathing complex constructed and continuously renovated between the 4th and the 1st centuries BCE.

Remains of ancient lime adjacent to the modern Huerva river at Villadoz in spain have been interpreted as a Roman bridge, likely associated with a road or route between Sermonae and Carae, two road stations attested in Roman itineraries.

The remains of a Roman bridge known locally as Puente Viejo or Puente de Cañete lying one mile west west of Obulco on the Arroyo Salado. The bridge may have been associated with a conjectured secondary Roman road or route between Corduba and Catulo because although unmentioned in the Antonine Itinerary, the bridge's location lies between two mentioned stations: Calpurniana and Vircao.
An ancient settlement, lying on a hill east of the modern village of Ullastret in Catalonia.
A first millennium B.C., pre-Roman settlement of Majorca.

A Roman fort located in and around the modern village of Pumsaint in Wales, it is probably the "Louentinon" mentioned by Ptolemy. The Latinate form "Luentinum" is common in the literature but is not attested by any ancient source.

A Punic-Roman sanctuary, possibly of Hygieia/Salus or Aesculapius/Eshmun was identified to the northwest of Carthage in the direction of Cape Kamart (Tunisia), mostly on the basis of an assemblage of extremely fragmentary polychromatic terracotta statues, numbering at least 30.
Modern location in the vicinity of Mamallapuram that may have been the site of a port or harbor facility for the ancient city.
A now-submerged nymphaeum that dates to the reign of Claudius.
An Etruscan necropolis dating to the seventh-fifth centuries B.C. The ancient settlement associated with the site may have been Palmule.
Pupput was an ancient city of Africa proconsularis.
A fortress in the vicinity of Til-garimmu fortified by the Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721-705 BC) against Urarṭu.
Late Bronze Age settlement on the Dnieper River in Northwestern Ukraine covering over 30,000 square meters.
A Gallic site in the French commune of Vayrac, near the village of Saint-Denis-lès-Martel, often considered to be identifiable with the ancient cite of Uxellodunum, mentioned by Caesar.
A late Bronze Age settlement on Cyprus, abandoned after a brief occupation.
Pyra is a place with preserved ruins of a Doric temple dating to the third century B.C. The sources connect Pyra with the pyre of the hero Herakles.
Pyramid of King Ameny Qemau located in Dahshur.
The pyramid of the Third Dynasty pharaoh Djoser was built at Saqqara by architect Imhotep ca. 2267-2648 B.C.

A pyramidal structure located near the modern village of Hellenikon in Greece, whose ancient name is unknown. It is variously interpreted as one of several mass graves mentioned by Pausanias or as a fort or guard tower for a farm or other installation. Possibly of classical date.
The pyramid of the Pharaoh Khendjer (Thirteenth Dynasty) who ruled Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period (ca. 1760 B.C.)
A pyramid complex dating to the Fifth Dynasty of Ancient Egypt and associated with the Egyptian pharaoh Sahure.
Senusret II was a pharaoh of the Twelfth dynasty of ancient Egypt.
The Pyramid of Teti is a smooth-sided pyramid situated in the pyramid field at Saqqara. Teti was the first king of the Sixth Dynasty of Ancient Egypt.
A pyramid at Saqqara built for Unas, the final ruler of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty.
The pyramid tombs of the kings of the Kushite kingdom.
The Prut river flows from the Carpathian Mountains to the Danube.
Settlement and industrial site in southern Cyprus dated to the Early and Middle Bronze Ages.
Settlement featuring a Hellenistic tower west of the cemetery in the Berbati Valley occupied from the Iron Age to the Early Roman period.
Mentioned by Ptolemy, the Pyr(r)on Pedion is generally considered to be unlocated, but BAtlDir offers that it may correspond to the modern Gharb (Rharb) plain in Morocco.
An ancient city of the Peloponnesian Mani, located near the modern village of Kavalos/Pyrrhikhos.
An ancient city, located on the western slope of Mount Olympos to the southwest of modern Pythion.
A river of Pontus that drains into the Black Sea near Prytanis.
A fifth-century fort in the modern Iranian province of Golestan, located two kilometers south of the Great Wall of Gorgan.
An ancient city in Oman that was a key location for Indian Ocean trade networks.
An ancient castle, located in modern Syria. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006 as part of the "Crac des Chevaliers and Qal’at Salah El-Din" listing.

Değirmendüzü (formerly Qamişvan/Kamişvan) is a modern village situated ca. 8 km in the east of Pathos (Aznavurtepe / Anzavurtepe) in the Ağrı Province in eastern Turkey. Here a column base with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua, son of Išpuini (9th/8th century BCE) has been found (CTU I A 5-70)

Early Islamic structure in Eastern Jordan, likely constructed before the eighth century CE. Though its outward appearance suggests a castle, it does not seem to have had any military function, and the structure's original purpose is unknown.
A Hellenistic palace constructed in the second century CE at the southern end of the Tyrus/'Iraq al-Amir site.
A late Roman fort in Egypt's Kharga Oasis
A late Roman fort in Egypt's Kharga Oasis.
Site in Luxor (Egypt) associated with a Ptolemaic temple dedicated to the god Thoth.
Qasr el-Banat is a fortified site in Egypt's Eastern Desert, some 15 km from Wadi Hammamat.
A ruined Roman fort in modern Libya, possibly to be identified with "Thebunte", a road station listed in the Antonine Itinerary.
A tell located in Tal Afar in Nineveh Governorate, Iraq, that was the site of a Neolithic settlement established ca. 8500-7900 BCE. Neolithic roundhouses were documented at the site.

The Roman fort of Qreiye-Ayyash was established by the early third century CE and was abandoned by the mid-third century CE. It is situated on the outskirts of the modern village of Ayyash in Syria. It measures 220 x 220 m. Poidebard discovered the site in 1929. In the twenty-first century, the site has been the subject of several campaigns of geophysical prospection.
The Quadi, mentioned by Tacitus, were an ancient Germanic tribe and a part of the Suebi.

A Roman villa near the line of the Aqua Claudia located in the modern Via del Quadraro. The villa is dated to the first century B.C. or first century A.D. Following remodelling in the third century, the villa's occupation ends in the fourth century.
A suburban villa built by Sextus Quintilius Maximus and Sextus Quintilius Condianus (consuls in A.D. 151).

A villa located near the sanctuary of Madonna di Quintiliolo (Tivoli) that is traditionally associated with Quintilius Varus. The remains of the basis villae may date as early as the third century B.C.
One of the hills of Rome comprises several smaller peaks. According to tradition, its first inhabitants were Titus Tatius and the Sabines; during the Republic, the hill was mostly residential.
A desert castle built in the early eighth century CE by Walid Ibn Yazid, who would become the future Umayyad caliph Walid II. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.
A Greek trading settlement in northeastern Spain founded by the Rhodians.

A major, but relatively short-lived, fortified site in the Zagros mountains of modern Iraqi Kurdistan comprising two settlement loci within a large fortified area. Remains include stone foundations for mudbrick fortification walls and buildings, a stone-cut stairway, and two rock-reliefs depicting an unnamed ruler in elaborate costume. The complex has some evidence for reoccupation in Sasanian, Is
An unlocated city/town in the kingdom of Suhu that was situated on an island in the Euphrates River.
An ancient people, described by Ptolemy as inhabiting an area along the Danube that scholars interpret as being in the vicinity of Vienna.
Ram Hurmizd was a town and district in K̲h̲ūzistān in southwestern Persia.
Ramla Bay is located on the island of Gozo. A Roman villa was discovered on its shores in 1910-11.
Raphon/Raphana was an ancient city of the Decapolis that is now in modern Jordan. The ancient site was the legionary base of Legio III Gallica and of Legio XII Fulminata.
Rapidum was a Roman camp of the Mauretanian limes.
Rapinium is located on the coast of Etruria between Centumcellae and Graviscae, at modern Bagni Sant'Agostino.
A Punic-Roman sanctuary site located on the western coast of Gozo (Gaulos), Malta.
Rassvet is a Bosporan agricultural settlement dating from the second century BC to the first century AD.

An island offshore from modern Northern Ireland with evidence of human habitation stretching back to the Mesolithic period. It is one possible identification for an ancient "Riginia" island mentioned in ancient sources.

Excavations on site of post office at 49 Ben Ami St. revealed Hellenistic remains, including a dedication to Zeus Soter on behalf of Antiochos VII by a courtier (SEG XIX 9094). This inscription was associated with Hellenistic architecture of a temple-like character. Nearby workshops also uncovered.
A river of northern Italy emptying into the Adriatic just north of the Po delta. The modern Lemene.
Site of a Roman temple and possible small town near the confluence of the rivers Soar and Trent near Ratclifffe-on-Soar, Nottinghamshire. Findspot of at least three curse tablets (defixiones).
The site of a Roman camp located in Newbrough, Northumberland, England, United Kingdom.
The third pyramid built by Pharaoh Sneferu.
The Tomb of Annia Regilla (vix. A.D. 125-160), the wife of Herodes Atticus. The tomb is also erroneously known as the "Temple of the God Rediculum" and was used in the Middle Ages as a hay barn.
Regma/Rogmoi (also Rhegma) is an ancient lake or lagoon formed by the Cydnus river in Cilicia, approximately 5 km from Tarsus.
An ancient walled city, modern Resafa in Syria.
The modern Volga river is the longest river in Europe.
The Rhebas river, the modern Gökçesu, is a left-hand tributary of the Lower Sangarius river.
The Rhebas river, the modern Rıva deresi, is a river of Bithynia.

Pausanias describes this complex of two drainages near the Bay of Eleusis as sacred to Demeter and Persephone and as demarcating a territorial boundary between Athens and Eleusis. It was here that participants in the procession of the mystae were obliged to disembark from wagons and continue on foot to Eleusis. An inscribed decree of 422/421 BCE specifies the construction of a pedestrian bridge fo
The Reno river in northern Italy
An ancient name for a promontory on the island of Corsica, probably to be identified with the modern Cap Cargese.
The river now known as the Rhône is the second longest river in Gaul.
A group of small islands in the Propontis.
An ancient city located in the northern part of the Troad.
The Tavignano is a river of Corsica that flows into the Tyrrhenian Sea near Aléria.
The ruins of a Hellenistic tower located on the island of Amorgos near the church of Ag. Ioannis Prodromos.
A Roman road station along the Via Aemilia Scauri on the Mediterranean coast of Italy, thought to have been located in the vicinty of modern Recco.
The chief town of the Dalmatae.
A Roman auxiliary fort at present-day Castleshaw.
Rigomagus (Remagen) was the site of a Roman fort built west of the Rhine.
The Ring of Brodgar (also known as Brogar, or the Ring o' Brodgar) is a Neolithic henge and stone circle monument in Orkney, Scotland.
In antiquity, Ripatransone was a significant Picene center. It now lies in the Province of Ascoli Piceno, in the Italian region Marche.
Gate in the eastern city walls of Dura-Europos, no longer extant.

The River Yeo (South Somerset) is found in North Dorset and South Somerset, England. It is a tributary of the River Parrett. The ancient Roman road known as the Fosse Way crossed the River Yeo at the site of Lindinis.
A stretch of Roman road attested by a milestone discovered just north of Sidi-Ali-Medioumi, attributing construction to the emperor Augustus and the Legio III Augusta.
A hypothetical road route south from Buraq, connecting to an archaeologically attested road segment in the vicinity of Umm ez-Zeitun/Omra and continuing south to Dionysias.

A route via Roman roads, partly based on archaeologically attested routes and their conjectured continuation and connection, from ancient Tyre through Caesarea Philippi and thence northeastward to Damascus.
Roads: Via Nova Traiana → Umm el-Jimal
An archaeologically attested secondary road, branching off to the southeast from the Via Nova Traiana to the nearby fort at Qasr el-Ba'iq and thence to the settlement at Umm el-Jimal.
The sanctuary of the god Robigus, located at the sixth mile of the Via Cassia. The Romans celebrated the festival of Robigalia on 25 April.
A group of nine Bronze Age barrows in Somerset, England.
A promontory attested in ancient sources, Robogodion Akron is possibly to be identified with modern Fair Head.

The Rocca San Silvestro is a tenth century fortified village on Monte Rombolo near Campiglia Marittima in the Alta Maremma. The village was built in order to exploit rich mineral resources in the area.

The Rocca di Cerere (Rock of Ceres) is a rocky outcrop located in the city of Enna, Sicily. It was used as a fortified acropolis in antiquity. Roman soldiers are reported to have sacked the temple atop the rocca in 173 BCE.

The site of a Roman fort and an adjacent settlement is located on a terrace south of the River Ure to the west of Boroughbridge. The Roman fort was identified via geophysical survey and test excavations.
A fortified pre-Roman center connected with the Aequi. The ancient name of the site is unknown.
A complex of three Neolithic and Bronze Age megalithic monuments dating from the fourth to second millennia B.C. located on the borders of Oxfordshire and Warwickshire in the English Midlands.
The Roman agora at Athens is located to the north of the Acropolis and to the east of the ancient Agora.
A Roman Amphitheater at Syracuse, Sicily, that was in use from the first through third centuries. The structure measured ca. 140 x 119 meters.

The Roman Amphitheater of Serdica was built during the third and fourth centuries CE atop remains of an earlier theater complex. The complex was abandoned by the fifth century CE. The site was rediscovered beginning in 2004.
A well-preserved section of the 26 km aqueduct that supplied Mytilene on the island of Lesbos.
A roman contour-grade aqueduct, carrying water from the Fundana spring, south of Knossos, to an inverted siphon bridge at Spilia and thence to Knossos.

The Roman Bath House, Castleford, consists of the now-buried archaeological remains of a Roman military bath house that was built in the mid to late AD 80s. The site was excavated in 1978. The ancient bath was situated within the site of a former defensible annex that was constructed to the north of Castleford Roman fort.
Public baths at Parium used from the second century BCE and renovated several times in the late Roman and Byzantine periods, likely being used until at least the seventh century CE.
The Roman Baths of Como were in use from the later first century until the third century CE.
A hypothesized Roman bridge over the river Arly just above its confluence with the Isére at modern Albertville in France.
Roman Bridge: Le Vistre de la Fontaine Palaeochannel

Remains of a Roman bridge spanning a former channel of Le Vistre de la Fontaine south of Nîmes have been excavated. Work at the site also provided significant evidence for Roman-era waste and lead contamination transported down the river from the urban center of Nemausus.

A two-aisled Doric stoa ran along the south side of the Panathenaic Way from the Stoa Basileios towards the Dipylon Gate, which contained shops. It was constructed over a long period beginning in the early second century BC and repeatedly modified. The building was destroyed in the Herulian Sack of 267 AD, rebuilt, damaged in the Gothic Sack of 396 AD, rebuilt again, and was finally destroyed in t

The Roman Mausoleum of Villa Gordiani is a two-storey cylindrical tomb with pronaos executed in opus latericium. It fronts on the ancient via Praenestina. The rotunda has a diameter of more than 19 meters. Based on brick stamps, chronology is potentially wide and likely should be assigned anywhere in the period from Constantine I to Theodoric.
Palace building located at the northeast within the military sector at Dura-Europos.
The Roman Odeum of Tauromenium dates to the reign of the Roman emperor Hadrian.
The Roman Temple of Évora, also referred to as the Temple of Diana, is a Roman temple of the first century A.D.
A Roman theater in Baelo that dates to the reign of Claudius.
A theater constructed in Minturnae under Augustus or Tiberius, and further embellished under Hadrian.
The Roman theater at Caere (modern Cerveteri, Italy) is known especially for the sculptural program honoring Julio-Claudian emperors, including Tiberius and Claudius.
This extensive villa (ancient name unknown) was located at modern Welschbillig in Germany (in the ancient territory of the Treveri).
Remains of a Roman amphitheater dating to the later first century A.D.
The Roman amphitheater at Albano Laziale is generally dated to the mid-third century A.D.
A Roman amphitheater dating to the first century A.D.
The Roman amphitheater at Ariminum is dated to the second century, perhaps during the reign of Hadrian.
A small, first-century amphitheater with an ellipsoidal plan.
The so-called "Palais Gallien" is an early second century A.D. amphitheater.
The Roman amphitheater at Béziers dates ca. A.D. 80, during the Flavian period. It measured ca. 110 by 90 meters and could accommodate 15,000 spectators.

The Roman amphitheater at Calleva Atrebatum began as a timber structure ca. A.D. 55-75. Its remains lie north of the east gate of the third century A.D. town wall and the site was first identified by William Stukeley in 1724. The amphitheater measures approximately 90 by 75 meters.

The Roman amphitheater at Corinth was located northeast of the Temple of Apollo. It has been suggested that it dates to the early days of the Roman colony, perhaps placing its construction in the first century B.C.
The Roman amphitheater at Frusino measures ca. 78 by 57 meters.
Grumentum's amphitheater (first century B.C.) is the only known example in Lucania. The arena measures ca. 62.5 by 60 meters.
The Roman amphitheater at Hispellum dates to the first century.
The Roman amphitheater at Luca dates to the second half of the first century.
The Roman amphitheater at Luna was built in the second century, perhaps during the Antonine period.
The Roman amphitheater at Lupia(e), modern Lecce, was built in the late first and early second centuries A.D.
The Roman amphitheater at Ocriculum lies outside the city walls.
Roman amphitheater at Santa Maria Capua Vetere

Sometimes referred to as the "Anfiteatro Campano", the Roman amphitheater at Santa Maria Capua Vetere is the second largest in the Roman world. Begun under Augustus, it was further renovated under Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.
The Roman amphitheater at Segobriga dates to the Flavian period. It measures approximately 75 by 65 meters and could seat 5,500 spectators.
The remains of the early Imperial amphitheater were discovered within the Caserma Minervio during the early nineteenth century.
The Roman amphitheater at Suasa dates to the first century A.D.
The Roman amphitheater at Trier dates to the reign of Antoninus Pius and was renovated under Constantius Chlorus. The arena measures ca. 71 x 47.5 meters.
The Roman amphitheater at Verona dates to ca. A.D. 30.
The Roman amphitheater of Catania is the largest known ancient amphitheater in Sicily. Its external dimensions measure ca. 125 x 105 meters. It likely dates to the second century.
A Roman amphitheater in Tarragona, built in the first century A.D. The structure was renovated under Elagabalus.
The amphitheater of Italica, built in the second century A.D., was one of the largest in the Roman world and could accommodate an estimated 25,000 spectators.
The Roman amphitheater of Martigny likely dates to the reign of Trajan.
The Roman amphitheater of Milan was built near the Porta Ticinese during the second and third centuries. It was destroyed by the time of the Gothic Wars, most likely during the fifth century.
A Roman amphitheater at Tours that dates to the first century CE.
A Roman amphitheater dating to the first and second centuries.
The so-called "Arch of Drusus and Germanicus" at Spoleto.

The Imperial Baths at Trier (also referred to as "Kaiserthermen") are a large Roman bath complex in Trier, Germany. The site was designated as part of the "Roman Monuments, Cathedral of St. Peter and Church of Our Lady in Trier", a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The complex dates to the fourth century A.D.
An ancient Roman bridge along the Via Aurelia.
The Roman bridge (Puente romano) at Mérida spans the Guadiana River. It is included as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida".
The Roman forum at Cupra Maritima.
The Roman forum of Sarsina has been excavated in its northern reaches.
Roman engineers began modifying the Punic harbor by the late second century B.C.
Sandstone quarries located some 4 km west of Cartagena, in the Diputación de Canteras.

An extensive complex of structures dating to the 1st - 3rd centuries of the Roman imperial period sited at a pair of springs known today as "Viktoriaquelle" and "Schwefelquelle," near modern Heckenmünster in German. This site, whose ancient name and tutelary deities are not known, was extensively excavated in the 1960s. It comprised religious and performative spaces, as well as baths and hostelry.
A pseudodipteral, hexastyle, Corinthian order temple begun under Claudius and completed under Domitian. The temple is likely sacred to the imperial cult.
The Roman theater at Asculum was discovered during excavations in 1932. The structure dates to the first century A.D.
The Roman theater at Augusta Bagiennorum
A Roman theater of the second century A.D. constructed during the reign of Hadrian.
The Roman theater at Ferentium dates to the early Imperial period.
Pliny the Younger discussed the restoration of the theater in a letter sent to the Roman emperor Trajan.
The Roman theater at Italica could accommodate 3,000 spectators. It predates the Hadrianic rebuilding of the city.
The Roman theater at Spoletium dates to the first century B.C.

The Roman theater at Suessa Aurunca was built in the first century A.D. and then restored under Antoninus Pius. Amedeo Maiuri initiated excavations at the theater site in the 1920s. The excavation was not completed until 2003.
The Roman theater at Tusculum was first excavated in 1839.
The Roman theater at Verona dates from the late first century B.C.
The Roman theater of Volaterrae was built during the during the Augustan period under the consulship of Aulus Caecina Severus.
The Roman theater at Aspendos dates ca. AD 155 and is perhaps the best preserved example of a Roman theater building.
A Roman theater in Lyon, France, that originally dates ca. 15 B.C.
The Roman theater of Herculaneum was constructed during the Augustan period. The theater was discovered first in 1709 while a well was being dug.
The Roman theater of Milan was built during the Augustan period and could accommodate 7,000 to 9,000 spectators.
The Roman theater in Plovdiv, Bulgaria.
Roman vicus and harbor at Lousonna
The site is located in modern Lausanne-Vidy

A Roman villa rustica dated between the first and fifth centuries. The site occupies a low hill located to the south of Cerro de Robledo, near the Roman settlement of Aratispi. Archaeological fieldwork has demonstrated that the site was involved in the production of olive oil until the later Roman period.
Roman villa of Torre di Pordenone

A Roman villa and bath complex located in the valley of the Noncello River. The villa complex, whose original construction dates to the first century BCE, was likely rebuilt during the second century CE.
The remains of the Roman villa located in via Michelangelo Tilli are located close to the Aniene. The late republican villa remained in use until the fourth century.
Galerius commissioned the Late Roman fortified palace compound and memorial complex of Gamzigrad-Romuliana in the late third and early fourth centuries.
Site of an important Bronze Age and Iron Age city located in the Bet She'an Valley about 5 km south of Beit She'an and 3 km west of the Jordan River.
What would become Medieval Rota was once a pagus of Etruscan Caere. Writing in PECS, Mario Torelli describes this an an important Archaic center in the area of Tolfa.

A brick rotunda of the fourth century AD ordered by the emperor Galerius for use as either a tomb or temple; later incorporated into the Christian Church of Agios Georgios. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988
A Minoan site in eastern Crete.
A nomadic Sarmatian people who occupied territory between the Don and Dnieper rivers, later migrating toward the Danube, to the Baragan steppes of Romania.

Tomb VI at Qatna, known as the Royal Hypogeum, is a tomb complex located approximately 12 meters below the Royal Palace of Qatna. The tomb consists of a long corridor and 4 burial chambers, and contained approximately 20 burials.
Two stone buildings (west and east) located 30 m apart were excavated at modern Rujm al-Ḥenū in Jordan. The pottery found has been dated largely to Iron Age IIc.
A Roman military site in Jordan, it was bulldozed out of existence between 2013 and 2017.
A fortress or fortified settlement in northern Jordan dated to the Middle Bronze Age.
Rural settlement between Oppidum Novum and Arbaoua
An unnamed settlement consisting of small farmsteads.
Rusahinili (modern Toprakkale) was an ancient fortress of Urartu built by Rusa I.
A Gallic tribe whose territory corresponds roughly to the modern region of Aveyron.
A Roman villa, identified and initially excavated since 2018, located in the modern district of Rutland (England, United Kingdom), east of Foster's Bridge and southwest of Ketton.
The Roman fort at Rutupiae was erected at the location where the Claudian landings took place in A.D. 43.
An archaeological site at Braga located close to the forum of the ancient city that preserves remains of domestic architecture dating from the first century BCE until the fifth century CE.

The Alcudia River, also known as the Cabra River in its upper course, is a tributary of the Guadalmez River, which in turn is a tributary of the Zújar River, a tributary of the Guadiana. Its course runs more than 70 km.
A Roman fortification founded during the principate of Augustus that was located some 50 km from the legionary fortress at Mainz-Mogontiacum.

A spring that was a cult site used in the Early Neolithic, Middle Neolithic, Late Neolithic, Early Bronze Age, pre-Roman Iron Age, and Roman Iron Age, the Röekillorna Spring is located in modern south-east Scania, Sweden.
A 'villa rustica' located to the west of Höflein, Austria, on the Danube frontier.
This extensive rural villa of the Roman imperial period (ancient name unknown) was built in the territory of the Treveri. Located at modern Fliessem-Otrang in Germany.
A Talaiotic village dating between the ninth and second centuries B.C.
S. Agata di Campobello di Mazara
BAtlas 47 B3 S. Agata di Campobello di Mazara

A titular church on the Via Nomentana, S. Agnese houses the remains of the eponymous saint. The present church was built by Pope Honorius I in the seventh century AD, on the site of a fourth century basilica built by Constantine I.
The basilica and catacombs of S. Alessandro are located at the seventh milestone of the Via Nomentana.

The Roman Villa of Baños de Valdearados, also known as the Villa de Santa Cruz, is located in Baños de Valdearados, Burgos region of Ribera del Duero, in Castilla y León (Spain). A Late Imperial Roman villa (fourth and fifth centuries CE) with polychrome mosaics is located at the site.
S. Giovanni Lippioni is the site of a pre-Roman sanctuary that was later repurposed as a Christian church.
Site of a small Samnitic sanctuary atop Colle Rimontato (709 m. a.s.l.)

The Papal Basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the Walls (Basilica Papale di San Lorenzo fuori le Mura) is one of the Seven Pilgrim Churches of Rome. The basilica serves as the shrine and tomb dedicated to Saint Lawrence and its earliest phases likely belong to the fourth century AD.
BAtlas 45 A4 S. Marco di Castelabbate
BAtlas 41 C2 S. Maria del Giudice

On the hill of Grignano, located on the outskirts of Montebuono, the remains of a Roman villa were first excavated in the nineteenth century in the area of the church of "S. Pietro ad centum muros". Excavation in the 1990s revealed further villa remains beneath the church and in the vicinity of its cemetery. Epigraphic evidence attesting to the consulship of M. Vipsanius Agrippa was discovered imm
S. Sebastianus (San Sebastiano fuori le mura) is a Christian basilica outside the walls of Rome; the earliest phase belongs to the fourth century AD.
The protocoenobium of San Sebastiano is a monastery located in the territory of Alatri, to the east of the city center on the slopes of Mount Pizzuto.

The fortified Saint Simeon Monastery (Aswan, Egypt) dates to the seventh century. It was initially sacred to the local saint Anba Hedra. The site was rebuilt in the tenth century and re-dedicated to Saint Simeon. Saladin partially destroyed the monastery in 1173.

Remains of at least two Roman villas have been identified in the frazione of San Valentino, part of the larger comune of Poggio Mirteto. One is the so-called Villa dei Casoni, while this site is sometimes known as the Bagni di Lucilla. This villa was the findspot in 1801 of a mosaic pavement now in the Chiaramonti museums of the Vatican.
A Christian catacomb along the Via Flaminia dedicated to S. Valentino.
A Phoenician settlement of the eighth and seventh centuries B.C.
Saalburg was a Roman auxiliary castrum associated with the Limes Germanicus.
A volcanic lake in Latium north of Rome (modern Lago di Bracciano).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group whose territory was located in the Valle Sabbia in Northern Italy.
An ancient river mentioned by Caesar. It is possibly to be identified with the modern Sambre, a tributary of the Meuse that flows through France and Belgium.
Sabrina fl. (River Severn) is the longest river in the United Kingdom.

Sabu-Jaddi is the site of multi-period Nubian rock art and is located along the Nile River downstream of the third cataract region on the east bank of the Nile. These rock drawings are found on sandstone cliffs between the Sudanese villages of Sabu and Jaddi.
A promontory described by the geographer Strabo as the most westerly point of the inhabited world. The modern Cape St. Vincent (Portugal).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Śātavāhanas, dominant political power in Deccan Skt.: Śātavāhana.
An enclosure in the Campus Martius surrounded by porticoes built by Marcus Agrippa before ca. 26 BCE.
An ancient river, attested between Kaulonia and Lokroi Epizephyrioi. The Sagra(s) is perhaps to be identified with the modern Allaro.
A river of eastern Italy (modern Sangro).

A fourth-century AD church was rebuilt in the seventh-century AD to house the remains of the eponymous saint. The church is located in the city of Vagharshapat (Etchmiadzin), in the Armavir Province of Armenia. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
An archaeological site covering some 3 ha in the modern French commune of Gruissan (Aude department), with occupation beginning in the first century BCE and continuing to Late Antiquty.
An urban quarter of Roman Vienne, now presented as an archaeological museum.
Remains of a rustic temple and a menhir were discovered in the early 1960s near Boutaran.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Śakas, after occupying Sindh and (briefly) N Deccan IND/PAK.
Sal(a)pia(i)/Salinae was an ancient city of Daunia.
An ancient settlement located at modern Cortijo de la Coria in Spain's Sevilla province.
An ancient coastal lagoon on the coast of Apulia, drained in modern times.
A river, attested in ancient sources, that is probably to be associated with the modern Thüringische Saale.
The Salassi were a Celtic tribe in the Alpine region of northern Italy and Gaul.
Archaeological site in the upper Tigris region inhabited in the early Bronze Age.
An ancient settlement mentioned only in Avienus. If it is not fictional, it might possibly be identified with modern Salou.
Modern Bozdağ in the Tavas district of Turkey's Denizli province.
A river, placed by ancient sources to the west of Malaca (modern Malaga in Spain), the Salduba may correspond to either the Vélez or the Guadalhorce river.
The modern town of Salemi, near Trapani, has been associated with the location of the ancient settlement of Halicyae.
The modern Río Sella in the Spanish principality of Asturias.
Salt pans located to the east of Ostia and to the north-east of Portus around the Tiber river estuary.
Salinae *Tubunenses, a shallow, saline lake and marshland located in northeastern Algeria.
Salinarum L./Tritonis Palus (modern Chott el Djerid) is a large endorheic salt lake in southern Tunisia.
Sallentini were a tribe of an ancient Apulia, the 'heel' of the booth of the Italian peninsula. They spoke the Messapian language.
Cape Leuca, known as Sallentinum and Iapygia in ancient sources, is a headland that forms the extreme southeastern point of Italy and separates the Gulf of Tarentum from the Adriatic Sea.
The river Jalón of the northeast of Spain is one of the principal tributaries of the Ebro river.
Ancient tuff quarries and a bridge at Salone on the Anio River.

The ancient Salsum river has been identified with the modern وادي المالح (Oued Melah) in Algeria's Aïn Témouchent province. It debouches into the Mediterranean at the modern beach resort area of Shati Tariqa.

A Roman senatorial estate located southwest of ancient Sufes, epigraphically attested in the second century CE, and owned at least for a period by the otherwise unknown senator Lucilius Africanus. Its location and extent is thought to have corresponding roughly to the later, late-antique province of Byzacena.
A Chalcolithic necropolis with tumulus-type tombs.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
Modern Cape Sideros at the extreme northeast tip of the island of Crete.
The River Somme flows some 245 km (152 mi) from Fonsommes near Saint-Quentin to the Bay of the Somme in the English Channel.
The so-called "Samnite House" is a domus in Herculaneum that originally dates to the second century B.C., making it one of the oldest buildings discovered at the site.
The so-called "Samnite Palaestra" (VIII, 7, 29) lies behind the temple of Isis. A dedication in the Oscan language dates to the second half of the second century BC.
An ancient, Oscan-speaking people who lived in the central southern part of the Apennine mountains in Italy.
Scholars tentatively associate the ancient name Samnitum with modern Ile de Noirmoutier.
Samothrace is an island of the northern Aegean Sea.
The modern Șomeș/Szamos river, which flows through the modern countries of Romania and Hungary

San Crisogono (sacred to San Crisogono) is one of Rome's early parish churches (tituli). Pope Sylvester I (314–335) likely builds the first iteration in the fourth century AD; later reworkings occur in the twelfth and seventeenth centuries, respectively.
Remains of a late Roman villa with mosaics have been excavated at a site named San Cromazio in the municipal territory of modern Villaspeciosa on the island of Sardinia.
A settlement that was an important center of the Vestini in the Abruzzo.

The Roman Catholic church of San Gervasio dei Bulgari is located in Mondolfo, province of Pesaro and Urbino, Marche, Italy. Built in the Romanesque style, the church was likely founded in the fifth or sixth century.
San Gimignano, which originated as an Etruscan settlement, is best known as a Medieval town renowned for its fortified towers.
A church dedicated to St. George located in Rome's Velabrum. Legend connects the church's location with the spot where the Roman she wolf found the abandoned twins, Romulus and Remus.
The San Lázaro Aqueduct is located to the north of Emerita Augusta in the locality Rabo de Buey-San Lázaro, as noted by the Barrington Atlas Directory.
An Etruscan hypogeum tomb dating either to the third or the second century BCE. The tomb is located beneath the medieval church of San Manno in the comune of Perugia.
San Martino ai Monti is a minor basilica in Rome. The basilica was founded on a site donated by Equitius during the reign of Pope St. Sylvester I in the fourth century.

The Catholic church of San Paolo alla Regola located in the modern Rione of Rome named "Regola", to which it gives its name. The current edifice of the church dates to the seventeenth century. Excavations carried out from 1978 to 1982 documented multiple layers of architecture dating from the imperial period when this district was used primarily as one of warehouses (horrea) located near the Tiber

San Pietro in Vincoli is a Roman Catholic titular church and minor basilica in Rome, Italy. It is located on the Oppian Hill and it houses relics connected with the Catholic Saint Peter. The basilica was founded as the Basilica Eudoxiana ca. 432-440. Pope Sixtus III consecrated the site in 439. The basilica has undergone numerous stages of building and rebuilding, notably under Pope Adrian I and P
A church on the Palatine Hill in Rome, sacred to Saint Theodore of Amasea, dating originally to the sixth century AD.

The basilica of Saints Vitalis, Valeris, Gervase, and Protase, commonly known as the Basilica di San Vitale, is a titular minor basilica church in Rome. The church was built ca. AD 400 by Pope Innocent I.
An island in the Red Sea to the east of Tiran island.
The modern Acıgöl in Turkey's Aegean region.
Sanctuaries of Apollo Deiradiotes and Athena Oxyderkes
At Argos, Pausanias mentions both the sanctuary of Apollo Deiradiotes (Apollo of the ridge) and the sanctuary of Athena Oxyderkes (Athena the clear-sighted).
