A Late Helladic sanctuary was excavated by Helene Konstolakis-Jiannopoulou in 1990 near the chapel of Agios Konstantinos and Elenis. Activity at this site dates between 1500 and 1300 B.C.

The Sanctuary of Apollo near Amyklai is a stoa-like building that enclosed a colossal statue of Apollo on three sides and was decorated with reliefs. The tomb of Hyacinthus is used as a statue base, combining the two local deities together.
At Thebes, the foundations of a Doric temple dating to the Archaic and Classical periods were excavated by the American School of Classical Studies in 2015-6.
A partially excavated artificial platform and temple at modern Kato Phana on the Greek island of Chios (ancient Phanai).

A Doric-order temple with a hexastyle in antis plan measuring 31.15x16.05 m. According to Mazarakis-Ainian, the cella is divided into two parts by means of an axial colonnade. The altar stood at the east front of the temple.
The Sanctuary of Apollo at Halieis is a temple complex dedicated primarily to Apollo, constructed outside of the city of Halieis and dating between the seventh and fourth centuries BCE.
The famous sanctuary of Apollo on the Cycladic island of Delos.
Sanctuary of Artemis Anaiitis in Lydia

Pausanias describes the Sanctuary of Artemis Anaiitis in Lydia in his third book. Central to his discussion is the xoanon of Artemis that may have been present in the sanctuary, one which he associates with the object Orestes has carried off from Taurus, an episode described by Euripides in his play, Iphigenia in Tauris.
A now mostly destroyed ancient temple dedicated to Artemis Munychia on the promontory above Mikrolimani. A Yacht Club in the 1930s was built on top of the promontory.

Pausanias describes a Sanctuary of Artemis Soteira located at Phigaleia, noting that it stood atop a level hilltop and that there was a standing cult image made of stone. A sacred procession of the local people commenced from the sanctuary site.
Sanctuary of Artemis Soteira in the Kerameikos

This sanctuary is located in the Kerameikos of Athens, south of the street of the tombs and was established in the early Hellenistic Age. It has often been identified as a sanctuary of Hekate, but more recent research suggests that it was dedicated to Artemis Soteira. It also contained a prophetic well associated with Paian.

A small sanctuary of Athena Hygieia ("of health") on the Acropolis of Athens, consisting of a statue and an altar, next to the Propylaia. The sanctuary may have been established in 430/29 BC in response to the Periclean plague or have older roots on the Acropolis.
Sanctuary of Bendis located on the Acropolis of Salamis
An ancient sanctuary to Despoina located at Lykosoura, Arcadia.
The Sanctuary of Dionysos, which includes a theater, choregic monument, statue bases, and at least one temple, formed part of the civic center of the Attic deme of Ikarion.

An ancient cult site to Dionysus described by Pausanias in Sicyon, Argolid. Now likely destroyed, Pausanias puts the temple between the theater and the agora, and may well have been located closer to the former.
A sanctuary of Aphrodite Erykine near Psophis in Achaia that is mentioned by Pausanias.

The Sanctuary of Hercules Victor in Tivoli is a significant cult place of the second century B.C. The sanctuary is composed of a vaulted, terraced platform that support the temple, its porticoes, and a theater.
The Sanctuary of Iuno Gabina at Gabii.
The Sanctuary of Metaneira was located near Eleusis. Its precise location has not been determined.
A site sacred to Minerva with activity from the Early Iron Age onward, the Sanctuary of Minerva at Spinera is located at Breno on the banks of the river Oglio.
The Sanctuary of Montélu lies to the west of Chassenon. The building, only partially excavated, is of an octagonal plan and oriented to the cardinal points.

A sanctuary located by the Ilissos River, east of Athens, consisting of a rock-cut courtyard, where over 50 votive reliefs were found, dedicated to an older god called Pankrates ("all-powerful"), Palaimon, Plouton ("wealth") and "God", and a younger god called Pankrates and Herakles Pankrates.
Pausanias describes a Sanctuary of Poseidon located at Onchestos that preserved a grove sacred to the god and that Homer had once praised.
Described by Pausanias, this sanctuary was located near Akraiphiai in Boeotia.

The remains of the Sanctuary of Sol Indiges are located near Pomezia, Italy. The original phase of the sanctuary dates to the last quarter of the sixth century BCE, with subsequent rebuilding in the late fourth century BCE.
Pausanias mentions the Sanctuary of Zeus Aphesios as being located atop a mountain. The site was excavated ca. 1890 and has views over the Saronic Gulf.
The sanctuary of Zeus Lykaios on Mt. Lykaion.
The Sanctuary of the Helikonian Muses in Boeotia is celebrated by Hesiod. Archaeological remains of part of the sanctuary in the valley of the Muses date to the third and second centuries B.C.
An islet near Lesbos, the modern Garbias.
An ancient settlement, located on the Athos/Akte peninsula.
Sanisera was a Roman settlement of Menorca.
A paleochristian site located at the thirtieth mile of the ancient via Labicana, near to the ancient road station 'ad Bivium'.

A maritime villa of Roman imperial date, located on the northwest shore of the Porto Conte bay in western Sardinia. Use of the site for various purposes continued into the 8th century of the modern era.
A nuragic sanctuary centered on a sacred well that was in use from ca. 1200 to 700 BC.

A minor Catholic basilica in Rome, Santa Croce in Gerusalemme is also a titular church in rione Esquilino and one of the Seven Pilgrim Churches. The church was consecrated ca. 325 to house relics of the Passion of Jesus Christ brought to Rome from the Holy Land by Empress St. Helena.
A fifth-century A.D. Christian church built in the Forum Romanum at the foot of the Palatine Hill.

Santa Maria Maggiore is a major papal basilica as well as one of the Seven Pilgrim Churches of Rome. Located on the Mons Cispius, the origins of the church date to the reign of Pope Celestine I (422–432).
The church of Santa Maria dell'Orto is a Roman Catholic church located in Rome's Trastevere district. Its foundation is traced to 508.

A minor basilica church in Rome, Italy. Tradition holds that the church was founded in the sixth century to serve the Greek community at Rome. The beginnings of the present edifice lie in the eighth century.

Santa Maria in Monterone is a Catholic church located in Rome's Sant'Eustachio neighborhood. The church gives its name to the street on which it is located. The church building is situated on first-century BCE ruins in the area of the artificial basin known as the stagnum Agrippae. The present edifice dates to 1682.

A large seaside villa on two terraces overlooking the modern Santa Marina bay near Varbiga, Croatia. The villa lies on the northern coast of a headland; the major amphora workshop at Loron occupies the southern coastal site.
The castro of Santa María de Cervantes is located on the banks of the Ancares river the municipality of Cervantes, in the province of Lugo.
A titular church on Rome's Aventine Hill dedicated to Saint Prisca. A Mithraeum dating to the late first century A.D. was discovered on the site in 1934.
A Late Imperial catacomb located in the territory of Nepet. The Christian church of San Tolomeo alle Sante Grotte developed at the site of the catacomb.

The current Church of Saint Susanna at the Baths of Diocletian located on the Quirinal Hill in Rome dates from 1585. A titular church has existed on the site since ca. A.D. 280. The remains of an elite house (domus) are preserved beneath the church.
A Galician oppidum located located on the mountain of Santa Tecla in the extreme southwest of Galicia.
An archaeological area in Sicily, near Acireale, possibly related to the ancient settlement of Acium.

The Roman sanctuary of Santalla de Bóveda dates to the second through fourth centuries A.D. It is located in the parish of Santalla de Bóveda de Meralocated near Lugo. Discovered in 1926, the site is a protected national monument.
Santi Quattro Coronati is an early Christian basilica on Rome's Caelian Hill begun by Pope Miltiades in the fourth century A.D.

The Basilica of Saint Stephen in the Round on the Caelian Hill is an ancient titular church located on the Caelian Hill in Rome. Its earliest phase belongs to the reign of Pope Simplicius (468-483). The early martyr Saint Stephen was honored in the church's consecration. Its circular plan is highly unusual.
A sanctuary with twin temples located at the Etruscan port. The Pyrgi sanctuary was initially excavated by Massimo Pallottino in 1957. The so-called Pyrgi Plaques were discovered here in 1964.
Santuario di Santa Maria di Barbana
The Santuario di Barbana is an ancient Marian shrine that dates ca. 582. It is said that Elia, the Patriarch of Aquileia, built a church near the hut of a hermit from Treviso by the name of Barbanus.

The Cirencester amphitheater is the second largest known in Britannia. Its earthworks supported tiered seats that could accommodate about 8,000 spectators. The amphitheater was converted to a fortified site in the fifth century during the Saxon invasions.
The modern Ghaghara river in India, a major tributary of the Ganges.
Cave with Neolithic, Mesolithic, Palaeolithic, and Bronze Age remains in Boeotia, Greece.
The earliest of the three shrines sacred to Serapis identified by archaeologists working at Delos in the nineteenth century.
An ancient, proto-urban site located in north-western Tajikistan.
An Urartian fortress constructed in the eighth century BCE and destroyed in the seventh century BCE.
Important pre-Roman center in Dacia (cited: BAtlas 21 F4 Sarmizegetusa (Regia))

The Sarnios corresponds to the lower course of the modern Hari/Tejen river in Turkmenistan, from around its junction with the Kashafrud river to the Tejand Oasis beyond which it disperses into the Karakum Desert.
The Saronic Gulf (also called the Gulf of Aegina) is a part of the Aegean Sea that delimits the eastern side of the isthmus of Corinth.
Pliny notes that this island was notorious as a pirate refuge.

The Sasso Pinzuto necropolis is linked with the Etruscan culture and is located near Tuscania, Italy. The necropolis was in use from the middle of the seventh century BCE until the fifth century BCE. A new cult area was discovered at Sasso Pinzuto in 2024.
A minor river of the southern Troad.
The Savo River of Campania; the present-day Savone.
Savo/Vicus Virginis? (modern Savona) was a Ligurian settlement that came under Roman influence after the Second Punic War.
A river of Central Europe and a right tributary of the Danube.
The modern-day site of a Roman-British settlement dates from the second to fourth centuries AD.
The Scaldis was a river of Gallia Belgica. It separated the territory of the civitates of the Atrebates and the Menapii from that of the Nervii.
An ancient settlement on the eastern bank of the Nile, located between Meroe and the fifth cataract. Probably modern Berber in Sudan.
On Castle Hill, Scarborough, a Roman signal station/fortlet was established ca. A.D. 370 that remained in use until the early fifth century. A medieval castle was established ca. A.D. 1135.
A fortified Medieval site in the Maremma region of Italy with evidence for earlier fortified centers.
A monastic complex on Skellig Michael established in the seventh century A.D. and enrolled as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
Twin Italic temples located atop the Colle della Torre.
A Roman fort with associated vicus located at modern Schirenhof in the German municipality of Schwäbisch Gmünd, Baden-Württemberg.
School of Homer Ag. Athanasios excavations (Ithaca)

A site on Ithaca that local tradition links to both Homer and Odysseus. Excavations in 1998 near the Church of St. Athanasius documented a series of walls including both Bronze Age and Iron Age phases, as well as a Hellenistic building constructed using orthostates, and a circular structure with a diameter of more than 7 meters.
Celtic settlement site in eastern Austria inhabited during the 1st-2nd centuries CE.
Scicli is the site of settlement beginning in the third millennium BC. The town of Scicli is believed to have been founded by Sicels ca. 300 BC.
An ancient Slavonic people who settled in the area north of the Carpathian mountains from the 5th century CE onward.
A Roman sanctuary in use from the first century B.C. through fifth century A.D.
An ancient settlement occupied from the fourth century B.C. to the fifth century A.D. noted for an Italic sanctuary and a production center for terra sigillata.
The Scordisci were a Gallic people of the Iron Age inhabiting what is now Serbia. Their territory centered on the confluence of the Savus (Sava), Dravus (Drava), and Danube rivers.
The Scultenna, the modern Panaro river, is a tributary of the Po river in northern Italy.
An island in the Red Sea, mentioned by Pliny, that cannot be precisely identified today; however, some modern scholars have conjectured its association with Shadwan island.

The Sebasteion at Aphrodisias was a temple complex dedicated to Aphrodite and the Iulio-Claudian emperors that local patrons financed. It was built between ca. 20 and 60 CE. The complex was excavated between 1979 and 1981.
The third western-most ancient mouth of the Nile River.

When Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud) became the principal administrative center of the Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC, king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC) built (or rebuilt) numerous temples. One of those was dedicated to the divine Sebetti. The location of this building is not known.
The so-called "Second Temple" in Jerusalem stood on the northern edge of the Dome of the Rock and was destroyed in A.D. 70 during the Roman siege.
Segisamo was located on the road from Tarraco to Asturica.
The Segovellauni were a Celtic tribe in Gallia Narbonensis whose territory lay between the Rhodanus and the Druna.
Segovii?, a Gallic tribe whose territory was located in the Alpes Cottiae.
A Roman settlement along the Via Domitia.
A settlement or people within the territory of the Suessetani, known only from coins they issued. The precise location is not known.

The Seleucid Empire was a Hellenistic kingdom, founded by Seleucus I Nicator, and ruled by the Seleucid dynasty from 312 to 63 BCE. At its height, it stretched from the Aegean Sea to northern India, but it steadily lost territory and prestige. The remnants of the kingdom were eventually incorporated into Roman territory as the province of Syria in 64 BCE.
BAtlas 67 G2 Seleukeia epi tou Zeugmatos
Selge was an important city of Pisidia; Strabo claims it was founded as a Spartan colony.
Modern Krestena, in the Elis regional unit of the Peloponnese.
A wetland in the neighborhood of Ephesos, mentioned by Strabo, from which the temple of Artemis derived income. Modern scholars identify it with the modern Lake Gebekirse.
The Selvicciola Roman villa is the site of a vast Roman rural complex as well as a Longobard cemetery.
A prehistoric (Eneolithic) necropolis in mid-Tyrrhenian Italy with activity beginning in the early fourth millennium BCE. The Selvicciola necropolis is located in the valley of the Fiora River.
The Semnones were a tribe of the Germanic Suebi whose territory lay between the Albis and Viadua rivers.
A road station during the Roman period, attested by the Antonine Itinerary. Its exact location is not known today, but may have been in the Upper Sinni Valley in southern Italy.
An ancient Gallic tribe that entered Italy after 400 BC and settled on the Adriatic coast from Forlì to Ancona, marking the so-called Ager Gallicus.
The Senones were an ancient Gallic tribe of the Seine River basin.
The tomb of C. Publicius Bibulus, a plebeian aedile, located at Rome at the foot of the Capitoline Hill. It most likely dates to the close of the Republican period.
A family tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones near the Porta San Sebastiano in use from the third century B.C. to the first century A.D.
An ancient people of Etruria inhabiting the area around Nazzano Romano.

The so-called "Sepolcro dei Veienti" is a ruined tomb of Roman imperial date. Built in opus caementicium and travertine, only the core of the rectangular structure remains. Likely located along the ancient Via Veientana, the tomb today stands in the modern Parco Papacci.

An ancient Roman brick tomb of the second century that is located in the Via Bisignano between the fifth mile of Via Appia Antica and the seventh kilometer of Via Appia Nuova. The tomb has also been known as the Temple of Salus. Its typology is comparable to that of the tomb of Publius Aelius Callistion.
The Serapeum in Alexandria was a temple to Serapis erected by Ptolemy III in the third century B.C. It was destroyed in A.D. 391.
One of three shrines sacred to Serapis identified by archaeologists working at Delos in the nineteenth century.
The ancient Serbes river, mentioned by Ptolemy, is probably to be associated with the lower course of the modern Yusr (Isser) in Algeria.
A large, saline lake in Egypt on the north coast of the Sinai Peninsula; the "Serbonian Bog" described by Herodotus.
One of the "Dead Cities" of northern Syria, Sergilla (or Serjilla) was founded in 473. It lies close to the ruins of Bara in the Jebel Riha.

An ancient bronze column that was displayed in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, the Serpent Column was part of a monument originally installed at Delphi and relocated to Constantinople by Constantine I in A.D. 324. The monument was originally built to celebrate the Greek defeat of the Persian Empire at the Battle of Plataea in 479 B.C.
An ancient settlement in the Propontis near modern Ganos, Turkey.
A New Kingdom Egyptian town on the west bank of the Nile opposite Delgo, Sudan.
A river of northwestern Italy and a tributary of the Po River.
Setelsis was a settlement of the Jaccetani in Hispania Tarraconensis.
An archaeological site located at the midpoint of the Via Tiburtina linking Rome and Tibur.
A Late Republican Roman slave-run villa owned by the senatorial family of the Volusii.
An ancient settlement near modern site of Magrusa
An ancient settlement near modern site of Magrusa
An ancient settlement near modern site of Magrusa
An ancient settlement near modern site of Magrusa
Settlement north of Buridava Roman fort and Vicus
A Dacian settlement, probably of indigenous origin, lying a few kilometers north of the Roman fort and vicus known as Buridava. It may have originated the toponym.
A modern city and associated municipal district in Turkey's Konya province.
A fortified Parthian-Sassanid city with extensive remains of mudbrick architecture.

Shanidar Cave is a cave located in the Zagros Mountains, within the Erbil Governorate of the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq. The cave was the site of hominin activity beginning some 65,000 years ago. Following the first archaeological investigation of the cave in 1951, fieldwork has continued and, among other finds, has documented the remains of a dozen Neanderthals. There was proto-Neolithic a

Large temple at Tell Jokha/Umma dedicated to the Sumerian god Shara. The temple was constructed by king Šu-Suen of the Third Dynasty of Ur (2035-2027 BCE), and was used during the Ur III-Old Babylonian periods.
Site on the western bank of Shaytanskoe Lake, Sverdlovsk Oblast, containing remains dated to the early Bronze Age.
A necropolis located on the West Bank at Thebes in Upper Egypt that is now part of the archaeological area of Deir el-Bahari.
Oasis region in Southern Uzbekistan centered around the city of Sherabad/Sherobod containing 126 archaeological sites dating from the 2nd half of the 2nd millennium BCE to the 5th century CE.

Monastery near the town of Mtskheta in Georgia. According to tradition, the monastery was founded in the 6th century CE by St. Shio the Anchorite. It was one of Georgia's largest monastic communities in the early Middle Ages, and it remained in active use throughout the Medieval and Early Modern periods.

The ruins of VII.4.22 at Pompeii are identified as a shop with an associated dwelling and are linked to VII.4.21. The site was excavated in 1822 and again in 1833 and was bombed during the Second World War (13 September 1943). Among the themes depicted in the wall paintings of the structure are those to do with Adonis and his tomb at Byblos.
The so-called "Shore Temple" of Mahabalipuram is a granite-built tomb at the "Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram" UNESCO World Heritage Site. It dates to the eighth century CE.
An ancient trading colony on the Oxus river in the vicinity of the lapis lazuli mines of northern Afghanistan dating to ca. 2000 BC.
A rural shrine sacred to Dionysos located at Peristeria, Salamina in Salamis, Attica. The shrine is in the vicinity of the so-called "Cave of Euripides".

The Sacrum Cloacina was a small shrine dedicated to Venus Cloacina, patron divinity of the sewer, and was located near the Tabernae novae in the Forum Romanum. The foundation of the sacellum is extant while images of its likely elevation are found on Roman coins.
An ancient settlement in the Abruzzo mentioned by Polybius in the account of the Battle of Geronium during the Second Punic War.
One of the three indigenous tribes of Sicily present at the time of Phoenician and Greek colonization.
The modern Bolaman Irmağı in Turkey, which rises in the Pontic mountains and flows into the Black Sea.
A cape mentioned by Skylax. Modern scholars identify it with the Adrasan Burnu on Turkey's southern coast.

South of the marabout of Sidi el Mekki on the upper Beht river in modern Morocco, archaeological survey in the late 20th century identified pottery remains consistent with a small rural establishment of the Roman imperial era.
Tunisian location of ruins of an "agglomération urbain" tentatively identified in AAT with the attested "Elephantaria" (whence BAtlas).
The Sidicini were a people of ancient Italy; their territory bordered that of the Campani and the Samnites.
A town of Lycia located on the southern slope of Mt. Cragus and northwest of the mouth of the Xanthus river.

Thucydides relates that the Sikels (or Sicels) who would settle the island of Sicily and impart their name thereto got their start in the Italian peninsula and would eventually migrate to Sicily via raft. Thucydides goes on to relate that Italy, in fact, takes its name from Italus, a Siceliote king.
The archaeological site of an oppidum of either Punic or bastulo-Punic origin located in the Spanish municipality of Tarifa (Cádiz). It was likely a precursor of Baelo Claudia.
A mountain mentioned in ancient sources.
A tell settlement, located 20km west of Thessaloniki.
A mountain range, now called Sinjar Mountain (Shengar/Shengal), located in northwestern Iraq.
Singilis fl. (Genil river) is a tributary of the Baetis/Certis fl. (modern Guadalquivir).

An ancient city, located in modern Syria, with remains of an ancient church and residential buildings. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 as part of the "Ancient Villages of Northern Syria."
A small island that is part of the Pontine Islands.
The island of Siphnos has been inhabited since the Neolithic period and was a major center of Cycladic civilization.

A large Roman or late Roman fortress that was at least partly maintained into the medieval period. Known today as Rabat Kalesi, it is located to the northeast of the village of Hisaraltı in modern Turkey.
A mountain peak in modern Turkey, also known as Mount Sipylus, Mount Spil (or, in Turkish: Spil Dağı).

The ancient Sira corresponds to the modern Oued El Hammam in Algeria, which originates above Hammam bou Hanifia (ancient Aquae Sirenses) and the modern reservoir there. At modern Mohammadia (ancient Castra Nova), the river leaves the mountains and becomes known as the Oued Habra. Its course north across the plain and associated wetlands to empty into the Mediterranean east of modern Mers El Hadjad

Sirsukh is a ruined urban center that forms part of the archaeological landscape at ancient Taxila (Punjab, Pakistan). This urban center may have been founded during the Kushan era at the end of the first century CE and represents the last of the ancient cities of Taxila.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: vicinity of Sises.
Sitagroi is the location of an important archaeological site from the late Neolithic period and early Bronze Age.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: E middle Hebros valley TKY.
Sito archeologico Le Tombe di Amplero
A Pre-Roman settlement and necropolis of the Marsi.
Six Windows Building Complex at Sikait

A complex of three stone-built structures in the ancient settlement of Sikait in Egypt's Eastern Desert. The structure seems to have served a primarily residential function, certainly during the 4th and 5th centuries CE and (in a previous phase) during an as-yet undetermined earlier period. It may also have had a commercial function.
Skardon M., the Šar Mountains, is a mountain range in the Balkans that extends from Kosovo to northeastern Albania.
An island in the Atlantic Ocean located just west of the coast of Ireland.
Skidros or Scidrus was an ancient Greek city located on the Tyrrhenian coast of Lucania between Pyxus (Buxentum) and Laüs.

An ancient river that flowed by Edessa (modern Şanlıurfa in Turkey) and into the Euphrates. Much of its modern course is now diverted or built over, although ancient water gates and pools associated with the river are still extant in the southern portion of the ancient city of Edessa.
Skolopoeis was a settlement of Ionia. Herodotus notes the presence of a sanctuary sacred to the Eleusinian Demeter. The ancient place was located near Doğanbey in Asiatic Turkey.
Settlement mound in Northwestern Russia with archaeological remains from the 8th-1st millennium BCE.
A Hellenistic temple, possibly of Zeus, the foundation of which was excavated on the southern outskirts of the residential area of modern Skydra in Greece.
Skylax fl. (modern Çekerek river) is a tributary of the Iris river in Asia Minor.
Site 34 (“Slaves' Hill”) was an Iron Age copper smelting site in the Timna Valley. The peak of productive activity occurred in the tenth century BCE.
Small Roman Theater or Odeon at Sisak

Documented in media released by the Croatian Ministry of Culture and Media in 2025, remains of a small theater or odeon of Roman date have been identified and consolidated under the early 20th-century city hall of modern Sisak in Croatia (ancient Segestica/Siscia). Existence of a theater at Sisak was previously mooted on the basis of a Latin inscription mentioning a "magister mimariorum" (leader o
The remains of a triple arch in opus latericium marking the pomerium of Capua. It is perhaps originally constructed under the Flavians.

The ruins of an ancient building with a large peristyle, probably built around the second century AD, in the southwest area of the archaeological site of Sidi Khiribech, in Berenike (modern Banghazi).

A small basilica located outside the walls of the ancient Greek city of Akragas, at the foot of the so-called Temple of Juno, on the eastern slopes of the Hill of the Temples, in an area previously occupied by the necropolis of the late Roman period.
A large and rich Early Christian necropolis on the Via Sacra in Agrigento, dated to the fourth century A.D.
A Roman peristyle house located in Cyrene.
A very large Roman house on the acropolis ridge of Cyrene.
So-called House of the Doric Peristyle
A large private house in Cyrene.

A large building complex located on the western hill of Apollonia, probably built between the fifth and sixth centuries A.D. Its position and size, the presence of a chapel with a reliquary, and some public rooms led Goodchild to identify it as the residence of the Dux.

An architectural complex located on the West side of the East Church in Apollonia (Cyrenaica). Excavated in 1954-55, it was first thought to be a temple of Isis (Stucchi 1975). According to Kenrick (2013), it is more likely to have been a small production centre, maybe for the fermentation of wine.

A monumental complex in the ancient city of Syracuse, probably built around the first century AD. It was initially identified as a gymnasium or a thermal bath; it includes the ruins of a theatre, a quadriporticus, and a temple.
Temple 1, also referred to as the "Great Temple", is located in the lower city of Hattusa. It dates to the thirteenth century B.C.
A temple located on the acropolis of Cyrene.
A recently discovered temple on the acropolis of Cyrene.
A site on the Via Appia that is likely commercial in nature but that has long been associated with a shrine mentioned by Martial.

The ruins of an architectural complex in Sezze that acquired the misnomer of "Temple of Saturn" in the early modern period. The ruins are likely those of a platform villa and include visible remains in opus incertum and polygonal masonry of Lugli's "fourth" typological category, meaning the blocks approach isodomic forms.
The ruins of an ancient theatre in Cyrene, known as "Theatre 2".
A Roman theatre on the acropolis ridge of Cyrene, conventionally numbered "3".

A large architectural complex that includes a three-aisled church with a projecting western apse, a small atrium, a baptistery, and other structures built up against the inner face of the western stretch of the city wall of Apollonia.

An unusual structure close to the water edge, on the western side of Apollonia, refurbished in Byzantine times. The presence of Maltese crosses led to its interpretation as a martyrion, but an administrative role has also been suggested.
A double sanctuary on the forum of Carsulae. It is no longer clear to which gods these temples belonged.
An ancient river mentioned by Ptolemy. It may be identifiable with the modern Salween.
At Solforata along the Via Ardeatina activity related to the extraction of sulfur has been identified.
The so-called "Solomon's Pools" are three ancient reservoirs located in the south-central West Bank, approximately 3.5 kilometres (2.2 mi) southwest of Bethlehem. They date to the early Roman period.
Solsbury Hill is a flat-topped hill in Somerset, England, that is the site of an Iron Age hill fort.

The Talaiot de Son Fred is a prehistoric building on the island of Mallorca. It is located in the municipality of Sencelles in the Pla de Mallorca region. The building is attributed to the Iron Age Talaiotic culture and dates from the ninth to sixth centuries BCE.
Son Mercer de Baix is a naviform settlement on the island of Menorca. These "boat-shaped" stone settlements belong to the prehistoric cultures of the Balearic Islands.
A prehistoric necropolis near punta Fenicis that remained in use through the Roman period.
A burial site on the banks of the Om River in western Siberia containing a number of non-contemporaneous Bronze Age tombs.
Sorano was a Villanovan and, later, Etruscan settlement.
An eleventh and tenth century B.C. settlement in south Etruria.
The modern Riu Serpis, which debouches into the Mediterranean at modern Gandia in Valencia, Spain.
A pre-Roman tribe of the Aquitani.
Scholars associate the Souastos river, mentioned in ancient Greek sources, with the modern Swat river in Pakistan.
An ancient settlement, now known as al-Suriyya in Syria.
One of two gates providing access from the west through the southern end of the citadel defense walls at Dura-Europos.

South Stoa I is the modern name for the stoa that bounded the southern edge of the Agora of Athens from the late 5th century BC until the mid-2nd century BC, when it was demolished and replaced with South Stoa II. It contained rooms for communal dining and was probably the headquarters of the metronomoi and other officials.

The Southeast Stoa lined the east side of the Panathenaic Way at the southeast corner of the Athenian Agora, between the Library of Pantainos and the City Eleusinion. It was built in the mid-second century AD and incorporated into the Post-Herulian Wall after 267 AD.
Southwest Temple in the Agora of Athens
A tetrastyle Doric temple in the Athenian agora, built in the Augustan period using material from a Classical stoa at Thorikos and unidentified Hellenistic structures.
A region near Carthago Nova in Hispania Tarraconensis.

A temple in Acarnania, located between Stratos (modern Sourovigli) and modern Lepenou. The temple seems to have been constructed in the Greek Archaic period on the site of an earlier Helladic settlement. The temple continued in operation into the Roman period.
Sphettos was an inland deme of Akamantis, in Attica, near modern Koropi.
An archipelago off the east coast of Greece in the Aegean Sea consisting of 24 islands.
An island now known as Yılanlı Island.

The Square Peristyle is the modern name for a large square peristyle in the northeast corner of the Agora of Athens, begun around 300 BC, but never completed. It may have functioned as a lawcourt in the early Hellenistic period. It was demolished and used to build South Stoa II in the early 2nd century BC. The site was subsequently used for the Stoa of Attalos

Main temple in Ahobilam dedicated to the man-lion form of the Hindu god Vishnu built or expanded in the 14th century, sacked by the Mughals in 1578, then restored and expanded at various times up to the present day.
St-Aubin-sur-Gaillon was the site of a Gallo-Roman sanctuary.

A copper mine located about 4 kilometers southeast of the Alpine village of modern St-Véran (France). It was exploited as early as 2,000 BCE, and was in use in Roman times and again in the 20th century of the modern era.
A Byzantine castle in Cyprus likely built in the late eleventh century. The site was a holiday retreat for Cyprus's Frankish rulers, and the Venetians destroyed it in the fourteenth century.

Church in Geneva, Switzerland that was originally a Roman Catholic cathedral but was converted into a Protestant church during the Reformation. The original church was built in the 4th century but the present building began construction around 1150.
Mid-11th to mid-18th century church built on top of an older church that was an important pilgrimage site in Nubia. The church is located in the modern Sudanese village of Banganarti.
An Oscan and Roman settlement located on the bay of Naples.
A Roman city gate at the southern terminus of Strada Stabiana in Pompeii.
Domitian built the Stadium Domitiani in the Campus Martius at Rome.
A stadium of ancient Puteoli constructed under Antoninus Pius in the second century A.D. that was revealed by excavation in 2008.
An ancient city on the east coast of the Chalcidian peninsula. Birthplace of Aristotle.
An Iron Age ring fort, dating perhaps to the fourth century AD.
The Standing Stones of Stenness is a Neolithic monument on the mainland of Orkney, Scotland, generally dated to the third millennium BC.
An important Roman military road built in what is now northern England, linking Corbridge in the east and Carlisle in the west. A later western addition may have linked the fort at Kirkbride.

A group of four Roman buildings that includes a bathhouse with a hypocaust was discovered in 1957 and 1958. These remains indicated the presence of a Roman-style villa. The remains date from the second to fourth centuries A.D.
Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications or Stanwick camp is an Iron Age site in Britain covering approximately 300 hectares.
Stari Ras, the first capital of Serbia, is the site of an impressive group of medieval monuments consisting of fortresses, churches and monasteries listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
A 4th century BCE tholos tomb, embedded in a tumulus known as Chetinyova Mogila (Chetinyova Mound), located northwest of the modern Bulgarian village of Starosel.
An archaeological site at Starotitarovskaya 4, Russia, is included as numbered feature 165 on the Barrington Atlas map 87 M2.

Bronze and Iron Age burial ground in the Baraba forest-steppe containing 75 burials of the Pakhomovka culture (late second millennium BCE), plus additional burials from the Andronovo culture (ca. 2200-900 BCE) and Sargat culture (ca. 500-250 BCE).
A tribe of Liguria whose territory was located on the northern slopes of the Apennines in the Bormida valley.

Statues of the tyrannicides Harmodios and Aristogeiton, the assassins of the tyrant Hipparchos and symbols of the Athenian democracy. An initial pair, made by Antenor were erected in the Athenian Agora ca. 510 BC, taken away to Susa by the Persians in 480 BC and returned by Alexander or one of his successors in the late fourth century BC. A replacement pair, made by Kritios and Nesiotes were erect

Remains of this paleochristian church, located at modern Loupian in Hérault, France, were discovered and excavated in the 1980s. The structure lies immediately north of the current church of Ste-Cécile, which dates to the 14th century.

The stele of a Roman military officer dating to the first century A.D. located at modern Dikilí Tas (Ντικιλί Τας), an archaeological site with evidence for both prehistoric and Byzantine occupation. The stele stands just to the east of modern Krenides, only 2km from the center of the ancient city of Philippi, which lies on the west side of the modern town.

The Stoa at Brauron, within the larger Artemis Brauronia complex, housed dining spaces as well as votive offerings to the goddess Artemis. The Stoa was Π-shaped, wrapping around a courtyard that separated it from the temple of Artemis at Brauron, which it faced. Worship at the cult site began ca. the eighth century BCE. The site was abandoned after a flood in the third century BCE.
A group of four islands off Hyères, France, in the Mediterranean Sea.
Stomalimne/Mastramela Stagnum is a coastal lagoon on the Mediterranean coast of France, located som 25km northwest of Marseille.
The Stone of the Pregnant Woman in Baalbek, Lebanon is one of the largest monoliths ever quarried.
An ancient formation of stones set in a field near Salisbury (Wiltshire County, England).
Palace located in block C9 at Dura-Europos.
An auxiliary fort located just to the north of Watling Street.
The modern Sturma river originates in what is now Bulgaria, flows through the ancient region of Thrace, and empties into the Aegean Sea.
A river of northern Italy and a tributary of the Po river.
A nuragic spring sanctuary in use from the thirteenth to ninth centuries BC.
Suana (Sovana) has Etruscan origins but later became a Roman municipium. In the fifth century A.D. it became an episcopal see.
A first century BC bath complex in Pompeii built against the walls near the Porta Marina
The Júcar river flows 509 km from its source at Ojuelos de Valdeminguete to the Gulf of Valencia.
The Suebi were an ancient tribe in Germany, first mentioned by Iulius Caesar ca. 58 BC.
The Suessetani were a pre-Roman people of the northeast Iberian Peninsula that inhabited the Alba (Arba) river basin.
The Suessiones were a Belgic tribe located in what is now western Belgium.
Suessula was an important ancient city of Campania.
A Germanic people located along the Rhine river during the time of Caesar.
A northern Germanic people whose territory was located in Scandinavia; described by Tacitus in his treatise Germania.

The Sulayman-too Sacred Mountain (Taht-I-Suleiman, Sulayman Rock or Sulayman Throne) located in the city of Osh was once a major place of Muslim and pre-Muslim pilgrimage. The mountain is located in the plains the Fergana Valley.
A fortified area at Merv covering some 400 hectares.

A site with a long history of occupation, beginning in the Mesolithic period. In the Roman imperial period, a Roman auxiliary fort replaces a La Tène phase of occupation. A vicus is associated with the fort.

Armenian monastery in East Azarabaijan province, Iran. The first church was constructed on the site in 62 CE. A monastery was constructed there in the 7th century, and the structure was expanded in the 10th century.
Surkh Kotal is an archaeological site of southern Bactria and one of the most significant sites connected with the Kushan civilization.
An ancient settlement along the Via Salaria, the exact position of which remains unknown.
Ritual complex in central Mongolia consisting of eight deer stone monuments surrounded by nine stone rings and several cairns.
A Roman bridge along the Via Claudia Augusta.
Sweet Track is an ancient timber causeway of Britain built at the end of the fourth millennium BC.
A site in Cilicia Aspera near Demirtaş.
Synagogue adapted from a private house building in Dura-Europos.

An ancient sanctuary of Zeus attested in inscriptions found on "the upland plain of Makas Alan between the [Phrygian] cities of Kotiaeion (Kiitahya) and Nakoleia (Seyitgazi)" in modern Turkey (Drew-Bear). Its precise location cannot be determined today.
Syriai Pylai (Belen Pass) is a narrow pass through the Nur Mountains. This may be the location at which Alexander the Great pursued Achaemenid King Darius III after the Battle of Issus.

The largest island in the modern Khawr al-Bayḍā lagoon in the Emirate of Umm al-Quwain. Archaeological surveys conducted between 2012 and 2021 have identified two major and a variety of minor archaeological sites while beginning to establish dates and sequences for human occupation and exploitation of the island.
The T(h)onabaei were a tribe of southern Arabia mentioned by Pliny the Elder.

According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, TE.E (read as either Tê or Kisīri) was one of the six city districts of the eastern half of the inner city of Babylon and it contained one temple and two daises.
Taberna Frigida was a road station on the Via Aemilia Scauri at the crossing of the Frigidus river, located between Pisae and Luna.
A fruit shop in Pompeii (I, 8, 1) with an entrance on to the Via dell'Abbondanza.
Remains of a Roman vicus and hilltop temple complex excavated at modern Tawern in Germany.
A Kushite site located on Argo Island in Nubia, the location of a large Amun temple.

In 1997, during work to restore and consolidate the "Blue Mosque" in modern Tabriz, Iran, an extensive Iron Age cemetery was discovered and excavated. Since 2007, the site has been partly open to the public as an open-air museum.

The Tabula Traiana is a monumental inscription in what is now Serbia commemorating the completion of a Trajanic road along the Danube. The inscription was moved from its original spot to its present location in 1972.
The modern Segura River, flowing from the Sierra de Segura to the Mediterranean Sea in southeastern Spain.
Tafis was the site of a Roman fortress in Nubia.
Late Bronze-early Iron Age necropolis on the Tagisken plateau used throughout the first half of the first millennium BCE.
Saka necropolis with burials from the 7th-5th century BCE on the Tagisken plateau.
Takyris is an ancient royal Egyptian necropolis located in the desert on the west bank of the Nile.
Talatí de Dalt is a Talaiotic site located on Menorca.
Iron Age site in the Central Jordan Valley, sometimes identified with the historical place Adama.
Find spot (large mound) for an inscribed door socket.
A place from the TAVO Index
Find place for cuneiform inscription: high mound with eroded brick walls, north of Babylon.
An archaeological site of western Jordan that dates from the Early Bronze Age (ca. 3200–2100 BC) to the Hellenistic period (323–30 BC).
Mound with remains from third millennium BCE.
Prehistoric archaeological site located 3 km south of Persepolis. The site consists of two mounds (Tall-e Bakun A and B).
A settlement of the Mandalai located on the lower Ganges River.
A river name provided only by Ptolemy and thought by scholars to be identifiable with the modern Plymouth Sound estuary and its contributory, the Tamar (southwest England).
Tanarus fl. (Tanaro river) is a 276 km-long river in northern Italy that flows from the Ligurian Alps to the Padus fl. (Po river).
16th-century city of Bengal in South Asia
A circular Hellenistic tomb of the second century BC.
A third to second century B.C. tomb in the hinterland of Cortona.

A valley of the Pulvar River near Pasargadai in Fars/Persis, Iran. Rescue excavations before the completion of Sivand Dam revealed settlements and cemeteries from 5000 BCE to the Sassanian period, including the first rural site from the Achaemenid period to be excavated in Iran.
The second eastern-most ancient mouth of the Nile river.
A place from the TAVO Index
Taposiris Mikra was a town located to the east of Alexandria in the delta of the Nile river.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: E coast of Sri Lanka.
The Tarbelli (Quattuorsignani) were a people of western Aquitania.
The chief settlement of the Nantuates.
Tartessos was a harbor city and surrounding region located on the southern coast of the Iberian peninsula at the mouth of the Guadalquivir River.
Tarus fl. (Taro river) is a tributary of the Po river in northern Italy.
Tatta L. (Lake Tuz or Tuz Gölü) is one of the largest of the world's hypersaline lakes and the second largest lake in Turkey.
Taulantioi, a group of ancient Illyrian tribes.

Now unlocated, Taurianos Skopelos seems to be a rock formation in the Vibonensis Sinus, known in modern times as Golfo di Sant’Eufemia. As described by Ptolemy, this place is probably near Temesa on the Tyrrhenian Sea coast. The compilers of the Barrington Atlas note that the ancient place may be the same as the modern "Scogli Isca", which is now incorporated in a protected marine habitat area adm
A small island located just off the northeast coast of Sardinia. It may correspond to a "Hermaia" mentioned in Ptolemy's Geography.

This reconstructed (in-situ) temple complex stands on a hill called Metzenberg, just to the southwest of modern Tawern in Germany. A partially excavated Gallo-Roman vicus lies at the foot of the hill, closer to town.
An ancient city with the ruins of the Gandhāran city of Takṣaśilā, an important Hindu and Buddhist center. (cited: BAtlas 6 C3 Taxila)
The major mountain range of the Peloponnese, running north/south for over 100km. In antiquity, it separated Laconia from Messenia.
A large Roman bridge at Adana in the modern country of Turkey. It spans the Psaros/Sinarus/Koiranos river (modern Seyhan).
A town in ancient Apulia located between Larinum and and Sipontum. Rome took control of the site in 318 BC, granting it municipal status.

The so-called "Maritime Theater" at the Villa of Hadrian in Tivoli is sometimes referred to as the 'island villa'. It served as a kind of inner sanctum within the larger complex of the Villa Hadriana.
The Tech river flows some 84 km from its source is the Parcigoule Valley to the Mediterranean Sea.

An ancient river. Ptolemy places its mouth on the Adriatic coast of what is now Croatia, between Lopsica (modern Sv. Juraj) and Ortopla (modern Stinica). BAtlas followed prior scholarship in identifying it with the former course of the Gacka river, which was diverted in the 1960s for power generation. Other prior scholarship assumed Ptolemy was in error, suggesting the Tedanius be identified with
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Puebla de Trives region.
Teithras was an inland deme of Aigeis in Attica.
Tel Anafa is an archaeological site of the Upper Galilee in Israel. The site was inhabited from the Early Bronze Age through the early Roman period and has a notable Hellenistic phase.
Tell in northern Israel with remains from the Late Bronze Age, Iron Age, Persian period, and Byzantine period. The tell was not fortified but did have a fortress in the Iron Age.
Teleboas? fl. (the modern Karasu (Euphrates)) is a river of eastern Turkey and one of the sources of the Euphrates.
A small Aegean island in the Sporades, located just west of Kalymna.
A Bronze and Iron Age archaeological site in Gilead in the eastern valley of the Jordan river
BAtlas 89 E4 Tell Ahmed Agha Kabir
Settlement in western Syria inhabited from the 3rd Millennium BCE through the Byzantine period.
Tell on the southwestern corner of Failaka Island containing the remains of two large buildings, tentatively identified as a palace and a temple, dated to 1900-1400 BCE.
Settlement site in the Deh Luran Plain in Iran rich in pottery remains. The site has remains from the Chalcolithic, Uruk and Early Dynastic, Elamite, Parthian, and Sasanian periods.

Tell in the Hamrin Basin with settlement remains from the Early Dynastic, Early Akkadian, Late Akkadian, Ur III, Old Babylonian, and Partho-Sassanian periods. The site was flooded by the creation of Lake Hamrin in 1981.
Religious and administrative center in Syria with two temple complexes. This site was in use in the Early Dynastic Period and the Uruk and Abaid periods.
An early and middle Bronze Age site in the Jordan valley.
Neolithic settlement in the Azmak River Valley inhabited from the 7th-2nd millennia BCE. The hilltop settlement is the type site of the Karanovo culture.
A settlement mound with evidence of human activity stretching from the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period to the Hellenistic period.
An unusual circular "fort" dating to the Old Kingdom period of ancient Egypt.
Tell in Mesopotamia occupied during the Proto-Dynastic period I, the early Akkadian period, and the Seleuco-Parthian period. Tell Sabra was submerged with the creation of the Hemrin Dam in 1981.
Mound east of Aleppo, Syria which was inhabited from 2400 BCE until its destruction in 2000 BCE. The site was deluged by the creation of the Tabqa Dam in 1973.
An archaeological site in East Jerusalem, identified as a possible location for the ancient sites of Gibeah or Perath/Parah.
Archaeological site in Jordan, located approximately 10 km northwest of Madaba. The site shows signs of primary occupation during the Iron Age II (900-600 BCE).
A small but tall settlement mound located in the Jordan Valley with archaeological remains from the eighth-fourth centuries BCE.
Temenion was located in the Argolid. It was built by Temenus, the son of Aristomachus. Temenion lay 50 stades from Nauplia and 26 from Argos.
An ancient city located on the west coast of Bruttium, just north of the Gulf of Hipponium.
An Archaic settlement in Lucania located near moderm Oliveto Lucano.
A major urban sanctuary at Vulci with a long period of use, stretching from the archaic period into the Roman period.

The temple of Grasceta dei Cavallari is an Etrusco-Roman sanctuary located in the municipality of Tolfa. This sanctuary sits at the foot of Mount Mazza, above a pass near Tarquinia and Caere's ancient borders. The temple was small, with a rectangular platform and an octastyle arrangement.
The so-called Temple C at Selinus is a Doric temple that dates to the second half of the sixth century B.C.
Temple at Santa Maria in Canale

A temple of Tuscan type with cella and lateral alae built of ashlar masonry and dated to the 3rd century BCE, now built into a rural church and farmstead complex. The temple is situated along the Via Amerina between Ameria and Tuder, and marks the boundary between those two Umbrian communities. A fragmentary Umbrian bronze inscription (Vetter 229) of around 300 BCE mentioning a deity characterized
The so-called "Temple de Diane" is a first century Roman monument on the Gard river dedicated to Augustus.

Church in Geneva, Switzerland that has existed in some form since the 4th century CE. The 4th century building was followed by a 10th century Romanesque church which was destroyed by fire in the 14th century. The current church was constructed in the 15th century.
An area of the upper city of Hattusha with the remains of up to 30 temples.

A temple sacred to the goddess Al-Lat in Palmyra. The earliest shrine on the site was constructed in the mid-first century BCE, and was greatly expanded during the second century CE. The temple was closed and its altar destroyed during the 380s CE.

The Temple of Amada is the oldest Egyptian temple known in Nubia. Founded by Pharaoh Thutmose III (18th dynasty), the temple was dedicated to Amun and Re-Horakhty. The decorative program is attributed to Amenhotep II, his son and successor. The temple was relocated to its current position in 1964 along with the Temple of Derr.
Amenhotep II built a temple at Giza that he dedicated to the god Horemakhet, a sun-god identified with the Great Sphinx. It lies northeast of the Sphinx itself.
Temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal
Large temple dedicated to the Amun located at the base of Jebel Barkal. Designated temple B500, the structure was likely constructed by the Napatan king Piankhi in the 8th century BCE.

The Temple of Apollo Patroos on the west side of the Agora of Athens was built at the end of the fourth century BC. It contained a famous statue of Apollo by Euphranor. The structure wraps around the tiny fourth-century BC shrine of Zeus Phratrios and Athena Phratrios. The existence of an earlier temple, destroyed during the Persian Sack of 480 BC, is disputed.
The Temple of Apollo Zoster is a sanctuary of the god Apollo located in Vouliagmeni in Attica, Greece. The temple's foundations date to the sixth century BC.
The second temple of Apollo at Corinth whose reconstructed remains are visible on the site today. The structure dates ca. 540 B.C.
Temple of Artemis on Thasos Island with remains from the Archaic period to the 1st century CE.
Archaeological phase (c. 13-160 CE) of the Temple at Dura-Europos dedicated to Artemis Azzanathkona, probably the tutelary deity of the Euphrates island settlement Anath.
An Archaic temple dedicated to Artemis Orthia within the sanctuary of this goddess at Sparta. The site contained rich deposits of both votives and masks.

An archaic temple of Athena on the acropolis of Thasos was dismantled in the 5th century BCE. Planning, procurement of materials, and construction of its replacement seem to have begun shortly thereafter, but were never finished.
Pausanias describes the Temple of Athena Polias at Erythrai as containing a wooden image of the enthroned goddess.
Temple of Athena Skiras at Phaleron

This sanctuary, reported in Phaleron by Pausanias, is thought to have been located near the modern "old town" of Phaleron in Attica. It is not to be confused with the Temple of Athena Skiras on the island of Salamis, reported by Herodotus.
Temple of Athena Skiras on Salamis

This sanctuary, reported by Herodotus, is thought to have been located on the modern Cape Arapis in the northeast part of the island of Salamis, just north of the modern naval base. It is not to be confused with the Temple of Athena Skiras in Phaleron, reported by Pausanias.
The Temple of Athena at Sounion (ca. 470 B.C.) with its L-shaped colonnade was built on the site of an earlier temple (sixth century B.C.) at the same location.
An early Imperial (first to third centuries) temple at Centuripae that has been associated with the priestly college of the Augustales.
The Temple of Augustus in Pula is a Roman temple that dates to the time of Augustus. The tetrastyle Corinthian temple sites a high podium.

The Temple of Augustus and Roma at Ankara likely dates ca. 20 BCE. It is also known as the "Monumentum Ancyranum", highlighting the structure's role in preserving the most complete copy of the inscription known as the "Res Gestae Divi Augusti", which was promulgated in both ancient Greek and Latin following the death of emperor Augustus in 14 CE.

The so-called Temple of Augustus et Livia dates ca. 10 B.C. and was originally dedicated to Roma and Augustus. The temple was located on the ancient forum of the city. By the fifth century the temple had become a Christian church. It was extensively restored in the nineteenth century.
The Temple of Augustus dates to the second century A.D.
Temple in Palmyra dedicated to the Canaanite god Baalshamin.
Located at the southeast corner of the Forum Romanum, the aedes Castoris is a temple of ancient Rome vowed by the dictator Postumius in 499 BCE.
Temple of Castor and Pollux, Cora
The Temple of Castor and Pollux at Cora was originally built between the fourth and the second centuries B.C. The partially extant architrave carries an inscription of the first century B.C.
An ancient temple relocated in the 1960s before the completion of the Aswan dam.

An ancient Egyptian temple that was dedicated to Dedwen, the Nubian serpent goddess. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, as part of "Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae". It was relocated to its current location.
A Punic and Roman temple sacred to Demeter and Kore located at Bagoi, Perdaxius, Sardinia.
The temple in the forum of Augusta Emerita is conventionally known by the misnomer "Temple of Diana", yet was actually dedicated to the Imperial cult.
According to Cassius Dio, Tiberius dedicated a temple to the deified Augustus at a location marking the site of the princeps' death. Its precise location is not known.

A small rock-cut temple dedicated to Amun, Horus, and Satis dated to the 18th Dynasty. Originally located near Qasr Ibrim/Premis, the temple was relocated to the Museo Egizio in Turin, Italy, in the 1960s prior to the area's flooding beneath the surface of Lake Nasser.

The Temple of Hathor at Deir el-Medina dates to the reign of the Ptolemies. It was later repurposed as a Christian installation known as Deir el-Medina or "Monastery of the City", from which the site's modern toponym is derived.
The Temple of Heracles is one of the oldest temples in the Valley of the Temples in ancient Akragas, Sicily, dating from around the late 6th century BCE.
The Temple of Herakles at Cora was built during the 80s B.C. The temple is tetrastyle in its plan and built following the Etrusco-Italic temple tradition.
The Temple of Hercules is located within the Amman Citadel in Amman, Jordan. The temple was built during the administration of Geminius Marcianus, ca. 162-166.
Monumental Ptolemaic temple dedicated to Horus, constructed between 237 BCE and 57 BCE at the settlement of Apollinopolis Magna.
A major ancient sanctuary of the Capitoline Hill, the remains of which are likely to be found beneath Santa Maria in Ara Coeli.
A monumental first-century A.D. Romano-Celtic sanctuary located in Autun, Saône-et-Loire, France, to the northwest of the ancient city of Augustodunum.
A temple of the Doric order that was built at Akragas ca. 450 BCE.
Juno Caelestis, a successor divinity of the Punic Tanit, is celebrated by a sanctuary built at Dougga ca. 222-235 CE, and sponsored by Q. Gabinius Rufus Felix.
A second-century CE temple sacred to Jupiter.
A small temple to Jupiter the Thunderer, most likely located in the Area Capitolina. Vowed by Augustus in 26 BCE and dedicated in 22 BCE.
The Temple of Jupiter in Damascus was begun during the rule of Augustus and completed during the rule of Constantius II.
A temple dedicated to the god Khnum constructed during the Ptolemaic and Roman period in the city of Esna (Latopolis).
New Kingdom temple to the god Khonsu, constructed by Ramesses III and expanded by Ptolemy III Euergetes.
A Gallo-Roman temple of Mercurius, located atop the modern Puy-de-Dôme, commune Orcines in France.
A temple sacred to Montu located at El-Tod, Egypt. The temple's foundations were laid during the Fifth Dynasty and the sanctuary continued in use under the Ptolemies.
The Temple of Olympian Zeus is located approximately 3 km southwest of Syracuse on the Cyane river.
Temple of Poseidon and Amphitrite on Tenos
The Poseidon sanctuary at Isthmia lies 16 km to the east of Corinth. The initial phase belongs to the seventh century BC, although the sanctuary was destroyed ca. 470 BC and rebuilt in 440 B.C.

A temple dedicated to a local form of the Egyptian god Sobek, Soknebtunis, at Tebtunis. The temple was built by Ptolemy I in the late fourth-early third centuries and was greatly expanded by Ptolemy XII in the first century BCE.

An Etruscan temple of the fourth century BCE, associated with the ancient settlement of Telamon. It lies on Mount Talamonaccio, across the bay from the modern village of Talamone, north of Orbetello, Italy.
The Temple of Tellus (Thugga) dates to the reign of Gallienus ca. 261 CE.
The Temple of Trajan at Pergamon, also referred to as the Traianeum, was dedicated to Trajan and Zeus Philios and completed during the reign of Hadrian.
The Temple of Venus Genetrix located in the Forum Iulium was dedicated ca. 46 BCE.
A temple in the Roman Forum dedicated to the deified Vespasian that was begun by Titus and completed under Domitian.
The Temple of Vesta in Tivoli dates to the early first century B.C. It was once situated on the acropolis of the ancient city. Its ruins now lie within the grounds of the Villa Gregoriana.
Temple building located on the southwest side of Dura-Europos.
A partially reconstructed Doric temple, dating to the 4th century BCE.
The Temple of Zeus at Olympia was built in the second quarter of the fifth century B.C. Libon of Elis served as architect.
The Temple of the Ship Carpenters at Ostia dates to the later second century CE.
Near a bath complex built under Commodus, a Severan complex that included a plaza, porticoes, and a temple dedicated to the Severan family was added.
Temple or Large Administrative Building at Sikait

A significant, large structure at Sikait in Egypt's Eastern Desert that has been variously identified as an administrative building and, most recently on basis of finds from the first systematic archaeological excavation of the structure, as a temple.

The main sanctuary at Ai Khanoum, built in a mixture of Greek and Mesopotamian styles under the Seleucids and rebuilt under the Diodotids in the 240s BC, again in the early 2rd century BC and in the reign of Eukratides (ca. 170-140 BC).
The Temple of Peace in Rome was vowed by Vespasian following the Jewish War.

An archaeological site in the modern Parc National de l'Isalo in southern Madagascar. The site comprises rock-cut terraces, niches, walls, and other features in a style unique in the region. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and stylistic dating of imported ceramics place activity at the site to a period spanning the 10th - 12th centuries CE. The excavators tentatively interpret the site as part of a
An archaeological site located in the central Zagros mountain range where human occupation begins as early as the sixth millennium BCE.
Termas Romanas do Alto da Cividade
A monumental public bath (thermae) at Braga, dating from the first to third centuries CE.
Remains of Roman baths at Antequera in Spain.
A Roman bath located at Aquae Passeris.
The largest known bath complex of Roman Mediolanum, built in the late third to early fourth centuries CE.
The Roman baths of ancient Ferentium are located adjacent to the Roman theater.

The so-called "Baths of the Swimmer" or "Terme del Nuotatore" (V,X,3) in region 5 of the ancient city of Ostia takes its modern name from a partially preserved black-and-white mosaic pavement. These baths were built in the late first century CE during the reign of Domitian. The complex was rebuilt during the Antonine period. The complex remained in use until ca. 250. The site was first excavated d

Mineral springs located at modern Lamezia Terme in Italy's Cantanzaro province. There is some archaeological evidence for exploitation of the springs in antiquity, but the current spa complex is completely modern in date. Some scholars have suggested that the Terme di Caronte may correspond to the "Aquae angae" mentioned on the Peutinger Map.
The so-called "Terme di Tito" is a terraced Roman villa site located in the modern comune of Castel Sant'Angelo near Lago Paterno.
The so-called "Terrace of Zeus" or "Terrazza di Zeus" at Elea-Velia.
Terrace of the Lions at Delos
Nine white marble lions arranged in a single row along a terrace facing the sacred lake. The pathway marks an entry point into the city from the Bay of Skardana towards the shrine of Leto.
The land where the Pieres, a Thracian tribe, resettled after being driven from Pieria in the 7th century BC
The monumental columnar entrance to the sanctuary of Aphrodite
A mountain group in Italy, part of the central Apennines, the Tetricus mons is known today as the Monti Sibillini (Sibylline Mountains).
An ancient settlement of Boetia, probably to be located at modern Mesovouni.
Mount Tabor is located in the Lower Galilee at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley, approximately 18 km west of the Sea of Galilee.
A river in the modern region of Calabria, flowing from the Sila plateau (Sila Piccola) to the Gulf of Squillace.
An ancient city of Arabia, located west of the Persian Gulf.

An ancient place included in the Peutinger map between "Arcamo" (Arzamon) and Nisibis (modern ). Its precise modern location is unknown today, not least because the map in this section seems rather confused with regard to the relative locations of known sites (like Arzamon and Nisibis) and the river Tigris.
A Roman city located in the province of Mauretania Tingitana, along the road from Tingi to Sala. The city is mentioned by Ptolemy, the Antonine Itinerary, and the Geographer of Ravenna.

Thanahat Church is a Christian church situated in a mountain village at the right shore of the Vorotan river near the village Arevis, 17 km west of Sissian in the Sjunik province in southern Armenia. In the ruins of the church, a stele of the Urartian king Argišti II., son of Rusa (eighth century BCE) was found, which describes his success and conquest of the land Etiuḫi, resulting in the deportat
A Celto-Roman sanctuary situated at an ancient high-mountain pass in the eastern Alps near Grossglockner, excavated beginning in the 1990s. Its ancient name is unknown.

Monumental religious building carved out of rock in Petra, Jordan which was used for a variety of complex religious ceremonies and customs after the time of its completion in the mid-first century CE.
The Frith is an Iron Age hillfort in Hampshire, England, that covers 1.6 hectares.
A monumental limestone sphinx situated on the Giza plateau, likely connected with the reign of Pharaoh Khafre.
A Roman fort on the island of Alderney in the English Channel. Its ancient name is unknown.
The Ridgeway is an ancient trackway that runs from Wiltshire along the chalk ridge of the Berkshire Downs to the River Thames in England.
A sanctuary of the Pentrian Samnites on the flanks of Monte Capraro, north of the modern Italian village of Vastogirardi.
The Sanctuary of the Nymph Ionides
Healing spring described by Pausanias on the Kytherios River, in Salmone, Elis
Treasury building erected by the citizens of the island city of Siphnos at Delphi in the late Archaic period, famous for its caryatid columns.
The Temple of Athena Polias at Priene
The temple of Athena at Priene, designed by the architect Pytheos, is an especially good example of the Late Classical form of the Ionic order.
The now destroyed Temple of Janus near the Forum Romanum, Rome, was originally built in the reign of Numa, according to Livy.
The theater at Larissa was a large stone theater built around the end of the third century BC and used for dramatic performances and as a political meeting place.
Tomb of the mythic figure Protesilaus, first to die in the Trojan War. According to ancient testimony, the tomb was located on the Chersonesus, near Elaeus, its precise location is not known today.
A Greek and Roman theater at the site of Butrint.
The largely preserved classical theater at Thorikos is dated ca. 525-480 B.C.
The Theater of Aphrodisias dates to the second half of the first century B.C. and stands on the eastern slope of the acropolis.
The Greek theater of Cyrene was constructed in the sixth century BCE and transformed into a Roman amphitheater in the second century CE.
Theatre on the south slope of the Acropolis in Athens.
The Theater of Melos likely has Hellenistic origins but the visible phase belongs to the Roman period.
A theater-temple complex that stands within pre-Roman walls belonging to a period of Samnite occupation on Monte San Nicola in the municipality of Pietravairano, Italy.
Originally the Saite tomb of Ankh-Hor, this site was reused from the 4th century BCE by the Late Dynastic/Ptolemaic period family of Pa-di-Amun-neb-nesut-tawy, a high-ranking priest of Khonsu.

TT69 is located in the Theban Necropolis on the west bank of the Nile. It served as the tomb of an Egyptian official known as Menna, among whose titles were "Overseer of Fields of Amun", and "Overseer of Fields of the Lord of the Two Lands". The tomb is generally dated to the reign of Thutmosis IV.
Theganoussa island, the modern Venetiko, Peloponnese, Greece.
An ancient settlement in Arcadia that flourished from the Archaic to Roman periods.
The circuit wall of Athens, built by Themistokles in 479 BC. It was abandoned as indefensible in the aftermath of the Herulian Sack of 267 AD.
The Theodosian Walls (Murus Theodosii) were erected during the reign of Emperor Theodosius II (r. 408–450) to defend the landward approach to the city of Constantinople.

"Theon Ochema" is a toponym that describes a place in West Africa. Scholarship suggests that this toponym appears in the treatises of Mela and Pliny the Elder via the Greek version of the Periplus written by Hanno the Navigator. Some scholars suggest that this place be identified with Mount Cameroon.

An island of the southern Aegean Sea, Thera is the southernmost of the Cyclades. The island's present form is the result of a Middle Bronze Age volcanic eruption that destroyed a Minoan settlement on the island.
Ancient settlement southeast of Sparta associated with the Menelaion (sanctuary of Helen and Menelaos).
Public baths near the Viminal Hill in Rome constructed under Diocletian from 298-306 CE.
The site of thermal spings, founded as a sub-colony of Selinus in the seventh century B.C. Thought to be in the area of modern Sciacca.
A monumental public bath of ancient Rome that was built between 104 and 109. The architect Apollodorus of Damascus built the baths for Trajan.
The Terme River or Terme Çayı.
A dining establishment that served drinks and hot food in antiquity. There are several well-preserved wall paintings in the interior.
The house and thermopolium of Vetutius Placidus (I,8,8) opens directly onto the south side of the Via dell'Abbondanza.
One of the three main ancient tribes of Epirus.
Thizica was a civitas in the Roman province of Africa Proconsularis.
The residential and production district of Thorikos features the remains of a number of classical period houses and a silver refinement center.
Lake Van, the largest lake in Asia Minor, is a saline soda lake.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: MOL/UKR.
The Thriasion Lager was a fortified camp in ancient Attica located 3 km. west of the so-called Dema Wall.
Thubursicum Numidarum (now Khamissa, Algeria) is an indigenous site that became a Roman municipium by A.D. 100 (Municipium Ulpium Traianum Augustum Thubursicu).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: SE Tipasa.
The Tirso river, one of the most important rivers of Sardinia, flows from the Punta Pianedda to the Gulf of Oristano.
An ancient settlement, located on the Athos/Akte peninsula.

The ancient theater of Tarquimpol is located at the ancient settlement of Decempagi, present-day Tarquimpol, in the Moselle department. The theater was revealed by aerial photography in 1981; the theater measures approximately 117 meters in diameter and could accommodate up to 16,000 people.
An ancient right tributary of the Eurotas, joining it south of ancient Sparta. It is to be identified probably with the modern Langada/Langkada (BAtlas) or Skatias (ToposText).
An ancient population of Scythian descent inhabiting the southern shores of the Black Sea in Asia Minor.
An island in the Tiber River at the site of Rome.
The Sea of Galilee, also known as the Sea of Tiberias, is the largest freshwater lake in Israel.
Tiberias was founded by Herod Antipas ca. 20 BC.
Tibiscum was an ancient settlement of Dacia mentioned by Ptolemy that later became a Roman castrum and municipium.
Ticinus fl. (Ticino) is a left-bank tributary of the Padus fl. (Po river) in northern Italy.
The Tifernus (modern Biferno) is a river of Molise that flows from near Bojano to the Adriatic Sea.
Tigava Castra was a fort located in Mauretania Caesariensis, between Oppidum Novum and Malliana.
An elite villa dated to the first century B.C.
A Hellenistic city founded under either King Tigranes I, or his son and successor King Tigranes the Great.
A river in north-east Italy, flowing from the Alps to the Adriatic Sea.

Tillya tepe ("Golden Hill" or "Golden Mound") is an archaeological site in northern Afghanistan near Sheberghan. A hoard of approx. 20,000 gold ornaments and coins were discovered in six tombs dating to the first century BC.
A promontory on the north coast of Corsica mentioned by Ptolemy. Modern scholars identify it with the Punta Cavallata, which is located just west of the Gulf of Saint Florent.
Timonitis was a region of the interior of Paphlagonia.

The archaeological site of Timpone del Ponto in Lucania indicates occupation from the Bronze Age through to the the Hellenistic period. The built fortifications of the Hellenistic period command a narrow point of the Sinni river valley between the hills of Coppola and Colobraro.
Timur is a mountain that is situated between Meliddu and Tabal.
An island in the Ligurian Sea designated as part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Tino is connected with the life of the seventh-century AD Christian Saint Venerius.
Tiran (Arabic: جزيرة تيران‎ Jazīrat Tīrān) is an island located in the Straits of Tiran, which separate the Red Sea from the Gulf of Aqaba.
A Roman fortlet in Tripolitana (modern Ksar Ghilane in Tunisia).
An ancient place in Bruttium mentioned by Appian. Its precise location is unknown today.
An ancient Aeolian city, Tisna was built on a pair of volcanic hills northwest of modern Uzunhansanlar (Aliağa, İzmir, Turkey).

A Chalcolithic cemetery located at modern Polgár, Hungary, with at least 156 graves. This site is the typesite for the Tiszapolgár or Tiszapolgár-Româneşti culture, an Eneolithic archaeological culture. This archaeological culture has been identified on the Great Hungarian Plain and elsewhere in eastern, central Europe. It dates ca. 4500-4000 BCE.

Fortified site associated with the Saltov-Mayatskaya culture (8th-10th centuries CE) located northwest of the modern village of Titchikha, Voronezh Oblast'. Remains dated to the Scythian period have also been found in the vicinity of the site.
A people settled on the coast of south-western Corsica (area of modern Tizzano).

An ancient settlement mound located 45 kilometers north of Şanlıurfa, Turkey, Titris Hoyuk lies near the Euphrates River valley. There were several phases of occupation in the third and second millennia BCE.
The modern Boz Dağ in Turkey, which lies immediately east of the city of Izmir.
To-Bener was an ancient site in Lower Egypt, located east of ancient Xois. It is thought to have been near modern Kafr Matbul.

A village located in the valley of the Omecillo River, a tributary of the Ebro. Tobillas has been the focus of a case study interested in the processes of village formation from both archaeological and historical perspectives.
A river of the Venetia, possibly in the territory of Patavium.
A river of Lazio and Abruzzo that is a tributary of the Velino.
The modern Italian comune of Tolfa is 24 kilometers northeast of Cerveteri. Its environs contain several ancient sites, dating from prehistory as well as the time of the Roman Empire.
A location at the most easterly point of England that, in antiquity, was separated from the mainland by the River Wantsum.
One of the three Gaulish tribes found in ancient Galatia.
Tomb 3 is a rock-cut tomb with a peristyle courtyard in the "Tombs of the Kings" necropolis of Nea Paphos.
Tomb of Annedia and Lucius Caesius
The Tomb of Annedia and Lucius Caesius is an aedicula tomb in the Porta Nocera necropolis.
The Tomb of Arellia Tertulla, daughter of Numerius and wife of Veius Fronto.
A tomb at Pompeii's Herculaneum gate that may be that of Aulus Umbricius Scaurus.
A Roman tomb on the right bank of the Anio discovered in 1929. The tomb dates to the first century A.D. and is associated with Cossinia, a priestess of the cult of Vesta.
A burial mound described by Pausanias as the Tomb of Theban general Epaminondas. Located near Mantineia, east of Milia.
A monumental exedra-type tomb built at the Porta Nocera between ca. A.D 1-30 that served as the tomb for the family of Eumachia.
The Late Republican tomb of the freedman Hilarus Fuscus along the Via Appia (ca. 30 B.C.).

The Tomb of Marcus Alleius Minius is located outside the Porta Stabia of Pompeii. It is a schola-type tomb, excavated 1888-1890. The tomb carries a Latin inscription and it was buried by debris following the 62 CE earthquake.
The mastaba tomb of the vizier Mereruka at Saqqarah dates to the Sixth Dynasty of ancient Egypt.

The Tomb of Nigidius Alleius Maius was excavated in 2017. The tomb includes a 'res gestae'-style inscription in Latin that describes the life, career, and patronage of the decedent. Although the name of the decedent is no longer extant, the tomb has been linked to prominent citizen Nigidius Alleius Maius.
Tomb of Petosiris at Tuna el-Gebel

The Tomb of Petosiris at Tuna el-Gebel dates to the late fourth century BCE. Petosiris, also called Ankhefenkhons, served as the high priest of Thoth at Hermopolis during the 28th Dynasty of ancient Egypt.
A Roman tomb along the Via Appia that belonged to one Priscilla, wife of Titus Flavius Abascanto, a freedman of the emperor Domitian.

The tomb of Publius Aelius Callistion, a freedman (libertus) of the emperor Hadrian, is colloquially known as the "Sedia del Diavolo". It is located in a piazza that derives its name from the tomb's occupant (piazza Elio Callistio) in Rome's Trieste neighborhood.

An aedicula tomb built near the Porta Nocera ca. A.D. 25-50 by Publius Vesonius Phileros for himself, his patroness Vesonia, and his friend Marcus Orfellius Faustus. A later added inscription shows a falling out between the two friends.
Tomb TT39 in the Theban Necropolis, the burial site of Puimre (or Puyemre), an Egyptian official of the 18th Dynasty.
The tomb of the boy poet Quintus Sulpicius Maximus on the Via Salaria in Rome. He died in 94 CE, aged just 11 years.
Theban Tomb 100 (TT100), the burial place of Rekhmire, a noble of the 18th dynasty.
Tomb KV17 in the Valley of Kings was the burial place of the 19th dynasty Pharaoh Seti I.
A Late Antique hypogeum tomb discovered in 1911 and dedicated to Trebius Iustus and Honoratia Severina.
An imperial Roman tomb of Publius Vibius Marianus, erroneously identified as the Tomba di Nerone (Tomb of Nero) by G. B. Piranesi.
Tomb of the Five Chairs, Caere
An Etruscan tomb at Caere dated ca. 625-600 B.C.
The Tomb of the freedman Marcus Lollius Lucrio and his familia at Pompeii.
Tomb of the Shields and Chairs, Caere

The so-called Tomb of the Shields and Chairs at Caere dates ca. 520 - 500 B.C. The organization of this tomb is similar to that of the Tomb of the Capitals and the Tomb of the Cornice. It has a short dromos and a large vestibule. In the vestibule are two seats carved from the tuff bedrock as well as a series of hanging shields carved in relief.
The Tomb of the Stronnii at Pompeii is a monumental altar tomb that is flanked by lions carved in tuff.

A painted Etruscan tomb at Chiusi that dates ca. 170-150 BCE. The tomb has acquired a constellation of modern appellations, including "tomba della Tassinaie", "tomba della Tassinara," and "tomba della Tassinaia".
The so-called Tomb of the Winged Demons (Sovana, Italy), a third-century BC Etruscan tomb located in the Poggio Felceto necropolis.
