The Grotta Campana at Veii is an Etruscan burial complex discovered by Giampietro Campana in 1843.
A Hellenistic, rock-cut tomb at Norchia. The site is located within the modern municipal boundaries of Viterbo in Lazio, Italy.
An Etruscan tumulus-type tomb in the Monte Abatone necropolis of Caere that dates ca. 320-200 BCE.
An ancient tomb located along the via di Terrano on the outskirts of Falerii Novi.
A Roman tomb near Albano Laziale connected in tradition with the story of the contest between the Horatii and Curiatii.
A mid-seventh century BCE tumulus at Populonia with a diameter of 28 meters; part of the San Cerbone necropolis.
The so-called "Tomb of the Roaring Lions" at Veii is considered to be among the earliest, if not the earliest, known example of a painted tomb in Etruria. It is dated ca. 700-690 BCE.

The so-called Tomba del Peccato has been a well-known rock-cut tomb in the hinterland of Falerii Novi since the nineteenth century. The tomb collapsed following heavy rains in 1991 and is in a ruinous condition.
A corridor-type tomb in the territory of Vetulonia dating to the Orientalizing period.
A Roman chamber tomb now located on the grounds of the Policlinico Umberto I hospital in Rome.
A Roman tomb on the Via Flaminia at Grottarossa that is associated with Annia Aurelia Fadilla, the daughter of the emperor Marcus Aurelius.
A single-chamber tomb carved in tufo bedrock at Cortona dates from the third and second centuries BCE. The Tomba di Mezzavia was discovered in 1950.
The so-called tomb of Tulliola is a Roman mausoleum located at Formiae. Situated about 100 meters from the so-called tomb of Cicero, this tomb is held to be that of Cicero's father.
Tombs of the Buccii and Melissaei
The Grave enclosure of the Buccii and the Melissaei located on the west side of Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate.
Tombs of the Festoons and Frontespizio

Two collocated tombs on the Via Appia - a Republican tomb belonging to the time of Sulla known as the 'Tombs of the Festoons' and a second tomb called the 'Tomb of the Title Page' by Luigi Canina who studied and restored it.
The "Tombs of the Kings" archaeological site is a Hellenistic and Roman-period necropolis associated with the city of Nea Paphos and characterized by large, rock-cut, subterranean tomb structures.
A canal that connects the Nile River with the Faiyum Oasis in Egypt.
The Hingol River flows some 350 miles (560 km) through Balochistan.
A large, fortified Kushan urban center (first to third centuries).
The Tor de' Schiavi is a medieval tower (thirteenth century) built atop the remains of the octagonal hall of the Villa Gordiani.
A Roman villa of the early second century BCE, constructed in opus incertum and so named because of the presence of a torcularium.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Gelendzhik.

A Roman tomb, known as the Torraccia dell’Inviolata. This tomb has a cruciform plan that is inscribed within a circular structure. Based on masonry techniques the tomb dates to the later first or second century.
A Medieval tower located on Tiber Island.
A Roman columbarium tomb located on the Via Latina.
A Medieval tower (12th or 13th century) is now located within the grounds of the Caffarella park.
The archaeological site of Torre d'Ischia was identified in 1982, with evidence for Proto-Villanovan occupation.
A first century AD tower tomb built 6 km from Tarraco, the Torre dels Escipions has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A fortified Medieval tower located in Rome, dating to AD 1238, and built by Richard Conti, brother of Pope Innocent III.
The Torre dei Graziani is a twelfth-century tower on the Esquiline Hill in Rome.
Torre del Giudizio is a Medieval tower built atop a pre-existing Roman site located near the fluvial harbor of vicus Alexandrini.
A Medieval tower in Rome's Largo Argentina.
A fortified Medieval tower built adjacent to the Forum of Trajan in Rome.
A Medieval tower that was originally built in the twelfth century and is located near the crossroads of the present-day via Casilina and viale Palmiro Togliatti in the city of Rome.
An Etrusco-Roman fortified hilltop settlement that later served as a fortress of the Della Gherardesca family from the twelfth to the fifteenth centuries.

Torres de Auençala was a rural castle located in the west of Jaén. This type of settlement consisted of a fortified perimeter and small tower. This site belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X (thirteenth century). Today the site is known as Torre Venzalá and is located in Torredonjimeno.
Toshbuloq or Tashbulak was a high-altitude urban center located along the medieval Silk Route (6th–11th century CE).
Situated atop Mount Cavalier, the so-called "Tour Magne" is a tower on the fortified walls of ancient Nemausus. The tower dates to the time of Augustus.

An ancient river of the northwest Peloponnese, described by Pausanias as flowing into the Ladon at the border of Thelpusian and Heraian territory (i.e., prior to the Ladon's confluence with the Alpheios).

A rectangular defensive tower located on the northern end of the defensive circuit walls around the city of Dura-Europos. The fortifications were built ca. 150 BCE. They were breached in 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.

Rectangular defensive tower located on the northern end of the defensive circuit walls around the city of Dura-Europos. Built ca. 150 BCE, the city's fortifications were breached in 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.

Rectangular defensive tower externally added to the western defensive circuit wall around the city of Dura-Europos and intended to cover a junction between stone and mudbrick curtain wall near the city's northwest corner. Built ca. 150 BCE, the city's fortifications were breached in 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.

Rectangular defensive tower externally added to the western defensive circuit wall around the city of Dura-Europos and intended to add additional protection in a section of mudbrick curtain wall on the city's northwest corner. Built ca. 150 BCE, the city's fortifications were breached in 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.

Rectangular defensive tower externally added to the western defensive circuit wall around the city of Dura-Europos and intended to add additional protection in a section of mudbrick curtain wall on the city's northwest corner. Built ca. 150 BCE, the city's fortifications were breached in 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.
Also known as the Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestes, the Tower of the Winds is an octagonal Pentelic marble clocktower located in the "Roman" Agora that functioned as a horologion.
A tributary of the Danube in lower Austria.
Traianoupolis in Thrace was re-founded on the site of Doriscus, a site that Darius the Great founded in 512 B.C.

The ancient monument referred to as "Trajan's Kiosk" or the "Pharaoh's Bed" is an incomplete hypaethral temple that dates to the second century CE. The monument is currently located on Agilkia Island although it was originally built on the island of Philae. It was relocated in the 1960s as part of the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia.
The hexagonal Trajanic harbor basin at Portus was built between 100 and 112. Its maximum diameter is approximately 716 meters.

The remains of a Roman bridge at Tramatza cross the Riu di Mare Foghe. Gosner and Nowlin assert that this bridge likely dates to the first century BCE and that its construction may have allowed for better access to the Sardinian interior in the direction of Forum Traiani (Fordongianus). The bridge was repaired in the Middle Ages and again in 1826.
An ancient road station, possibly to be associated with or sited in the vicinity of modern Kratovo in the Republic of North Macedonia.
Trasumennus lacus (modern Lake Trasimeno) is the largest lake of the Italian peninsula and the site of a major engagement of the Second Punic War on June 21, 217 B.C.

Tratturo Caniò is an archaeological site in the territory of the ancient city of Setia, on the Pontine Plain of Lazio, Italy. An archaic temple sacred to Iuno is known at the site, and archaeological prospection in 2009 revealed earlier Bronze Age and Iron Age remains.
A Bronze Age tholos tomb with a corbeled dome and monumental ashlar facade on the Panagitsa Hill at Mycenae.
The Treasury of the Massaliots at Delphi is an in antis building built of Parian marble with Aeolic capitals. It stands in the area of the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia. It dates ca. 510 BCE.
An Iron Age settlement covering some 20 ha was identified at Trebbio, located to the south of Sansepolcro.
A river of Liguria and Emilia-Romagna and one of the four main right-bank tributaries of the river Po.
An ancient tribe of Umbria that Pliny places in the sixth Augustan region.
An ancient city of Campania that became enfranchised in the Roman system in the late fourth century B.C.
A sanctuary in NW Kea located at Treis Ammoundas dating from the Archaic to Hellenistic periods.
A multi-phase settlement - Neolithic to Medieval periods - that is now preserved as an archaeological site.
A castle located above the town of Trenčín in western Slovakia that preserves epigraphic evidence of Roman military activity during the Marcomannic Wars.
A river of central Italy, identified by scholars with the modern Sacco, and a right tributary of the Liris.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Trevi.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Qukës ALB.

From Hesiod onward, Greek writers locate the Nemean lion in a cave or ravine in this mountain and explain the mountain's name ("perforated") from being split by the ravine. Wiseman (in PECS, whence ToposText) identifies the Tretos as "the mountain on the W side of the main road between Kleonaia-Corinthia and Argolis" and the ravine as the modern Dervenakia pass. Camp in BAtlas silently suppresses
An ancient Gallic people, later part of the Roman Empire. Their chief city was Augusta Treverorum.

Trevinano is a human settlement in Italy, located in the Province of Viterbo of northern Lazio. In antiquity the site was settled by Etruscans. In the eleventh century, the powerful Boncompagni-Ludovisi family built a castle there.
A triangular plaza with an Ionic propylon that was surrounded by 95 Doric columns. A Doric order temple sits in the forum.
The Triboci were a Germanic people inhabiting eastern Gaul, comprising what is now Alsace.
Gallic tribe dwelling on the upper Seine and the Aube rivers during the Roman period
Small, rocky islets in Galicia located adjacent to Cabo Ortegal.
An ancient river, identified by modern scholars with the modern Truyère in France.
Triopion, the modern Cape Deveboynu Cape, is a promontory located at the extreme end of the Datça Peninsula.
Sanctuary of Apollo Triopios, known as the Triopion, in the territory of Knidos, was the federal sanctuary of the Dorian hexapolis.
The modern river Arun, which drains into the English Channel between modern Portsmouth and Brighton.
A town (polichnion) in ancient Macedonia, mentioned by Stephanus. Its precise location is unlocated today.
A triumphal arch most likely built during the reign of Augustus to honor veterans of the Gallic Wars and Legio II Augusta.
Known now as Lake Suğla, or in Turkish, Suğla Gölü, the ancient Trogitis is a lake that is located in Turkey's Konya Province.
The modern Lake Suğla is a lake located in Turkey's Konya Province.
The greater mountain range of Cyprus. Its highest point is 1952 meters.
An ancient Celtic people who likely migrated into Anatolia in the early third century BCE.
A river of Picenum that flows from its source on the Gran Sasso d'Italia to the Adriatic Sea at Porto d'Ascoli.
An alpine people dwelling in the area of Brixia; the name is connected to the Val Trompia.
Trypillia (Obukhiv Raion, Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine) was the site of an extensive proto-urban settlement of the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture ca. 4300-4000 BCE.
The site of a large Roman town located on the Troia peninsula on the left bank of the Sado river.
According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon, Tuba was one of the four city districts of the western half of the inner city of Babylon and it contained three temples.
Tugunbulak was a Medieval city on the Silk Route covering an area of ca. 120 hectares (300 acres).
A mountain in the Ligurian Apennines cited in the Sententia Minuciorum; the modern Monte Leco.
Neolithic burial site located near the eastern bank of the Sarygamysh Lake in modern Turkmenistan, containing remains dated to the 5th-4th millennia BCE.
An Etruscan tumulus-type tomb at Asciano with artifactual evidence dating to the Orientalizing period.
A seventh-century B.C. Etruscan tumulus is located near Pisa.
An Etruscan tomb located at Castellina in Chianti in Italy.
Tribe, or group of tribes, who lived in the Belgic part of Gaul, during the times of the Roman Empire.
An approximately 6 km. long tunnel built under Roman emperor Claudius in 52 CE for the purposes of attempting to drain the Lacus Fucinus.
The Turmog(id)i/Mourbogoi were a tribe of Hispania Tarraconensis whose territory bordered that of the Cantabri to the south.
An ancient people who lived in western France just south of Caesarodunum, modern Tours.

An assemblage of four Middle Neolithic tumuli located in the territory of the commune of Tusson in the French department of Charente. The four tumuli are known colloquially as "tumulus de la Justice", "le Petit Dognon", "le Gros Dognon", and "le Vieux Breuil".

Toutzis (Dendur) is located in Nubia, approximately 80 km south of modern Aswan. In 23 BCE the Roman provincial governor Petronius built a temple at the direction of Augustus. The temple was dedicated to Isis and the deified Nubian brothers Pedesi and Pihor. Imperiled by the Aswan High Dam project, the temple was relocated by UNESCO in 1963. Egypt gifted the temple to the Metropolitan Museum of Ar
Tylos is the ancient name for Bahrain, renowned in antiquity as a center of pearl trading.
A mountain at the western edge of the Spercheios valley on which the river itself rises. In modern times, the mountain has been known both as Timfristos and Velouchi.
A Greek settlement on the coast of the Sea of Azov.
The Dniester river flows from Ukraine to the Black Sea.
The Tyrrhenian Sea is part of the Mediterranean Sea off the western coast of Italy. It takes its name from the Tyrrhenian people, another name for the Etruscans.
A Middle Helladic settlement excavated near Nemea.
Settlement site near the Georgian village Edisa in South Ossetia. Archaeological remains, including burials, were found in this site dating from the 11th-12th centuries CE.
The Ubii were a Germanic tribe settled on the right bank of the Rhine River. Iulius Caesar encountered them during his campaigns. Their capital was Ara Ubiorum.
Uchi Maius was a township of Africa Proconsularis where Marius settled veterans. It did not achieve the status of colonia until the third century.
Fortified settlement on the banks of the Cheptsa River, inhabited from the 9th-13th centuries CE and associated with the Cheptsa culture
A Roman fort on the Pannonian Limes, at modern Szentendre in Hungary.

At West Hill, Uley, Gloucestershire, excavations revealed the remains of a multi-period ritual site. This site remained in use from the Neolithic period to the Middle Ages. An Iron Age sanctuary was replaced by a Romano-British temple dedicated to Mercury in the early second century A.D.
The Roman capital of Dacia established by Trajan and located some 40 km from the indigenous center of Sarmizegetusa Regia (cited: BAtlas 21 E4 Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa)
The ruins of a Late Gothic Church of St. Ulrich which gave its name to the mountain on which it stands.
A river of Etruria that flows from Castelnuovo Berardenga to the Tyrrhenian Sea.
An ancient settlement at modern Umm el-Gbur in Libya.
A necropolis at Abydos, Egypt, with royal tombs from the Pre-dynastic period as well as from the Early Dynastic (First and Second dynasties) period.

While Arthur Evans gave this archaeological site the moniker "Unexplored mansion", it was in fact an annexe of the "Little Palace" and post-dates it. The "Unexplored Mansion" was built in MM IIIB or LM IA.

The site of an unnamed Gallo-Roman temple is situated in Thésée, Arrondissement of Romorantin-Lanthenay, Centre-Val de Loire, France. This temple site is located close to the ruins at Bâtiments des potiers de Pouillé.

Majonelle, Cm. Montlauzun, France, was the site of a long-lived villa of substantial size. According to M. Labrousse writing in PECS, the presence of a "Byzantine coin of Phokis" denotes a very late occupation.
Unnamed Roman fort, Cheeke Street, Exeter
A previously unknown Roman fort was discovered in Exeter between Bampfylde Street and Cheeke Street during the construction of a bus station in 2019.
Unnamed Settlement at mouth of Oued Titinguel
A small Roman-era settlement noted by Gsell in AAA, whence BAtlas 30 inset 2
An unnamed ancient bridge located on the Via Aurelia over the Osa river at Telamon.
Located between Costa Balenae and Portus Maurici (at or near modern San Lorenzo al Mare, over the Rio della Torre, Italy).
The remains of a bridge of Byzantine or Turkish construction located northwest of Sardis.
The so-called "Ponte di Bard" located at Bard, to the southeast of Vitricium.
Unnamed bridge at Isturgi on the Guadalquivir river
According to the Barrington Atlas directory, an ancient group of bridges crossing the river Duria (Bautica) is found at Villeneuve/Leverogne to the west of Aosta.
Unnamed bridge in the Piazza Eugenio Biffi
The remains of an ancient Roman bridge in the present Piazza Eugenio Biffi in Rome. This bridge is thought to have spanned the Almo river.
Unnamed bridge over the Nar river near Terni
An ancient bridge near the *Via Curia.
Unnamed bridge over the River Burbia
At modern Toral de los Vados.
A Roman legionary camp, approximately dating to the years 4-6 CE, located at modern Anreppen, Stadt Delbrück (Germany).

Remains of an ancient fortification recorded by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas). The location should lie within a kilometer of the BAtlas coordinates: a point east-northeast of modern Bousâada in the municipal territory of modern At Muḥli/Beni Mouhli in Algeria's Setif province.

Remains of an ancient fortification of Roman date, recorded by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas). The location should lie within a kilometer of the BAtlas coordinates: a point along the modern CW 43 road to the east of Djaafra and just past the intersection with the road linking Ouchanene Kebira and Tiâroussine (Bordj Bou Arreridj willaya, Algeria).
Unnamed lead mines at Halkyn Mountain
A Roman-era lead mining operation at modern Halkyn Mountain, Flintshire, Wales, United Kingdom.
Unnamed quarries to the west of Thiounta

Waelkens 1987 describes the discovery of a quarry district referred to as Taşlı Göl. It is to be located between the villages of Doğanlı, Gözler, and Çindere. This site is approximately 25 km northwest of Pamukkale. The marble from these quarries is identified as Thiounta marble on the basis of comparison with the coarser marble of Hierapolis.
Referred to today as "Gisacum", this vast Gallo-Roman religious complex (with major spa), is located largely in the French commune of Le Vieil Evreux.
Connecting Tremithous → Kition via Kelliake?; exact route uncertain.
An unnamed ancient road station located between Makhareg and Ujra Zena and included on Barrington Atlas map 77.
A rural settlement near Tremuli consisting of small farmsteads.
Unnamed rural settlement north of Souk el Arba
A rural settlement consisting of small farmsteads.
An unnamed ancient settlement, located near modern Baugy in France (BAtlas 14 H1 Baugy)

M. Cristofani describes terracotta antefixes discovered at Tre Fontane, in the general location of the abbey of the same name. These antefixes form part of a set of evidence relevant to a discussion of the functioning of regional coroplastic workshops in central Italy in the late archaic period. They are dated from the later sixth to the early fifth centuries BCE.
A tuff quarry located at Castelporziano, to the east of Ostia Antica.
A Neolithic chambered cairn dating to the fourth and third millennia BC.
Castellum Menapiorum → Minariacum? → Nemetacum → Bagacum → Atuatuca
Bracara Augusta → Nemetobriga → Asturica Augusta (Via Nova)
Unlabeled feature captured from the Barrington Atlas
BAtlas 42 B4 unnamed bridge (near Aquae Apollinares? on road to Tarquinii at La Mola)
The Ura Fons was a source of water for ancient Nemausus.
A stone circle measuring 33 by 26 feet with 11 standing stones located near Gleninchaquin Park, Tuosist, County Kerry, Ireland.
The northernmost island in the Tuscan Archipelago.
The Urius (modern Río Odiel in Spain) rises in the Sierra de Aracena to join with the Río Tinto in the Huelva estuary, which empties into the Atlantic.
An island off the Croatian coast in the Adriatic Sea, now known as Sveti Juraj (San Giorgio).
Settlement from the Late Bronze Age Srubnaya Culture located in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, 1.8km southwest of Yampil.
A Roman bath structure of the fourth century A.D. whose remains were reused to construct the Medieval church of San Lorenzo.
Attested in ancient sources, the Utens river is possibly to be associated with the modern Uso.

A Bronze Age archaeological site with Deer Stones located at Uushigiin Ovor (UO), Mongolia, that is included in the cultural landscape "Deer Stone Monuments and Related Bronze Age Sites", inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
A Roman site with evidence for a series of ditched enclosures of the first century.
Roman fort on Hadrian's wall in Stanwix.
Uzita was a settlement of Byzacium located south of Hadrumetum.
The Vaccaei were a Celtic tribe of the Durius river valley.
A partially dry lake of ancient Etruria near Orte. The Romans were victorious in two battles fought against the Etruscans there (310 and 283 BC).
A villa, vicus, and necropolis site in modern Puglia, Italy, located near the modern city of Gravina. The site was active from the first to fourth centuries CE.
Hill in Southern Iran with pottery remains from the end of the Bakun period, through the Uruk period, and into the Proto-Elamite period.

Architectural remains consistent with a Roman-era villa maritima have been identified on both the north and south sides of a small bay at modern Valbandon in Croatia. Originally thought to represent a single establishment that wrapped the entire bay, more recent interpretations would see two separate architectural complexes.
A valley in Egypt where Pharaonic burials took place from the sixteenth to the eleventh centuries B.C. (Eighteenth to the Twentieth Dynasties).
A valley in Egypt where the burials of both Queens and Princes took place from the sixteenth to the eleventh centuries B.C. (Eighteenth to the Twentieth Dynasties).

An ancient "princely" grave was discovered in the 19th century at the village of Valløby in Denmark. Among the grave goods were some Roman imports. It is not known if the tomb, which was reportedly marked by a circular stone structure, was singular or part of a larger cemetery.
The name of an ancient people inhabiting the northeastern portion of Corscia
Vani (7th -1st centuries BCE) is an ancient city located in the Colchis Lowlands on the western bank of the Sulori River.
Vappincum was a pre-Roman settlement captured by the Romans in 14 BC.
The modern name of a seventh-century Pallava cave temple in Mahābalipuram.
A villa maritima in eastern Liguria, inhabited from ca. 100 BC to the fifth century AD.
Probable Roman fort and settlement in St Asaph, Wales
A square, stone tower known today as Varnava Tower (Ο πύργος του Βαρνάβα), located outside the modern village of Varnava in Greece.
A Roman municipium of the first century A.D.
An ancient, pre-Roman Iberian people that inhabited the regions of Navarre, Lower La Rioja, and northwestern Aragon.
A bath-gymnasium complex at Ephesus dating to the middle of the second century CE.
Veleia was an ancient Ligurian settlement (regio VIII).

Veliki Preslav was a fortified site that served as the capital of the Tsar Simeon I of the Bulgarian Empire. The site flourished during the ninth and tenth centuries CE. The site includes both 'inner' and 'outer' fortified areas.
A lake formed by three rivers (Avens, Himella and Tolenus) in the territory of the Sabines.

In the Roman period, the Lacus Velinus was a larger body of water than the surviving remnant that is now known as Lake Piediluco. Modern intervention drained water away from the lake into the lower Nera River.
Vellaunodunum, now unlocated, was a Gallic oppidum of the Senones tribe two days' march from Agedincum.

At Velletri the remains of a Late Archaic sanctuary (ca. 530 BCE) were discovered beneath the church of the SS. Stimmate di S. Francesco. The site is often referred to as "Tempio delle Stimmate"; Cardinal Stefano Borgia discovered it in 1784. The architectural terracottas from the sanctuary are part of the so-called "Veio-Roma-Velletri" decorative system.
A Roman fort associated with the Antonine Wall at modern day Carriden House. It does not lie on the Wall itself, but rather is 1.3 km to the south east of the Wall's eastern terminus at Bridgeness.
A late Roman cavalry fort located in the modern German municipality of Isny im Allgäu (Baden-Württemberg).

According to the Verona List (ca. A.D. 303–324), Venetia et Histria was a province of the later Roman Empire located in northeastern Italy. It succeeded the tenth region (regio X) of the Augustan administrative re-organization. Diocletian reorganized the region to become "VIII provincia Venetia et Histria" in the third century CE. The capital was located at Aquileia. The province stretched from th
Venonis was a Roman site located at the intersection of Watling Street and Fosse Way in Britannia.
Venta or Venta Icenorum was a central place, and perhaps market-town, of the Iceni, the tribe that revolted against Roman rule in 61 CE.
The River Wharfe, located in northern England, flows from the Yorkshire Dales to join the River Ouse near Cawood.
A burial mound dated to the fourth-third centuries BCE located northwest of the city of Stavropol'.
An extensive Pre-Roman settlement near Roman Verulamium connected with the ruler Tasciovanus, whose coins bear its name as 'Verlamion'.

Verlucio is the site of a Roman settlement. An incomplete fortified enclosure has been identified from fieldwork and aerial photographs. The site was located along the Roman road from Cunetio to Bath (Aquae Sulis).

The Vestini were an ancient tribe of Italy and lived in the southern part of the modern Abruzzo, between the Gran Sasso and the northern bank of the Aterno river. A major center was located at Pitinum.
Monte Viso is the highest peak of the Cottian Alps and the source of the Po River.
An Early Medieval royal property located in the area of Scarlino (Grosseto) in Tuscany.
Vetus Salina was the site of a Roman castrum on the frontier of Pannonia Inferior.
Mentioned in ancient sources, the Vi(n)genna is probably to be identified with the modern Vienne, a major river of France and a tributary of the Loire (ancient Liger).
A road named Via *Quinctia linked Florentia (Firenze) to Pisae (Pisa) in northern Etruria. Its construction is ascribed to the consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus starting in 123 BCE.

An early Roman road (via publica) originating at Rome and terminating at Brundisium, the Via Appia was begun in the fourth century B.C. by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus. The Latin author Statius described the Via Appia as "queen of the long roads".
An ancient Roman road begun ca. 241 B.C. by the censor C. Aurelius Cotta.

An ancient necropolis located in the modern Parco della Serenissima that was initially discovered via construction works in 1997. The necropolis is located, in ancient terms, in a landscape between the line of the via Collatina and that of the via Praenestina. The excavations also revealed traces of first-millennium BCE agricultural activity.
A road located on the right bank of the Tiber River leading to the Campus Salinarum romanarum and sharing the first part of its course with the Via Portuensis.
A major Roman road connecting Rome and Ariminum, by way of Narnia and Nuceria. The road was begun under the censorship of Caius Flaminius Nepos in 220 B.C.
Two suburban villa sites and a Late Antique granary were excavated at a site along the Via Gabina 14 km east of central Rome. Walter Widrig and Philip Oliver-Smith directed the excavations.
A necropolis at Ostia that began during the second century B.C. on the south side of the Via Ostiensis.
A road from Ariminum up the Adriatic Coast toward what is now Venice.
The Via Sublacensis was built in order to connect the Villa Neronis (Nero's villa at Sublaqueum) to Rome. It split from the Via Valeria near Varia.

The Via Vitularia was a Roman road that is now unlocated, but was originally located in the territory of Arpinum. Cicero mentions it in his correspondence. It likely led from Arpinum in the Italian interior to the Tyrrhenian coast. Its name is derived from the first-declension Latin noun vitula, -ae, meaning "heifer"; thus, the road's name may reflect its function, similar to the case of the Via S

Vicopisano is located in the Province of Pisa, some 50 km west of Florence and 15 km east of Pisa. In the Middle Ages, Vicopisano was a fortified center of the Republic of Pisa that was conquered by Florence in 1406. W.V. Harris asserts in the introductory essay for Map 41 of the Barrington Atlas that it is possible that the toponym "Vicopisano" has roots in the ancient Roman world.
A settlement of the Celtic Insubres located in the territory of Vercellae.
A settlement at the third milestone of the Via Ostiensis.

A Roman vicus, attested by name in inscriptions discovered in the 19th century. Based on the reported findspots of the inscriptions, the vicus seems to have been located in the vicinity of modern Spechbach, located southeast of Heidelberg, Germany.

The Vicus Patricius was a street of ancient Rome that crossed both the Cispian and Viminal hills and led, either directly or indirectly, to the Porta Viminalis. The Vicus Patricius bounded both Regio IV and Regio VI of the ancient city. Its course is thought to have been similar to that of the modern Via Urbana.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
Vieille-Toulouse was located on the Garonne River and was connected with trade in Italian wine and other craft products.

A fortified acropolis, discovered in 1989 on the Vigla hill south of the modern Greek town of Hagios Nikolaos (Plagia Community, Palairos Municipality). As yet unexcavated, monumental stone remains as well as pottery of the 5th/4th centuries BCE have been reported at the site. Some scholars have suggested that the attested city of Sollion could have been located here.
An imperial necropolis with columbarium tombs and a family tomb connected with the gens Atilia Romana.
A Jewish catacomb along the Via Appia discovered in 1859.
A Gallo-Roman settlement of the third to fifth centuries A.D.
The villa dates from the first century B.C. to the third century A.D. when it was transformed into a bath complex. It was partially reclaimed as a villa in late Roman and Medieval times.

The Villa Aldobrandini is located on the outskirts of Frascati. The current villa of the site was built in 1550 by a Vatican prelate named Alessandro Rufini. Subsequently, Pope Clement VIII gave the villa to his nephew Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini in 1598. The Papal villa and gardens occupy the site of a Roman terrace villa.
The so-called "Villa Arianna" at Stabiae is typically considered one of the earliest villas at the site and is often dated to the second century B.C.

The so-called “Villa of Augustus” at Somma Vesuviana was first discovered in the late nineteenth century. The villa has been shown to have survived the 79 CE eruption of Mt. Vesuvius but was eventually destroyed by a volcanic event in 472.
Remains of a Roman villa discovered in the Collatino archaeological park in Via Grotta di Gregna consisting of 14 rooms, a cistern, and channelization for water works.

A Roman-period urban 'villa' at Knossos was excavated by R. W. Hutchinson (1935) and M. R. E. Gough (post-World War II). Based on pottery evidence, the villa dates to the second century CE and comes to be destroyed ca. 170-180.
Villa Domitiani, a large imperial villa near the Alban Lake, now the site of the Papal retreat at Castel Gandolfo.
A third century A.D. villa complex along the Via Praenestina connected with Gordian I, Gordian II, and Gordian III.
The Villa of Hadrian (Villa Adriana in Italian) is a sprawling archaeological complex at Tivoli, Italy. The villa complex was designed and used by the emperor Hadrian in the second century A.D.
A complex on the Via Appia constructed by Maxentius in the early fourth century A.D.

The Villa Muti in Grottaferrata occupies, at least in part, the site of a Roman republican villa built on a series of terraces and likely dating to the third and second centuries B.C. Lanciani excavated a series of rooms at the site. The site also had an early to mid-Imperial phase that included elaborate floors and decoration in imported marble.

The church of San Pancrazio was founded in the sixth century A.D. by Pope Symmachus. It stands beyond the Porta San Pancrazio on the Ianiculum. Below the church is a massive catacomb referred to as S. Pancrazio or Ottavilla.
A seaside villa located in Oplontis, possibly owned by Emperor Nero, based on decorations, date of construction, and pottery fragments inscribed with the name of a freedman of Poppaea Sabina.

The site of Villaricos lies 5 km east of Mula (Murcia), Spain. The Roman villa at the site was large and well-appointed, including rich mosaics and a bathing complex. There is also an industrial area that includes a torcularium (facility for pressing of olives or grapes). The site's use ranges from the first to the fifth century CE.

Also known as the Villa Tuscolana, this structure was built in the 16th century on the site of a terraced Roman villa. The site occupies one of the most commanding positions on the slope above what is now Frascati, placing it in the environs of ancient Tusculum.
The remains of a Republican temple podium now support a Christian church at Villa S. Silvestro in Umbria. The temple's podium likely dates, in its first phase, to the third century B.C.
The Villa San Marco originates in the Augustan period and was subsequently expanded during the reign of Claudius. Its owner may have been a freedman of Claudius.
A Jewish catacomb discovered in 1919 on the grounds of the Villa Torlonia park in Rome.
The so-called 'Villa of the Antonines', located near Genzano di Roma in the Alban Hills, lies just south of the Via Appia between the road's 18th and 19th milestones.

A monumental villa complex that is known as the “Villa dei Quattro Venti” is situated on a south-eastern offshoot of the Circeo promontory, approximately 100 meters southeast of the historic center of S. Felice Circeo.

A massive Roman maritime villa that stretched across multiple platforms and the hill known as Poggio del Castellare at Giglio Porto. It was continuously occupied from the first century BCE through the fourth century CE and was renovated and expanded multiple times. During the empire, it was equipped with a large fishpond (the so-called Bagno del Saraceno/Cala del Saracino), which had been converte

The Forma Italiae notes the presence of drainage channels, foundations, and a cistern that are taken to be indicative of a Roman villa in the locale known today as Torrenova in the eastern portion of modern Rome.
A large villa rustica inhabited from ca. 100 B.C. to A.D. 500, located near Montelupo Fiorentino in the mid-Arno Valley of northern Tuscany, approximately twenty km west of Florence.
A late Republican and early Imperial villa in the ager Cosanus noted for its turreted enclosure wall.

A villa complex at the eighth mile of the Via Cassia, to which it was linked by means of a paved diverticulum. The first phase dates to the first century BCE and the villa remained in use until the Late Antique period.
The remains of the so-called villa of Fralana belong to the villa rustica type. Mosaic floors have been discovered at the site, in addition to a productive area that may have included a Torcularium.
A Roman villa located near Castel di Guido.

The ruins of a Roman villa rustica were discovered in the 1990s along via Diego Fabbri. The site dates to the first century B.C. and remained in use at least until the fifth century A.D. The remains of a bath complex are substantial.

A palatial Roman villa and bath complex that has been connected with Theodoric the Great, with twentieth century interpretations labeling it as Theodoric's "hunting lodge". More recent excavations have uncovered evidence for earlier building phases, dating from the first century B.C. through the third century A.D.
The so-called Villa of Vibius Varus is located south of the Villa Adriana at Tivoli. The site has three architectural phases stretching from the first century BCE to the fourth century CE

The Villa of Agrippa Postumus was discovered at Boscotrecase in 1903 on land owned by Cavaliere Ernesto Santini. Works for the Circumvesuviana railroad line brought the site to light. Excavations supervised by Matteo Della Corte were carried out from 1903 to 1905. In 1906, however, a new eruption of Mount Vesuvius reburied the site. Della Corte published a plan of the excavated portion of the vill

A Roman villa excavated at Boscoreale in 1903 and 1904 under the supervision of Vincenzo De Prisco and located on the property of one Giuseppe De Martino. Wall paintings and artifacts were recovered from the site, and the villa was subsequently reinterred. Records as to its precise location are less than optimal.
Villa of Caesar and Maxentius at San Cesareo
The so-called Villa of Caesar and Maxentius at San Cesareo is located at the 18th mile of the Via Labicana.

A 'Villa rustica' associated with one Caius Olius Ampliatus, located in the Ponticelli of Naples, Italy. The site was excavated in 1986-1987, with additional work in 2007. The site covers some 2,000 sq. meters.

A Roman villa associated with a Caius Furius Octavianus who was a member of the Senatorial order during the Severan period. The villa was identified along the via Aurelia in the locality of Massimina - Casal Lumbroso. Excavations were carried out between 2011 and 2017.
A villa dating to the first century BCE that is associated with Lucius Licinius Lucullus.

A villa site near Tivoli that has long been associated Manlius Vopiscus, who Statius mentions. Excavations began in 1825. In 1835 Pope Gregory XVI began construction of his eponymous Villa Gregoriana on the grounds of the Roman villa.
A Roman villa along the via Herculea near Oppido Lucano.
A Roman villa located northwest of Pompeii.
A suburban villa located northwest of Herculaneum that was originally owned by Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus.
A Roman "villa rustica" with an olive-oil press (torcularium, hence "Torchio") was discovered in 2006.
A villa dating to the final quarter of the first century BC located on a headland overlooking Portoferraio on the island of Elba.

Since antiquity, the 6,000-ha estate at Castelporziano has been an elite seaside compound. Where a modern pleasure villa for the Italian president now sits are remains of Roman villas on the Laurentine shore; these remains have been the object of continued study since 1983.
The Viminal Hill, located between the Quirinal and Esquiline hills, is the smallest of the so-called seven hills of Rome.
Vindelicus/Soulgas fl. (Sorgue river) is a river of southeastern France, situated between the Alps and the Rhone river.
A Roman fort at present-day Ebchester.
A Roman legionary base first established ca. AD 15.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Dorgali.
A Roman fort at present-day Bainbridge.

Although the present city in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh seems to have been founded in the 11th or 12th century CE, archaeological evidence indicates the natural harbor at Visakhapatnam has served as a center of maritime trade from the 4th or 3rd century BCE onward.
The basilica of Cabeza del Griego at Segobriga dates to the fifth and sixth centuries CE.
A villa rustica was excavated at Vittimose in 1969 and 1970.
A mountain range, identified with the modern Sierra de la Virgen, near Bubierca in Spain.
The Vocontii were a Gallic people living to the east of the Rhone river.
The Volcanal was an open-air sanctuary of Vulcan located in the valley of the Forum Romanum on the slopes of the Capitoline Hill. The earliest phases of the sanctuary likely predate the forum itself.
Voley Castle is an Iron Age hill fort located in Devon, England, on a promontory on Heale Down.

Site on the Kerch Strait inhabited from the 6th century BCE-4th century CE, and resettled in the 8th-9th, 12-13th, and 17th-18th centuries CE. Rescue excavations were conducted on the site from 1996-2012.

The Volsci (Volscians) were an Italic tribe of central Italy during the first millennium B.C. They inhabited parts of southern Latium and were bounded by other tribes, including the Aurunci, Samnites, and Hernici.
A volcanic lake of northern Latium formed by the collapse of the Vulsini volcano. Roman sources record volcanic activity at the site as late as the second century B.C.
Volturnum was located at the mouth of the Volturno River.
The Volturno River flows 175 km from the Apennines to the Tyrrhenian Sea at Castel Volturno.
A town of Mauretania Tingitana and a Roman colony.
A villa associated with the Volusii Saturnini built ca. 50 B.C.
The Vomano river in Abruzzo flows into the Adriatic Sea.

Vouni is located on the northwest coast of Cyprus, some 7 km west of Soloi. The rocky hill was occupied in antiquity and the settlement included a fortified palace enclosure, the ancient name of which is unknown. According to PECS, the palace is to be dated ca. 500 to 380 BCE, with two main architectural phases (I: ca. 500 to 450 BCE, II: ca. 450 to 380 BCE).
A fortified site located at Trypimeni Petra, between the foothills of Mount Kerdyllion and the coastline at Vrasna, dating to the fourth-first century BCE.
A Bronze Age settlement located on the south coast of the island of Tinos to the west of Agios Phokas.
One of the few known coastal Early and Middle Bronze Age sites in Cyprus. This site is a cemetery located in modern Lapithos, Cyprus.

Site in the Qena Bend of the Nile, approximately halfway between Luxor and Hou, containing hundreds of rock inscriptions. Most of the inscriptions are dated to the late Middle Kingdom through the early New Kingdom periods.

The Wall of Media, also known as Mēdías teîchos or the Wall of Semiramis, at Habl as-Sahr is mentioned by Xenophon in the Anabasis as a defensive ditch at the Euphrates built on the orders of Artaxerxes in the fifth century BC.

The city walls of Venta Silurum (modern Caerwent) are among the best-preserved Roman period city walls in Britain. The walls were constructed around the 3rd century CE, augmenting an earlier earthwork defense system, with external towers added in the mid 4th century.

Walwick Fell Roman temporary camp is an archaeological site located in Warden, Northumberland, England, United Kingdom. It is part of the distributed UNESCO World Heritage Site "Frontiers of the Roman Empire".
An ancient settlement site located in what is now Bangladesh.

The site of a Roman fort has been identified via aerial photos. It is situated in agricultural land on Dunston Hill overlooking the River Tyne, 3 miles southwest of Newcastle and ca. 1 km southeast of Whickham.
A twelfth-century, moated, fortified manor in Weeting, Norfolk, near Brandon, Suffolk, England.
At the modern town of Welzheim in the Rems-Murr district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany, a complex of two Roman forts with associated settlement (vicus) have been documented.
A Roman fort of the Limes of Germania Inferior.
Remains of a Roman camp or fort, located in the modern German town of Wesseling.
Western gate of the city of Carchemish, constructed in the Middle Bronze Age and in use through Late Antique period.
The West Kennet Long Barrow is a chambered long barrow located near the village of Avebury in south-western England. It dates to Britain's Early Neolithic period.
A small Romano-British courtyard villa was excavated at Lippen Wood, West Meon, by A. Moray-Williams in 1906. The villa had 16 rooms, three of which had mosaic floors.

Fortification at the western edge of the settlement of Serdica, constructed in the 2nd century CE and disused by the end of the 6th century CE. The site was excavated in 2011-2013 and is now an archaeological park.

Weycock Hill is the site of a Roman temple excavated in 1847. According to Lewis, this was an octagonal temple with a portico. It dates to the early fourth century CE with abandonment in the fifth century.
A Belgic oppidum in England, founded sometime after 50 BC.
A pyramid built by Pharaoh Amenemhat II.

The Romano-British settlement at Wickham Bushes is located due south from Caesar's Camp. A range of archaeological material was recovered, including numismatic evidence that ranges in date from Agrippa to Valentinian II.

A fortlet was identified via aerial photographs in October 1965. In this vicinity, the Antonine Wall runs roughly parallel between the River Kelvin to the north and the Forth and Clyde Canal to the south.
A Roman industrial site of the late first century A.D. located at the crossing of the river Mersey.
Stone archway constructed as part of the expansion of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem during the early Roman period.
The site of a Romano-British settlement located in Wimblington, Cambridgeshire, England.
A now-disappeared terrace wall and rock cuttings were thought to be the remains of an ancient sanctuary of uncertain identity.
A "villa rustica" located at Seeb is situated near the village of Winkel, canton of Zurich, Switzerland. By the first century CE, the villa included a thermal bath.
The Roman-British corridor villa at Withington was discovered in 1811. The site is located to the south of Withington village along with another Romano-British building/villa complex.
Site of late Iron-Age and Romano-British settlement near present-day Saham Toney in Norfolk. An Neronian-era fort is directly adjacent.
A Middle Iron Age-3rd/4th century A.D. settlement complex at Worthy Down, lying 8 km. NNW of Winchester.

The Western Xia mausoleums are located in northwestern China in the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. This UNESCO World Heritage Site includes nine imperial mausoleums and 250 tombs of imperial relatives and officials of China's Western Xia dynasty.
Extensive groups of Iron Age tumuli in the Lesser Caucasian mountains. A Neo-Assyrian seal bearing the name of Adad-nirari II (911-891 BCE) was found here during excavations in 1895.
Ancient Xois was located on an island that was formed by the Sebennytic and Phatnitic branches of the Nile. It became the capital of its own nome, the Xoite nome.
An ancient fort on Karnos island (modern Kalamos) with polygonal masonry and black-glazed pottery.
A Mycenaean necropolis located on the island of Amorgos that includes several chamber tombs.

The Yaoshan Site is part of the larger UNESCO cultural heritage landscape, "Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City". According to UNESCO, the Yaoshan Site dates ca. 3300-3100 BCE and covers an area of some 66.56 hectares (164.5 acres).
A mound site in Kırşehir province in Turkey containing a palace or temple structure dated to the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE or the first half of the 1st millennium BCE.
Yaz tepe was an ancient settlement located in southeastern Turkmenistan.

A sacred rock-cut sanctuary of the Hittites. The sanctuary was in use from the late sixteenth century B.C. Many of the reliefs date to the reigns of Tudhaliya IV and Suppiluliuma II in the late thirteenth century B.C.
Fortified site atop a limestone terrace in the Tur 'Abdin, constructed during the Iron Age and in use into the Medieval period.
The Yeavering Bell is a twin-peaked hill fort in Northumberland, England, that forms part of the Cheviot Hills.

An ancient granite quarry known today as "Yedi Taşlar" (Seven Stones), located near the modern Turkish village of Koçalı (Ezine District, Çanakkale Province). Several partially quarried monolithic columns remain on site today.
The Yeha Temple is alleged to be among the oldest known extant structures in Ethiopia. It is executed in the Sabaean style and may date to the seventh century BCE.

In 1925, Alderman Mitchelmore excavated a Roman courtyard villa at Yeovil. This site is located to the west of Seaton Road, Westland, Yeovil. Excavations continued in 1927/8 under Ralegh Radford. On September 15, 1916, a coin hoard containing more than 4,000 fourth-century CE coins was found on the site. The villa was a large building (200 by 170 feet) with a paved courtyard.
Quarry and sculpture workshop founded under the Hittite king Suppiluliuma in the 14th century BCE.

Yoncalı is located near the modern cities of Malazgirt and Bulanık, at the western end of the Bulanık-Malazgirt plain. The Assyrian king Tiglat-pileser I placed an inscribed, rock-cut relief here to commemorate his victories in the region.
Site for Urartian palace and citadel.
Rural settlement of the Roman and Late Antique periods in Thrace, located near the modern village of Stroyno, Bulgaria.

A modern village in the Refahiye region of Turkey's Erzincan province where remains of ancient roads and routes converge and where a Roman milestone has been found. In Roman times, it was likely a walled town or fort, garrisoned at some point by the cohors I Lepidiana. Scholarly opinions differ as to its possible names in antiquity.
The Yığma Tepe Tumulus is the largest ancient tumulus in the vicinity of Pergamon.
A fortified Bosporan site near Temriuk that was founded no later than the fourth century B.C.
The ancient Zagatis has been identified with the modern Pazar/Hemşin river in Turkey's Rize province.
A fortified citadel located in Hashtrud, East Azerbaijan Province, Iran. It takes its name from the mythological figure Zahhak. The site is in use from the second millennium BC until the Timurid era.
Zarai or Zaraï is an ancient place in the Roman province of Numidia. It was a Berber, Carthaginian, and, later, Roman settlement located near the site of present-day Aïn Oulmene, Algeria.

Bactrian walled settlement in Southern Uzbekistan that had a walled citadel and a palace within and probably had a moat outside. The settlement also had a Buddhist sanctuary. The site dates from the 4th-2nd centuries BCE and was occupied until the 5th-7th centuries CE.
The main naval harbor of the Peiraeus with 196 ship sheds.
The Khuriya Muriya Islands are a group of five islands in the Arabian Sea.
Diodorus refers to Zereia/Zeira as a fortress and places it near the location of Chalcidice. It was razed by Philip V. It is now unlocated. (cited: BAtlas 51 unlocated Zereia/Zeira)
A sanctuary of Zeus Aglaios located west of Metapontum.
A temple of Zeus Ainesios located atop mount Ainos on the island of Cephallania.
A sanctuary dedicated to Zeus Atabyrios located on the summit of Mt. Atavyros in Rhodes.
An oracular mountaintop sanctuary of Zeus on the island of Aegina.
Zeus Thenatas, T. is an archaic Greek sanctuary built atop earlier Minoan cult remains. The open-air temple remained in use until the second century AD.
A Ziggurat in the city of Nippur that was constructed under Ur-Nammu during the 21st century BCE and renovated under Esarhaddon and Assurbanipal during the 7th century BCE.

A river on the northern Atlantic coast of what is now Morocco, presumably near the ancient settlement of Zilil/Zilis. The lower course of the modern Lhachef/Hachef is the obvious match, although its precise ancient path through the coastal wetlands to the mouth mentioned by Ptolemy is uncertain.
Zilil/Zilis was an Augustan colony of western Mauretania (Iulia Constantia Zilis).
Zimara was a fort near the Euphrates River on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire.
A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources; the modern site is Zaytān.

Elmalık (formerly Zivistan, Zewestan) is a village in the Van Province in the southeast of Turkey ca. 12 km to the south of Van. Two small Urartian fortresses have been found in the immediate vicinity, which are known as Aşağı Zivistan Kalesi ("Lower Zivistan Castle") and Yukarı Zivistan Kalesi ("Upper Zivistan Castle"). On the basis of several Urartian stone inscriptions of the Urartian king Išpu
The Zoelae were an ancient Celtic tribe of Gallaecia in the Iberian peninsula.
A peninsula at modern Vouliagmeni in Attica, in myth the location where Leto loosened her girdle before giving birth to Artemis and Apollo.
Strabo provides the ancient Greek name Zouchis for the modern Bahiret el Bibane, a coastal lagoon located in Tunisia.

A seventh century AD church built by Catholicos Nerses the Builder (AD 641-653) and located in the Armavir Province of Armenia. The ruins of the church were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
An ancient town of the Zygritai on the ancient Libyan coast. Ptolemy provides the name and coordinates; BAtlDir tentatively associates it with modern Zawiet el-Chammas in Egypt's Matruh governorate.
A Roman camp located in the middle of the modern village of Zăvoi in Romania. The site may be associated with a road station known as Acmonia/Augmonia/Agnavi(a)e in ancient sources.
A significant site, estimated at 150 hectares during the Sassanian period, contracting to 100 hectares during the Early Islamic-Sāmarrān period.
Numerous ex-votos were excavated from a spring at La Source des Roches.
A small island in Lake Como.
BAtlas 40 D1 [Equilum] now Jesolo, located in the Veneto
The only island located in the Lago d'Orta.

Sabalan is an inactive stratovolcano located in the Lesser Caucasus mountain range (Ardabil Province, northwestern Iran). The mountain rises to 4,794 meters (15,728 ft) in elevation and is the third-highest mountain in Iran.
A brook in the Campus Martius of ancient Rome that flowed from the Cati fons to the Tiber River.
Ruins of a Roman era settlement noted by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas) at Koudiat el Azari, on a slope to the north above the Oued Kassob.
An ancient settlement site in modern Algeria, located 4 km inland on a ridge above the Oued Sebt (a tributary of the Oued Outar).
Predynastic and Early Dynastic burial site containing over 1,000 burials. It is the type-site of the Amratian culture.
el-Deir (also known as Deir el-Munīra) is the site of a Roman fort and necropolis in Egypt's Kharga Oasis.
A tumulus at Lavinium located near the Latin federal sanctuary that has been associated with the tomb of Aeneas and/or a heroön dedicated to him.
A rock-cut Phrygian monument dating to the seventh century BCE that carries an inscribed dedication in Old Phrygian by Ates, son of Arkias, to Midas.
The tribus Clustumina (or Crustumina) was a rural tribe of Rome which was established in 495 B.C.
The tribus Pomptina (or Pontina) was a later rural tribe of Rome, which was established in 358 B.C.
A later rural tribe of ancient Rome, which was established in 332 B.C.

The so-called "Villa of the Jurist" was discovered in 2013 during salvage excavations connected with the expansion of Italy's A24 motorway. A significant villa of the Late Republican period was documented and attributed to the jurist Quintus Mucius Scaevola.

Located 3 km south of the town of Auxerre, France, on the right bank of the Yonne River, archaeologists excavated the remains of an extensive Gallo-Roman villa covering an area of approximately 1.6 hectares. The villa site includes a bath complex. The site has been noted for its archaeological potential since the nineteenth century. While some excavations took place in the 1960s, the open-area exc
Çemka Höyük is a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site located in Mardin, Türkiye, dating to the tenth millennium BCE.
A Roman bridgehead fort, located near Carnuntum (modern Bad Deutsch-Altenburg in Austria).
Örvényes, County of Veszprém, Hungary, was the site of a Roman settlement.

An island in modern Iran at the head of the Persian Gulf, bounded today on the southwest by the Shatt al-Arab and on the northeast by the Bahmanshir. Its name first appears certainly in 9th century CE sources, but it may relate to an apparent cognate preserved in Ptolemy and its general topography (or that of an earlier island in the vicinity) may have been known to some Greek and Roman geographer
Burial site in North Ossetia–Alania containing 58 burials associated with the Koban culture (8th-7th centuries BCE), as well as 26 medieval burials (14th century CE).
A village in Turkey, the site of a late antique Georgian church constructed in the 7th century.
Iron Age fortress in the Northern Negev Desert with a solid wall and ten towers. Inside the fortress are building complexes with streets between them.
A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources; the modern site is ʿAzāz.
A place from the TAVO Index
A place from the TAVO Index
‘Ad Nonum’/Ornithon Polis, a road station between Tyrus and Sidon probably located at modern day Adlun in Lebanon, cited: BAtlas 69 B3
The ‘Bacuntius’ was a river of Lower Pannonia that flowed into the Savus River near Sirmium.
‘Cicutio’ is a Roman fort located near modern-day Brecon in Wales. The fort was originally built ca. A.D. 75.
A Roman fort at present-day Chester-le-Street.
An ancient road station recorded in the Antonine Itinerary, the name is likely corrupt. The site is possibly to be identified with the modern coastal town of Camogli in Liguria, Italy.
The Diyala River is a major tributary of the Tigris.

A large fanum sacred to ‘Herculis Rani’? at Campochiaro, the name of which is then preserved in the station mentioned on the Peutinger Table. Scholars like Adriano La Regina support linking this fanum to a place mentioned by Livy, although see the discussion by Oakley.
A Roman auxiliary fort in Wales.
A Roman fort at present-day Old Carlisle.
Site of a Roman fort and civilian settlement in the Castlefield area of modern Manchester.
A Roman fort at present-day Hardknott.
A fortified Roman town along the line of Watling Street.
The so-called "Great Basilica" is an early Christian basilica dating to the sixth century.
A Trajanic bridge spanning the Danube River at Drobeta-Turnu Severin.
Digitized by eye in Google Earth on 13 July 2012 at an eye altitude of 683m. Dates are general settlement dates, following Foss and Mitchell in BAtlas.
A Ghassulian public building dating ca. 3500 B.C. near the oasis of Ein Gedi on the western shore of the Dead Sea.
*Aquae or pagus Aquensis was a bath site located along the Strei river in the territory of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa.

The Chienti River is found in Italy's Marche region. It flows from near Serravalle di Chienti to the Lago di Pievefavera, and from there it joins the Fiastra River, eventually flowing into the Adriatic Sea.
Colijnsplaat, The Netherlands, is the site of an ancient sanctuary dedicated to Nehalennia.
*Glannoventa was a Roman fort and naval base on the coast of Cumbria.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: AUS.
*Panamara was as site in Caria that was a dependency of Stratonikeia and site of the sanctuary of Zeus Panamaros.
*Ponte Navata, a late Roman fort on Sibrik hill, Visegrád, Hungary.
A monastery constructed in the fifth century CE on the site of a cave previously inhabited by St. Paul the Anchorite.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: S Hodna.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A province of the Sasanian empire with its capital as Nishapur. The name and regional/administrative connotation outlasted the Sasanians.
An important monastery founded probably in the seventh century of the common era.
The church of San Claudio al Chienti is a Romanesque church building located in the municipality of Corridonia in the Chienti valley. It was founded in the eleventh century.
Abbazia di San Vincenzo al Volturno
An historic Benedictine monastery located in the Province of Isernia, near the source of the river Volturno.
Abbotsbury Abbey is a Benedictine abbey located in Dorset, England. It was founded in ca. 1026 for secular canons, became a monastery of the Benedictine order in 1044, and was dissolved in 1539.

Abric Pizarro is a prehistoric rock shelter located in the Spanish Pyrenees near the modern geopolitical border between Spain and France. Archaeological evidence shows that Neanderthals occupied the site for some 40,000 years, notably during the MIS 4 period, which lasted from around 71,000 to 57,000 years ago.
A peninsula in the South Caucasus, extending approximately 60 km into the Caspian Sea.
Fortified site in Upper Nubia dated to the late Meroitic and post-Merotic periods.
Abusir South, located north of Saqqara, refers to an archaeological area where a large cemetery of lower-ranking officials of the Old Kingdom has been identified.
Acanthus is an island in the Propontis named by Pliny the Elder.

The Acarnanian League was a tribal confederation of the Acarnanians that later transformed into a league by the 5th century BCE. The league was incorporated into the Roman province of Achaea following the battle of Actium in 31 BCE.
A monopteral nuraghe located near Quartu Sant'Elena.
An ancient spring said by Pausanias to be near Dorion in Messenia, its precise location is unknown.
The Acropolis of Aletrium, often referred to as the "Civita", is the fortified citadel of the ancient city. Surrounded by polygonal walls, it is accessed via two gates.
The polygonal masonry walls of the Acropolis of Circeii enclose an area of approximately two hectares. The walls likely date to the middle republican period.
The Hellenistic acropolis of Halos lies just beneath the summit of the hill and its later Byzantine successor, according to Reinders (1988, 58).

The fortified Acropolis of Selinus occupies a limestone plateau. It was planned following the Hippodamian fashion and it is most noted for the numerous Doric temples that occupied its sacred precincts.
A statio located at the mouth of Aesis fl. on the Adriatic coast; the Antonine Itinerary places it between Ancona and Sena Gallica.
An ancient place in Baetica located located 12 Roman miles from Astigi (Écija).
A station (statio) located in the territory of the Batavians between Grinnes and Noviomagus.
An ancient mine and quarry, located in the modern French commune of Peret.
A Roman road station attested in ancient sources, possibly to be identified with modern Kuršumlija in Serbia.
An attested Roman road station that modern scholars have associated with Laktaši near Banja Luka in Bosnia.
Ad Novas was a station along the road from Rimini to Ravenna.
Ad Sponsas was a road station on the Via Appia.
Ad Turres was located on the Via Aurelia, some 10 miles from Lorium and 12 miles from Pyrgi.
Ad Turres Albas lay on the Via Severiana, midway between Circeii and Astura.
Ad Vicesimum was a Roman road station located near modern Morlupo, Italy.
A villa and associated road station, located (on the basis of itinerary evidence) approximately 25-30 miles south of Hippo Regius. Its precise location has not been determined.
A site of rock-cut relief sculpture, perhaps dating to the second century.
A place from the TAVO Index
Medieval castle of the town Adilcevaz on the shore of Lake Van where Urartian inscriptions have been found. Not to be confused with Kef Kalesi which is located further north and outside of Adilcevaz.
The remains of a Roman villa and necropolis.
The Inn river is a right tributary of the Danube.
Aequinoctium was the site of a Roman fort on the Danube in Upper Pannonia.
The Sanctuary of Agios Lot is located at the southeastern end of the Dead Sea.
A 3,246 meter mountain at the NE end of the Antitaurus range.
An ancient river, mentioned by Ptolemy, that is probably to be associated with the modern Berda river in Ukraine.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: FRA.
A barren, uninhabited island in the Nikasiai islands (Naxos).
An island that is part of the Nikasiai islands (Naxos).
At Agios Vasileios is the archaeological site of the only Mycenaean palace thus far discovered in Lakonia. It is located near the village of Xerokambi in Lakonia, Greece.
A small bay known today as Agios Sostis, located on the western peninsula that partly bounds the prominent gulf of Kissamos in northwest Crete.

A building in the southeast corner of the Agora of Athens, built in the late fifth century BC, which was used for minting bronze coinage from the third century BC until it was abandoned in the first century BC.
The agora of ancient Elis included the Stoa of the Hellanodikai, who served as judges in the games at Olympia.
Ancient Agora of Messene, adjacent to the Asklepieion and Theatre of Messene.
Agora of the Ancient City of Palmyra.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: upper Struma valley BUL.
Agryle Kathyperthen ("Upper Agryle") was a deme of ancient Attica and one of two demoi of Agryle.
The Villa Romana di Aiano-Torraccia di Chiusi, located near San Gimignano, is notable for a tri-apsidal courtyard.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Goa region.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: S Kerala coast.

The Ajanta Caves are among the earliest Buddhist cave monuments and date from the second and first centuries B.C. During the Gupta period (fifth and sixth centuries A.D.), additional decorated caves were added to the group.

Noted by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas), modern Akbou des Beni Chénacha was the site of a large establishment of the Roman period, probably a villa. The location was approximately 2 kilometers to the southwest of colonial Camp-du-Maréchal (now Tadmaït in Algeria's Tizi Ouzou province.
An ancient mausoleum located at modern Akbou on the north slope of a prominent hill in the southwestern neighborhood of Bouzeroual (Béjaïa Province, Algeria).
An island group of the Cilician coast located between Pityoussa and Anemurion.
The modern Ulu Burun on the southern coast of Turkey.
Burial site on Lake Aktash on the Crimean peninsula made up of at least 12 mounds from the Scythian, Taurian, and Greek cultures.
Alanya Castle is a thirteenth century fortification built on the site of Korakesion.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
Alburnus M. is a mountain of Lucania near the river Silarus.
Aleion Pedion (the Aleian Plain) in Cilicia.
Algidus (mons) refers to the eastern rim of the dormant Alban volcano in the Alban Hills of central Italy, known today as Monte Artemisio.

Alhambra, Generalife, and Albayzín together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site that preserves elements of the medieval heritage of Granada, Spain. The Alhambra is a fortified palace complex that was begun by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, the first Nasrid emir and founder of the Emirate of Granada, in 1238.
An alignment of menhirs that form a rectangular area.
A megalithic complex located near Guadalupe, Portgual, dating to the Early Neolithic period.
A copper smelting site located near the modern town of Agia Varvara in Cyprus. The site contains remains dated to the Iron Age.
The Alps are one of the great mountain ranges of Europe stretching some 1,200 km. (750 miles).
The Carnic Alps, a part of the Julian Alps.
Altar at the temple of Amphiaraos
An altar located to the east of the temple of Amphiaraos.
A Roman sanctuary located at the mouth of the Colares river.
BAtlas 25 C3 Alto de los Casares
An ancient marble quarry located immediately north of the ancient settlement of Alyke, which is located on the southeast coast of the Aegean island of Thasos.
Alyscamps is a necropolis located outside the walls of Arles, France.
Amasya Castle or Harşene Castle, is a fortress located in Amasya in northern Turkey.
Cape Zoluphi, the northwest promontory of the island of Patmos, was known in ancient Greek as the Amazonion promontory.
Ambresbury Banks is an archaeological site in the Epping Forest of Essex, England. It contains the remains of a 4.5 ha Iron Age hillfort on a site that is now forested.
An ancient promontory on the southern coast of the Arabian peninsula: the modern Little Aden (Yemen).
A promontory on the southeastern coast of the island of Samos, mentioned in Strabo and Ptolemy.
A Mycenaean tholos tomb located southeast of Amphissa, Phokida.

Discovered in late 2021 on the site of the Basler Ruderclub in Augst, this amphitheater lies just west of the Roman fort of Castrum Rauracense. It seems to have been built in an abandoned quarry sometime in the 4th century CE.
The so-called Amphitheater house at Mérida is a second-century CE funerary complex connected with one C. Iulius Sucesianus.
The Roman amphitheater of Durrës dates to the reign of Trajan. A small chapel built inside the amphitheater has mosaics likely dating to the 6th-8th centuries CE.
A cave sanctuary, dedicated to Pan and the Nymphs, located near modern Ag. Marina in Phocis and therefore also near the site of Psilo Kastro (possibly ancient Patronis).

Also known as the "Long Wall of Thrace," this fortification line (nearly 60km in length) spanned the Thracian peninsula west of Constantinople. It was built in the 5th century CE and refurbished and modified by the emperor Anastasius in the early 6th century.
Anatolikon Stoma, the mouth of Baetis/Certis fl.

Anavyssos, Greece, is the findspot of the kouros of Kroisos, a fallen warrior. The kouros dates ca. 530–520 B.C. and is housed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens (inv. no. 3851). The kouros was discovered in 1936.
Originally constructed during the Hellenistic period, the theater at Teos was extensively modified during the early Roman empire.
Ancient bridge on Via Egnatia at modern Arisvi
