A domus in Pompeii excavated in 1818. It is linked to VIII.3.28 and VIII.3.30.
A Roman villa with a long occupational arc from the first century BCE to the third century CE.

Approximately 41 burials from a Roman cremation necropolis were excavated in 2021 at Cascina Torretta, a locality in the municipality of Calvignasco (southwest of Milan, Italy). The tombs were poorly preserved, appeared to be relatively shallow pit graves, and were likely connected to a rural settlement.
The House of Bacchus and Ariadne at Ostia dates to the Hadrianic period and adjoined the Serapeum.
A Late Bronze Age nuragic site.
Casteddu di Tappa is a Bronze Age archaeological site in Corsica connected with the Torréen culture.
The castle was the site of the Holy Emperor Frederick II's death in 1250.

An imperial necropolis with at least 326 tombs was identified at modern Castel Malnome (Ponte Galeria) in Italy. Archaeological evidence marks these as burials belonging to working-class people of the Roman imperial period, with most graves having either no grave goods or very few. The osteoarchaeological analysis led excavators to speculate that the individuals buried here many have worked in the
A 13th-century castle near Andria in the Apulia region of southeastern Italy built during the 1240s by the Emperor Frederick II. The castle was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
Situated along the via Severiana are the remains of an anonymous Paleochristian basilica that was in use between the second and the seventh centuries AD.
Castell Collen is the site of a Roman auxiliary fort dating to the Flavian period.
A Medieval fort dating from the mid-ninth to the eleventh century CE.
Castello D'Evoli is located at Castropignano in the Italian Province of Campobasso. The castle's construction dates to the fourteenth century and it may occupy the site of the Samnite fortifications.

The Castello della Pietra is a Medieval fortificaiton located in the comune of Vobbia in the province of Genova. The castle is occupies a position some 540 meters above sea level. It dates to ca. 1252.
Castello di Agira is situated atop Mount Teja in the province of Enna, approximately 820 meters above sea level.
A Medieval castle built atop Byzantine foundations.
A mausoleum dating to the Roman Imperial period located at Centuripe in Sicily.
A fortification located in the valley of the Treja River, in use from the tenth century until its abandonment in 1431.
A tenth-century castle located near the di Sant'Alessio in Sicily.
The Norman-Hohenstaufen Castle (Sannicandro di Bari, Italy) is a Medieval castle that dates from the tenth century.
A fort constructed ca. 11 BC to protect a wooden bridge built to span the Rhine river.
BAtlas 26 D4 Castilleja de la Cuesta
The Castle of Montalban is a ruined castle located in San Martín de Montalbán, province of Toledo, Spain.
A Medieval castle (thirteenth to seventeenth centuries) located near Ucero in Spain's Soria province.
Castle Hill is located about 350 m south-east of Round Hill and was the site of an Iron Age hill fort.
Castle Rising Castle is a ruined medieval castle located in Castle Rising, Norfolk, England. It was established by William d'Aubigny II ca. 1138.
Remains of a Venetian castle atop the former ancient citadel of Astypalaia.
A castle at Bominaco in Italy that originally dates to the twelfth century.
A medieval castle located in the municipality of Guimarães, in northern Portugal. The castle may have been founded in the tenth century.
Site of a Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
The Roman legionary base at Bonna.
A modern location in Sicily that has been associated with the location of the ancient settlement of Krastos.
A fortified site of the later Byzantine period located at Finale Ligure.
The Catacombs of Marcellinus and Peter lies some 3 km southeast of Rome along the ancient Via Labicana. They date to the fourth century A.D.
A paleochristian catacomb dating to the fourth century CE.
The Catalauni were a tribe of Gallia Belgica.
The First Cataract of the Nile is located at Aswan.
The Fourth Cataract of the Nile is located in the Manasir Desert. Since 2008, it has been flooded by the Merowe Dam.
The Fifth Cataract of the Nile river is located near the confluence of the Nile and Atbarah Rivers.
The Sixth Cataract is where the Nile cuts through the Sabaluka pluton.
The Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta on the island of Torcello is a Roman Catholic basilica initially founded in 639. The second basilica was begun in 1008.
A 12th-century Armenian church in Jerusalem, the principal church of the Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem.
Cattigara was a port city of the Sinae, located south of Thinae near the mouth of the river Cottiaris. Ptolemy considers the city to be the extreme southeastern-most point of the known world.
The Caucasus Mountains, located between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
A Samnite tribe that was subjugated in 275 BC by L. Cornelius Lentulus.

Excavated in the nineteenth century and only recently re-assessed, this cemetery is located east of Vulci itself, across the modern river Fiora from the ancient acropolis. The cemetery was in active use from the Villanovan period through Hellenistic times.
The Cavares were a Gallic tribe of the lower Rhone valley.
The southernmost cave at Udayagiri, dedicated to an unidentified god.
Cave 13 at Udayagiri, known as the Nārāyaṇa cave, contains a large relief panel of Vishnu's Nārāyaṇa avatar.
The largest cave temple at Udayagiri, known as the Amrita or Viṣṇupada cave.
Cave 5 at Udayagiri is dedicated to Vishnu and contains a monumental relief panel of Vishnu's Varaha avatar.
Sacred cave dedicated to the goddess of childbirth, Eileithyia, at Inatos, Crete. The site was in use from the Geometric period to the Roman period.

The so-called "Cave of the Apocalypse" on Patmos was enrolled in 1999 by UNESCO as a joint World Heritage Site together with the Monastery of Saint John the Theologian. This cave is said to mark the location where St. John of Patmos received the visions that he recorded in the Book of Revelation.
A Roman necropolis along the Via Amerina.
Site of a Roman fortress near Eastern Galcantray that some consider one of the northernmost Roman forts in Great Britain.

Mentioned only by Avienus, the Celebandicum Iugum is to be identified with the modern Cap de Begur on the Mediterranean coast of the Spanish province of Girona. The Barrington Atlas treated it as an unlocated, possibly false, toponym.
BAtlas 25 E4 Celsa/Col. Victrix Iulia Lepida
A group of cemeteries treated as a single entry by the Barrington Atlas.

A Roman villa located in the municipality of Constantí, in Catalonia. Among its finds are a dome mosaic with a Christian theme that numbers among the earliest known examples in the Roman world (4th century AD.)
Centum Cellas, also referred to as Centum Cellæ, Centum Celli, or Centum Cœli refers to a Roman villa rustica of the first century A.D., located in the Castelo Branco district of Portugal.
Roman era centuriation has been detected in the vicinity of ancient Trebula Balli(ni)ensium.
A Late Roman palace complex at Cordoba that may have been built to serve as the headquarters of the vicarius of the diocese of the Hispaniae and then later passed into the control of the church.
Cerro da Vila, the ruins of a Roman villa in the Algarve region of southern Portugal.
BAtlas 26 E3 Cerro de los Castillejos
A mountain placed by ancient authors east of the Euenos river on the Aetolian coast. Scholars identify it with modern Barasovon/Varasova in Greece.

During archaeological excavations beginning in 1969, Champigneulles (Meurthe-et-Moselle, France) was revealed to be the site of a settled, productive landscape that included the remains of a Gallo-Roman villa. The entry authored by R. Billoret included in the Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites describes what sounds like an assemblage of archaeological loci as opposed to a single locus.
The fortification located at Chancy dates initially to the reign of Valentinian.

Chani Kokkonas is an archaeological site in Tempe valley, Thessaly, Greece. The excavations revealed remains of a Hellenistic complex with both ritual and workshop areas, as well as a Byzantine church and guesthouse (khan).
The chapelle Sainte-Agathe was originally a Roman-period thermal complex that was converted to a Christian church by the seventh century.
Necropolis of the Jūybāri shaikhs located approximately 5 km west of Bukhara. The complex was constructed during the 16th century around the tomb of the scholar Emām Abu Bakr Saʿd.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Chamars, inhabitants of Bundelkhand.
The thermal baths of Chassenon are among the best preserved in the Gallo-Roman world. They are part of the ancient city of Cassinomagus.
Site of an Iron Age oppidum.
Understood to be the oldest necropolis in Alexandria that dates back to the Ptolemaic period and is located in the modern Chatby area of Alexandria.
Khatri, an ancient people in Malwa, also a caste.
The Chatti were an ancient Germanic people whose homeland centered on the valley of the Weser River.

The Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc Cave in southern France contains the earliest known and best preserved figurative cave paintings in the world, dating from the Upper Paleolithic. The cave was discovered on December 18, 1994, and was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List on June 22, 2014.
The Cheddar Gorge is a limestone gorge in the Mendip Hills, near Somerset, England. The gorge and its many caves are the site of human activity dating back to the Upper Paleolithic.
A large Roman-style villa in Britain, dating from the second to fourth centuries A.D.
An ancient peak in Arcadia (Greece) whose precise location is not known today. Pausanias names it and associates it with Kyllene.
Chersonesos Kimbrike, the Cimbric or Cimbrian Peninsula, is the modern Jutland peninsula.
The Cherusci were a Germanic tribe occupying parts of northwestern Germany.
Chervony Mayak (Kherson Oblast, Ukraine) is the site of a necropolis associated with the Late Scythian culture (second and mid-third centuries CE).
Chew Green is the site of a Roman encampment located in Northumberland.
The Chiarone is a river of the Maremma. It creates one of three major valley systems in the Ager Cosanus.

An extensive Roman villa located at Chiragan, in the French Commune of Martres-Tolosanes. The site produced significant architectural and sculptural finds that are now in various museums. Most of the site is covered by farmland today.
The Choaspes flows from the Hindu Kush mountains to the Indus river in what is now Afghanistan.
Cemetery site in the Altai Mountains containing burials associated with the Bulan-Koba culture (4th century CE).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: people of Coromandel coast?
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: in Khoyt district in Taurus Mts.

The Chrysopolitissa complex in Paphos is an archaeological area that includes various ruins. Among these are those of an early Christian basilica (fourth to seventh centuries), a medieval Franciscan church (thirteenth century), and the so-called Pillar of St. Paul.
The archaeological remains of a small Minoan settlement of approximately 12-20 houses on the island of Chryssi. Evidence for murex processing was discovered during excavations conducted in 2008.
7th-century Armenian church in the Kars region of Turkey. This church is now ruined, but still is the second-largest domed basilica from the 7th-century Caucasus still extant.
A paleochristian sanctuary located along the Via Francigena.
The so-called Church of San Primitivo in Monte Compatri. The church's bell tower was converted to a defensive tower around 1200.
Church of St. Etchmiadzin at Soradir
Sixth-century Armenian church in the town of Soradir (modern Yanal, Turkey).
One of a group of eleven rock-hewn monolithic churches located in Lalibela, a city in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia. The church likely dates to the twelfth or thirteenth century.
A fourteenth-century A.D. church in Thessalonica.
A fifth century A.D. Byzantine church.
A fourteenth century church at Thessalonica.
The Church of the Saviour, Thessaloniki, is a fourteenth-century Byzantine church.
Chûn Castle is an Iron Age hill fort near Penzance in Cornwall, United Kingdom.
The Cibarci were an ancient Celtic tribe of Gallaecia.
A first century BC Roman villa in Basilicata.
A small island in the Pagasitic Gulf.
Cinyphii, an ancient tribe dwelling in valley of the Cinyps river.
A circus was identified at the site in the nineteenth century. John Humphrey dubbed this site "the most impressive circus in Egypt outside Alexandria".
The Circus at Lepcis Magna is located to the southeast of the city and measures ca. 100 x 450 m.
The area of the Roman Circus at Segobriga had been occupied in the earlier Roman period (at least since the Augustan period) by a cremation necropolis.
Modern Pag Island in Croatia, an island in the Adriatic Sea.
A large Roman cistern associated with the so-called Villa di Marmura at modern Gianola in Italy.
A group of 15 large cisterns constructed during the late Punic era as a water supply for the city of Carthage.
Walls and towers surrounding the citadel hill inside Dura-Europos on the city's eastern side.
Fortified hill inside of Dura-Europos, located on the eastern side of the city.

The fortified wall encircling the city of Dura-Europos built primarily of locally-quarried ashlar limestone blocks. Built ca. 150 BCE, the walls were breached in 256 CE and went out of use thereafter.
The polygonal masonry circuit wall of ancient Ameria.
Cosa's polygonal masonry fortification wall, reinforced with interval towers, has a length of ca. 1500 meters. Traditionally the wall has been dated between ca. 273 and 264 B.C.
The city walls of Pompeii surround the ancient urban center and have several architectural phases.
A set of buildings and a stoa built in the Athenian Agora in the 2nd century AD, to provide space for official business in addition to the Metroon and Tholos.
The ruins of a Roman amphitheater.
Clasius? fl., a river of Umbria and part of the basin of the Tiber River.
A Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall in Scotland.
A Broch tower with other associated Iron Age structures.
The Clivus Victoriae was a steep street located at or near the southwest corner of the Palatine Hill in Rome.
Cluturnum was a site in Samnium, located near Aesernia. Its exact location cannot be determined.
The archaeological area of Cocciano located in the comune of Frascati, Italy, is the site of an imperial-period villa that is associated with Livia Drusilla and her son, the emperor Tiberius.
A Bronze Age megalithic gallery grave on Sardinia that belongs to the "giants' tomb" classification.
A Roman auxiliary fort in the Neath valley located at the confluence of three streams (Camnant, Nant-y-Bryn, and Nant-y-Fedwen), which join to form the Afon Pyrddin.
The encampment of the Cohors I Celtiberorum equitata civium Romanorum, an auxiliary unit of the Roman army.
BAtlas 26 F4 Colina de los Quemados
A plaform villa at Colle Nocello.
A Roman villa rustica in use from the middle Republican period until the 4th century A.D.
A Roman villa has been identified in the modern neighborhood of El Collet, which is located in the Catalonian municipality of Calonge i Sant Antoni.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Skt.: Kolūta.
Le Colonnacce refers to preserved elements of the lateral, north-south Corinthian-order colonnades that flanked the Forum Transitorium.

The so-called "Colonne della Sabatina" are located at the southeastern end of the territory of Campagnatico territory, between Arcille and Baccinello. These fortifications date originally to the thirteenth century and were initially a possession of the Abbey of San Galgano.
Columbarium of the freedmen of Augustus
An early imperial columbarium tomb on the Via Appia.
Site of a Romano-British villa of courtyard type.
The comitium is a component of a monumental forum complex constructed at Paestum after the city became a Latin colony in 273 B.C.
An island mentioned by Pliny, said to be located in the Naracustoma, one of the mouths of the Danube river.
The so-called Constantinian Columbarium is actually a second-century AD tomb on the Via Appia.
A palatial Roman villa, built in the 4th century CE and subsequently used as an imperial summer residence by the emperor Valentinianus I. Located at modern Konz bei Trier in Germany.
Contra Florentiam was a late Roman fort located on the Danube frontier.

The Conventus Bracaraugustanus or Conventus Bracarus was a sub-provincial administrative district of the Roman empire located in the northwestern part of the Iberian Peninsula, in Gallaecia. Its capital was located at Bracara Augusta.

Evidence of Roman quarrying activity was discovered at Coombe Crag, a site some 350 meters south of the line of Hadrian's Wall. The quarry was used as a source of building materials for the Wall and at least eight inscriptions were identified on the sandstone cliff.
Copper and Gold Mine at Kantanos
Southeast of the ancient settlement of Kantanos on Crete (BAtlas 60 A2)
A Roman-era villa in the vicinity of modern Corduente (Las Casulillas).
The abbey was first founded in 815 by Charlemagne's cousins, Wala and Adelard.
A Dacian fotress located near modern Costești village, Hunedoara County, Romania, built in the first century B.C.
The Cotini were an ancient Celtic people of the northern part of the Carpathian basin.
A Roman villa site in Northamptonshire first observed in 1736.
A site with evidence for large-scale pottery production.

The cave known as Cova de les Dones is located in the Millares municipality, province of Valencia, Spain. This site shows evidence of human activity across a broad period stretching from the Paleolithic to the time of the Roman Empire.
A shrine to a Celtic water goddess situated near the Roman fort of Brocolitia at present-day Carrawburgh, along Hadrian's Wall.
Covili sa Serra su Sipiri nuraghe
Remains of a single tower nuraghe.

Roman settlement, with evidence for agricultural, quarrying, and settlement activity during the second to fourth centuries CE, together with a possible mutatio (horse-changing station) along the Roman road linking Glevum (modern Gloucestershire) and Corinium (modern Cirencester).
Site of Roman fort occupied during the Antonine period, located 4.5 miles NNW of Castle Rock, Edinburgh.

Cave approximately 17km Northwest of El Maabdeh, Egypt where thousands of mummified crocodiles were found in addition to several other types of animals and human mummies as part of the Egyptian crocodile cult. All discoveries at this site were from the Ptolemaic or Roman periods.
A promontory fort on the Isle of Man.
Cross dyke and bowl barrow on the northern spur of Beacon Hill
A cross dyke in Burghclere, Basingstoke and Deane, England, United Kingdom.
The site of a Roman fort and fortlet on the Antonine Wall.
A rectangle of 21 menhirs ranging in height from 0.91 m to 2.4 m.
A Roman fort in Pannonia Superior east of Brigetio that was the base of the cohors V Callaecorum Lucensium.
Crypt and church of San Lussorio
The Romanesque church of San Lussorio dates to the early twelfth century.
A rock-cut tunnel of the Via Domitiana built during the first century BC under the direction of Lucius Cocceius Auctus.
An aisled Cryptoporticus at Alife that dates to the Augustan period.
A fortified Roman villa within the territory of Norba Caesarina. Re-occupation occurred during the Islamic period in Spain.
Two Roman forts and two Roman camps at St Andrew's Hill, Cullompton, Devon, England.
Cuneiform findspot close to the citadel of ‘Ammān
Location on a slope south-east of the citadel of ‘Ammān (modern Jordan) where cuneiform texts were discovered.
A grouping of burial mounds (named Cursus Barrows) located very close to Stonehenge.
A temple sacred to Cybele located at Neuss am Rhein.
Dabanas, a fortress of Justinian, situated between Dara and Amida.
At Dalswinton are the remains of a series of Roman forts from the Flavian period that guarded the river Nith.
Dam at source of the Aqua Anio Novus
Unlabeled feature captured from the Barrington Atlas
Dangstetten was the site of a Roman military camp.
The Dani were a North Germanic tribe inhabiting parts of southern Scandinavia.
A Roman auxiliary fort at present-day Doncaster.

South of modern Dar bel Amri, a settlement on the east side of the upper Beht river in Morocco, there are remnants of watch tower dating to the Roman imperial period. The fort's ancient name is not known.
Darb Qirmiz is a residential neighborhood in the tenth-century Fatimid quarter of Cairo, Egypt, with the oldest remaining monuments dating from the fourteenth century.
The Darinoi were an ancient tribe of northern Ireland mentioned by Ptolemy.
A cemetery site in southern Tajikistan containing burials from the Vaksh culture (mid-late 3rd millennium BCE).
Darsa is an island in the Socotra Archipelago of Yemen.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A mountain range of southern Italy that constitutes the eastern appendix of the Campanian Apennines.
Roman building interpreted either as a villa or a shrine at Borough Hill hillfort, United Kingdom.

Once known as İririn or Érérin and now known as Dağönü, this modern Turkish village located in the Van Province of eastern Turkey at the eastern coast of Lake Van lies ca. 10 km north of Ayanis. Here a stela with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) has been found (CTU I A 5-18).
Decennovium refers to a 19-mile stretch of the Via Appia from the Forum Appii to Tarracina that continued through the paludes Pontinae.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
Belonging to Vulci's Roman phase, the Decumanus Maximus is the well-preserved east-west road of the city paved in basalt.
The fortification wall of the Late Roman fortified palace compound at Gamzigrad-Romuliana, commissioned by Emperor Caius Valerius Galerius Maximianus, in the late third and early fourth centuries.
A Coptic Orthodox monastery located in the Wadi El Natrun northwest of Cairo.
Late antique monastery at Saqqarah constructed around 470 CE and abandoned by the middle of the 9th century.
A small temple dedicated to Isis on West bank of the Nile at Luxor. Its ancient name is unknown.
An ancient place, located in modern Syria, with remains of a monastic chapel. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 as part of the "Ancient Villages of Northern Syria."
A country house in Attica dating to the fourth century BCE located near the fort and wall at Dema.
This Pleiades place resource was moved to errata because it is a doublet for another place resource (see details for link).
Site of a Roman fort that was first occupied ca. A.D. 55-65. The fort later moved to a new site during the governorship of Cn. Julius Agricola.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
Iron age tomb where cuneiform inscription was found.
A place described by Pausanias who indicates that three sanctuaries are to be found here, namely those of Apollo, Poseidon, and Demeter.
Dinogetia, a Roman castrum located in the province of Moesia.
The Diolkos was a paved tract near ancient Corinth that allowed boats to portage the Isthmus of Corinth. It was in use from ca. 600 B.C. until ca. A.D. 50.
The name assigned by some writers, including Livy, to the plain of Canusium, in which the battle of Cannae was fought in August of 216 BC.
Highest point (1745 meters) on the island of Euboea
A place from the TAVO Index
The Dobunni were a Celtic people of pre-Roman Britain.
The ruinous remains of a dolmen-type tomb, its tumulus no longer extant, are located on the same axis as the Tusson tumuli.
Domus Augustana, a topographic appellation for the central block of the Flavian palace complex on the Palatine Hill attributed to the emperor Domitian.

The remains of a private domus that date to the second and third centuries CE and include a Mithraeum. This complex eventually became incorporated into the fourth-century basilica on the site of the later basilica of San Clemente al Laterano.
West corner of the museum built on the site of a Roman Villa. Time periods following the Barrington Atlas (BAtlas 47 inset Melita).
The remains of a Roman domus and a bath complex adjacent to the area of the Forum of Trajan.
Domus and Episcopal Palace at Aquileia. The second phase of the Episcopal Palace at Aquileia belongs to the fourth and fifth centuries CE.
Domus de Janas on Monte Crobu
A prehistoric chamber tomb of the third millennium B.C. The 'Domus de Janas' tombs are typical of the Ozieri and Beaker cultures and are found chiefly on Sardinia.
The so-called "Domus dei Ritratti" is located in the archaeological area surrounding Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome. The domus dates to the later Roman Empire.
The so-called "Domus della Fortuna Annonaria" (V,II,8) is an ancient peristyle house with a nymphaeum located in Ostia. Its initial construction likely dates to the reign of Antoninus Pius.
The House of Titus Macer at Aquileia dates to the middle of the first century CE when at least two pre-exisiting domus were merged to form a single domus covering more than 1,500 square meters.
The ruins of a Republican-period 'domus rustica' located on the via Alexandre Gustave Eiffel in Rome, Italy, near Ponte Galeria.

An archaeological site in Tarsus, Turkey, that has been interpreted in various ways and assigned to various periods. The current consensus suggests that the ruined concrete structure is of a sacred nature and dates to the second century CE.
An Archaic Greek temple at Corfu built in the Doric order ca. 500 B.C.
The so-called "Doric nymphaeum" is located on the shores of the Alban lake and was a component of the Villa of Domitian.
The Doric Temple at Caulonia has been dated ca. 420 B.C.
Doss Trento is a small hill that lies along the course of the Adige River. A Paleochristian basilica was located on the hillside.

An unfinished Doric stoa with colonnades on both long sides, built at Thorikos in the late fifth century BC, of uncertain function, perhaps a gateway to a sanctuary of Demeter. Material from the structure was spoliated in the Augustan period to build the southwest temple in the Athenian Agora.
The twelfth-century medieval castle of Dover, England, sits atop earlier Roman fortifications.
Dowth is a Neolithic passage tomb in the Boyne Valley, County Meath, Ireland.
BAtlas 30 G3 Dra Zeg et Ter
An unexcavated Roman fort established circa 47 CE near Drayton, United Kingdom.

An ancient promontory on western end of the island of Kos, mentioned by Strabo. Its precise location cannot be determined today with full confidence, but the Ákra Dafní and the Ákra Kríkellos are the two likely candidates.
The modern Cape Drepano, located at the western narrowing of the Corinthian Gulf, just east of Rhion/Antirrhion.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Trissino.
A megalithic stone circle monument, also known as the Druid's Altar, consisting of seventeen closely spaced stones with a diameter of 9.3 m. Thirteen stones survive today.
Iron Age promontory fort near Loughshinny, Ireland
A Roman auxiliary fort located at Drumlanrig in Scotland.
The Dulgubnii? were a Germanic tribe whose territory was located to the north of the Angrivarii and Chamavi.
Dun Carloway Broch is a well preserved broch in Scotland that was in use from ca. the first century BC until ca. AD 1300.
Roman fortlet and fort on the Antonine Wall in West Dunbartonshire, Scotland.
A road station (mutatio) located along the Via Egnatia to the east of Thessaloniki.
The Durotriges were a Celtic tribe of pre-Roman Britain.
A Roman villa rustica dating to the first century A.D. located in the Punta Grande beach, in the territory of Realmonte, province of Agrigento, Sicily.
Early medieval church in the modern village of Akhalsopeli, Georgia, constructed in the 9th-10th centuries CE.

Džanfida is a village located in the Armavir province of southwestern Armenia, ca. 9 km south of Sardarabat. Here a stone block with an inscription of Sarduri II (8th century BCE) was found which curses anyone who dares to damage or destroy his fortress or inscription.
The shrine/seat of the god Ennugi in the Egipar temple at Ur. The name is damaged and the complete Sumerian ceremonial name of the structure is not known.
The shrine/seat of the god Nusku in the Egipar temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eadgigi means "House of the Counsellor."
The temple of the goddess Ningal at Kissik. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eamaškuga means "House, Pure Sheepfold."
The shrine in the Egipar temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Eanšar means "House of All Heaven."

A series of decorated early Christian tombs dating to the fourth century CE is located in the town of Sopianae, in the Roman Province of Pannonia. The Early Christian Necropolis of Pécs was enrolled as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
An unexcavated, eroded fortified site at the gold-processing complex at al-Ghuzza in Egypt's eastern desert. It may date to the New Kingdom period.
Eastern theater at Laodicea ad Lycum
Digitized by hand in Google Earth in July 2012 at an eye altitude of 683m. Dates are general for the settlement, following Foss and Mitchell in BAtlas 65.
The Eaton House Roman Fort was a Roman auxiliary fort located just outside Pennocrucium.
Archaeological excavations in 2008 and 2010 revealed an ecclesiastical complex at the west side of the port of Sanitja on the Spanish island of Menorca. This complex may date to the sixth century CE.
A group of islands in the Ionian Sea off the coast of Acarnania.
An Alpine tribe included on the Tropaeum Alpium inscription.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: W Asturias.
An Alpine tribe mentioned on the Tropaeum Augusti.
A megalithic tomb dated ca. 1700 BC located near Waterville, County Kerry, Ireland.
Archaeological investigation and geophysical prospection at Eilsleben, Germany, have documented the presence of a notable Early Neolithic settlement dating to the later sixth millennium BCE.
The shrine/seat of the goddess Ninimma in the Egipar temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Ekišibgalekura may mean "House, Keeper of the Seal of the Ekur."
Located in the Upper Agroa, the Ekklesiasterion at Akragas dates to the fourth and third centuries B.C.

The seat of the popular assembly of Poseidonia/Paestum, the Ekklesiasterion was built ca. 480-470 B.C. and could accommodate, at most, 1,700 persons. The structure retained its function after the Lucanian conquest but was abandoned, buried, and built over after the Roman conquest.
A Roman limestone quarry that served Tarraco and is now included in the UNESCO World Heritage listing.
The Elaitic Gulf, now Çandarlı Körfezi.
An island in the Sea of Oman is home to the "City of Caves", where an important assemblage of rock-cut art dating to the fifth through eighth centuries and linked to the cult of Shiva may be found.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: on Red Sea coast near Mouza and Okelis YEM.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
The temple of the gods Adad and Apla-Adad at Anat (Anatho). The Sumerian ceremonial name Enamhe means "House of Plenty."
Located in ancient Elis, the Enipeus was a right tributary of the Alpheius, which it joined downstream (west) of ancient Olympia. It has been identified with the modern Lestenitsas.
The cella/shrine of the goddess Ištar in the Eanna temple at Uruk. The Sumerian ceremonial name Enirgalana means "House of the Prince of Heaven."
The shrine/seat of the goddess Ningal in the Egipar temple at Ur. The Sumerian ceremonial name Enun means "Princely House."
An Arab tribe mentioned only by Pliny the Elder.
A headland (no modern name?) in Taşucu bay (Mersin province, Turkey), now occupied by a NATO port facility. An Ottoman-era fortification (Liman Kalesi) occupies the high point.
A substantial plateau that is roughly triangular in shape and extends to the north and west of Syracuse.
A river of the Argive plain, emptying into the Argolic Gulf: the modern Erasinos/Kephalari.
A rock-cut Christian sanctuary located on Monte Altino in the Monti Aurunci that was begun ca. A.D. 830.
A place from the TAVO Index

A branch Roman road (Margary 41) running from Calleva Atrebatum (modern Silchester) to the legionary fortress at Col. Glevum (Gloucester). Not to be confused with the major north-south road named Ermine Street (Margary 2).
This place resource has been removed from the Pleiades "places" section of the gazetteer because it is a duplicate for https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/54081048
An island mentioned in an Roman itinerary. It is possibly to be identified with the modern Île Plane, which is located a few kilometers off Cape Farina, Tunisia.
The Esaro River in Calabria is a tributary of the Coscile River.
The Esquiline Hill is one of the seven hills of Rome. The eastern section of the hill lay outside the Servian Wall, and served as a pauper's cemetery during the archaic and Republican periods.
A rock-cut altar dating to the first half of the sixth century B.C.
The Gulf of Euboea is an arm of the Aegean Sea.
Modern Alinnia, an island of the Dodecanese.
The temple of the goddess Anunnītu at Sippar-Anunnītu (=Sippar-Amnanum).
A barracks of the seventh cohort of the Vigiles, Rome's urban fire brigade, was located in the Transtiberim.
A rural tribe of Rome, which was established in 318 B.C.
The site of a Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
An archipelago made up of 18 islands situated between the Norwegian Sea and the North Atlantic Ocean.
Fectio was a castellum along the Roman frontier system (limes) of Germania Inferior.

An amphora production site with kiln was identified in the 1990s at a place called Felceto, approximately 10km south of ancient Tifernum Tiberinum (modern Città di Castello) and 2km east of the Tiber on a tributary (i.e., somewhere to the east of modern Cinquemiglia and Promano). The site has not been excavated.
A promontory on the east coast of the Iberian peninsula, modern Cabo de la Nao in Spain.
Foundations of a bath facility with mosaic pavement and other structures were discovered during rescue excavations in 2006 at the corner of Daidalou and Kadmou streets in modern Levadeia, Greece.
A Roman signal station/fortlet of the Yorkshire coast, England.

A multi-acre site, now located within the bounds of the Fingringhoe Wick Nature Discovery Park in Colchester. The site may have been or included a Roman military supply base that was in use until ca. A.D. 120. The site included several structures, a ditched enclosure, and a possible villa.
Fishbourne, in West Sussex, is the site of a palatial villa built soon after the Roman conquest of Britain in the first century A.D.
A small coastal river in Picenum located between Ancona and Firmum.
Flower's Barrow hill fort overlooks Worbarrow Bay in Dorset on England's south coast.
A river included on the Peutinger map.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: W Veldidena.

The Tower of Fonias (meaning "murderer" in Greek, named after the nearby river) is located on Samothrace island's northeastern coast and has been attributed to the military activity of the Genoese Gattilusi family.
An ancient necropolis documented during rescue excavation in the early 1970s at a location known as Font-du-Buis or La Fontaine du Buis between Saze and Avingon in Gard, France.

One of the interval forts spaced along the Great Wall of Gorgan.

One of the interval forts spaced along the wall.
