A fortress at modern Civitavecchia in Italy. It was begun in 1508 and completed in 1537 during the reign of Pope Paul III. Antonio Sangallo the Younger designed the fortress.
The polygonal masonry fortifications of the ancient settlement now known as Civita di Artena. These fortifications today measure more than 2.5 km in length.
The forum-basilica at Venta date to the first and second centuries A.D. and are of the so-called "principia" type. The basilica measures ca. 54.6 x 20.1 m and was of the Corinthian order.
The Forum of Carsulae is supported by terraces and it includes the basilica and a twin sanctuary, in addition to tabernae.
The Forum of Saepinum assumes a trapezoidal shape and is aligned with the decumanus.

The Forum of Theodosius in Constantinople was founded by Constantine as the Forum Tauri. In 393, Theodosius I rebuilt and remodelled the forum to resemble the Forum of Trajan in Rome. The forum occupied the area of what is now Beyazıt Square in Istanbul.
Fossae Papirianae refers to a navigable coastal canal and road station location along the Via Aemilia Scauri between Luna and Pisae.
A minor tributary of the Anio river in the vicinity of Guidonia.
The stream known as the Fosso del Manganello is a stream that delimits the northern part of the tuff plateau upon which the Etruscan metropolis of Caere developed.
One of the sources of the Aqua Traiana.
A stream that drains into the Tyrrhenian Sea at Santa Marinella, Italy.
The Fosso di Pratolungo is a small tributary of the Anio. Its lower course is also known as Fosso di Marco Simone.
The site of a Roman villa with two parallel ranges of rooms dating from the second half of the first century to the fifth century.

A stips votiva was discovered at the site of the Christian church of San Martino a Poggio - Frascole in 1887. The main ancient activity at the site likely took place during the middle of the third century B.C.
A Roman outpost of the Rhaetian Limes.
The strait separating Gallia and Britannia.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.

The Friars Wash Roman Temple was noted first in 1965. Aerial photography and subsequent archaeological investigation identified a system of ditches and two rectangular structures that were considered to be Romano-British temples.
"Frigidae" is the site of a Roman castellum located 18 km south of Lixus that is mentioned as a station on the Antonine Itinerary.
An Umbro-Roman temple of Iuppiter on the slopes of Monte Catria.
A brackish lake ca. 90 km southeast of Rome.
A subterranean funerary chamber with three frescoes walls depicting animal and vegetal life, located around the third mile of the Via Appia.
Gabreta? Hyle (Gabreta Forest) is an ancient forest of continental Europe mentioned by Strabo and Ptolemy.
The modern Strait of Bonifacio separates the Tyrrhenian Sea from the western Mediterranean Sea. The strait measures 11 km (6.8 miles) in width.
A Gallo-Roman amphitheater dating to the early third century CE.

A Gallo-Roman structure including hypocaust and other remains of a bath, located beneath the later Church of Saint Martin in modern Moissac, France. The bath may have belonged to a villa of the fourth-fifth centuries CE.
The Gallo-Roman amphitheater at Grannum dates to the late first century B.C.
A Gallo-Roman bath complex located at the modern town of Mackwiller in the French commune of Waldhambach.
A suite of Roman-period public baths in Lyon, France. The site is located in the rue des Farges on the slope of the Fourvière hill. The baths may have been linked to the cult of Apollo.
The remains of a possible Gallo-Roman fanum were recovered, including an enclosure surrounding a rectangular structure along with terra sigillata from La Graufesenque.
The fanum of a Gallo-Roman cult that was in use from the first century B.C. to the fourth century A.D.

Remains of a series of structures dating to the first 3 centuries of the common era -- including a probable villa -- were excavated in 1989 at a village called Perron in the French commune of Saint-Sauveur, on the north bank of the Isère river.
Remains of a Gallo-Roman at Vannes.
Gallo-Roman temple of Forêt d'Halatte (cne. Ognon, Oise)
A Gallo-Roman temple built ca. mid-first century AD that remained in use until the fifth century.
Gallo-Roman villa of Bapteste at Montcrabeau

The first phase of this Gallo-Roman villa belongs to the first century A.D. The site was subsequently rebuilt on a grander scale in the fourth century. This later phase was centered on a courtyard and covered some 5,000 square meters.
Modern name of a seventh-century Pallava rock-cut temple at Mahābalipuram.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: upper R. Ganges-Ghaggar Doab.
Tributary of the Rhodanus (Rhone), famously spanned by the Pont du Gard Roman aqueduct bridge. The river's ancient name is unknown.
Garden and Pool Complex at Petra
Garden terrace and monumental pool with island pavilion dates to the Nabataean/Early Roman periods, 9 BCE-c. 200 CE. Formerly called the "Lower Market."
An archaeological area in Vienne that includes remains of municipal and domestic architecture.
A Roman-era garden, with terrace, dining room, water feature, and other components, located next to the small baths at Cuicul (modern Djemila) in Algeria.
A hypothesised gate in the Themistoklean city wall of Athens, through which the road to Phlya and Athmonon would have run.
The Gate of Athena Archegetis is the Doric-order gateway at the west of the Roman Agora in Athens. It was dedicated to Athena Archigetis in 11/10 BCE.
Remains of a large villa that was in use from the Augustan period to the seventh century A.D.
Gebel al Silsila is a mountain that was the site of quarrying activity in ancient Egypt.
The Greek and Roman period necropolis at Gebel el-Muzawaka, in Egypt's Dakhleh Oasis.
Royal residence in Georgia initially constructed in the 8th-9th centuries CE, and expanded several times through the 14th century.
The Monastery of Gelati was founded in 1106 in western Georgia. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Tempio.
A monumental fountain dating to the second century CE at Gerasa (modern Jerash in Jordan).
Ancient Germanicum, also referred to as Kastell Kösching, was a Roman military camp built ca. 80 CE. It was located in Kösching in the district of Eichstätt in Bavaria.
The Sulak river flows into the Caspian Sea, draining most of the mountainous interior of Dagestan.
Gerulata, located in Pannonia, was a Roman limes fort located near Rusovce, Slovakia.

A Romano-British villa site located in Gestingthorpe parish, Essex, that has been sampled through survey, magnetometry, and partial excavation. Artifact evidence indicates occupation from the first to the fourth centuries.
Gheriat el-Garbia was the site of a Roman fort in Libya that was part of the Limes Tripolitanus.
Gheriat esh-Shergia is the site of a fortified farm of the Limes Tripolitanus.
A roman-era fort at Al-Ghuzza in Egypt's eastern desert.
The Gialia Monastery is a ruined medieval Georgian Orthodox monastery located in the village of Gialia, Paphos District, northwestern Cyprus.
A passage grave associated with the nuragic complex at Lu Brandali near Santa Teresa Gallura.
Giants' grave of Sa Dom'è s'Orcu (Quartucciu)
A "Giant's tomb" of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries B.C.
The Glinditiones were an ancient people of Illyria.
Known now as the "Dolaucothi Gold Mines" or "Ogofau Gold Mine," this was a major gold mining and ore processing site in the Roman period.
According to the Historic England registry, a Roman signal station/fortlet was identified at Goldsborough. This station was part of a system along the cliffs of north-east Yorkshire.
Kuntalas, an ancient people in Mysore.

A complex in Peshawar, constructed as a caravanserai in the 16th century CE. The site itself seems to go back much earlier (to perhaps the 3rd century CE) and may be mentioned in early travelers' accounts.
Ptolemy locates the Goryaia below the Lambatai and Sovastini.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
The Gothi were an East Germanic people with multiple branches.
Grabbist Hillfort is an Iron Age hillfort located west of Dunster in Somerset, England.
A theater founded ca. 390 B.C. with subsequent Hellenistic and Roman renovations.
Graeco-Roman theater at Marina di Gioiosa Ionica
A second-century B.C. theater that represents a point of architectural transition from the Greek-style theater building to the Roman typology.
The theater at Oinoanda is believed to date from the second century B.C. It sits on the northern fringe of the city.
The Gran Sasso d'Italia is a mountain located in the Abruzzo region of central Italy.

A mausoleum near Cillium dates to the second century CE. Tiberius Flavius Secundus built the family tomb, dedicating it to his father, and inscribing two poetic texts totaling some 110 lines on its facade. Located in what is now Kasserine, Tunisia.
Alexander's famous battle at the Granicus river in 334 BCE may have taken place in the vicinity of modern Güleç, Adliye, and Höyükbayırı Tepe in the Biga district of Turkey's Canakkale province.
The Great Church of Hippo Regius is located in the Christian quarter of Hippo. The church is associated with Saint Augustine, who was bishop in Hippo from 395 until he died in 430 CE.
The so-called Great City Baths at Salona or Great Thermae were built in the second or beginning of third century A.D.
Great Dolmen of Comenda da Igreja
A megalithic dolmen of the fourth to third millennia BC.
The Great Mosque of the Umayyads is located in the old city of Damascus and is one of the largest and oldest mosques in the world. It was completed in 715.
A Roman-style villa in Britain in use from the first to the fifth centuries AD.
Remains of a mud-brick theater with building inscription in Greek were excavated at Babylon. The structure was substantively rebuilt in modern times.
The Greek theater at Alabanda dates to the Hellenistic period.
Remains of a Greek theater at Segesta that was first built in the first half of the third century B.C.
Remains of a Roman villa excavated in Lincolnshire.
Grimes Graves is the site of a Neolithic flint mining complex near Brandon in England that was in use from ca. 3000 to 1900 BC.
The site of a Roman military tilery operated by the Fourth Cohort of the Breuci.
The site of a Roman fort on the river Waal.
A cave near Oliena, Sardinia, where evidence for the earliest human occupation of the island of Sardinia has been recovered.
A cavern discovered in 1931 near Manfredonia with evidence for ritual activity dating to the Neolithic period.

A karstic cave located near Porto Badisco in southern Apulia, Italy, the so-called Grotta dei Cervi was first discovered in 1970. The cave system, although not completely documented, contains a wealth of parietal art and pictograms dating to the late Neolithic and Eneolithic periods, ca. 6000 to 5000 years BP.
The Grotta dell'Uzzo is an important archaeological site in Sicily with traces of human settlement beginning 10,000 years BP.
The so-called "Grotta della Vipera" is the hypogeum tomb of a Roman woman named Atilia Pomptilla. It dates to the first century CE.
Architectural remains near Lago Fusaro that may have been associated with a so-called "villa maritima".
The Pertosa Caves, a system of karst caves located in the comune of Pertosa, province of Salerno, Campania, Italy.
The River Guadalimar is a right-bank tributary of the Guadalquivir.
Today is known as the Guadalmez, the Guadarmes is a river located in the south of the province of Ciudad Real, Spain.
Archaelolgical site in Azerbaijan containing the remains of an Achaemenid palatial structure. The primary occupation of the site is dated from ca. 600 BCE-330 CE.

The Gymnasium of the Roman period at Corinth was excavated by the University of Texas and the American School of Classical Studies beginning in 1965. It is possible that Hellenistic and Classical phases preceded the Roman phase, although evidence is scanty.
An epigraphically attested promontory on the Aegean island of Tenos. Its modern identification is unknown.
Göd-Bócsaújtelep is an unfinished late Roman fort from the reign of Valentinian along the Limes Sarmatiae.

Göllü Dağ is an extinct volcano with a lava dome that contains rhyolite, dacite, and basalt. The formation dates to 1.33 to 0.84 million years. Obsidian at the site was exploited by humans beginning in the Lower Paleolithic period, approximately 800,000 years ago.
A place from the TAVO Index
A sanctuary dedicated to Mithras located near modern Heilbronn, Germany, in use during the second-third centuries CE.

The largest stream of the southern Negev, the HaBesor Stream (Hebrew: נחל הבשור‎, Nahal HaBesor) is a wadi that flows from Mount Boker into the Mediterranean Sea near Al-Zahra in the Gaza Strip, where it is known as the Wadi Ghazzeh.

Kocapınar (known as Hagi/Aği until officially renamed in 1959) is a modern town in the administrative district of Erciş in the Van Province in eastern Turkey. Here a stela with an inscription of Argišti II., son of Rusa (8th / 7th century BCE) was found which reports the creation of an artificial lake in front of Mount Quria.
A church to Saint Sophia dating originally from the third century A.D.
An unlocated well in the middle Euphrates region, near the city Ḫindānu.
A swampy plain that was located to the north of the main harbour of the Piraeus.

Hamam is a modern Turkish village near Erzurum in the Northeast of Turkey. Here an inscription of the Urartian king Argišti I, son of Minua (eighth century BCE), was found which reports the filling of a grain silo.
At Hambleden the ruins of a Roman villa just north of the river Thames were excavated in 1912.
Harlow is the site of a pre-Roman and Roman sanctuary.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.

A karstic cave located in northeastern Libya that is a significant site for modern human prehistory. The cave was occupied during the Middle and Upper Paleolithic, the Mesolithic and the Neolithic periods. Evidence for modern human presence in the cave dates back to 200,000 BP.
Haut Bécherel is the site of a major Gallo-Roman sanctuary sacred to Mars.
The heavily reconstructed remains of the Hellenistic theater at Dion. Parts of the ancient underground stage system are preserved.
Henchir el-Hadjar is the site of a Late Roman fortlet of Africa Proconsularis.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Ras Carcura.
The "Herculaneum Gate" was a city gate of Pompeii located at the northern terminus of the Via Consolare. The gate originally incorporated three passageways.
An islet in the Gulf of Naples.
BAtlas 26 B3 Herdade do Monte do Outeiro
A sanctuary located north of Syracuse.
A mountain of Crete mentioned in ancient sources, probably Mt. Drapanokephala.
Modern Flini island (Greece), south of Anaphe.
Histria (modern Istria) is the name given to a peninsula at the head of the Adriatic Sea between the Gulf of Trieste and the Bay of Kvarner.
A Romano-Celtic temple site dating between the second and fourth centuries AD.
One of the Seven Gates that surrounds the city of Thebes according to ancient sources. If it was indeed historical, no archaeological evidence for it has yet been found.
Early Bronze Age mound located near the town of Erbaa in Northern Anatolia.
A set of warehouses in Regio VIII.
A warehouse complex on the Palatine slope adjacent to the Sacra Via.
The gardens of Sallust in Regio VI of the ancient city of Rome.
Fortified site in Upper Nubia dated to the late Meroitic and post-Meroitic periods (6th-7th centuries CE).
A Hospitium located at the Porta Stabia of Pompeii.
A Roman hospitium located near the Porta Stabia in Pompeii (I, 1, 8).
Remains of a large building and baths uncovered between Bilbury Lane and Lower Borough Walls, beneath what is now known as the Gainsborough Spa in Aquae Sulis, modern-day Bath.
A large private house located in Block D1 of Dura-Europos.
Private house converted later into the barracks of K5.
Private house later adapted for use as synagogue phase 1.
Private house located in Block M7 of Dura-Europos.
Private house later converted for military use as X7 Barracks.
Roman villa and caupona in Pompeii.
Roman villa at Nea Paphos on Cyprus containing extensive mosaic floors.
Residence named for a mosaic floor with an emblem showing Hylas carried off by the nymphs. The mosaic has been removed to the Archaeological Museum in Sevilla.
House of Leda and the Swan
The so-called House of Leda and the Swan at Pompeii (Regio V 6,12) is located along the street referred to as Via del Vesuvio. The domus is well-appointed with Fourth Style wall paintings.

A house located southwest of the Agora in Athens, which was built ca. 475-450 BC and demolished ca. 275 BC. It was used by marble workers, including the sculptors Mikion and Menon. The courtyard contained two cisterns, known as the Demeter Cistern and Menon's Cistern.
The House of Paquius Proculus at Pompeii, also known as the House of C. Cuspius Pansa, is a domus which was excavated in 1911 and then from 1923 to 1926.
The House of Aulus Trebius Valens (III,2,1) is an atrium-style house in Pompeii that lies on the north side of Via dell'Abbondanza. It was first excavated in 1913.
The so-called House of Venus numbered among the most opulent houses of Volubilis. It possesses a private bath and a richly decorated interior.
House of the Cryptoporticus at Vulci

A well-appointed Roman domus with a large, well-preserved cryptoporticus. The earliest phase belongs to the late second and early first century B.C. with subsequent modifications during the early Imperial period.
House of the Deep Trench at Italica
House inside the city wall, located on a street that leads directly onto the east end of the Traianeum, the great temple erected in honor of the emperor Trajan.
A Roman domus that once belonged to Cn. Poppaeus Habitus (VI 16,7).
House of the Rhodian Peristyle at Italica
Roman house at Italica, also known as the House of the Rhodian Patio. Constructed on a slope, the house has a multileveled patio, with sections of different heights connected by stairs.
House of the Scattered Branches and Flowers

According to Leveau (1982), this is a vast domus identified in 1963-1964, located on the Berbache property to the south-east of the coastal plain. The structure measured at least 30 by 60 meters but excavations were not carried to completion.

According to Leveau (1982), the so-called "House of the Two Pools" is located to the south of the Rivet barracks. This was a large peristyle-type domus that included two nymphaea. The latter were published by Cumont and Stern.
The so-called House of the Wooden Shrine may have been owned by one Lucius Autronius Euthymius. Its remains include a notable wooden shrine.
Temple of Mithras at Roman fort of Housesteads (Vercovicium)
A Roman corridor villa with both bath facilities and mosaics. Excavated in 1911 and 1993 and dated to ca. A.D. 150 to the 5th century.
A Trajanic fort located at Hawara (modern Humayma in southern Jordan).
An Iron Age and early Roman farmstead located near Orton Longueville, Cambridgeshire. Salvage excavations were conducted in 1974 prior to highway construction that destroyed the site.
Husn Niha is the site of four Roman temples that were constructed between the first and third centuries AD.
Findspot of two Roman distance slabs along the line of the Antonine Wall: RIB 2198 (found in 1865) and 3507 (found in 1969).
A river in Carmania mentioned by both Pliny and Strabo.
BAtlas 80 C3 Hydreuma to epi tou Paneiou
An island of the Aegean Sea between the Saronic and Argolic gulfs.
Located on a secondary peak of Mt. Hymettos are the remains of a circular tower, 8.3 m in diameter, and preserved to a height of 1.7 m.
A late eighth to early seventh century B.C. hypogeum tomb on the main plateau of ancient Caere.
A sixth century B.C. sanctuary located on the island of Naxos.
The church and convent "I Cappuccini" in Frascati was the site of a Roman villa.
Iabakchos fl. (Zarqa River (Arabic: نهر الزرقاء‎, Hebrew: נחל יבוק, Yabok river)) is the second largest tributary of the Jordan River.
The remains of a Roman arch may mark the boundary between the Roman provinces of Hispania Baetica and Hispania Tarraconensis.
Asin Körfezi, a bay in the southern part of the Güllük Gulf.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
Iberia was an ancient region of southern Caucasia.

The Iberian Peninsula, the westernmost portion of the continent of Europe, bounded in the northeast by the Pyrenees Mountains, in the east and south by the Mediterranean Sea, the west by the Atlantic Ocean, and the north by the Bay of Biscay.
Icknield Street was a road of Roman Britain running from Fosse Way to Templeborough.
A place from the TAVO Index
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: mountains near Auzia.
Area in the Altai region of extreme western Mongolia containing a number of burials and other structures dated from the Bronze Age and the Turkic Period.
The Ilercaones were an ancient people of Hispania Tarraconensis.
An early Christian basilica on the Ilissos River in Athens that may date to the fifth century.
A Roman fort, most likely called Verbeia, at modern-day Ilkley in the U.K.
The island known as "La Maddalena" is grouped in an archipelago of the same name.
The city wall of Nippur according to the so-called "Kuyunjik Ziqqurrat List" (7th century B.C.). Its Akkadian ceremonial name means "The God Marduk Showed Favor."
An ancient road station recorded on the Peutinger Map. It is probably to be identified with the modern Passo del Bracco.
A river located near Argos in modern Greece.
The Incastro is a river of Latium that drains the waters originating from the Lago di Nemi. Its ancient name is unknown.
The delta of the Indus river.
Extensive archaeological evidence of the fish processing industry is evident at Sexi/Saxetanum.
An ancient people, localized in Liguria (BAtlas 16 F1 Ingauni)
The Intemelii were a tribe of Liguria.
Site of a small Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
The site of a Roman fort occupied during the Antonine period near present-day Musselburgh in East Lothian.
A rock-cut relief depicting the investiture of Ardashir I, ca. A.D. 226-242. This relief is the earliest Sasanian monument at Naqš-e Rustam.
An Ionic stoa with four dining rooms on the south slope of the Acropolis of Athens, built ca. 420 BC. It may have been part of the Asklepieion complex.
An ancient island off the northwest coast of Crete, probably to be associated with the Tigani peninsula.
A sanctuary sacred to Jupiter located on the western slopes of Tifata Mons (Monte Tifata).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Pelion, near Cape Puri.
A nuragic complex located near Monte Nai, Sardinia.
A menhir located near the Is Calas nuragic complex near Monte Nai, Sardinia.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Yazd IRN.
The modern Usk river in the UK, draining into the Bristol Channel.
A church and monastery in Tao-Klarjeti, first constructed in the 7th century.

The ruined tower of Isola Conversina, also known as Torre della Stroppa, is located on a tuff ridge with steep margins that has likely been inhabited since the Bronze Age. This hill is located along the line of the Via Amerina. The present ruined castle dates to the Medieval period.
The Isole della Marmorata off the coast of Sardinia provided the grey granite (also known as granito della Sardegna) that was exported to Rome during the Imperial period.
The Issedones were an ancient people of central Asia.
The modern Aegean island of Giali.
One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Liguria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.
One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Etruria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.
One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Aemilia. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.
One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Venetia and Histria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.
Unlabeled on the Barrington Atlas, this dam is popularly known as the "Devil's Bridge."
The sacred 'Grove of Iuno Curritis' located in Falerii Veteres.
Iunonis Pr. is a headland in the Province of Cádiz in southwestern Spain.
The Jura Mountains, a sub-alpine mountain range located to the north of the western Alps, separate the Rhine and Rhone rivers.
The Bridge of Justinian or Sangarius Bridge is a Late Roman bridge built by the emperor Justinian I across the Sangarius river. The bridge's original span was ca. 430 m.
An ancient river of Italy, identified by modern scholars with the Giovenco River.
BAtlas 92 D4 Ivan-i Karkheh/Eran-Khurra-(kard-) Shapur?/Karkha de Ladan
The modern Oued Ksob of western Morocco.
Unexcavated military barracks south of House J1-A in Block J1 at Dura-Europos.
Military barracks in the southern part of Block J6 at Dura-Europos.
Military barracks reworked from private houses in Block J7 at Dura-Europos.
An island of the Socotra archipelago.
Jazīrat Sāy, an island in the Nile River located in Sudan.
Jebel Moneijah was the site of a Nabatean sanctuary in the Southern Sinai.

Jebel Moya is an archaeological site located in the southern part of the Gezira Plain in Sudan. The 25-acre site was the locus of the largest-known pastoralist necropolis in Africa, with more than 3,000 burials dating between 5000 BCE and 500 CE. Sir Henry Wellcome first excavated the site from 1911 to 1914.
At Jebel Oust [Jbel al Wost] (Tunisia) are the remains of a large Roman bathing complex with a number of built cisterns.
Jebel Shams (Arabic: جبل شمس‎, (mountain of sun) rises to 2,818 m (9,245 ft) asl and is the highest summit of the Al Hajar Mountains in Oman.
Jebel Shaqadud (Sudan) is an archaeological site located 115 km northeast of Khartoum. It preserves at least 7 meters of in situ stratified deposits that date from ca. 8,200 to 4,000 cal BP.
The Jerash Hippodrome dates after the middle of the second century. While among the smallest of the attested examples of Roman period hippodromes, it numbers among the best preserved.

The Assyrian king Sennacherib had an aqueduct constructed between 703 and 690 B.C. near the ancient city of Girmua. The structure is part of the "Khinnis [Canal] System." The identification of the structure's builder is confirmed by means of several inscriptions.
A sanctuary near Thebes where the mystery cult of the god Kabeiros and his son, Pais, was celebrated.
Kadousioi, an Iranian tribe settled between the Caspian and the Black seas.

The Kaiadas cave is located near modern Trypi in the Peloponnese. Ancient testimony identifies it as a place of execution used by the ancient Spartans. Exploration in the modern era identified a significant number of skeletal remains, but these have not been effectively dated.
A Hellenistic fort located on the Kainys promontory (modern Punta del Pezzo) in southern Italy.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: N Scotland.
Kalaiou Nesoi, a group of nine islands in the Gulf of Oman.
The site of a Roman fort in the eastern desert of Egypt.
A small Aegean island located between Kalymnos and Pserimos (modern Plati).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A Middle Helladic to Late Helladic settlement located near Kalloni, Troizenia, Attiki, the Kalloni site was excavated in 2005.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Lake Prespa GRE.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Kavalla.
An ancient people of S Panjab. Skt.: Kapiṣṭhala.
A Roman fort on the island of Lesbos.
A rock-cut tomb dated to the second century BCE.
A Roman-era bridge spanning the Arabkir Çay south of Hastek Kale in Turkey. Now submerged and inaccessible.
A coastal promontory located northwest of Doğanyurt, Turkey. Modern Kerembe burnu.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Irgoli area?.
An ancient people located on Gulf of Mannar.
An Iron Age tribe of Britain describe by Ptolemy.
A Doric-order temple, hexastyle in antis (23.20x11.10 m). The building utilizes stone from both Aegina and Paros.
Byzantine castle on the northeastern coast of Corfu overseeing the village of Kassiopi. May have been built over roman ruins.
One of the two known Genovese fortresses on Andros.

Kasımoğlu (Ghusnents) is a modern settlement situated 30 km north of Van in the southeast of Turkey. Here a stela with a military account of the Urartian kings Išpuini and Minua (9th / 8th century BCE) was found (CTU A 3-5).
The oldest surviving church structure within the boundaries of modern Yerevan, constructed in the late 6th century CE.
An ancient people located along the Parthenios (modern Bartın Irmaği/Bartin Su in Turkey).

Kavuncu is a modern settlement situated near Van in the southeast of Turkey. Here a cylindrical stone (probably a column base) with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua, son of Išpuini (9/8th century BCE) was found (CTU I A 5-53 B).

The small village of Babil (now Kebili) is located about 25 km southwest of Cizre, near the Tigris river, directly on the Turkish-Syrian border. The name of the ancient site whose ruins lay beneath the modern village is not known.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Gublan YEM.
An ancient fortification system at the multiperiod Glauberg site in Germany.
A Roman segmental arch bridge over the Xanthos fl. near the ancient city of Xanthos in Lycia.

A tertiary hill (154 m high) dominating the surrounding flatland in Belgium's West Flanders province close to the French border. Archaeological remains ranging from the Middle Paleolithic to the 5th century BC. Also the site of heavy fighting during World War I.
One of the islands of the Cyclades.
A dolmen that is still covered by its original cairn, the Kercado tumulus was built ca. 4600 B.C. and remained in use for approximately 3,000 years.
A complex comprised of 1029 megaliths arranged in 10 rows.
A Roman villa which emerged from a late Iron Age settlement located in the London Borough of Bromley, England.
A circular Roman mausoleum was located at the Keston Roman villa. It dates to the third century CE and is located in a cemetery to the north of the villa.

The Khalij was a canal in Cairo. It was created during the Arab conquest in the seventh century CE, when a Pharaonic, Hellenistic, and Roman canal was rebuilt in order to once again link the Nile River to the Red Sea. It remained in use until the eighth century.
BAtlas 29 G1 Kherba Oum el Adame
BAtlas 30 B4 Kherba Sidi el Ahmar

The early Byzantine monastery located at Khirbet ed-Deir in the Judean desert was excavated from 1981-1987 by Yizhar Hirschfeld. The remote site yielded important evidence about monastic life from the fourth to seventh centuries CE.

An archaeological site located in the middle Jordan Valley in the West Bank that includes the largest known of the complex oval compound type habitation sites connected with the Israelite Settlement period.
Located some 70 km from Petra, Khirbet et-Tannur is the site of a well-preserved, open-air Nabataean sanctuary.

A partially-excavated complex near modern Qum in Iran. The site was possibly a sanctuary and likely dates to the Seleucid age. There is some evidence that the site continued in use into the Parthian period.

A state once located in the southern part of the continent of Africa, near the confluence of the Shashe and Limpopo Rivers, south of Great Zimbabwe. The Kingdom of Mapungubwe collapsed in the fourteenth century.
The site of a Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall. The fortlet measures ca. 21.5 x 18.5 m, covering an area of ca. 0.04 ha.
Kinvaston Fort, a Roman vexillation fort located near the point where the Watling Street crossed the River Penk. The fort was discovered via air photos in 1946.
A Roman fort at Bowness on Solway on the Stanegate.
Roman fort on the Antonine Wall, in East Dunbartonshire, Scotland
A Roman fortlet in Scotland discovered from the air by the RCAHMS in 1989.
A modern village near the Pazarcik dam in Turkey. The Pazarcik Stele, which bears inscriptions of the Assyrian kings Adad-nerari III and Shalmaneser IV, was discovered here.
A place from the TAVO Index
A river of the Peloponnese and tributary of the Alpheios, which it joins from the north at the ancient site of Olympia in Greece.
An archaeological site located on a coastal hill near Samikon, Kleidi presents evidence for both prehistoric settlement and a cemetery.
A megalithic complex located between Macroom and Millstreet, in County Cork, Ireland, and thought to have been constructed ca. 3,500 years ago.
A cluster of Neolithic and Bronze Age earthworks with a twelfth-century Norman church built in the center.
Settlement on the right bank of the Don River inhabited from the Roman period and associated with the Maeotians.
Nisída Koínyra, an island in East Macedonia and Thrace, Greece.
Modern Agioi Theodoroi, a pair of islands off the northwest coast of Crete.
A deme of ancient Athens, probably located at Varnava Tower in northeastern Attica.
A modern settlement in Sri Lanka catalogued as the findspot of 220 Roman coins dating between the reigns of Constantine I and Honorius.
The modern Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin), southernmost tip of the Indian subcontinent.
Komedai, an ethnonym recorded by Ptolemy.
A Mycenaean Tholos Tomb dating to the middle of the second millennium BCE located to the north of Koronida/Komiaki on the island of Naxos in the Aegean Sea.
Kophos Limen, (the "Still Harbor"), was a Classical period harbor located at Halai in the Piraeus, Attica.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A peninsula on the east coast of Attica.
The Aegean archipelago lying between Ikaros and Samos, known today as the Fourni Korseon. Its two main islands are known today as Thymena (to the west) and Fourni (to the east).
The westernmost of the two pairs of peninsulae of northwestern Crete (with the other being the Rodopos Peninsula).
Circular, stone, pit-like structures built into the ground at the edge of the West Court of the Minoan palace at Phaistos.
The ruined city of Koumbi Saleh in south-east Mauritania may have been the capital of the Ghana Empire.
Kouriannon? Akroterion is a headland or spit that separates that Atlantic Ocean from Arcachon Bay.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: W Scotland.

A small river of the northern Peloponnese, draining into the Corinthian Gulf between Aigeira (modern Vitrinitsa) and Aristonautai (modern Xylokastro). The modern Fonissa in the Greek municipality of Xylokastro.
Fortified Berber granary (ksar). The surviving structure dates to the 14th century CE, but the site may have been in use as early as the Roman era.
A peak of the Ararat massif, known as Little Ararat.
A large Gallo-Roman villa located north of Béziers on the banks of the Libron river.
A Roman tomb at Centuripe known as "La Dogana".
A Neolithic ritual site that includes a passage grave dating ca. 4000-3500 BCE.
An early Christian necropolis with tombs dating to the fourth through sixth centuries CE in the Italian comune of Vieste.
The modern city of La Spezia, Italy, is located what was in antiquity the territory of the city of Luni. The area of La Spezia has been surveyed by archaeologists.
BAtlas 26 D3 La Torre de Miguel Sesmero
A Medieval watch tower (thirteenth to fourteenth centuries) that is part of a system that appears to follow the line of the ancient Via Amerina.
The Labotas was a river of the plain of Antioch and a tributary of the Orontes.
Lacetani, a pre-Roman people of the Iberian peninsula.
A mountain ridge of Campania that is a spur branching off the Apennines. Many Roman villas in this vicinity were destroyed (and thus, preserved) by the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius.
Formerly an island northwest of Miletus.
Ladle Hill is an Iron Age hill fort located in north Hampshire, England.

A 70-km long river in the Peloponnese that is a tributary to the river Alfeios. The Ladon flows from its sources on the western slope of the Aroania mountain and joins the Alfeios some 3 km southeast of the village of Tripotamia.
The Leitha river is a right tributary of the Danube.

The Lago di Biéntina was once the largest lake in Italy's Tuscany region. While it was finally drained in 1859 and converted to arable land, the extent to which it was a standing body of water in antiquity remains debated.
An ancient caldera lake near Gabii (ancient name unknown) that has been drained and filled in modern times.
A villa of the emperor Domitian located in the area of Circeii.
A confederation of Libyan peoples, cited: BAtlas 35 F3 Laguatan
A Roman road station located along the ancient route leading from Berenike to Edfu (the ancient Apollinopolis Magna).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: upper Struma valley BUL.
Lake Bafa (Bafa Gölü) in Ionia formed as a result of the silting of the Latmian Gulf.
Lake Tana is the source of the Blue Nile and the largest lake in Ethiopia.
A Gallo-Roman villa that is expanded upon the second and third centuries A.D.
The Amato River (ancient Lametus) is a river in Calabria that rises in the Sila Piccola and flows into the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia, flowing along a course of some 56 km.
Lamnae/Ad Lam(i)nas, a road station located 33 miles from Rome and 13 miles from Tibur.
A Medieval castle that was established in the eleventh century on the site of a Roman fort that overlooked a crossing of the River Lune.

Multiple phases of a Romano-British villa were excavated at Langton, East Riding, Yorkshire, England. The site was discovered in 1899 and excavations took place in 1926 and 1930-31. The original phase of the site might have been either a military outpost or an indigenous farmstead.
The modern Punta dos Aguillóns, which is the eastern component of Cabo Ortegal, a cape on the Atlantic coast of modern Spain.
Two distinct Roman forts; the smaller covering ca. 1.9 ha and the larger up to 8 ha.
A large rock-cut temple at Sikait in Egypt's Eastern desert.
A Roman tomb of the second or third century CE.
The Venetian Castle of Argos, which incorporated and replaced a series of fortifications dating back to the classical period (with Mycenaean antecedents).

A rectangular structure in the Athenian Agora, consisting of 11 rooms surrounding a central courtyard, built in the early 5th century AD in connection with the Palace of the Giants. It appears to have been an administrative building.
A round building constructed in the northwestern corner of the Athenian Agora in the 5th century AD over the Crossroads Enclosure. It was ruined in the late 5th or 6th century AD.
According to Strabo, the Lathon/Leton fl. flows into the lake of the Hesperides.

The Latin League is the name given by scholars to a confederation of about 30 tribes and villages located in ancient Latium that was created for mutual defense purposes and existed from the seventh century BCE until 338 BCE. Its ancient name is unknown.
A late fifth century AD church, later associated with a small monastery in Thessaloniki, Greece.
Ancient thermal baths in use from the Etrusco-Roman period onward.
Le Carrozze-Gravetta, the site of a Daunian sanctuary of the fourth century BCE.
BAtlas 14 D2 Le Moulin des Vignes
A villa rustica at Tortoreto, in the province of Teramo, with occupation beginning in the Late Republican period.
BAtlas 17 H4 Le Plan de Phazy
A Roman villa located on via Lemonia in Rome's suburbium attributed to Quintus Servilius Pudens.

Rescue excavations in 1980 documented the remains of an unusual funerary structure dated ca. 1000 to 950 BCE that contained a double human burial alongside a horse burial. The structure's scale (50 by 13.8 m) and nature have led some scholars to identify it as a heroon.
The River Rother located in East Sussex and Kent, United Kingdom.
Lemannonios Kolpos, a sea-loch located in Argyll and Bute, Scotland, United Kingdom.
A modern Sicilian town in the province of Enna, thought to be located in the area of the ancient settlement of Assorus.
A center of mining and ore processing.
Leuka M., a mountain range of Western Crete, located in the Chania prefecture.
A site located along the Roman frontier (limes) in Germania Inferior.
A necropolis with four dolmens surrounded by small kerbstone circles.
Libicii, an ancient tribe of Cisalpine Gaul.

The Libraries' Courtyard belongs to the republican period and is one of the most ancient gardens at Hadrian's Villa. It is enclosed in a large peristyle 48 m wide, 72 m long, and is located at the northern end of Villa Adriana.
An ancient people of North Africa who, according to Ptolemy, lived in the north of Marmarica.
Mountains that border the Nile river valley to the west.
The Licca river (modern Lech) is a right tributary of the Danube.
An island group off North Euboea, Greece. Near the Malian Gulf.
The site of a 29-room Romano-British villa located in present-day Gloucestershire.
An Ottoman-era fortification located on a headland in Taşucu bay (modern Mersin province, Turkey)
A well-preserved Classical-period blockhouse, located northeast of Fichti in the Argolid.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: W Azov UKR.
The so-called "Lion gate" of Butrint is a fifth century A.D. gateway that reuses an Archaic Greek sculpted relief.
former Greek Eastern Orthodox church in Istanbul converted to a mosque

The Little Metropolis church or Panagia Gorgoepikoos is a Frankish, Late Byzantine, or Ottoman-period domed cross-in-square church in central Athens. It is decorated with spolia from earlier structures.
The site of two monopteral nuraghi.
Località De Santis I at Pontecagnano
Necropolis in Pontecagnano containing fifty burials from the Orientalizing Period (725-550 BCE) and an additional six burials from the Lucanian period (4th-3rd centuries BCE).
A standing megalith located near the mouth on the Solway Firth and dating ca. 3000 B.C.
At Locmariaquer, Brittany, are the remains of a complex of Neolithic structures.
A Benedictine abbey that is located 7 km south of Poitiers and was founded by Martin from 361 to 371.

A civic basilica in ancient Londonium, the remains of which the Museum of London archaeology service (MOLA) has documented at a site located at 85 Gracechurch Street, London. The site is dated ca. 70 CE.

London's original Roman wall in stone was built ca. A.D. 190 to 225. The wall originally had a length of ca. 4 km (2.5 miles and enclosed an area of ca. 134 hectares. It once included four city gates.
Fortified structure near the modern village of Lori Berd (Armenia) constructed in 1065 CE.
An ancient town on the Via Aurelia.

Located in the territory of Parentium (Poreč, Croatia), Loron was one of the largest Dressel 6B amphorae workshops in Adriatic (1st-4th centuries CE). It belonged to important senators like Sisenna Statilius Taurus and Calvia Crispinilla before its integration in the imperial property from the reign of Domitian (81 CE).
BAtlas 26 D4 Los Castillejos de la Sierra

A Roman villa about 200 meters south of the center of the modern village of Santervas del Burgo and about 100 meters south of the left bank of the river Cejos. Included in the Barrington Atlas (25 B4 no. 129) under the toponym "Los Villares (Fuentearmegil)".
Loudoun Hill was the site of a Flavian Auxiliary Fort (ca. A.D. 69–96) that had four occupational phases.

Loughcrew (County Meath, Ireland) is the site of a funereal landscape of the fourth millennium BCE that includes more than twenty megalithic tombs spread across four hilltop areas: Carnbane East, Carnbane West, Carrickbrack, and Patrickstown Hill.
Loutra Hypatis Early Christian basilica and bath
An excavated Early Christian site at Varka hamlet south of Loutra Ipatis, Phthiotida.
At Low Borrowbridge, northeast of Kendal, are remains of a Roman auxiliary fort that was in use from the time of the Flavians until the fifth century A.D.
A fourth-century A.D. Roman courtyard villa (ca. 340) known particularly for its mosaics, including a famous pavement featuring Aeneas and Dido from the frigidarium of the villa's bath complex.
The lower agora of the ancient city of Agrigentum contains shops, a sacred area, and the gymnasium complex.
District in Hattusa located northwest of Büyükkale, enclosed by the oldest wall of the city, the Poternenmauer, and including the structure known in modern times as Temple I.
A modern settlement in Poland where ancient graves have been found.

A Roman bridge over the the modern Pancrudo river south of Luco de Jiloca in Teruel province, Aragon, Spain. The bridge crosses the river just below the modern Lechago dam, less than 100m before the Pancrudo's confluence with the Jiloca.
Now unlocated, Lucos was a statio located on the Via Herculia near Potentia in south Italy.
Plutarch describes a villa owned by Lucullus near Tusculum.
A grove sacred to Stimula, located at the southwestern foot of the Aventine Hill.
The Lukmanier Pass or Passo del Lucomagno is a mountain pass in the Swiss Alps (elevation 1915 meters above sea level).
A turf and timber Roman fort near Coventry, England. The site's ancient name remains unknown.
The Roman Bridge of Lurs is located to the northeast of Alaunium (modern Lurs, France). It was a bridge of the ancient Via Domitia.
An ancient Egyptian temple that was initially built ca. 1400 BCE.
A fourth century AD temple dedicated to Nodens.
An ancient river placed by Ptolemy on the northern side of the Sea of Azov. It is probably to be identified with the modern Kal'mius river.
A Roman auxiliary fort in Scotland guarding the road from Trimontium to Castledykes.
BAtlas 66 A1 Lystra/Col. Iulia Felix Gemina
Site of a rural sanctuary dedicated to Aristaeus, son of Apollo.
A place located in the eastern part of Cilicia on the river Cydnus.
The Macedonian palace at Pella, now only partially excavated, occupied an area of perhaps 60,000 square meters. The palace consisted of up to seven large architectural groupings.
The Macellum of Hippo Regius originates in the early imperial period and is then renovated in Late Antiquity.
A small tribe on the coast of the Syrtis Minor
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Babors.
A Shiva temple at Banavasi in India whose foundation may date as early as the 7th century CE.
A necropolis of the early Dilmun culture, dating to the second millennium B.C.
Madinat Hamad 3 Burial Mound Field (Dar Kulayb)
A necropolis of the early Dilmun culture, dating to the second millennium B.C.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Skt.: Mādhyandini.
Maen Castle is an Iron Age promontory fort near Land's End in Cornwall.
Maes Howe is a Neolithic chambered cairn and passage grave on Mainland, Orkney, Scotland.
Maesbury Castle is a small ring hillfort in the Mendip Hills in Somerset, England.
BAtlas 93 D3 Maghlub/Forat?/Perat de Meshan?/Bahman Ardashir?/‘Oratha’?/Furat al-Basra?
Renovated during the early Roman imperial period, this theater at Magnesia on the Maeander was located close to the city's agora.
One of two theaters found at Magnesia on the Maeander, this so-called "theatron" was built in the late Hellenistic or early Imperial period and was destroyed by a landslide in antiquity.
A plain, mentioned by several ancient authors, that lies to the southeast of Bulla Regia (modern Hammam-Darradji in Tunisia), across the Bagradas (modern Medjerda) river.

Mahmudabad is a modern settlement in the West Azerbaijan Region in the Northeast of Iran. Here a stone slab with an inscription of the Urartian king Rusa I. (8th century BCE) was found which lists offerings for undertaking a royal campaign.
An ancient island along the coast of Syrtica, identified by modern scholars with the Legarah reef (Gharah island / Al-Hebri).
A twelfth-century monument in the Old City, Baku, Azerbaijan.
The Maisaimaneis were an ancient people of northwestern Arabia.
A large, centrally located Roman townhouse in Augustoritum (modern Limoges), built in the first century CE and decorated with elaborate wall paintings.
A Libyan People, cited: BAtlas 37 E2 Makatoutai
Scant remains of a tower of the Classical and Hellenistic periods located at Makri Louri (Kaminaros), island of Siphnos.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Madhhig SAU.
A Mycenaean tholos tomb located to the north of Margarites, Rethymno, Crete.
Maliacus Sinus (Malian Gulf) is a gulf of the Aegean Sea in eastern central Greece. The gulf is located in the region of Phthiotis.
An ancient Indian people that settled at the confluence of the rivers Hydaspes, Acesines, and Hydraotes.
Malling is the site of a Roman fort first re-discovered in 1968 to the west of the Lake of Menteith.
Sometimes associated with the Montgrí massif in Girona or a part thereof. The ancient name is known only from Avienus and is otherwise unattested.

An archaeological site with Iron Age funerary megaliths located in the vicinity of the modern Moonamkutty-Mangad Road in the northeastern portion of India's Kollam municipality. The site was damaged by cashewnut tree farming and is now not visible due to habitation on the site.

The site of a Roman corridor villa with a separate bathhouse. Three phases dating from the late first century AD into the fourth century. It possibly forms part of a complex with the villa uncovered ca. 250 meters to the south and east.
A peripteral temple built of basalt that includes an altar to Nemesis. Epigraphic data provides a chronology of late second to third centuries A.D.

The beginnings of the early Christian monastery of Saint Elian at Al-Qaryatayn, Syria, are linked with the saint Julian of Emesa. The Medieval iteration of the monastery was badly damaged - or perhaps nearly destroyed - by Islamic State terrorists in 2015.
A complex quarry landscape near Karystos, heavily exploited especially in Roman times, for highly prized Cipollino Verde (marmor Carystium).
An unnamed marble quarry near Simitthus (modern Chemtou, Tunisia). The marble variety is known as marmor numidicum or giallo antico.
The Marcomanni were a German tribe.
The modern Sierra Morena mountain range in Spain.
Marica, an Italic goddess, was worshipped in a sacred grove located between Minturnae and the estuary of the Liris river.
Marmos is a settlement in the Ağrı Province in Eastern Turkey. Here a stele with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua (9th/8th century BCE) was found which reports the construction of a canal.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: W India (name preserved in modern Maruha tribe?).
Mashnaqa, Lebanon, is the site of a monumental altar that dates to the first and second centuries A.D.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Petra.
The site of a Roman imperial-period villa in the modern Italian comune of Massaciuccoli Romana.
The site of a Roman imperial-period villa in the modern Italian comune of Massaciuccoli Romana.

Masseria Muro (comune di Mesagne, province of Brindisi, south Italy) is the findspot of a hoard of ancient coins. In 1976, a deposit of coins originating from a number of Greek cities of south Italy was discovered. The coins range in date from the Archaic to the Hellenistic periods.

The Mastaba of Khentika at Qila ad-Babba near Balat in ad-Dakhla depression, Egypt, dates from the Sixth Dynasty of ancient Egypt. Khentika was a wealthy official and served as the governor of the Dakhla Oasis during the reign of Pharaoh Pepi II, (2284 – ca. 2216 BCE).
Maternum was a settlement of ancient Etruria that is known from the Peutinger Table. It is located along the Via Clodia between Saturnia and Tuscana.
A mountain range that defines the center of Matiene.
A Gallo-Greek oppidum founded at the end of the sixth century BCE.
A circular, domed, apsidal subterranean structure of the Hadrianic period that is referred to as a tomb but may have had a cultic function.
The ruins of a first century B.C. Roman tomb along the Via Appia at Mesa di Pontinia.
A first-century B.C. circular funerary monument at Gaeta.

Quintus Lollius Urbicus served as a governor of Britannia between 139 and 142. His career is detailed on a pair of inscriptions from his hometown of Tiddis. His mausoleum is located a few kilometers north of Tiddis.

A circular mausoleum dating to the time of the Roman Empire is visible today at Tor di Quinto. Elements of this marble funereal monument were uncovered in excavations conducted by a landowner in 1876 along the Via Flaminia, not far from the Porta del Popolo. The marble elements were expropriated by the state and then fell into neglect for more than 20 years. By 1897 the Museo Nazionale Romano had
Mausoleum of the Atilii at Sádaba
The Mausoleum of the Atilii is a Roman mausoleum dating from the second or third centuries A.D. The ruins are located in the municipal territory of Sádaba, Aragon, eastern Spain.
Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

The mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of the Qin dynasty of China, was built between 246 and 208 BCE. The mausoleum itself was outfitted with numerous ancillary features, including the famed "terracotta army" discovered in 1974. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
A Berber tribe of North Africa.
Site of two caves containing finds dated to the Chalcolithic period.
The Mesima river of southern Italy.
The Brenta river flows from near Trentino to the Adriatic Sea.
The modern Bacchiglione river flows through the Veneto. It originates in the Alps and then, following a course of about 90 km, empties into the Brenta river near Chioggia.
Meduana? fl., a river in France, now the Mayenne river.
Megalithic, polygonal masonry walls atop Mount Pugliano are generally interpreted as Samnite fortifications associated with ancient Telesia.

Through a series of survey and rescue excavations, the modern lignite mines just west of modern Megalopolis (and southwest of the ancient site of Megalopolis) in the Peloponnese have produced important evidence for ice age activity, especially at (but not limited to) a Lower Paeleolithic site known as Marathoussa 1.

Pliny the Elder describes the "Megisba Stagnum" as an inland marsh or lake of Sri Lanka that has a circumference of 375 Roman miles. He says that from this wetland once flowed two rivers: one called Palaesimundus and the other called Cydara.
An Eastern Orthodox Christian monastery overlooking the Kidron Valley located between the Old City of Jerusalem and the Dead Sea.
Modern Pachia island, southeast of Thira in the Aegean Sea.

According to an inscription of the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus, the name of the wall of Kish was Melem-kurukurra-dulla, whose Sumerian ceremonial name means "(Whose) Radiance Spreads over (All) Lands."
Etruscan tumulus-type tombs of the seventh through fourth centuries B.C. located near Cortona, Italy, in località Il Mulino.
Mendesios Nomos, the 16th nome of Lower Egypt.
A fortified area of indeterminate chronology located on Mount Merenda in Attica.
An island located in the Blackwater and Colne estuaries to the south-east of Colchester.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: around Shikarpur, Sindh (modern Mazari) PAK.
Modern Gramvousa island off the northwest coast of Crete.

A Roman fort, cited: BAtlas 9 F6 Piercebridge
A Roman bridge that carried Dere Street across the River Tees in northern England.
The Roman legionary fortress at modern day Inchtuthil.
An archaeological site that yielded a rich votive deposit located south of the road leading from Nemea to Leontio, in the foothills of Mt Koukougeras on the south side of the Phliasian plain.
Paşa Dağ, mountain and village above Thebe.
BAtlas 15 C2 Plan de la Tour
A tumulus at Marathon associated with the Boeotian Plataeans. Marinatos identified the mound in 1970. It rises to a height of about 3 meters.
Plinth in D Street Outside The Temple of Artemis Azzanthkona
Probable statue base placed outside the temple of Artemis Azzanathkona at Dura-Europos.

The hill of Poggio Civitella near Montalcino, Italy, rises to a height of 661 meters above sea level. Beginning in 1993, excavation campaigns revealed a series of settlement horizons dating to the first millennium BCE, ranging from the archaic to the Hellenistic periods. The hilltop was fortified during this period.
A Roman villa overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea located within the former territory of Populonia.
Modern town in Sicily, near Cefalù, that has been associated with the ancient settlement of Apollonia.
The polygonal masonry wall of the Roman castrum at Pyrgi encloses an area of ca. 5.7 ha.
A building complex in Regio I of ancient Pompeii that in its final phases was devoted to commercial use that included the production of woven mats.
The Pomptinae Paludes (Pontine Marshes) is an area of former marshland in Latium.
A Roman aqueduct dating to 3 B.C.
A bridge across the Tiber river built either by Caius or Nero in order to connect the western part of the Campus Martius with the Campus Vaticanus.
The Chateau de Fontager (13th century) is the site of the discovery of an ancient necropolis, including Early Christian tombs as well as pre-Christian tombs.
A bridge over the Vidourle and road station on the Via Domitia.
A Roman aqueduct built to supply the city of Tarraco.
A Medieval bridge spanning the Tech river that dates between 1321 and 1341.
A Roman bridge in the modern French commune of Boucieu-le-Roi (Ardèche department).
A Roman segmental arch bridge in the Aosta Valley in Italy that dates to the first century BC. The bridge spans 31.4 m across the Betuctelum to the NNW of Eporedia.
A second-century Roman bridge on the Riu Brabaciera.
A Roman bridge on the Via Cassia.
A Roman segmental arch bridge across the Bacchiglione river in Padua, Italy.
A Roman bridge crossing the river Temo; the bridge is said to have originally had a five-arch span.
The Roman bridge at Ponte Fonnaia carried a branch of the Via Flaminia over the river Naia. It is located north of modern Acquasparta in Umbria.
A stone bridge at Genga, Italy, that is purportedly of Roman origin.
A Medieval bridge across the river Trebia that is said to have Roman origins.
A Roman bridge on the Volturno river located near Capriati.
A bridge of Roman origins crossing the Sabato river on the outskirts of Benevento.

The Roman bridge known as "Ponte Manlio" carried the Via Flaminia across the Bosso torrent, whose main channel is now some hundreds of meters to the south. This is a well-preserved Roman vaulted arch bridge that dates to the second century B.C.
A bridge along the Via Amerina, just south of ancient Nepet (modern Nepi in Italy)
A Roman bridge, perhaps originally dating to the first century BC, was substantially transformed to carry a provincial road in 1872.
A bridge near Ferentinum (modern Ferentino in Italy) that is traditionally dated to A.D. 260 or after. A substructure in polygonal masonry supports the bridge.
BAtlas 45 C4 unnamed bridge (Ponte Silla, over R. Tanagro, SE Tegianum)
A rock-cut tunnel (cuniculus) at the northwest margin of ancient Veii.
The so-called Ponte Spiano is a Roman bridge located along the Via Flaminia in the modern comune of Sigillo.
A bridge of Roman origins located near Montesarchio.
A bridge that crosses the Tronto River at Ascoli Piceno that dates from the later eleventh century.
A Iulio-Claudian bridge located in Ariminum.
A bridge in the territory of Blera known as the "Devil's Bridge".
A Roman bridge across the Torrente Gran Caso located south of Ascoli Piceno.

The bridge known as the Ponte del Viceré de Ribera crosses the Fosso di Sant'Andrea on the line of the Via Appia. The viceroy of Naples, one Parefàn de Ribera, renovated the bridge in 1568. During the Second World War, the bridge was bombed and was eventually restored in 2005.

A bridge over the Metauro River built initially in the thirteenth century. The original bridge was destroyed in 1765 and rebuilt in 1782. The bridge was again destroyed in 1944 and was rebuilt in 1946.
Ponte della Mola di San Gregorio da Sassola
A Roman aqueduct bridge that was part of the Aqua Anio Vetus. The remains of the bridge preserve a series of 22 arches stretching approximately 155 meters.
A Campanian sanctuary located in the territory of Cales in Campania.
An arched Roman bridge across the Titerno near Cerreto Sannita in Campania.
A Roman bridge known by a variety of local toponyms that crosses the Savuto river. It is located in the modern Italian municipality of Altilia, Calabria.
A Roman-period bridge along the via Praenestina built of lapis Gabinus.
The Ponte di San Francesco or Bridge of Saint Francis is a single-span medieval segmental arch bridge that crosses the River Aniene in Subiaco, Lazio, Italy. It was built in 1358.
An early segmental arch bridge, built between 47 and 30 B.C.
The Ponte sul Fosso di Biserano is a Roman aqueduct bridge of the Aqua Anio Vetus.
Pontecorvo is a comune located in the province of Frosinone, Lazio, Italy.
One of two castra defending the Trajanic bridge across the Danube.
An island between Lesbos and Asia Minor, attested in multiple ancient sources and site of the homonymous city. The island has been identified with the modern Cunda Adası, Turkey.
The Mius River flows into the Sea of Azov.
Porphyrites M. was the site of important quarries that supplied the Roman empire with porphyry.
Port-sur-Saône may be the ancient “Portus Abucinus” included in the Notitia Galliarum. This may have been the location of the martyrdom of Saint Valerius.
A gate in Rome's Servian Wall located on the Quirinal Hill.
A city gate of the first century B.C.
The main gate, defended by a bastion, of the Middle Republican fortifications of the city. The gate still stands to a height of ca. 13 m.
The so-called Porta Marina of Paestum is a gate in the Hellenistic fortifications and is located along a main street axis leading to the port of the city.

The Porta Mugonia was one of the three gates of the original Palatine city of Rome (often referred to as "Roma quadrata"). Its precise location can no longer be established and it remains a hotly debated issue for topographers.
A city gate of Pompeii located at the southern terminus of Strada di Porta Nocera.
A city gate located at the eastern terminus of the Strada di Nola. In antiquity, the gate was known as Porta Urbulana.
A surviving turreted gateway of the Roman circuit wall of Augusta Taurinorum.
The Porta Pinciana is a gate passing through Rome's Aurelianic wall and was added during the principate of Honorius in the fifth century.
A gateway in the polygonal masonry circuit wall of Segni.
The Porta Settimiana is a gate in Rome's Aurelianic walls.
The Porta Solestà is one of the gates of Ascoli Piceno.
The so-called "Porta Vesuvio" was damaged in the earthquake of A.D. 62.
The Porte de Mars is a Roman triumphal arch in Reims, France, that dates from the third century A.D.

Portus ‘Adurni’? was likely a third-century A.D. Roman fort (now Portchester) mentioned by name only in the Notitia Dignitatum. The Roman fort was converted to a Saxon castle and is thus well preserved.
Poseidon?, T. a sanctuary of Poseidon on the island of Samos.
Post-Archaic necropolis at Poggio dei Cavallari
A necropolis located along a road that once led to the Mater Matuta sanctuary composed of approximately 50 tombs.
Remains of a Roman imperial villa incorporated into a post office that later became a hotel.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Gibelit.
A Middle Bronze Age hillfort near Dorchester, England.
An architectural complex dating to Sardinia's nuragic period.
A tract of suburban land located southwest of the Aventine Hill that would come to be the location of the Horrea Galbae.
A Roman fort along the Limes Tripolitanus in Africa Proconsularis.
The Praetuttii were an ancient tribe of central Italy.
An ancient people of Paripātra (W Vindhyas).
Large island formed by two branches of the eastern Indus River Delta.
An ancient tribe of India, whose capital was Palimbothra.
Temple constructed in the city of Hariharalaya, dedicated in 880 CE by the Khmer king Indravarman I.
Pseira is a small island of the Gulf of Mirabello of the northeastern coast of Crete where the archaeological remains of Bronze Age and later civilizations have been excavated.
An Aegean island located between Kos and Kalymnos.
A Libyan People, cited: BAtlas 37 C2 Psylli
A lake of the Troad, mentioned by Strabo following his discussion of the grove of Hector.
The main gymnasium in Athens in the Hellenistic Period, built with the support of one of the Ptolemies, gradually superseded by the Diogeneion.
Known locally as the Puente Romano or Puente Viejo, this single-arched bridge crosses the modern Río Guadalimar at Puente de Génave in Andalusia, Spain.
The Puente del Bibey or ‘Ponte Bibei’ crosses the river Bibei at Mendoya.
Relocated remains of a 300m-long Roman stone bridge originally located southwest of modern Tourmogon at Alconétar, over R. Tajo in Spain.
A bridge, originally of Roman date, over the modern Arroyo Rabanales (a tributary of the Guadalquivir) just east of Cordoba, Spain. The bridge was in use as late as the 1920s.

A hilltop fortified site southwest of modern Biosca in Catalonia, Spain. The site exhibits architecture and pottery indicating its function as a Roman military castellum during the second century BCE.
A Roman mausoleum dating to the early fourth century CE located at Punta del Moral, Isla de Canela, Ayamonte.

A coastal fortified settlement dating to the late Bronze and early Iron Ages, known in modern times as Castro de Cociñadoiro and A Punta de Muros. The site was excavated ahead of its complete destruction in the first decade of the 21st century as part of the development of the Porto Exterior da Coruña at Punta Langosteira.
A coastal Etruscan sanctuary that dates ca. 540-530 B.C. with additional architectural phases dating to the fourth through second centuries B.C.
A Roman villa that was likely in use from the first century BC until the third century AD.
An island group off the western coast of Morocco.
Sassanid fort located about 3.5km south of the Iranian town Puskan. The fort is square shaped with a round tower at each corner.
A large, multi-period site in modern Afghanistan. One of its key feature is a large, fortified enclosure with 48 towers.
The Puy de Dôme volcano is a lava dome and volcano located in the Chaîne des Puys region of the Massif Central in France. This volcanic feature emerged approximately 10,700 years ago.
The Pyramid of Amenemhat I is an ancient Egyptian pyramid located at Lisht. It was built for Pharaoh Amenemhat I, the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt.
The Pyramid of Djedkare Isesi in South Saqqara was built for the Fifth Dynasty pharaoh Djedkare Isesi.
The Pyramid of Khafre is the second-largest of the ancient Egyptian Pyramids at Giza and served as the tomb of the pharaoh Khafre (Chefren), of the Fourth Dynasty of ancient Egypt.
Pyramid of Pepi I at Saqqarah
One of the pyramids at Saqqarah in Egypt. Pepi I was a pharaoh of the Sixth Dynasty and reigned from ca. 2332–2287 B.C.
The Pyramid of Senusret I dates to the Twelfth Dynasty of ancient Egypt. It is located at el-Lisht near the pyramid of Amenemhat I, the father of Senusret I.
There are three satellite pyramids, typically referred to as "Queen's pyramids", associated with the pyramid of Menkaure on the Giza plateau.
Buddhist temple complex in Swat, Pakistan occupied from the 1st century CE until the end of the 4th-5th centuries CE.
Site for the city of Pikasi dating back to the Old Babylonian period. A large number of cuneiform tablets were discovered there during excavations around year 2000.
Stronghold with traces of Assyrian buildings where inscribed blocks have been found. Possibly ancient Alše.
BAtlas 89 H2 Qara Zia Eddin tepe
Bronze age burial site associated with Wadi Suq culture. The site is located alongside a limestone ridge in the Sir Plain east of the city of Ras al-Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates.
Qasr Neba is the site of a Roman temple in the Bekaa valley of Lebanon.
An ancient fort located in the Timna Valley, Israel.
Qasr Wurtij (also Gasr Uertig) is a fortified Roman site located in Cyrene.
A late-Roman fort at Ain Labakha/Lebekha in Egypt's Kharga Oasis
An Old Kingdom cemetery located in the Dakhla Oasis, Balat, Egypt, that contains the tombs of royal officials who governed the area of the oasis.

A Late Neolithic to Chalcolithic settlement in the vicinity of the Medieval Torre Spaccata in Rome. The earlier settlement remains were truncated by activity in the Roman period that included road pavement.
The archaeological site of Pill'è Matta preserves remains of a Punic-Roman necropolis in use from the fourth century B.C. until the fifth century A.D.
A north African tribe that revolted against Roman rule in the late third century A.D.
Burial site dated to the Chalcolithic period.

Pliny the Elder mentions a river named Quosenum in the context of his discussion of the voyage of the historian Polybius beyond the Atlas Mountains that was said to have been facilitated by Scipio Aemilianus.

An eleventh-century caravanserai along the Silk Road, now located in Uzbekistan. Rabati Malik Caravanserai was built under Karakhanid Shams-al-Mulk Nasr, son of Tamgachkhan Ibragim who ruled in Samarkand from 1068 to 1080. The site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2008.
Raeburnfoot is a small Roman fort near the junction of the river Esk and the Rae Burn.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Veranjā, in Mathura region?.
A sanctuary of Ammon was located at Ras el-Haddagia. The rectangular temple (7.05 x 2.95 m) included an altar and a portico.
Rathgall Hillfort is a multivallate Bronze Age fort located in County Wicklow, Province of Leinster, Ireland.

The Ravenglass Roman Bath House, also known as "Walls Castle", is linked to the second-century CE fort at Glannoventa. English Heritage dates the site ca. 130 and deems it one of the tallest surviving Roman ruins in Britain.
Supplied Ravenna with water from the Bedesis fl.
A pre-Roman center located in the territory of Allifae.
A Celtic tribe living in the area of modern Brittany counted among the civitates maritimae or Aremorica.
The Reg(i)noi were a British Celtic kingdom and later a civitas of Britannia.
Regulbium was a Roman 'Saxon Shore' fort.
A Celtic-Ligurian tribe of Gallia Narbonensis.
A Late Republican temple at Fabrateria Nova.
Rharion Pedion, a plain near Eleusis in Attica that is now unlocated. Pausanias describes the plain as "the first to be sown and the first to grow crops."
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Çirağan.
The Rhodope Mountains are located in southeastern Europe. Golyam Perelik is the highest peak of the mountain range rising to 2,191 meters (7,188 ft).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Beylerbey.
Rhombites Elasson fl. (Lesser Rhombites) is the modern Kirpili River.
The northernmost of the Channel Islands.
Road Segment: Ad Mercuri → Oppidum Novum
A segment of Roman road in modern Morrocco, corresponding to a route listed in the Antonine Itinerary.
Road from Barbare east to Ad fl. Tigrim

A reconstructed road stretch from a station named Barbare (possibly modern Mohammed Khan in Turkey's Şanlıurfa Province) through Nisibis (modern Nusaybin at the Turkish/Syrian border) to a road station named Ad fl(umen) Tigrim (modern Cizre in Turkey's Şırnak Province).
A Roman auxiliary fort was identified via cropmarks in Kellington, Selby, England, United Kingdom.
Now unlocated, Roboaria was a road station of the fifteenth mile of the Via Latina. It was likely sited near Molara and some have suggested a nearby ruin as a possible location.
A Roman-style courtyard villa occupied until the fifth century AD.
Roman Aqueduct from Gorze to Metz

A Roman aqueduct with a course of about 22 km, originating from the Bouillons spring near Gorze (208 m) and flowing to the city of Divodurum (Metz) (184 m). Some 12.7 km of the aqueduct is subterranean. Arched aqueduct bridges are extant at Ars-sur-Moselle and Jouy-aux-Arches.
A Roman Army camp located on the northern side of the plateau of Avdat is generally assigned to the reign of the Roman emperor Diocletian.
At the Prestatyn Roman Site, a bath complex was identified via excavation (1934-7; 1981). The bathhouse measures approximately 11.7 by 4.5 meters.
Roman Bath-House at Little Chart, Kent

The remains of a Roman bath house were discovered in a field to the west of the village of Little Chart, Kent in 1942. These remains included fragments of mosaic pavement. Excavations in 1942 and later in 1947 identified the site as a Roman bathing complex.
Bathhouse complex in Aquae Sulis, modern-day Bath. This well-preserved site is now a museum and the bathing complex itself is below modern street-level.
A Roman bridge over the Torrente Marmore at Châtillon in the Valle d'Aosta, Italy.
One of two Roman siege camps at Burnswark Hill that flank the Iron Age hillfort. The camps are linked to the campaigns of the Roman commander Quintus Lollius Urbicus ca. 140 CE.
Constructed in the first century CE and in use through the fourth century.
The remains of a colonnaded square located near the Cortile di San Pantaleone in Catania are identified as those of the ancient Roman forum.
A Roman tower-type tomb that some local traditions label as the tomb of Cnaeus Pompeius Magnus. The structure is located at the so-called Villa di Pompeo, south of Castel Gandolfo in Italy.

A monumental Roman mausoleum, originally installed over a Hellenistic cemetery, was excavated in 2017 at a site known as "Old School" to the south of modern Chiliomedio in Greece. Its location helps indicate the extent and date of cemeteries at the ancient site of Tenea.
The Roman Odeion at Corinth dates to the first century A.D.
The Roman Theatre of Mérida was sponsored by Marcus Agrippa and dates ca. 16-15 B.C.

Remains of a Roman theater were identified in the 20th century in the vicinity of modern Piano La Roma in the municipal territory of Casoli, Italy. Its construction is estimated to date to the end of the first century BCE.
The remains of a Roman villa (first to fourth centuries CE) at Ladispoli. The surviving cryptoporticus gives the site its name.
A Roman villa located at the modern lighthouse on Avenida del Faro, Torrox, 29770, Málaga in Spain.
Roman Wall and Albarrana Islamic Tower
The Roman Wall and Albarrana Islamic Tower are included in the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida".
The Roman amphitheater at Moridunum is located in Carmarthenshire. It is one of only seven surviving Roman amphitheaters in Britain.
The Roman amphitheater at Aosta likely dates to the first century A.D. Its remains are englobed within Medieval structures.
The Roman amphitheater at Arretium was built during the late first and early second centuries. It measures 121 by 68 meters.
The second-century A.D. Roman amphitheater at Deva Victrix (modern Chester, England) was the largest military amphitheater in Britain.
The so-called Roman amphitheater at Egnatia/Gnathia dates to the Iulio-Claudian period. It is an elliptical structure with walls in opus Africanum that were revetted with painted plaster.
The Roman amphitheater at Lepcis Magna dates to the first century A.D. and was dedicated to Nero.
The Roman amphitheater at Lucus Feroniae was financed by one M. Silius Epaphroditus, who in turn received the title patronus. The structure dates to the reign of Tiberius.
The Roman amphitheater at Noviodunum was only discovered in 1996 and likely dates to the second century A.D. The arena measures ca. 50 x 36 meters.
The earthwork remains of the Roman amphitheater associated with the Saxon Shore fort at Richborough.
The Roman amphitheater at Purpan-Ancely dates ca. A.D. 40 and is the only significant Roman architecture to survive from ancient Tolosa.
The archaeological remains of the Roman amphitheater at Trebula Mutuesca are located at Monteleone Sabino in the Province of Rieti, Italy.

The archaeological remains of an amphitheater were discovered at Volterra in 2015. Preliminary work suggests that the structure measured ca. 70 x 90 meters and had three tiers of seats that could accommodate 8,000 to 10,000 spectators.

The Roman Aqueduct of Cádiz was built in the first century CE. It ran a course of some 80 kilometers, originating from springs near Tempul in San José del Valle and flowing into castellum aquae near the Roman amphitheater.
A triple-bay Roman Imperial arch near Medinaceli, Spain, that was originally dedicated to the emperor Domitian and later re-dedicated to Trajan.
A thermal spring where a Roman bath complex was first built in the third century A.D.
A two-phase complex of public baths at Fregellae dating to the third and second centuries BCE represents an important point in the transition from "Greek" bathing culture to "Roman" bathing culture.

Epigraphically and archaeologically attested bath complex at Capsa (modern Gafsa) in Tunisia. Two interconnected, open-air quadrangular pools, known collectively today as the "Roman basins" (Piscine romaine) remain. They were historically supplied by a mineral spring known today as Ain Dar el Bey.
Roman baths at calle Reyes Huertas

The Roman baths at calle Reyes Huertas date to the third century CE. They were located outside of the ancient city center in an area that has been categorized as industrial. Their exact nature is difficult to determine.

The site of Coriovallum is known for its well-preserved bath complex. These baths were first built ca. A.D. 40 and then re-built during the reign of Hadrian. They remained in use until the fourth century.
The Roman baths of Ebora were in use during the second and third centuries. The archaeological site was discovered in 1987.
The Roman baths of Taormina are built atop a public building of the Hellenistic period. The Roman baths originally fronted on the forum and were expanded in the second century.
Baths of the early imperial period at Carsulae.
A Roman bridge at Naples that was rediscovered and conserved ca. 2000. Its original phase may place it along the ancient road connecting Neapolis and Puteoli.
Structural remains of a Roman bridge located on the River Rede in the vicinity of Habitancum Roman fort. The bridge lay along the ancient Watling Street.
A bridge constructed across the Danube at the Roman fort of Valeriana.
A bridge across the Minho River at Lugo with Roman origins. Heavily restored in modern times, the bridge now serves as a pedestrian walkway.
The remains of a Roman bridge that once crossed the river known as Uso are located at San Vito, Italy, in the environs of Rimini.
An unnamed bridge located west of Hybla Gereatis at Pietralunga di Paternò, over the river Simeto.
The circus of Carthage could accommodate ca. 45,000 spectators and may date to the third century A.D.
The Roman cistern at Largo Zucchi dates to the second century A.D. It was discovered in 1957 and had an original diameter of ca. 6.90 meters.
A preserved gate of the Roman city wall in the district Mainz-Kästrich.
The Roman city wall of Zaragoza was begun under Tiberius, although work continued through the third century. The wall once stretched some 3,000 meters and had 120 defensive towers.

Located outside the city wall, the Roman amphitheater at Carnuntum dates to the later second century. It could accommodate some 13,000 spectators. The amphitheater likely went out of use by the fourth century.
Two-terraced forum at Thessalonica in use during the Roman period through the 6th century.
