The Roman forum of Col. Clunia (Sulpicia) dates to the Imperial period. It is equipped with a rectangular basilica and a small tribunal in addition to shops. The paved decumanus enters the square through a gate.
Once hypothetically identified by some scholars as an amphitheater, this structure at Aeclanum is now understood to be a Roman macellum.
The remains of a paved Roman road near Catribana in Portgual that is part of a cultural heritage assemblage that includes a bridge and ancient water mills.
A siege camp dating to the Roman siege of the fortress of Masada in A.D. 72.
A Roman signal station dating from ca. A.D. 370. Comprising a ditch, an inner wall with bastions, and a signal tower, it was used until the early fifth century.
The archaeological site of a Roman temple at Ain Amur.
The Roman temple of Vic dates to the second century A.D.
The remains of an early Imperial Roman temple on Sicily's Cape Mulini.
Structures thought to be temples set within a sacred area that includes a sacred well.
The Roman theater at Aizanoi is part of a theater-stadium complex. The complex is built after A.D. 160 with the patronage of one M. Apuleius Eurycles.
The Roman theater at Amiternum could seat approximately 2,000 people. It was abandoned after the fourth century and became a necropolis.
A second century Roman theater at Amman that could seat 6,000 spectators.
Roman theater at Carthago Nova/Col. Urbs Iulia
The Roman theater at Cartagena dates to the very end of the first century B.C. and was dedicated to Caius and Lucius Caesar.

The Roman theater at Cádiz was one of the largest in the Roman world, accommodating some 20,000 spectators. It dates originally to the first century B.C. In the thirteenth century it was incorporated into a fortress built by King Alfonso X of Castile.
The Roman theater at Herakleia dates to the time of Hadrian and remained in use until the fourth century. Its remains came to light in 1968.
The Roman theater at Lepcis Magna was financed in the first century by Annobal Tapapius Rufus.

The remains of the first century B.C. Roman theater are located adjacent to the Alcazaba of Málaga. The theater is not completely excavated, although epigraphic data places it in the Augustan period. Its abandonment came in the third century.
The Roman theater at Metellinum (modern Medelin, Spain) dates to the late first century B.C.
The Roman theater at Ostia was built under the patronage of Marcus Agrippa.
Salamis remained an important city of Cyprus during the Roman period and the theater is one part of a complex of monumental architecture there.
The larger of the two Roman theaters at Vendeuil-Caply was located at the northwest angle of the cardo and the decumanus.
The Roman theater of Alba Fucens
Crop marks, confirmed by a magnetometer survey reported in 2026, demonstrate the location and footprint of a monumental theater at the archaeological site of Fioccaglia di Fumeri.
The Roman theater of ancient Calama (now Guelma) was built in the early third century CE and substantially restored in the twentieth century.
The Roman theater of Neapolis is a structure of the first century B.C. that is built atop the pre-existing fourth century B.C. Greek theater.
The Roman theater of Suasa was discovered in 2003 during excavations near the amphitheater. The semicircular structure measures ca. 55 meters in diameter and dates to the first century A.D.
Roman villa at Anagnina Metro station
The archaeological remains of a villa in the suburbium of the city of Rome located adjacent to what is now a station of the Rome Metro system at Anagnina.
A Roman villa built atop the terraced platform of the so-called "Civita di Artena".
Roman villa at Híjar en Las Gabias
A Roman villa, of which the pars fructuaria has been excavated.

A Roman villa near the modern village of Maasbracht, Limburg, Netherlands, famous for its murals. The earliest structures on the site are dated to the second century CE, and the villa was abandoned by the middle of the third century.
The remains of a Romano-British villa on the Buckinghamshire bank of the River Thames just south of the village of Mill End. The remains were first observed via parchmarks in 1921.
A Roman villa rustica located in the bay of Verige, dating from the first century B.C. through the sixth century A.D. The villa's ruins lie within Croatia's Brijuni National Park.
Remains of a tessellated floor pavement likely indicate the presence of a villa.
The platform, including cryptoporticus, of a republican period villa originally dating to the first century B.C. with evidence for second century A.D. renovations.
Room W13, Military compound in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona
Room requisitioned for military record keeping and administration, formerly belonging to the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona in Dura-Europos.
Room W9 in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona
Pronaos in the Temple of Artemis Azzanathkona, Dura-Europos, also known as the salle aux gradins or stepped room. The steps of Room W9 carry inscriptions on them.
A Roman-era limestone quarry located to the north of Nîmes in modern France.
Rossano di Vaglio, a fourth century BC site dedicated to Mefitis, was a Lucanian federal sanctuary.

The so-called "Red House" is a large building at Dūr-Katlimmu that was built and occupied between the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. The structure included administrative, reception, and living areas, and a few Assyrian cuneiform texts were recovered during its excavation.
A Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
Rowberrow Camp is the site of an Iron Age defended settlement.
The so-called Palace V has been interpreted as a royal residence at Pergamum containing a peristyle watered by cisterns. It is noted for its mosaic decoration.

Royal residence of the rulers of the kingdom of Mari. Constructed in the 24th century BCE, the site is also known as the Palace of Zimri-Lim, the ruler who completed extensive renovations of the structure around 1800 BCE.
A large palace constructed in about 1600 BCE in Qatna, an important Bronze Age city in Syria.
Medieval fortress in the Netroknoa district, Mymensingh, Bangladesh dated to the 13th-14th centuries CE.
Ruborough Camp is a triangular-shaped promontory fort, comprised of double bank with a medial ditch.

A modern village in the East Riding of Yorkshire near which were found Neolithic cursus monuments and standing stones, two Iron Age Arras Culture cemeteries, and a fourth-century Romano-British villa.
The Tróia peninsula in Portugal is the site of a large facility for the production of Roman fish sauce (garum) and ruins of a large industrial area for the processing has been excacated there.
The remains of an extensive Roman villa dating from the first century B.C. onward, located at modern Russi, Italy.
The Roman Forum at Lahnau-Waldgirmes is the site of a fortified Roman trading outpost. It is located at the edge of the modern village of Waldgirmes.
The Tomb of the Giants Sa Perda 'e S'Altare is a giants' tomb located in the municipality of Birori, province of Nuoro, Sardinia.

A multi-phase rustic structure (fattoria) located near Olbia, Sardinia. The quadrangular structure consists of twenty-some rooms arranged around a central courtyard; the built surface covers ca 1,000 square meters.
BAtlas 25 F4 S. Antonio de Calaceite
BAtlas 25 B4 S. Esteban de Gormaz
Located some 16 km from Lugo, S. Eulalia de Bóveda is the location of a vaulted, three-aisled, underground building, likely dating to the middle Imperial period and functioning as a nymphaeum.
A catacomb connected with the Christian Saint Hippolytus of Rome along the Via Tiburtina.
BAtlas 39 H2 S. Maria di Minerbe
The oldest Orthodox church in Gaza, sacred to the fifth century Saint Porphyrius whose tomb lies within the church.
A monastery of S. Quiricus, mentioned by Gregory of Tours, that should be localized in the area of modern St-Cirgues-sur-Couze, in the French arondissement of Issoire (Puy-de-Dôme).
The San Rocco villa was built during the second quarter of the first century B.C. It was initially a simple villa rustica and it was later enlarged substantially.
BAtlas 48 A3 S. Salvatore di Cabras
BAtlas 47 G3 S. Venera al Pozzo
A nuragic complex consisting of a 'megaron-type' temple and a giant's grave.
A poorly preserved, single-tower nuraghe located near Olmedo, Sardinia.
A middle Bronze Age (ca. 1300 B.C.) nuragic settlement.
Burial ground near the Dilmun temple at Saar also from the Dilmun culture.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: DEN.
The Sagapa Stoma is a river mouth reported by Ptolemy. Erdosy (BAtlas) identifies it with the western mouth of the Indus river, contra Eggermont.
A seventh century AD church located in Vagharshapat (Etchmiadzin), Armenia and built by Catholicos Ezra I. The church was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

The abbey of Saint-Guilhem-le-Desert or Abbey Gellone, is Benedictine abbey founded in A.D. 804 by Guillaume Gellone. The abbey is a listed historical monument in France and was listed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1998 .
The Saint-Michel tumulus is a megalithic funerary mound in Brittany and one of the largest such mounds in Europe.
Remains of Gallo-Roman substructures that support the choir of the present church.
The Chapel of Saint Jean is built atop a temple once dedicated to Iuppiter Optimus Maximus.
A place from the TAVO Index
An ancient people between Kṛṣṇa and Godāvarīdeltas. Skt.: Śālankāyana.
An islet of the Cyclades with evidence of a Neolithic agricultural community dated ca. 5000-4500 BCE.
A Medieval castle dated to the thirteenth century in the Syrian village of Salkhad.
The Saltus Carminianensis was a large imperial property of northern Apulia mentioned in the Notitia Dignitatum Occidentis. Its precise location and borders are not known today.
A small islet off the southern coast of Samos. A locus of ancient shipwreck finds; unexcavated remains of a Roman-Byzantine settlement have been noted opposite Samiopoula on Samos.
Samḥa is located between the main island of Socotra and Somalia.
A Roman bath complex that was reused first as a monastic complex and then as the Medieval church of San Basilio.

A church in Venice, Italy. San Giacomo di Rialto is claimed to be the oldest church in the city, with AD 421 as the traditional date of its consecration. The first documented attestations of the church belong to AD 1152.
A church of the eleventh and twelfth century built along the line of the Roman Via Flaminia. The church incorporates Roman remains, including those of a bridge.
A Medieval church on the island of Sardinia that is dated to 1133.
San Pancrazio al Fango is an early medieval abbey built between the eighth and ninth centuries AD.
Ruins of a Roman-era villa/estate (ancient name unknown) at modern Burmarrad, Malta.
An abbey with tenth century origins connected to the pilgrimage route known as the Via Francigena.
San Pietro di Cantoni Italic sanctuary
An extra-urban Italic sanctuary located in the territory of ancient Saepinum.
A Roman military fortification at modern Trieste, dating from the third to the first centuries BCE.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: inhabitants of Sasun.
The sanctuary and grove of Feronia located at the site of Lucus Feroniae.
A small temple of Artemis Aristoboule ("of best deliberation") erected by Themistokles
The Sanctuary of Asklepios at Balagrae in Cyrenaica is dated to the Hadrianic period on the basis of epigraphic evidence.
Sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos at the Acropolis of Sparta
A Sanctuary of Cybèle located adjacent to the theater complex at Lugdunum and dating to the middle of the second century CE.
A sanctuary of the fifth century B.C. located to the east of the stadium at Olympia.
A sanctuary of Eros and Aphrodite, located in a fold of the rock on the north slope of the Acropolis of Athens, active from at least the mid-fifth century BC.
Sanctuary of Hathor built in the Middle Kingdom at Serabit el-Khadim.
Middle Kingdom sanctuary of Heqaib located on Elephantine Island near the Temples of Satis and Khnum.
Pausanias describes the Sanctuary of Herakles Hippodetos located in the Teneric plain
The sanctuary of Isis at Dion dates to the second century A.D.
Ptolemaic sanctuary originally situated in Kalabsha, relocated to the southwestern tip of Elephantine Island in 1961.
Sanctuary of Kodros, Neleus and Basile at Athens
A sanctuary located between the Phaleron gate and the Itonian gate of Athens.
A Catholic sanctuary on Mount Gargano, in northern Apulia, Italy. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.
The Palaimonion at Isthmia is a Roman sanctuary dedicated to an embodiment of the Isthmian games.
The site of a shrine assumed to honor to the hero Phrontis.
Sanctuary of Poseidon at Kalaureia, Poros
A sanctuary sacred to Poseidon on the island of Poros.
Sanctuary of the Dioscouri at Athens
Also known as the Anakeion, located likely East of the Acropolis.
Sanctuary of the Egyptian gods (Nea Makri)

A sancutary located at what is now Nea Makri at the south of the Plain of Marathon, dedicated to Egyptian gods and likely dedicated by Herodes Atticus ca. 160 CE. The site also included an opulent bath complex.
A mountain and extensive mining works mentioned by Strabo in the vicinity of Pimolisa in Pontus. Its exact location cannot be determined today.
A modern town in Sicily that has been associated with the location of the ancient settlement of Agathyrnum.

At Sant'Annèa are the remains of an extensive Roman villa located near the port of Gargano, about 3 km south of Lake Lesina. The villa probably originates in the late republican period and flourishes in the third and fourth centuries CE.
A subterranean Roman aqueduct in the modern Italian province of Salerno.
The church of Santa Lucia in Selci was founded by the eighth century and perhaps as early as the sixth century.
An eleventh century church near Aquinum built largely from spolia.
A Paleochristian church (fifth century CE) located near ancient Lavinium.
The church of Santa Maria di Devia is a Romanesque church of the eleventh century with Byzantine frescoes dating to the twelfth through fourteenth centuries.

St. Nilus of Rossano founded what is now known as the Territorial Abbacy of Saint Mary of Grottaferrata in 1004 on the site of a Roman villa that in local tradition was connected to Marcus Tullius Cicero and alleged to be the place where the latter wrote his Quaestiones tusculanae.

Site of a large Roman villa, the remains of which were incorporated into the church of Santa Maria in Legarano. The early phases of the villa likely date to the early imperial period. At some point the villa became an Imperial property as it was donated to Pope Sylvester by Constantine.

A vicus and villa of the Roman period that lay along a route connecting the Via Flaminia to the coast. Archaeological evidence for the production of ceramics and tiles has been identified. A Christian monastery is established in 1090.
A Longobard church in Benevento, Italy, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.
A settlement located at a favorable crossing over the Drau river that was an important road junction.
An octagonal structure covered by a cupola, dating between the second and sixth centuries A.D.
Santuario dei Tre Santi (Alfio, Filadelfio e Cirino)
A church of ca. 1200 AD onwards, containing ancient material from the site of Apollonia in re-use.

A Samnite sanctuary of ancient Capua that was initially discovered in 1845. Active from the sixth century B.C. until the first century B.C., the Santuario di Fondo Patturelli is noted for its architectural terracotta as well as for the presence of a sacred maternal cult.
Santuario di Maria Santissima del Lattani
Santuario di Santa Maria Regina di Anglona
A Marian sanctuary located on the hill of Anglona in the province of Matera, Italy, that originates in the eleventh century.
The so-called rock-cut sanctuary of Silvanus at Terracina.
Saos M., a mountain on the island of Samothrace rising to 1,611 m. above sea level.

Sar Mashhad, located in the Dadin Rural District, Jereh and Baladeh District, Kazerun County, Fars Province, Iran, is the site of a Sasanian rock relief of a lion hunt, along with accompanying inscriptions. The monument dates to the reign of the king Bahram II (r. 274–293 CE).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Jodhpur region. Skt.: Śālva(-vastya).
Masirah (or Mazeira) is an Island off the east coast of Oman.
The modern Saar/Sarre river, flowing through parts of France and Germany.
The province of Sardinia et Corsica was the second Roman province and came under Roman control after the First Punic War.
The Roman amphitheater at Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa was built in A.D. 108/110 and renovated in 158 under the legio IV Flavia Felix
Sarpedonion Pr., a promontory in Cilicia.
The Sassanid Palace at Sarvestan is an elite building of the fifth century A.D. It is located approximately 90 km southeast of Shiraz.
The Sasanian Empire was an Iranian empire from 224 to 651 CE. The Sasanian Empire succeeded the Arsacid dynasty of Parthia.

A locality in southern Etruria near the Via Aurelia some 50 km north of Rome that has yielded evidence for human activity across multiple periods. Notable is evidence of Protovillanovan and Villanovan necropoleis as well as ritual activity of the Etruscans.
Satala was the station of the Legio XV Apollinaris.
A Scythian people of the Tauric Chersonesus.
The modern Cabo de Palos, a Mediterranean peninsula in the modern Spanish municipality of Cartagena.
A Roman bridge on the Rubicon at Savignano sul Rubicone.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
The Gallo-Roman villa of Séviac was designed around a central peristyle courtyard and its fourth-century A.D. phase covered up to one hectare.
The ruins of a medieval castle built ca. A.D. 1135 by William le Gros, Earl of Albemarle. Now an English Heritage site.
The Scheggia Pass marks the division between the Central and Northern Apennines in northern Umbria. Its elevation is 632 meters above sea level.
Scratchbury Camp, Wiltshire, England, is the site of a 15 hectare hill fort.
The island of Skyros in the Aegean Sea.
Site of a Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall.
Minor gate in the western city walls of Dura-Europos.
A Roman fort at present day Caernarvon. The first Roman fort was built under Agricola ca. A.D. 77 and the site was occupied by Romans until ca. 338.
A pyramid, originally approximately 23m in height, built by the fourth dynasty pharaoh Snefru. The function of the pyramid, which seems to have lacked an interior chamber, is uncertain.
Ponte della Selciatella, a Roman-period bridge crossing the Fosso di Acqua Rossa in San Vittorino, Lazio, Italy.
The Selgoouai were an ancient people of southern Scotland attested only in the text of Ptolemy.
Seli, A Libyan People, cited: BAtlas 37 C1
The Pre-Aksumite settlement of Sembel, located near Asmara in Ethiopia, dates ca. 800 BCE.
A mountain range of northern Ethiopia first mentioned in the Monumentum Adulitanum and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
An ancient people of Sardinia thought to have been localized in the southwest portion of the island.

The tomb C. Maenius Bassus is located along the Via Valeria. This podium tomb with superstructure is dated to either the reign of Caius or that of Claudius. Epigraphic evidence mentions that C. Maenius C. f. Cam. Bassus was an Augustalis, an aedile, and praefectus fabrum.
A Roman tomb along the Via Appia that is traditionally believed to be that of Publius Septimius Geta, the younger son of Septimius Severus.
The Mausoleum of the Plautii dates to the first century B.C. It is located near Ponte Lucano at Tibur.
A Roman tomb of the fourth century C.E. built in opus listatum.
A station on the Via Popillia in the Po River delta (also known as Septem Maria).
The Serapeum in Ostia's Regio III was built between 123 and 126 CE thanks to private patronage.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Swāt. Skt.: Śveta.
The Setantioi were a pre-Roman tribe of Britain who lived in western and southern Lancashire, England.
A mountain probably near Mt. Tetricus.

A Middle Kingdom fortress that was originally located on the Nile's west bank at the Second Cataract of the Nile River. The ruins of the fortress are now situated on an island in Lake Nubia in northern Sudan.

Cave in Kandahar Province, Afghanistan, 3.5 miles NNE of Panjwai town, with archaeological remains from the Kushan period (100 BCE to 300 CE), Kushano-Sassanian (transition) period (300 to 700 CE), and the Early Islamic period (700 to 1222 CE).
Central coastal plain between the Carmel and Joppe in modern Israel.

A chapel located in the Palestinian village of Beit Sahour that is believed to be the site of the annunciation of Jesus Christ's birth to the shepherds. A Christian monastery was founded on the site in the early fifth century.

Burial site in western Mongolia that dates to between the 8th century BCE and the 3rd century CE. Nine tombs associated with the Pazyryk Culture and 7 tombs associated with the Xianbei Culture have been identified.

The Shrine of Sabazius was installed in part of a horreum (V, XII, 2) that was initially built ca. 120-125 CE. The Sabazius shrine likely dates to the early third century. Dante Vaglieri excavated the shrine in 1909.
The Shrine of Strenia was located in the valley of the Colosseum and is mentioned as the starting point of the Sacra Via.
An island in northern Albania, created in modern times when surrounding land was flooded by the creation of a reservoir. It is the site of the llyrian settlement of Sarda.
A strait separating the eastern tip of Sicily and the southern tip of Calabria in the south of Italy.

These names were sometimes used by the Romans to denote a portion of the Mediterranean Sea that RE asserts lies between southern Italy, Sicily, and Malta on the west and the Peloponnese and coast of Epiros on the east. BAtlas positions the label for this feature midway between Sicily and the Peloponese, some way below the label for "Ionium Mare".
BAtlas 26 D3 Sierra de la Martela
Modern Cape Sigri on the west coast of the Aegean island of Lesbos.

Silbury Hill is a prehistoric artificial chalk mound near Avebury and is part of the Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites UNESCO World Heritage Site. The mound stands to 40 meters (131 ft) in height.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: POL.

The remains of a church belonging to the early Medieval period (perhaps the seventh century) that perhaps was a project of Pymenius, Bishop of Asidonia. This edifice is located on the hill that was the site of the oppidum referred to as Silla de Papa.
An uninscribed Roman milestone discovered in 1970 at Sillian, Tirol, Austria. The milestone corresponds to the 24th mile from Aguntum.
The Silures were a tribe of South Wales.
Iron Age cemetery located on the eastern slope of the Kidron Valley, containing burials dated from the 9th-7th centuries BCE.
A series of three artificial lakes created along the river Anio.
The Roman theater at Simitthu, an ancient Roman-Berber town in northwestern Tunisia.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: around Umarkot (modern Sanghis) PAK.
A church and possible monastic complex identified in 2021/2022 on modern Siniyah Island in the emirate of Umm al-Quwain, UAE.
The Siris/Semnus fl. (modern Sinni) is a river of south Italy flowing through the region of Basilicata.
The Sitones? were a Germanic or Finnic people living somewhere in northern Europe.
One of the nomadic tribes of ancient Mesopotamia.

The Skerki Bank is an area of relatively shallow open sea lying between Sicily and Tunisia. The presence of several reefs made the area perilous for ancient mariners and, from 1988 onward, ancient shipwrecks have been investigated in this area.
The modern Wadi el Natrun: a valley in northern Egypt that developed as an important locus of Coptic monastic establishments, beginning in late antiquity and continuing to the present day.
A physical feature mentioned by Strabo as near Pylos in Elis. It may be identical with the mountain named "Skollis" mentioned later in Strabo.
A mountain that Strabo reports as lying on the border of Elis and Achaea in the Peloponnese, identified with the modern Santameri/Santomeri/Santameriotiko (also now often called by its ancient name).
The remains of a first-century A.D. earthwork and the buried remains of a Roman fort at Slack. These remains might be associated with the Roman toponym Camulodonum.
Small Down Knoll is the site of a Bronze Age hill fort near Evercreech in Somerset, England.

Snettisham is a village and civil parish located in the county of Norfolk in England. It has been the site of numerous archaeological finds, including notable Iron Age and Roman hoards. It is probable that it was a locus of settlement, including perhaps a villa, during the time of the Roman Empire.
Remains of large building found in the settlement of Aquae Sulis, modern Bath.
A temple dedicated to Octavian by a Lucius Calpurnius. It replaced a temple of ca. 194 B.C. that had in turn been restored by Sulla.
So-called House of the Mosaic Columns
Suburban villa outside the Herculaneum gate in Pompeii
A Ptolemaic temple to the god Sobek.
An Alpine tribe mentioned by Pliny the Elder.
Sohund M. (Sahand) is an eroded stratovolcano in northwestern Iran.
Burial mound of Sarmatian nobility from the 1st century CE in modern Mykolaiv Oblast, Ukraine with earlier remains from the Bronze Age. The mound has since been demolished by bulldozer.
Burial complex in the southern Ural Mountains region containing a number of Late Antique burials.
The modern Cap Spartel is a promontory in Morocco located at the entrance to the Strait of Gibraltar, some 12 km west of Tangier.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Oued el-Hammam area.
Near Parentium (today Porec/Parenzo in Croatia), Cape Sorna (Zorna) first hosted a large villa maritima, and then a small early Christian church.
The tumulus (burial mound) of the Athenian dead at Marathon.
Sorviodurum was the site of an auxiliary fort in Raetia (modern Straubing, Lower Bavaria).
Site approximately 1 km north of the modern village of Lapithos, northern Cyprus, containing several burials from the Early and Middle Bronze Age.
An islet located in Souda Bay on the northwest coast of Crete.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: CZE.
BAtlas 28 C5 Souk Jema el Haouafa
The southernmost tip of the Attic peninsula.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: S Astorga.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Mathura region. Skt.: Śūrasena.
One of three rivers called "Salsum" by the Romans, this river is probably to be identified with the modern Sous, which debouches into the Atlantic Ocean at modern Agadir in Morocco.
Cemetery site in southwest Cyprus lying 1.5km southwest of Souskiou Village with archaeological remains from the chalcolithic period.
Two-story palace near the western bank of the Nile used as an administrative center from the Second Intermediate Period to the early New Kingdom.

The South Square is the modern name for an enclosed area at the south end of the Athenian Agora, which was built in the mid-second century BC, incorporating some earlier structures. Parts of it were damaged in the Sullan Sack of 86 BC and demolished.

A bath complex at Herculaneum that was discovered in the excavations of the so-called "Insula Occidentalis". It was not in use as a bath at the time of the 79 CE eruption as it had been repurposed as a ship-shed.
The Southeastern Cluster of rock-cut churches at Lalibela.
Gate located between Tower 8 and Tower 9 in the southern city walls of Dura-Europos.
A fountain house at the southwest corner of the Athenian Agora, built ca. 350-325 BC, modified in the late 4th and 2nd centuries BC, and destroyed in the Sullan Sack of 86 BC.
A Romano-British villa located at Manor Hall Road, Southwick, England.
Now unlocated, Sphendale was an ancient place in Attica. Herodotus mentions it as a place located along the route of Mardonius' march from the Megarid to Tanagra by way of Dekeleia.
The Old Kingdom temple associated with the Great Sphinx of Giza and assigned to the reign of Khafre.
An archaeological site of the Roman period connected with the fluvial harbor of Rusellae.

Remains of a walled ancient city in the Ghazni province of Afghanistan. Its remains date to various periods according to W. Ball (1982): Late Sassanian and Turki Shahi (sixth–ninth century AD) and Early Islamic (tenth -twelfth century).
Large baray or reservoir at Angkor constructed in the 10th century CE.
A tidal island located in Mount's Bay, Cornwall, England. Known for the castle crowning the island, this place has been inhabited since the Neolithic period.
An archaeological site first excavated between 1894 and 1897 that has yielded remains of several villas, including a luxury villa of more than 117 rooms, and a sanctuary.
The stadium of ancient Ephesus originally dates from the Hellenistic period. It is expanded during the reign of Nero thanks to patronage from the freedman C. Stertinius Orpex.
A stadium south of the city proper at Anazarbos (modern Dilekkaya in Turkey)

This stadium, constructed in a natural depression near Epidaurus, was part of the sanctuary of Asclepius, the god of medicine and healing, and housed athletic contests in honor of the god. It dates to the fourth century B.C.
The ancient Greek stadium at the pan-hellenic sanctuary of Nemean Zeus.
Stadium in the settlement of Delos, constructed in the early 3rd century BCE.

A garden at the Villa Hadriani imitating the shape of a stadium, situated between the Three Exedras' Hall (to the west) and the Winter Palace (to the east), with a semi-circular nymphaeum at its southern end.

The Stari Grad Plain is located on the island of Hvar in the Adriatic Sea. This cultural landscape is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site due, in part, to its pristine state of preservation, which dates back to the time of Greek colonization by Paros in the fourth century BCE.
A stele carrying a Latin inscription that dates to the Severan period (ca. 206 CE) recording the restoration of the bridge that had been destroyed by the "fury of the sea".
Horemheb was the last pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty of Egypt. The deeds of his career were recorded on a stele that was mountaed at the foot of the Tenth Pylon of the Karnak temple.
Burial site in the Altai region dated to the Syanbi-Zhouzhan period (4th-5th century CE).
Stoa in the sanctuary of Zeus Lykaios
A 62 m long stoa, probably of the fourth century BC.
At Stoneyford in 1852 a burial and associated hoard showing Roman cultural affinity was discovered, although the find and its interpretation are now debated.

Findspot of the Stony Stratford Hoard, an urn discovered in 1789 containing three fibulae, two headdresses, and approximately 30 decorated silver and gilt bronze plaques, among which were three dedications to Jupiter, Vulcan, and Mars (RIB 215, 216, and 217).
A Roman auxiliary fort. Limited excavations in 1969 suggested a construction date of ca. A.D. 83 with abandonment ca. 87.
Strageath is the site of a Roman camp located near the River Earn in eastern Scotland.

A waterway connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. The author of the Periplus Maris Erythraei mentions this area, but does not explicitly name the strait, referring instead to the "mouth of the Persian Gulf". The origin of the toponym "Hormuz" remains debated.
Stravomyti is a Neolithic cave site with evidence for cultic activity. It is located on the slopes of Mt. Juktas in Crete.
The so-called "Street of Facades" is a necropolis that is lined with tall, rock-cut tombs that have elaborate facades.
Pre-Flavian Roman fort near present-day Derby, pre-dating the later fort at ‘Derbentio’ (Little Chester), directly across the modern river Derwent.
The remains of a Romano-British amphitheater were discovered on Studforth Hill, just outside the village of Aldborough between Harrogate and York in northern England.
A nuragic complex with three phases of occupation and construction, beginning as early as the sixteenth century B.C.
A nuragic site in Barumini, Sardinia that was named as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
A place from the TAVO Index
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: in Syrastrene. Pāli: Soratta.
The modern Bay (Gulf) of Valencia was known in antiquity as the Sucronensis Sinus.

Cemetery site in Khakassia containing numerous burials associated with the Karasuk Culture (14th-8th centuries BCE). The site was inundated following the construction of the Krasnoyarsk Hydroelectric Power Plant.
The Sultanahmet Camii (The Blue/Sultan Ahmed Mosque) was built on the primary site of the Great Palace of Constantinople between 1609 and 1616 during the rule of Ahmed I.
A place from the TAVO Index
Temple dedicated to the god Ra in the 5th dynasty by the pharaoh Niuserre (Nyuserre).
The Sunuci were a Germanic tribe in Germania Inferior.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: ALG.
The Surdaones were a people of Gallia Narbonensis.
Surviving colonnade of the imperial temple at Mérida
A promontory of the southern coast of Arabia.
The remains of a Roman bath complex that included mosaic pavements and marble statuary were documented during rescue excavations in 2004 to the west of Sykeon in Thessaly.
Synagogue adapted from a private house building in Dura-Europos.
An ancient river of the northern Peloponnese (modern Trikaliotikos) that was considered to constitute the eastern border of the region of Achaia.
Site of a temple dedicated to the Celtiberian/Lusitanian god Endovelicus.
A well-preserved 'giant's tomb' dating ca. 2000-1600 BC.
Khmer temple at Angkor constructed in 1186 CE under Jayavarman VII.
A Romano-Celtic temple complex located near the junction of Stane Street and Watling Street in modern Southwark.
A road station located on the via Aurelia between Centumcellae and Graviscae in Etruria, now unlocated.

A small fortified hilltop settlement located on private land in the modern Algerian village of "Crète Rouge" at Tachachit, which is approximately 8km north of El Adjiba. Noted already by Gsell for AAA, a 2012 cultural inventory notes visible remnants of walls, roof tiles, drainage conduit, a cistern, and a polychrome opus-tesselatum mosaic.
The Acacus Mountains are known for rock-art dating from 12,000 BC to 100 AD and were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985 because of the importance of these paintings and carvings.
A plateau in modern Uzbekistan near the Aral Sea containing two burial sites dating to the first millennium BCE.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A peak in the Taygetos range, mentioned by Pausanias. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
Mound of a small rural settlement at the confluence of the river Robal with Tigris in modern Iraq. The site is now submerged by the reservoir created by the Mosul dam.
A Middle Bronze Age nuragic complex near Macomer, Sardinia.
An ancient people that inhabited the South Caucasus and the mountainous region of northeastern Anatolia.
Tap o' Noth hill fort is located in Aberdeenshire, Scotland; a well preserved vitrified wall survives at the site.
Tapori or Tapoli, an ancient Celtic tribe of Lusitania.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: KYR.
Site in western Iran with a series of Sassanid rock reliefs carved in the fourth century A.D.

An ancient river of south Italy, debouching into the Gulf of Taranto to the northwest of the ancient city. The coastal landscape and river course have seen changes since antiquity, but the modern Fiume Tara is normally associated with its ancient predecessor.
A Roman cemetery at modern Tarnów Opolski in Poland.
According to Canmore, "a major Roman complex (Flavian to Antonine) at Milton (Roy's Tassieholm) was excavated between 1938 and 1950 by J. Clarke."

Tassili n'Ajjer is a mountain range of the Sahara Desert, covering an area of 72,000 square kilometers. The mountain range is the site of more than 15,000 rock art drawings and engravings dating from 6000 BC to the first centuries of the present era.
A ninth-century monastery located on a large basalt plateau in southeastern Armenia.
Armenian monastery located in Syunik Province, Armenia. Constructed beginning in 848, the monastery complex was expanded several times from the 10th-13th century.
The modern Habibas Islands, off the Algerian coast, are probably to be identified with the ancient Tauria island.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
A river flowing from Alpes Maritimae and emptying into the Ligusticum Mare near Costa Bellene.
The Tavşan Tepe Tümülüsü is a tumulus at Pergamon included in the UNESCO World Heritage site "Pergamon and its Multi-Layered Cultural Landscape".
A small theater at Soluntum, first erected in the middle of the fourth century BCE and then revitalized in the first century BCE.
Tell in the Negev desert with archaeological remains from an Iron Age town and a Hellenistic-early Roman settlement.
Tell in the Hamrin Basin with a Parthian settlement, possibly featuring a defensive moat. The area was flooded by the creation of the Hamrin Dam in the late 1970s.
Tell Abraq was an ancient Near Eastern city.
An archaeological site located in the Northwestern Negev Desert in modern Israel with identified with the Biblical city of Sharuhen. Two Middle Bronze Age cemeteries are located next to the site.
Citadel on the modern banks of Lake Assad in Syria located near the Emar site and containing remains dated to the late Bronze Age.
Tell el-Ajjul was a fortified Bronze Age settlement located in what is now Gaza. Evidence from the site indicates economic interaction with ancient Egypt.
Fortified site dated to the New Kingdom located on the eastern frontier of Egypt, just into the Sinai Peninsula.

Tell el-Retaba is a large, multi-phase settlement site located in the central part of Wadi Tumilat. Its human activity ranges from the period of Hyksos settlers to the Third Intermediate Period to the 19th century.
An Imperial Roman villa at Caddeddi on the Tellaro river in Sicily with elaborate floor mosaics.
A Gallo-Roman temple complex dated to the 1st-4th centuries CE.
The so-called "Tempio di Venere" is likely part of a bathing complex dating to the reign of Hadrian. The surviving structure has an octagonal plan.
Temple structure located south of the main Amun Temple complex at Naga, constructed during the reign of King Nebmaatre Amanakhareqerema (1st century CE).
A fifth-century B.C.E. Doric temple, sacred to perhaps Hera or Dionysus, located on the eastern hill at Selinus.
A Gallo-Roman sanctuary with an enclosed precinct that was linked to the oppidum.
The ruins of a Roman-period temple dedicated to Apollo located at the Oppidum de Gaujac (Gard, France).
Temple located in block L5 at Dura-Europos.
Middle Kingdom temple of Amon at the heart of the Karnak Temple Complex.
The remains of a marble temple executed in the Ionic order.
A Roman temple at Side dating to the reign of Antoninus Pius.
The Temple of Apollo Daphnephoros at Eretria dates originally to the late archaic period.
The Hellenistic Temple of Apollo Pythios on the Acropolis of the city of Rhodes.
The Temple of Apollo at Hierapolis, built during the Hellenistic period.
An Archaic Greek temple of the Doric order built ca. 580 BCE.
The Temple of Artemis Orthosia at Epidauros was founded in the Archaic period and continued in use in the Roman period. Pausanias mentions it as being on the city's temples.
An ancient sanctuary of Artemis and Apollo associated with the ancient settlement of Abai and located near the modern Greek town of Kallipodi.
The Temple of Artemis in Jerash.
Temple located in block H2 at Dura-Europos.
Temple of Ba'al (or Bel) in the ancient city of Palmyra.
A Doric temple ascribed to Demeter with origins in the fourth century B.C.
The Temple of Dionysos at Eretria dates ca. 350 B.C. It is located in the northwest sector of the city near the so-called West Gate.
A Temple of Dionysos in the Ionic order begun in the Hellenistic period.
Centerpoint of sanctuary at modern Jublains
A Punic temple founded in the first century B.C.
An archaic temple dating ca. 610 B.C.
Remains of the fourth-century BCE Temple of Hercules are preserved in the edifice of San Marco d'Alunzio.
Temple of Hercules at Montorio al Vomano
A sanctuary of Hercules located in the territory of Teramo near the Vomano river.
The Temple of Hercules at Lanuvium.
The Temple of Isis, Sabratha dates to the later first century CE.
A temple dedicated to the Capitoline triad is located on the forum of Saepinum.
A temple located at the fourth mile of the Via Appia.
Temple of Liber Pater at Sabratha
A Temple of Liber Pater at Sabratha that dates to the Iulio-Claudian period.
A temple sacred to Isis and Osiris of Roman date, relocated before the completion of the Aswan dam in the 1960s.
Temple of Mater Matuta at Satricum
A sanctuary dedicated to Mater Matuta that was in use between the seventh and fifth centuries B.C.
The Temple of Minerva at Theveste dates to the third century A.D.
A temple dedicated to the Babylonian god of wisdom.
The Temple of Ramesses II at Abydos in Egypt.
The Temple of Seti I at Abydos is also known as the "Great Temple of Abydos".
1st century CE temple to Minerva at the Aquae Sulis in Bath, England in use roughly until 410 AD.
A sanctuary dedicated to Trajan in the 'urbs nova' of Italica that flourished under the patronage of Hadrian.
The Temple of Zeus is Aizanoi's main sanctuary. The temple complex was built under Domitian.
The foundations of an ancient temple located to the west of ancient Astakos/Dragomestre in Aitoloakarnania.
A tetrastyle temple in the Corinthian order sacred to Zeus Megistos was built at Canatha by the first century CE.
The monumental sanctuary of Zeus Olympius at Jerash dates to the 160s CE.
An epigraphically attested temple at or near ancient Atyochorion (modern Akkent in Turkey).
The Doric Temple of Zeus at Cyrene.
BAtlas 75 D4 Tenis he kai Hakoreos
One of the 19 Roman bath complexes identified in Mérida.
Thermal baths at Catania dating to the fourth and fifth centuries CE. The archaeological remains are located near the present-day Piazza del Duomo of Catania.

The so-called Terme della Trinacria in Regio III of Ostia Antica were built in the Hadrianic period at the same time as the Temple of Serapis (III,XVII,4). The modern toponym is derived from a triskelion included in a mosaic decoration.
The excavations carried out following the earthquake of 1908 revealed a number of baths dating to the early centuries of the Roman Imperial period.
Known today as the "Women's Bath" at Gafsa, this open-air artificial pool built of opus quadratum is one of two that are associated with the ancient Roman bath complex at Capsa.
Known today as the "Men's Pool", this open-air, artificial pool in opus quadratum is one of two associated with the ancient Roman bath complex of Capsa.
Mound site in Khakassia containing burials associated with the Bronze Age Karasuk culture.
BAtlas 56 C5 Tes Kores to Gephyri
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: N and E Peiraieus.
A district of northeastern Attica that included the cities of Marathon, Probalinthus, Tricorythus, and Oenoe.
An island of the Dodecanese, modern Seskli.
Teutoburgiensis? Saltus (Teutoburger Wald) is a range of low, forested mountains in Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
An ancient peak whose precise location is not known, but which Pausanias implies was part of the Mainalion range in Achaia.
A monumental altar built during the reign of king Eumenes II.
The Queen's Megaron is a room in the Minoan "Palace of Minos" at Knossos. It includes the famous Dolphin fresco.

An excavated ancient theater at Telmessos (Fethiye) has been variously dated to the late Hellenistic or Augustan periods. Some components (e.g., the extant stage structures) date to later in the Roman imperial period.
The Theater at Bodrum is dedicated to Ares.
An ancient theater associated with the Letoon, a sanctuary of Leto near the ancient city Xanthos in Lycia. The theater is located on the Roman agora, to the the north of the acropolis.
The theater is located at the north-east end of Kouphonesi. It was a stone-built building that could accommodated ca. 1000 spectators.
The Theater at Limyra dates ca. 190 B.C.
The initial phase of the Theater at Philippi dates to just after 356 B.C. when Philip II conquered the city.
The intramural theater at Saepinum is one of the best preserved structures at the site. Located in the northern part of the walled area, it is likely built between 2. B.C. and A.D. 4.
The Theater at Termessos is a Hellenistic and Roman structure, with the Roman theater preserving elements of the earlier phase.
The Greek theater (second century BC) was renovated following a Roman design following the earthquake of A.D. 141.
Theater at the Sanctuary of Asklepios, Epidauros
The Greek theater in the Sanctuary of Asklepios at Epidauros, renowned for its acoustics
The ancient Greek Theater of Aigeira overlooks the Gulf of Corinth. The theater was built ca. 280-250 B.C.E. and enjoys a remarkable state of preservation.
The Theater of Ephesus sits at the foot of the Panayir mountains. It could host up to 25,000 spectators.
The Theater of Miletus was built in four phases between ca. 300 and ca. 133 B.C.

The ancient Theater of Nuceria Alfaterna was first built during the second century BCE and occupies a zone that abutted the city's fortification wall. The theater was identified and excavated between the late 1970s and early 1980s in the area between Pareti and Pucciano.
The Hellenistic theater at Dodona is linked to the reign of Pyrrhus in the third century B.C.
The remains of the Hellenistic theater of Tegea are to be found beneath the tenth-century A.D. Middle Byzantine church of Palaia Episkopi.
The Theater of ancient Sicyon dates to either the late fourth or early third century BC. It was restructured after 146 B.C.
A third- to second-century B.C. theater connected with the sanctuary of the Muses.
A Greek theatre at Parium that was reconstructed by the Romans in the second and early third century.
The New Kingdom tomb of the ancient Egyptian workman Inherkhau is located at Deir el-Medina and is part of the Theban Necropolis.

Collective name for the complex of tombs and temples on the western bank of the Nile, opposite the city of Thebes/Luxor. The necropolis was used for royal and elite burials throughout the Pharaonic period.
A mountain and pass in the Pontic range near Trabazon where Xenophon says the 10,000 first sighted the sea. Its precise location cannot be determined today.
Themistou Meris is a district that is part of the Fayoum.

Located in Thessaly, the Theopetra Cave is an important archaeological site with evidence of multi-phase prehistoric human occupation. Radiocarbon dates indicate human activity beginning at least 50,000 years ago. Archaeogenetics have focused on evidence related to Mesolithic inhabitants of the cave site.

A twelfth-century monastic foundation and fortified church in the modern town of Feres in Greece's Evros prefecture. The structure served as a mosque during the Ottoman empire and was returned to use as a church in the 20th century.
An unnamed bridge located north of Theveste (modern Tébessa, Algeria) on a Roman road between Theveste and Ammaedara (modern Haidra).

A hill in Boeotia located to the west of Chaeronea, Thourion is described by both Plutarch and Pausanias. The discovery of an inscribed trophy monument connected to the military campaigns of Lucius Cornelius Sulla in 86 BCE led to the identification of the site.
A Roman fort in Wales discovered with aerial photography in June 2018
Thrypti, a mountain range of eastern Crete.
A small river of the Troad and tributary of the Scamander.
A promontory on the west side of the central southern peninsula of the Peloponnese in Greece.
A prehistoric cairn located atop Tibradden Mountain.

The so-called Tigris Tunnel is a cave ca. fifty miles north of Diyarbakır, Turkey and it forms a source of the Tigris River. In its vicinity there are several Assyrian monuments, including five inscriptions.
Tilurium was the site of the fortress of Legio VII Claudia Pia Fidelis.
The Timna Valley is located approximately 30 km north of the Gulf of Aqaba and copper has been mined there since the fifth millennium B.C.
Tiquadra was part of the Menariae insulae.
Titos fl. (Trieux river) is a river of Brittany.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: middle R. Jalón valley.
A Roman fort located at Bolham Hill, Tiverton, Mid Devon, England. A Roman auxiliary fort of the Neronian period has been identified here.
Site of a Roman villa excavated in 1887-8. The site was an enclosed courtyard, with a main house, hypocaust, and baths, as well as an aisled farmhouse.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Altava area.
Latin inscriptions unearthed in 1792 between the second and third mile of the Via Appia near S. Sebastiano identify the tomb garden complex of one Claudia Semne.
A tomb located in Rome's Campus Martius. Its remains are now submerged in the channelized waters of the Euripus canal beneath the Palazzo della Cancelleria.
The Tomb of Caius Cartilius Poplicola, dating to ca. 30-20 B.C., is a monumental tomb outside the Porta Marina of Ostia. Poplicola was a prominent citizen of Ostia.
The Tomb of Derecia Methe is a house-type tomb located at the Porta Nocera.

The Tomb of Gaius Vestorius Priscus is located in Pompeii's Porta Vesuvio necropolis. Gaius Vestorius Priscus was an aedile and was granted 2,000 sesterces by the town council for his tomb and funeral. The tomb is decorated with paintings depicting a funereal meal.
Hetepheres I was a 4th Dynasty queen of ancient Egypt (ca. 2600 B.C). She may have been a wife of the pharaoh Sneferu and the mother of Khufu.
A painted Macedonian tomb located at Lefkadia, Imathia, Macedonia, that dates to the third century BCE.
The tholos-type Tomb of Lucius Ceius Serapio and his wife, Helvia, stands near the Porta Nocera at Pompeii.
The Tomb of Lucius Sepunius Sandilianus is a Roman-period tomb, possibly of tholos typology, located in the Porta Nocera necropolis of Pompeii.

The Tomb of Lucius Verginius Rufus was located at ancient Alsium. Lucius Verginius Rufus (d. 97 CE) was a colleague of Nero and guardian of the younger Pliny, with the latter recording Verginius Rufus' epitaph.

The schola-type tomb of one Marcus Tullius is located outside the Porta Stabia of Pompeii. The decedent is thought to have been the patron of the Aedes For­tunae Augustae and was three times duovir and tribunus militum a populo.
The largest private tomb in the Theban Necropolis, located in el-Assasif and containing the burial of a local ruler of Thebes during the 25th-26th Dynasties.
Tomb of Numerius Agrestinus Equitius Pulcher

A schola tomb at Pompeii located near the Porta Nocera necropolis. The inscription on the tomb's hemicycle honors Numerius Agrestinus Equitius Pulcher, a Roman who had an illustrious military career, including holding the role of praefectus of the Autrigones, an Iberian tribe.
Tomb of Orestes described by Pausanias in the Agora of Sparta, near a Sanctuary of the Moirai. Supposedly housed the bones of Orestes.
The tomb of Senwosret III, a pharaoh of the 12th Dynasty in Egypt.
A Roman tomb at the sixth mile of the Via Appia.
An elaborate tomb located near Kazanlak, Bulgaria. The Tomb of Seuthes III, who was King of the Odrysian Kingdom from ca. 331 to ca. 300 BC, is found in the Valley of the Thracian Rulers.
The so-called Tomb of Themistocles at Drapetsona.
Tomb of Thutmes I and Hatshepsut (KV20)
KV20 may be the earliest tomb cut in the Valley of the Kings. It was first the tomb of Thutmose I, although he was later re-interred in KV38. KV20 was adapted to accommodate both her and her father.
Tomb of the Mayor of Athribis

The tomb of Psenosiris, identified in a tomb inscription as the Mayor of Athribis, is a rock-cut shaft tomb with a richly-decorated burial chamber. The tomb was constructed in the necropolis of Athribis in the middle of the first century CE (ca. 37-54 CE).
Tomb of the Sempronii (Palazzo San Felice, Rome)
A late-Republican tomb located on the slope of the Quirinal Hill at Rome, now built into Palazzo San Felice (via della Dataria 21).

The Tomba del Sileno is an Etruscan tomb at the Sovana Archaeological Park in the province of Grosseto. Dating from the third century BCE, the tomb derives its name from a bas-relief resembling the head of a Silen.
An oval, embanked area of the north-east of the Roman fort has been identified as an amphitheater, one of only three known in Wales. The amphitheater is located near the site of the parade ground.
The Roman fort at modern day Tomen y Mur, presumably Flavian in date, was likely abandoned by the middle of the second century A.D.
The Tophet of Carthage, also known as tophet de Salammbô, is a hybrid sanctuary-necropolis of Punic Carthage.
The Tor di Mezzavia is a Medieval tower located along the modern Via Tuscolana, marking the midway point between Rome and Frascati.
Torcello is an island located at the northern end of the Venetian Lagoon that was first settled in 452 CE.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group.
The Toronaic Gulf, the modern Gulf of Kassandra.
A Medieval coastal fort of the Frangipani.
The remains of two towers of a Norman fortress near Spezzano Albanese.
A lighthouse that has served as a marker for the La Coruña harbor since the late first century AD.
An imperial Roman villa with a bath complex that emerged in the first and second centuries AD, transitioning to a fortified site after the sixth century AD.

The so-called "Torre del Filosofo" was a structure on Mt. Etna that may have been built by the Roman emperor Hadrian in honor of the Greek philosopher Empedocles as local legend held that he once climbed the mountain and died by falling into the volcano.
A Roman tower-type mausoleum located near Mondragone, Italy.
A coastal Roman villa that is succeeded by a Medieval coastal tower.
A Medieval tower along the Via Flaminia near Prima Porta.
One of five Roman-era aqueducts known from Sexi (modern Almuñécar, Spain). This one is represented by an extant aqueduct bridge located near the source of the Rio Verde, north of Sexi.
Torrellafuda is the site of a Talayotic settlement on the island of Minorca.
An ancient aqueduct, located to the west of Keresos.
The Torrente delle Ferriere or Fosso della Mola is a stream that bounds the tuff plateau upon which the Etruscan metropolis of Caere developed.
Torretrencada is a Talayotic settlement of the early first millennium BCE.
A Roman tomb that was adapted for use as a medieval fortification. It is located near modern Frascati, southeast of Rome.

This Roman courtyard villa that yielded ceramics dating to the 4th century CE was located on what is now Church Farm in Totternhoe (Central Bedfordshire, England). The survey and excavations were published in the 1950s; the site was backfilled after excavation and the villa's remains are no longer visible.
A monastery built by order of Emperor Justinian I. St. Catherine's at the foot of Mount Sinai in modern Egypt.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Castellum Tulei.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: Teruel.

The Tower of Amfikleia is a late Medieval tower located at Amfikleia, Phthiotis, Greece. It occupies a position on the acropolis of the ancient city of Amphicleia.
The Tower of Chrysokamaro Áyios Nikólaos is a small, fortified complex of Byzantine date located near the village Agios Nikolaos in Chalkidiki, at the beach of Trani Ammouda.
The Tower of Seneca is a sixteenth-century castle in Corsica built atop the remains of a Roman watchtower.
Tragia Ins. (modern Agathonisi) is a small island of the Dodecanese in Greece.
The site of a Roman fort on the right bank of the Danube, Transdierna played an important part in the Dacian Wars. Its name is not attested until the fourth century A.D.
A Roman auxiliary fort located on the river Ystwyth in Ceredigion, Wales. The fort overlooks a Roman bridge and was built during the AD 70s.
A necropolis along the Via Amerina, likely in use from the third century BC until the third century AD.
Tre'r Ceiri is an Iron Age hillfort located in Wales atop the easternmost summit of Yr Eifl, a mountain located on the north coast of the Llŷn peninsula in Gwynedd, northwestern Wales.
A group of small islands located in the Alboran Sea off the coast of Morocco.
A statio at the point where the Via Appia crosses the Via Ninfina.
A Thracian tribe of northern Macedonia.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: MAC/YUG.
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: N Aigaleos.
The Trinobantes were a Celtic tribe of Pre-Roman Britain.
BAtlas 65 A1 Tripolis ad Maeandrum/Apollonia ad Maeandrum/Antoniopolis
A megalithic "giant's tomb" in proximity to a nuragic settlement.
The modern Dip Burun in Turkey: a coastal promontory opposite the Aegean island of Samos extending from the Mykale mountains.
An oracular cave sanctuary at Lebadeia (modern Greece). Pausanias reports seeing a cult image here that was made by Praxiteles.
A large Early Helladic cemetery excavated at the Leoforos Plataion near Marathon, Attiki.
The archaeological site of Tsoungiza shows evidence of human activity since the Early Neolithic period. Modern excavations began under Carl Blegen in 1924.
BAtlas 31 E3 Tucca?/Fines Africae et Mauretaniae?

Tulul al-Baqarat is an archaeological site located seven kilometers northeast of Tell al-Wilayah, Iraq. The settlement was occupied from the fourth millennium BCE to the Islamic period. It may have been the Early Dynastic city of Kesh.

The Péré tumulus, or Pairé tumulus, is a Neolithic tumulus that dates from the fifth millennium B.C. The site is located in Prissé-la-Charrière, in Deux-Sèvres, in New Aquitaine, France. It is composed of three main megalithic structures, built at different times.
A sixth century B.C. aqueduct on Samos, the Tunnel of Eupalinos is an amphistomon, meaning it was excavated simultaneously from each terminus. The tunnel measures 1,036 m in length.
An ancient tribe dwelling in what is now southern Portugal.
Site of a major Roman villa complex in Gloucestershire, active from late second century CE until the end of the fourth century.
A turret situated on Hadrian's Wall. The site was excavated in 1930; there are no surface remains.
A turret situated on Hadrian's Wall.

Now unlocated, Turrita was a station (statio) near Pisae.
Nubian Cemetery site along the Nile in use in the Middle Kingdom and the Second Intermediate Period. The site was inundated by the creation of the Aswan Dam.
A Punic necropolis near Caralis in Sardinia.
The Tylihul Estuary, located in Odesa Oblast in the south of Ukraine, lies on the northwest coast of the Black Sea. It receives the waters of the Tylihul River.
A mountain, probably Mavrovouni (Khuka Loupou Range).
An ancient people, tribe, or cultural group. Located: near Tubusuctu.
A Roman villa located at modern Ucero in Spain's Soria province (Castilla y León).
According to an inscription of the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus, the name of the wall of Cutha was Ugal-amaru, whose ceremonial name means "Great Storm, (which is) a Deluge."
BAtlas 38 C1 no. 19 (Umm Heneia/Umm Henia el-Garbia/Esc-Shergia)
Although never completed, the 'unfinished obelisk' at Aswan in Egypt is the largest known ancient obelisk.

One of five aqueducts known from Roman-era Sexi. This one is represented by an aqueduct bridge whose extant remains parallel the SO-02 between the Ctra. de Málaga - Velilla and the Carrera de la Concepcion in modern Almuñécar, Spain.
A bridge near Col. Dea Vocontiorum
A Roman bridge located west of Akronios, near Akören.
This archaeologically attested Roman bridge was located east of Salaria on the Guadalquivir River.

A Gallo-Roman site located at the Villa d'Antone was partially excavated in 1931.
A Gallo-Roman villa identified, on the basis of mosaic remains, near modern Granéjouls in the French commune of Lhospitalet.
The remains of a large Gallo-Roman villa covering some 4 ha have been identified and studied at Petit-Bersac.
Unnamed Gate of the Themistoklean Wall
A gate of the Themistoklean city wall of Athens, detected during excavations at the northwest corner of modern Evripidou and Epikourou streets.
Unnamed Gate of the Themistoklean Wall
A gate of the Themistoklean city wall of Athens, whose existence is inferred from a break in the moat to the east.
According to PECS, the Roman aqueduct at Eporedia originates "at the Viona stream on the slopes of the Mombarone".

The remains of an unnamed Roman bridge at Fidenza are located in the public square known as "piazza Grandi". The bridge was part of the ancient Via Aemilia and carried the roadway across the Stirone stream. It likely dates to the first century CE.
An ancient Roman bridge over the River Ofanto, near Canusium on the Via Traiana.
The cryptoporticus of an Augustan-period villa that later came to be incorporated in the substructure of the abbey of Santa Maria Maddalena in Armillis.

The ruins of a well-appointed Roman Imperial villa are now to be seen immured in the esplanade of one of the beachfronts of Ladispoli, Italy. The visible remains include a portion of a peristyle courtyard with an elaborate mosaic pavement.
Unnamed Settlement north of Castellum Tingitanum
An unnamed Gallo-Roman villa located in the modern French commune of Castelferrus.
An unnamed aqueduct supplying water to Tarentum in south Italy that flowed from springs near Satyrion (aqua nymphalis).

The so-called "Acueducto de los Milagros" (miraculous aqueduct) that supplied Augusta Emerita from the Lago de Proserpina north of the city. A small portion of the impressive aqueduct bridge still stands in Mérida.
A group of Roman-era aqueducts (a "leat system" in regional parlance and the archaeological literature for the area), probably supplying the gold mining works at Dolaucothi.
An ancient bridge, known as "Ponte Rotto", over the Calore Irpino river along the Via Appia between Beneventum and Aeclanum.

The Vatican necropolis lies beneath Vatican City, specifically beneath the present St. Peter's Basilica, at depths ranging from 5 to 12 meters. The necropolis was partially exposed by means of archaeological excavations in 1940-1949. The necropolis was an open-air burial ground that included both mausolea and tombs. A hill located across the Tiber from Rome's traditional seven hills, the Vaticanus Mons now lies within the territory of Vatican City.

The Venetian Lagoon or Laguna di Venezia refers to an enclosed body of water that is linked to the northern Adriatic Sea by three inlets. This body of water is what remains of what was once a system of estuarine lagoons extending from Ravenna as far north as Trieste.
A Roman theater at modern Ventimiglia in Italy, dating to the early second century CE.

The compilers of the Barrington Atlas indicate that evidence for ancient silver working was identified at Verzino in the present-day Italian region of Calabria. This site is located in the valley of the River Neto (the ancient Neaethus).
The Via Ciminia was a Roman road that left the Via Cassia and continued toward the Ciminian hills. Its course likely ran from Sutrium to near Viterbo.
The Via Egnatia was a Roman road begun in the second century BCE that crossed the Roman provinces of Illyricum, Macedonia, and Thrace.
An ancient road, leading southwards from Rome toward Laurentum. Its course, endpoint, and coincidence with the Via Ostiensis and the Via Ardeatina are matters of scholarly contention.
A late republican to early imperial columbarium along the Via Praenestina. The columbarium is of rectangular plan and was last used during the early Flavian period.
An ancient road running from Rome to Ostia, exiting the city walls of Rome at the Porta Trigemina.

The Via Portuensis is an ancient Roman road that connected Rome and Portus. It proceeded along the right bank of the Tiber river, starting from the Pons Aemilius. In the first part of its course it is identical to the Via Campana.
An ancient road that originated at Rome and continued to Castrum Truentinum (Porto d'Ascoli).
The Via Severiana was a coastal route running from Ostia to Terracina, a distance of ca. 80 Roman miles.
A road running from the Pons Neronianus toward Monte Mario, eventually joining the Via Clodia some 7 miles from Rome.
An ancient road from Rome to Corfinium.
A hollowed roadway created by cutting the natural tufaceous bedrock. These roads link necropoleis and settlements in the area between Sovana, Sorano, and Pitigliano.
A necropolis at the thirteenth kilometer of the Via Aurelia excavated between 2007 and 2011. A total of 332 tombs were identified at the site.
A large, Roman imperial estate covering ca. 2,000 ha on the shores of Lake Bracciano. The name may derive from Vicus Aurelius, suggesting a connection with Marcus Aurelius.

A Roman villa first occupied in the Late Republican period and abandoned ca. the fifth century AD.

A Roman villa rustica at Boscoreale that was first discovered in 1868 by Modestino Pulzella. The villa is best known as the findspot of the so-called "Boscoreale Treasure". Following excavation, the remains of the villa were reinterred.
A villa with beginnings in the early Republican period, continuing in use to the middle Imperial period.
A Late Republican to early Imperial coastal villa located at the mouth of the Fosso delle Guardiole near Castrum Novum. Two artificial fish ponds are associated with the villa.

The so-called the Villa of Faonte was a Roman villa in Rome located between Via delle Vigne Nuove and Via Passo del Turchino. There are remains of a cistern (approx. 29.5 by 14 meters) now set in a garden area.
A Late Roman villa site near Ausculum.
The so-called Villa di Grotte di Piastra, ruins of a Roman villa at Castelporziano.

The Villa di Rufione is a villa rustica located along the via Flaminia Vetus, between the hamlets of Montecchio and Bastardo in località Toccioli. The site begins its life in the late republican period and continues in use until the fourth century CE.

An important villa that was excavated during the construction of the University of Rome 'Tor Vergata' in the 1970s, now reinterred. The Carcaricola villa begins in the middle of the second century B.C. and continues in use until the second century A.D.
The so-called Villa (or baths) of Agrippa on Planasia Ins. (modern Pianosa) is the putative location of exile for Agrippa Postumus, grandson of Augustus.

A well-appointed "villa" at Olynthus excavated in 1934, the so-called "Villa of Good Fortune" was considered one of the two "type" houses for the ancient site. It was located in the southeastern part of the city in the so-called "villa quarter". Its remains are no longer visible.
The archaeological remains of a villa near Licenza, Italy, that are traditionally connected with the Latin poet Horace.
The Villa of L. Crassius Tertius at Oplontis (modern Torre Annunziata in Italy) was discovered in 1974, approximately 250m east of the Villa of Poppaea.

The Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor was built after the middle of the first century B.C. and was ultimately destroyed by the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius. The villa may have been owned by P. Fannius Synistor and/or L. Herennius Florus.
Referred to both as the House and the Villa of the frescoes, this seaside Roman domestic complex with a peristyle garden covered more than 1,000 square feet and dates to the second century A.D.

One ashlar block bears an eight-line inscription recording the construction of a (subterranean) watercourse.

Wadi Haggag or the "Ravine of the Pilgrims" is located in the central, northeastern Sinai. It lies along one of the major roads leading from the Gulf of Elath to the monastery of St. Catherine and to Gebl Musa.
Late Roman-Early Byzantine cemetery at the point where the Wadi Qitna met the Nile. The graves were tumuli and covered 1200 meters. The site was deluged upon the creation of the High Aswan Dam.
The Wall of Constantine (Murus Constantini) was built during the AD 320s as Constantine organized his eponymous city. The course of the Wall of Constantine cannot be determined with precision today.

A series of fortification walls that surround Trabzon in northeastern Turkey and are referred to as "Walls of Trabzon". This fortification is sometimes referred to as the Trabzon Castle (Turkish: Trabzon Kalesi), although it did not serve as such.
The site of a Roman Saxon Shore fort known as "Walton Castle". The fort was built ca. A.D. 276-285 and was destroyed by sea erosion in the eighteenth century.
